[Theorem thm:dependency_encoding of arXiv:2604.18558, 'Uniform analyticity of local observables in FK-percolation and analyticity of the Ising sp'] Let $(d,p,q) \in \mathcal G_{\mathsf{FK}}$. 
Then there exists $L_0 > 0$ such that for any $L \geq L_0$, there exists a probability measure $\mathbb P$ on $  \{0,1\}^{E(\mathbb T_N)} \times (\mathsf{P}^L_N)^{\mathbb T_N^L}$ satisfying the following properties.
When $(\omega, (\mathcal C_x)_{x \in \mathbb T_N^L})  \sim \mathbb P$, then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\omega$ is distributed according to $\phi_{\mathbb T_N,p}$.
\item For any $x\in\mathbb T_N^L$, $\mathcal C_x$ contains $x$. 
\item For any $\Delta_1, \Delta_2 \subset \mathbb T_N^L$, any $F,G$ functions of $\omega$ supported on $\Delta_1$ and $\Delta_2$ respectively and any $C_1 \supset \Delta_1, C_2 \supset \Delta_2$ such that $C_1 \cap C_2 = \emptyset$, then
\[
\mathbb P[F(\omega)G(\omega) \ind{\mathcal C_{\Delta_1} = C_1} \ind{\mathcal C_{\Delta_2 = C_2}} ] = \mathbb P[F(\omega)\ind{\mathcal C_{\Delta_1} = C_1} ] \mathbb P[G(\omega)\ind{\mathcal C_{\Delta_2 = C_2}} ],
\]
where we call $\mathcal C_\Delta \coloneqq  \bigcup_{x\in\Delta}\mathcal C_x$. 
\item There exist two sequences $\tilde c_L, c_L > 0$ going to infinity when $L$ goes to infinity such that, for any $x \in \mathbb T_N^L$ and any $n \in \mathbb Z_{> 0}$, 
\[  \mathbb P[|\mathcal C_x| \geq n] \leq \tilde c_L\exp(-c_L n). \]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition of arXiv:2609.00233, 'A survey on mapping class groups of 3-manifolds'] For every $i$ choose a collar neighbourhood $T_i \times [0, 1]$ as above, and define $\iota_i$. By choosing small enough neighbourhoods, we can assume that they are pairwise disjoint, and then the elements in the images of different $\iota_i$ maps will commute with each other. Hence we obtain a map $\sum_i \iota_i \colon \bigoplus_i \pi_1 \Diff^+(T_i) \rightarrow \pi_0 \overline{\Diff}^+(M,(B_h),(T_i),(M_j))$. It follows from Lemma (lem:iota-properties of the paper) (b) that $\Image(\sum_i \iota_i)$ is a normal subgroup. We will denote the cokernel of $\sum_i \iota_i$ by
\[
\pi_0 \overline{\Diff}^+(M,(B_h),(T_i),(M_j)) \Big/ \bigoplus_i \pi_1 \Diff^+(T_i).
\]

[Lemma upper_bound_on_expected_number_of_occupation of arXiv:2505.07145, 'Nonamenable Poisson zoo'] Under the assumptions of 	Lemma~(lemma:size_biasing_for_Poisson_zoo of the paper),
	let $\mathcal{X} = \sum_{i \in I} \delta_{(x,H)_i} \sim \mathcal{Q}_{\nu}^\lambda$.

body:
[Theorem thm:main-thm-crit-window of arXiv:2606.06612, 'The limit shape and emergence of the \\ Discrete Gaussian level lines'] Fix any $h \in \mathbb Z_+$, and define with respect to $\underline{L}^{(h)}$ the probability
\[p_h(L) := \pi^0_{\Lambda}(\text{there exists an $h$ level-line loop with interior area $\geq .8\underline{L}^{(h)}$})\,.\]
Then the function $L\mapsto p_h(L)$ is increasing, and the probability that there exists a \texttt{large} $h$ level-line loop is $p_h(L)+o(1)$, where the $o(1)$-term goes to $0$ as $L\to\infty$.
Furthermore, if we define \[ \Lh = \min\{L : p_h(L) \geq 1/2 \}\,,\] 
then we have
\[ \Lh = (1+o(1))\frac{\lambda_* \beta}{{\widehat\pi}_\infty(\phi_o = h)}\]
and the following holds for every $h$:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item if $L < \Lh - (\Lh)^{1/2 + o(1)}$, then $p_h(L) = o(1)$;
\item if $L > \Lh + (\Lh)^{1/2 + o(1)}$, then $p_h(L) = 1-o(1)$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Critical window

body: In statistics, Gibbs sampling or a Gibbs sampler, also known in statistical mechanics as the heat bath algorithm, is a Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm for sampling from a specified multivariate probability distribution when direct sampling from the joint distribution is difficult, but sampling from the conditional distribution is more practical. This sequence can be used to approximate the joint distribution ; to approximate the marginal distribution of one of the variables, or some subset of the variables ; or to compute an integral. Typically, some of the variables correspond to observations whose values are known, and hence do not need to be sampled.
title: Gibbs sampling

Let G be a finite undirected loopless multigraph on n vertices with positive edge weights w_e, L its weighted Laplacian, and t > 0. A spanning rooted forest is a spanning forest with one chosen root in each tree; its weight is t^|E(F)| prod_{e in F} w_e (so an unrooted forest with trees T_1, ..., T_k counts prod |T_i| times). Z(t) is the total weight of spanning rooted forests, and Q_t = (I + tL)^-1. Draw a spanning rooted forest with probability proportional to its weight. Then tr Q_t is the expected number of trees, and t (d/dt) log Z(t) is the expected number of edges, which equals n - tr Q_t.

\]

body:
Let X be a normed space with dual X* carrying the weak-star topology sigma(X*, X). Then the closed unit ball B of X* is metrizable in the relative weak-star topology if and only if X is separable; in that case every bounded subset of X* is weak-star metrizable, and a compatible metric is d(f,g) = sum over n of 2^(-n) min(1, |f(x_n) - g(x_n)|) for any dense sequence (x_n) of the unit sphere of X. Combined with Banach-Alaoglu (B is weak-star compact), separability of X gives that B is weak-star compact and metrizable, hence weak-star SEQUENTIALLY compact: every bounded sequence in X* has a weak-star convergent subsequence. The dual statement also holds: for a Banach space X, the closed unit ball of X is metrizable in the weak topology sigma(X, X*) if and only if X* is separable. WHERE IT FAILS: (a) 'bounded' is essential - the weak-star topology on ALL of X* is metrizable only when X is finite dimensional; indeed if it were metrizable with countable base (U_m) at 0 and X is infinite dimensional, each U_m contains a nonzero subspace (it is cut out by finitely many functionals), so one can pick f_m in U_m with ||f_m|| >= m, and then f_m converges weak-star to 0 while being unbounded, contradicting the uniform boundedness principle; (b) the two directions are not interchangeable - separability of X does not imply separability of X*: X = l^1 is separable, so B of (l^1)* = l^infinity is weak-star metrizable, but (l^1)* = l^infinity is not separable, so the unit ball of l^1 is NOT weakly metrizable; (c) the metric above is not translation-invariantly compatible on the whole of X* and the equivalence is genuinely a statement about the relative topology on bounded sets; (d) for X = l^infinity, which is not separable, the unit ball of (l^infinity)* is weak-star compact but not weak-star metrizable, and weak-star compactness there is not sequential compactness.
X is a normed space (Banach for the uniform boundedness step in the failure remark and for the dual statement)
X* is the topological dual with the weak-star topology sigma(X*, X)
B is the closed unit ball of X*, or any bounded weak-star closed subset - the equivalence concerns bounded sets only
for the dual statement (weak metrizability of the ball of X iff X* separable), X is Banach

[Theorem 6 of arXiv:2605.06556, 'Probability of Quota Violations in Divisor Apportionment Methods with Nonzero Allocations'] \parencite{Self} \textit{(Lower Quota Violation Criteria Test)} Let $A$ be Adams's, Dean's, or the Huntington-Hill method, with divisor function $\delta(s)$. Order the populations such that $p_1 <p_2 < p_3$ and calculate the standard quotas $q_i$. Then the apportionment $A(p_1, p_2, p_3)$ on $M$ seats has a lower quota violation if and only if all three of the following statements are true: 
\begin{enumerate}
\item $q_3 \delta(\lfloor q_1 \rfloor) < q_1 \delta( \lfloor q_3 \rfloor - 1)$
\item $q_3 \delta(\lfloor q_2 \rfloor) < q_2 \delta( \lfloor q_3 \rfloor - 1)$
\item $\lceil q_1 \rceil + \lceil q_2 \rceil + \lfloor q_3 \rfloor = M+1 $ (equivalently for $q_1, q_2 \notin \mathbb{Z}$, $\lfloor q_1 \rfloor + \lfloor q_2 \rfloor + \lfloor q_3 \rfloor = M-1) $.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Proposition 118 (Operator-valued Hilbert--Fock isometry) of arXiv:2606.29292, 'Intrinsic Gaussian Tensor Geometry and Random Operator Spectra'] Let $\cH$ be a separable real Hilbert space, let $W$ be a real isonormal
Gaussian process over $\cH$, and let $\cC,\cE$ be separable Hilbert spaces.
Set
\[
 \mathfrak W_{0,2}:=\Sch_2(\cC,\cE),
 \qquad I_0(K_0):=K_0,
\]
and define
\begin{equation}

 \mathfrak F_2^{\mathrm{op}}
 :=\left\{(K_m)_{m\ge0}:
 \sum_{m\ge0}m!\,\|K_m\|_{\mathfrak W_{m,2}}^2<\infty\right\}.
\end{equation}
Then
\[
 \mathcal I((K_m)_{m\ge0}):=\sum_{m\ge0}I_m(K_m)
\]
extends from finite sequences to an isometry from
$\mathfrak F_2^{\mathrm{op}}$ onto the
$L^2(\Omega;\Sch_2)$-closure of finite operator-valued Wick polynomials.  In
particular,
\begin{equation}

 \left\|\sum_{m\ge0}I_m(K_m)\right\|_{L^2(\Omega;\Sch_2)}^2
 =\sum_{m\ge0}m!\,\|K_m\|_{\mathfrak W_{m,2}}^2.

Own work draft; proof (unaudited), initialization-only special case, no novelty claim. For distinct parity subsets S_t of uniform d-dimensional Rademacher skill inputs and one-hot task controls, use f(e_t,x)=m^(-1/2)*sum_j a_j ReLU(w_j dot x+v_jt+b_j). Initialize all a_j=0 and all hidden data weights, control weights and biases independently N(0,sigma^2), sigma>0. For conditional half squared losses with labels product_{l in S_t} x_l, let g_t be the full parameter gradient. Then for t!=u, E_init<g_t,g_u>=0 and E_init|<g_t,g_u>|^2<=3*(d+2)^2*sigma^4/(2*m). A union bound gives failure probability at most binom(n,2)*3*(d+2)^2*sigma^4/(2*m*epsilon^2) for any cross-gradient magnitude exceeding epsilon. This is not a trained-trajectory or nonzero-output-initialization theorem.

[Theorem 2 (Sampling active subspaces~\protect{\cite[Thm.~3.7) of arXiv:2604.27119, '\Large Applied Random Matrix Theory\relatedversion'] {Con15:Active-Subspaces}}]
Let $f : \R^d \to \R$ be $L$-Lipschitz and differentiable.
As in~\cref{eqn:sensitivity-matrix,eqn:empirical-sensitivity},
consider the sensitivity matrix $\mtx{\Sigma} \in \Sym_d(\R)$
and the empirical approximation $\widehat{\mtx{\Sigma}}_n \in \Sym_d(\R)$
determined by $n$ gradient samples.  The expectation of the relative approximation error satisfies
\[
\Expect\left[ \frac{ \norm{ \widehat{\mtx{\Sigma}}_n - \mtx{\Sigma} }}{\norm{\mtx{\Sigma}}} \right]
	\leq \sqrt{2\beta_n} + \frac{1}{3} \beta_n
	\quad\text{where}\quad
	\beta_n \coloneqq \frac{L^2 \log(2d)}{\norm{\mtx{\Sigma}}} \cdot \frac{1}{n}.

\]
For $\eps \in (0,1)$, the sample complexity $n \geq 4\eps^{-2} L^2 \log(2d) / \norm{\mtx{\Sigma}}$
results in expected relative error at most $\eps$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem thm:duality of arXiv:2602.19192, 'Bakry--\'Emery Curvature of the Fractional Laplacian\\ via Fractional Brownian Covariance'] For $\gamma \in (0,2)$ and all $\xi, \eta \in \mathbb{R}$ with
$\xi\eta \geq 0$ (same-sign frequencies):
\begin{equation}
  \Psi_\gamma(\xi,\eta)
  = \tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(|\xi|^\gamma + |\eta|^\gamma
  - |\xi - \eta|^\gamma\bigr)
  = R_{\gamma/2}(|\xi|, |\eta|).
\end{equation}
The carr\'e du champ of the $\gamma$-stable generator, evaluated
on same-sign Fourier modes, is the covariance of fBM with $H = \gamma/2$.

For opposite-sign frequencies ($\xi\eta < 0$), the carr\'e du champ
$\Psi_\gamma(\xi,\eta) = \frac{1}{2}(|\xi|^\gamma + |\eta|^\gamma
- |\xi-\eta|^\gamma)$ differs from $R_{\gamma/2}(|\xi|,|\eta|)
= \frac{1}{2}(|\xi|^\gamma + |\eta|^\gamma - \bigl||\xi|-|\eta|\bigr|^\gamma)$
since $|\xi - \eta| \neq \bigl||\xi|-|\eta|\bigr|$ when $\xi\eta < 0$.
The cross-sign kernel is treated separately in
Section~(sec:cross-sign of the paper).
title: Stable--fBM correspondence

[Theorem 5 of arXiv:2609.01574, 'A linear bound for Fujita's freeness conjecture'] Let $X$ be a smooth projective variety of dimension $n$, let $\Delta\geq0$ be a $\mathbb Q$-divisor, and let $x\in X$ be a closed point. Assume that $(X,\Delta)$ is log canonical near $x$ and is not klt at $x$. Let $W$ be the positive-dimensional minimal lc center through $x$, then 
$$
2\ebarone(\m_{W,x})\leq\bigl(\dim W-b_x(X,\Delta)\bigr)\mult_xW,
$$
where $\ebarone(\m_{W,x})$ is the first normal Hilbert coefficient of the maximal ideal of $\mathcal O_{W,x}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition 5 of arXiv:2606.02036, 'Self-intersection local times for Volterra Gaussian processes in stochastic flows with int'] A centred Gaussian process $\{u(t) : t\in[0,1]\}$ is called a Volterra Gaussian process, if  it admits the representation
$
u(t) = 

\int^t_0k(t,s)\differential{w(s)},
$ for each $t\in(0,1]$, 
where $k\in L^2([0,1]^2)$ is a Volterra kernel, i.e., 
$k(t,s)=0$  for all $s>t$, and 
$
\sup_{t\in[0,1]}\int^t_0k(t,s)^2 \differential{s}<\infty. 
$
title: Definition 5 of arXiv:2606.02036

[Thm T exact Haus of arXiv:2608.25471, 'Exact Hausdorff measures and fine geometry of collisions of independent Markov processes'] [Exact Hausdorff measure for collision times]
  There exist deterministic constants $c_1, c_2\in(0,\infty)$ such that,
  $\hat{P}_{\bm{\rho}}$-a.s., for all $t \in (0,\infty)$ and for every Borel subset $I$ of $[0,\infty)$,
  \begin{equation}
    c_1\mathcal{C}_t(I)
    \leq
    \mathcal{H}_{\Psi_{\mathrm{ct}}}(I\cap\mathcal{T}_t)
    \leq
    c_2\mathcal{C}_t(I).
  \end{equation}
  In particular, 
  $0<\mathcal{H}_{\Psi_{\mathrm{ct}}}(\mathcal{T}_t)<\infty$ for all $t \in (0,\infty)$, $\hat{P}_{\bm{\rho}}$-a.s. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Thm T exact Haus of arXiv:2608.25471

body: A probability distribution \mu with characteristic function \phi is said to be self-decomposable (or belonging to Lévy's class L) if for every c \in (0, 1), there exists a characteristic function \phi_c such that \phi(t) = \phi(ct) \phi_c(t) for all t \in \mathbb{R}. Class L distributions coincide with the class of all limit distributions of normalized sums \frac{1}{a_n} \sum_{k=1}^n X_k - b_n of independent (not necessarily identically distributed) random variables under the infinitesimal condition.
title: Self-Decomposable Distribution (Class L)

[Corollary cor:spectral-cross-section-lattice-induction of arXiv:2607.25616, 'Stealthy point processes and lattice induction'] Let $(X,\mu,Y)$ be an ergodic $\mathbb R$-cross-section system.
If
\[
    \int_{0<|\xi|<1}
    \frac{1}{\xi^2}\,d\sigma_{Y,\mu}(\xi)<\infty,
\]
then $(X,\mu)$ is lattice-induced.

[Definition 21 (Ollivier curvature) of arXiv:2605.24445, 'Matrix concentration inequalities for time-inhomogeneous Markov chains'] \label[definition]{def:curvature}
For any integer $t \ge 1$, we define the curvature at time $t$ as
\[
    \kappa_t
    \;:=\;
    \inf_{x \ne y} 1 - \frac{W_1(P_t(x, \cdot), P_t(y, \cdot))}{d(x,y)}.
\]

[Corollary cor:rho-intro of arXiv:2605.03703, 'Scaling Limits of Bivariate Nearly-Unstable Hawkes Processes and Applications to Rough Vol'] Under the assumptions of Theorem~(thm:main-intro of the paper) and in the
zero-start scaling regime,
the functional correlation satisfies
\[
\varrho(t)\sim C_\varrho\,t^{(3\alpha_1-\alpha_2)/2},
\qquad t\downarrow0.
\]
Since $\alpha_1>1/2$ and $\alpha_2<1$, the exponent is strictly positive.
In the homogeneous case $\alpha_1=\alpha_2$, it reduces to $\alpha_1$.
In particular $\varrho(t)\to 0$ as $t\downarrow 0$: the two components are decorrelated
at short time scales.
The explicit constant $C_\varrho$ and its proof are in Corollary~(cor:rho of the paper).
A stationary comparison, where the mean profiles are locally constant near
zero, gives the exponent $\alpha_1$; this is not the zero-start regime used
in the main theorem. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Short-time decorrelation, informal preview

body:
[Lem 149 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Fix $(b,\sigma,w,p,\zeta,\zeta^\Ising)$ satisfying the conditions of Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main}\ref{i:IAMP-main-centered}. 
Fix any vectors $\bx^{\dagger,0},\prxbx^{\dagger,0}\in\bbR^M$, and let $\tilde{\cA}^\dagger$ be the centered IAMP specified by Definition~\ref{d:centered.iamp}. 
Then, for $C\equiv C(L,\epsilon,\delta)$, 
there exists a $C$-Lipschitz map $\cA^\dagger$ which agrees
with $\tilde{\cA}^\dagger$ with probability $1-\exp(-cN)$, and satisfies
	    \[
    \cA(-\bG,-\bg^\aux)
    =
    -\cA(\bG,\bg^\aux)\,.
    \]
In particular, it follows that $\bbE[\cA(\bG,\bg^{\aux})~|~\bx^{\dagger,0},\prxbx^{\dagger,0}]=\bzero\in\bbR^N$.
\begin{proof}
    Let $(\hat\by^{\dagger,k},\hat\prxby^{\dagger,k},\hat\bx^{\dagger,k},\hat\prxbx^{\dagger,k})$ be the IAMP iterates corresponding to $(-\bG,- \bg^{\aux})$.
    We claim that for all $0\leq k\leq \ubl$ we have
    \begin{align*}
    (\hat\prxby,\hat\by,\hat\bu,\hat\bw)^{\dagger,k}
    &=
    (-\prxby,-\by,-\bu,\bw)^{\dagger,k}
      \,\\
    (\hat\prxbx,\hat\bx,\hat\bv,
    \hat\bm,\hat\bsig,\hat\bb)^{\dagger,k}
    &=
    (\prxbx,\bx,\bv,
    \bm,\bsig,\bb)^{\dagger,k}\,.
    \end{align*}
Indeed, the base case for the first statement above holds easily since
$w$ is even by the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main} \eqref{i:IAMP-main-centered}, the functions
 $\psi$ and $\prxpsi$ are odd (Lemma~\ref{lem:even-manual-init}), 
the vectors $(\by,\prxby,\hat{\by},\hat{\prxby})^{\dagger,0}$ are defined by \eqref{eq:mean-0-initialization},  and  we defined $\bu^{\dagger,0}=\hat{\bu}^{\dagger,0}=\bzero\in\R^M$.
The remaining statements follow by 
induction, using the formulas \eqref{eq:proxy-y-amp-def}--\eqref{eq:x-amp-def}. 

The above shows the desired symmetry for the mapping $\tilde{\cA}^\dagger$, and we must now transfer it to $\cA^\dagger$. This proceeds similarly as in the \hyperlink{proof:t.IAMP.main.main}{proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main}\ref{i:IAMP-main-main}}, using the Kirzsbraun extension theorem, except that we now need to ensure that the symmetry requirement is satisfied. 
First, we have by easy induction that $\tilde{\cA}^\dagger$ is $C$-Lipschitz on a subset $\mathcal{U}^{\dagger}\subseteq \bbR^{MN+N_{\aux}}$, similarly to the \hyperlink{proof:t.IAMP.main.main}{proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main}\ref{i:IAMP-main-main}}. To be precise, 
    \[\mathcal{U}^{\dagger}
    =\bigg\{
    \begin{array}{c}
    (\bG,\bg^\aux) : 
    \textup{$\bG_\circ$
    satisfies \eqref{eq:Brownian-bridge-condition},
    $\|\bG\|_\textup{op}\le C_0
    (M^{1/2}+N^{1/2})$,}\\
    \textup{$\|\bar\bg^{\ell}\|\leq 2\sqrt{N}$
    for all $0\le\ell\le\ubl$, and
    $\|\bar\bg^{\init}\|\leq 2\sqrt{N}$}
    \end{array}
    \bigg\}\,.
    \]
In particular, this choice of $\mathcal{U}^{\dagger}$ is origin-symmetric. 
(Again, see e.g.\ the discussion on ``standard optimization algorithms'' in \cite{HuangSellke2021} for the Lipschitz bound on such a domain.)

Thus, let $S=\{\bg_1,\bg_2,\dots\}$ be a countable dense set in $\bbR^{MN+N_{\aux}}$.
    For each $\bg_i$, we assume $\tilde\cA^{\dagger}$ has been extended to a $C$-Lipschitz function on $\mathcal{U}^{\dagger,i}\equiv \mathcal{U}^{\dagger}\cup \{\bg_1,-\bg_1,\dots,\bg_i,-\bg_i\}$.
    Then by the Kirzsbraun extension theorem, there exists a $C$-Lipschitz extension to $\mathcal{U}^{\dagger,i}\cup \{\bg_{i+1}\}$.
    Since 
  $\mathcal{U}^{\dagger,i}$ is symmetric,  
the unique odd extension to $\mathcal{U}^{\dagger,i+1}$ is still $C$-Lipschitz. Continuing in this way yields a $C$-Lipschitz extension to $ \mathcal{U}^\dagger\cup S\cup -S$. This set is dense by definition of $S$, so the result follows by continuously extending to all of $\R^{MN+N_{\aux}}$.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem 149 of arXiv:2608.29416

[Lemma 8 of arXiv:2609.02175, '2609.02175'] Let $g_1$ and $g_2$ be smooth Riemannian metrics on
	$\mathbb R^n$ which coincide with the Euclidean metric outside
	a compact set, and assume that their geodesic flows are
	non-trapping. If
	\begin{equation}
		\|S_{g_1,h}(\lambda)-S_{g_2,h}(\lambda)\|
		_{\mathcal B(L^2(\mathbb S^{n-1}))}
		=
		o(1),
		\qquad h\to0,
	\end{equation}
	then
	\begin{equation}
		\kappa_{g_1,\lambda}
		=
		\kappa_{g_2,\lambda}.
	\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 18 of arXiv:2605.06556, 'Probability of Quota Violations in Divisor Apportionment Methods with Nonzero Allocations'] (Asymptotic Apportionment) Let $(1,x,y_1(x,\tau_1),\ldots,y_{n-2}(x,\tau_{n-2}))$ be a reduced population vector with $\bm\tau=(\tau_1,\ldots,\tau_{n-2})$. Let $A$ be a divisor method that guarantees nonzero allocations on $M$ seats. Then for almost every $\bm\tau$ satisfying $-\tfrac13 < \tau_1 < \cdots < \tau_{n-2} < \tfrac13,$

$$\lim_{x\to\infty}A(1,x,y_1(x,\tau_1),\dots,y_{n-2}(x,\tau_{n-2}))=\tilde A_1(\tilde q_2,\dots,\tilde q_n).$$

The limiting quotas are 
$$\tilde q_2=\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{Mx}{P(x)},\qquad\tilde q_{i+2}
=\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{M y_i(x,\tau_i)}{P(x)},$$
where $P(x) = 1+x+y_1(x,\tau_1)+\cdots+y_{n-2}(x,\tau_{n-2}).$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Lemma lem:algebraic of arXiv:2608.04900, 'A Sharper Hoeffding Bound for Weighted Sums of Exchangeable Random Variables'] Let $I\subset\mathbb{R}$ be an interval and $h\in C^5(I)$. Let $x_1,x_2,x_3\in I$ be distinct and set $p(t)=\prod_{i=1}^3(t-x_i)$. If $h(x_i)=0$ for $i=1,2,3$ and $h^{(5)}(t)>0$ on $I$, then $\sum_{i=1}^3 h'(x_i)/p'(x_i)^2>0$.

[Proposition prop_prop_SL of arXiv:2603.26307, '\LARGE The incompressible Navier--Stokes--Fourier system with thermal noise'] Let Assumption (Ass:noise of the paper) hold, $(\Omega,\mathfrak{A},\mathbb{P})$ be a probability space equipped with a filtration $\mathscr{F}$ satisfying the usual conditions and $3$-dimensional standard $\mathscr{F}$-Brownian motions $(W_n)_{n\in \mathbb{Z}^3}$ and $3\times 3$-matrix valued $\mathscr{F}$-Brownian motions $(B_n)_{n\in \mathbb{Z}^3}$ with covariance structure (equation Eq_noise_matrix_covariation of the paper) be independent. Moreover, we let  $U\colon [0,\tau ) \to C^1(\mathbb{T}^3;\mathbb{R}^3)$ and $\Psi\colon [0,\tau )\to  C^1(\mathbb{T}^3)$ be continuous, adapted processes, defined up to a stopping time $\tau>0$, such that for a strictly increasing localizing sequence $0\le \tau_j\nearrow \tau $ properties (equation Item_pos_Phi of the paper) and (equation Item_U_eq of the paper) of Definition (defi_strong_sol of the paper) holds. 
	Then, $(U,\Psi)$ is a local strong solution to (equation Eq_new_var of the paper), 
	iff the temperature $\Theta = \Psi^2/2$ satisfies the following for any $j\in \mathbb N$:
	\begin{enumerate}[(i)']
		\setcounter{enumi}{2}

[Definition 16 of arXiv:2608.31171, '\bf Finite-energy spacetimes with torus symmetry. \\ \Large Cauchy stability of Einstein--'] A \textbf{Navier--Stokes triple} \((\mathscr F,\chi,\mathscr B)\) is called \textbf{admissible} provided the following \textbf{invariant-domain property} holds for each of the two associated Einstein--Navier--Stokes models 
\eqref{eq:pot-production-system} and \eqref{eq:pot-dissipated-system}, as follows. 

Let \(\{\Sigma_t\}_{t_0\leq t<t_1}\) be a spacelike foliation of a compact spacetime slab, and let \((g,\beta,\zeta)\) be a regular solution of the corresponding hyperbolic evolution-constraint system\footnote{A gauge must be chosen to deal with the spacetime metric and formulate a well-posed initial value problem; this is a standard topic, not reviewed here \cite{Choquet-book}.} on \([t_0,t_1)\). Assume that
\be
\zeta(t_0,\Sigma_{t_0})\subset\mathcal K_0
\qquad\text{for some closed fiber subset }\mathcal K_0\Subset\mathscr F.
\ee
Then one has
\be
\zeta(t,\Sigma_t)\subset\mathscr F
\qquad\text{for every }t_0\leq t<t_1.
\ee
Moreover, if the fields admit a continuous limit in the ambient bundles as \(t\uparrow t_1\), while the nonsingular coefficients in the equation for~\(\zeta\) remain bounded, then the terminal relaxing field satisfies
\be
\zeta(t_1,\Sigma_{t_1})\subset\mathscr F,
\ee
rather than merely taking its values in~\(\overline{\mathscr F}\). Equivalently, the constitutive boundary~\(\del\mathscr F\) cannot be the first cause of breakdown of a regular solution.
title: Definition 16 of arXiv:2608.31171

[Theorem 3 (Ruelle) of arXiv:2605.29030, 'Preferential relocations enhance survival \\ for Markov chains with killing'] Suppose that the defective kernel $\kk\in \mathcal{H}_{>0}(\S)$. Then there exist a unique probability measure $\boldsymbol{\mu}\in \calP(\S)$ --often called the quasi-stationary distribution-- and a unique functional
$\mathbf{h}\in \mathcal{H}_{>0}(\S)$  such that
\[\Kk \mathbf{h}= \mathbf{r}  \mathbf{h}, \quad \Kk^{*} \boldsymbol{\mu}= \mathbf{r}  \boldsymbol{\mu}, \quad \text{and} \quad \int_{\S}\boldsymbol{\mu}(\d \s) \mathbf{h}(\s)=1.
\]
Moreover, for any $\mathbf{f}\in \calC(\S)$, there is the convergence in $\calC(\S)$
\[ \lim_{n\to \infty} \mathbf{r}^{-n}\Kk^n \mathbf{f} =   \boldsymbol{\mu}( \mathbf{f}) \mathbf{h} , \qquad \text{where} \  \boldsymbol{\mu}( \mathbf{f})=\int_{\S}\boldsymbol{\mu}(\d \s) \mathbf{f}(\s).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition 1 of arXiv:2609.03143, 'Equilibria for Networks of Linear Translational Springs'] A translational spring network is a pair $N = (P, S)$ with set of nodes (points) $P = \{ p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n \}$ and a collection of linear springs $S \subseteq \{ s_{i,j}: 1 \leq i, j \leq n, i < j \}$ (with $s_{i, j}$ connecting points $p_i$ and $p_j$). Each spring $s_{i,j} \in S$ is given by a pair $s_{i,j} = (k_{i,j}, \tilde{\ell}_{i,j})$ where $k_{i,j}$ is the spring constant and $\tilde{\ell}_{i,j}$ is the resting length of $s_{i,j}$.

    An embedding of a network $N=(P,S)$ into $\RR^d$ is a function $f: P \to \mathbb{R}^d$ that assigns coordinates to the points and, in turn, determines the stretched lengths $\ell_{i,j}=|f(p_i)-f(p_j)|$.  
    We call such an assignment an \emph{equilibrium position} if for each $1 \leq i \leq n$ the net force on each point $p_i \in P$ from all of the springs incident to $p_i$ is $0$.
title: Definition 1 of arXiv:2609.03143

[Prop cor:explicitcondforXe of arXiv:2605.06488, 'Continuous-state branching processes with L\'evy-Khintchine drift-interaction: Laplace dua'] Let $\Psi$ and $\hat{\Psi}$ be mechanisms, and denote by $\pi$ the L\'evy measure associated with $\Psi$. Assume that $\hat{\Psi} = \hat{\Sigma} - \hat{\Phi}$ with $\hat{\Sigma} \not\equiv 0$. Then the following statements hold:
\begin{enumerate}[1)]
\item Assume $\Hone$ and $\hatHone$. Then the process $X^{\mathrm{m}}$ admits a $[0,\infty]$-valued Feller extension at $\infty$, denoted by $X^{\mathrm{e}\infty}$, which satisfies (equation def:Xeinftyviamonotonicity of the paper) and the $(0^{+}\cdot \infty, \infty^-\cdot 0)$ Laplace duality relation (equation eq:laplaceduality1 of the paper). Moreover, $0$ is absorbing for $X^{\mathrm{e}\infty}$, and $\infty$ is inaccessible for $Y^{\mathrm{m}}$.

\item If $\hat{\Phi}'(0+) \in (0,\infty)$ (which in particular implies $\hatHone$) and
\begin{equation}
\exists \,\kappa \in (0,\infty) \text{ such that } \int_{\kappa}^{\infty} \frac{1 + u \bar{\pi}(u)}{\hat{\Psi}(u)} \mathrm{d}u < \infty,
\end{equation}
then the extension $X^{\mathrm{e}\infty}$ exists and satisfies all the properties listed in (1). Moreover, $\infty$ is an instantaneous entrance boundary and $0$ is accessible for $Y^{\mathrm{m}}$.
\item If $\hat{\Phi}'(0+) \in (0,\infty)$, $\Phi'(0+) \in [0,\infty)$, and $\neg \hatHtwo$, that is,
$\int_1^{\infty} \frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\hat{\Sigma}(u)} < \infty$,
then (equation eq:JI of the paper) holds. Consequently, the extension $X^{\mathrm{e}\infty}$ exists and satisfies all the properties listed in (1) and (2).
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop cor:explicitcondforXe of arXiv:2605.06488

[Cor 83 of arXiv:2509.01797, 'Relation between Wick powers and excursion clusters of the 2D GFF'] Let $j\geq 0$.
Let $n\geq 1$
and let $\alpha_{n}>\alpha_{n-1}>\dots >\alpha_{1}>\alpha_{0}=1$.
Let $(c_{0}, c_{1}, \dots, c_{n})$
be the unique solution to the linear system
\begin{displaymath}
\forall k\in \{0,\dots, n-1\},
\sum_{i=0}^{n} c_{i} \alpha_{i}^{-(k+1/2)} = 0,
\qquad
\sum_{i=0}^{n} c_{i} \alpha_{i}^{-(n+1/2)} = 1.
\end{displaymath}
Then
\begin{displaymath}
\psi_{2n+1, j} = \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} (-1)^{n}\dfrac{2^{n} n! (n+1/2)}{(2\pi)^{n}}\vert\log\varepsilon\vert^{n+1/2}
\sum_{i=0}^{n} c_{i} \ind_{\Ns_{\varepsilon^{\alpha_{i}}}(\clus_j)},
\end{displaymath}
with convergence in $L^{2}(d\PP,\sigma(\Phi),H^{-\eta}(\C))$ for $\eta>0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Cor 83 of arXiv:2509.01797

[Lemma 9 (Descent closure) of arXiv:2609.01882, '\textbf{Coxeter Descents and Parabolic Homotopy Colimits}\\[2mm] \large A Hochster-type de'] If $L_{\mathcal K,D}\ne\varnothing$, the map
\[
  c_D:Q_{\mathcal K,D}\longrightarrow Q_{\mathcal K,D},
  \qquad c_D(I)=I\cap D,
\]
is a descending closure operator. Its image is the poset of nonempty faces of $\mathcal K_D$. Consequently
\[
  L_{\mathcal K,D}\searrow \sd\mathcal K_D
\]
by a sequence of unit simplicial collapses.

[Proposition prop:D15 of arXiv:2605.03718, 'Potential Hessian Ascent III:\\ Sampling the Sherrington--Kirkpatrick Model at $\beta < 1/'] Fix a finite number of replicas and let $G^-\in \mathcal Q$ be any quadratic bulk observable, where
\[
    \mathcal Q := \mathsf{span}\left\{(R^-_{\ell,\ell'}-q^*)^2, (M^-_\ell - m^*)^2, (R^-_{\ell,\ell'}-q^*)(M^-_\ell - m^*)\right\}\,.
\]

Then, for every $s\in[0,1]$,
\begin{align*}
    \nu_s\big(f^-\,G^-\big)&=O(4)\,, \\
    \nu_s\left(\widehat{f}^-\,G^-\right)&= O(4)\,.    
\end{align*}
The same statement holds with $f^-$ replaced by $\widehat f^-$ (and with $G^-$ allowed to include standardized overlaps).
title: Cubic moments of ``rectangular sums'' with quadratic weights are $O(4)$

[Lemma 8 (Unstable/stable splitting) of arXiv:2607.20882, 'An Eyring--Kramers Law for the Hypoelliptic Third-Order\\ Langevin Diffusion'] In an eigenbasis of $H_\sigma$, the full $3d\times3d$ linearized deterministic
matrix block-diagonalizes into one unstable triple $\mathsf A_\sigma$ (with
the single positive eigenvalue $\mu_\sigma$) and $d-1$ stable normal triples
whose spectra lie in the open left half-plane.  Lifting the orthogonal
diagonalization of $H_\sigma$ to phase space leaves
$|p|^2+|r|^2$ and the diffusion $\Delta_r$ invariant, so the saddle generator
decomposes accordingly and the quadratic Hamiltonian becomes
\begin{equation}

H_\sigma^{\rm quad}
=
U(\sigma)-\frac{\lambda_\sigma}{2}q_1^2
+\frac12\sum_{i=2}^d\lambda_i^\sigma q_i^2
+\frac L2|v|^2+\frac L2|w|^2 ,
\qquad
-\det H_\sigma=\lambda_\sigma\prod_{i=2}^d\lambda_i^\sigma .
\end{equation}

body:
[Theorem 14 of arXiv:2601.16377, '2601.16377'] Consider an off-critical ensemble \eqref{eq_measure_general_intro} with fixed filling fractions. There exists functions $\mathcal{F}_{h_1,h_2}(z_1,z_2)$ indexed by $h_1,h_2 \in [H]$ depending only on $\boldsymbol{\Theta}$ and the endpoints of the bands, and having the following properties. First $\mathcal{F}_{h_1,h_2}(z_1,z_2) = \mathcal{F}_{h_2,h_1}(z_2,z_1)$. Second, for any $h_1,h_2 \in [H]$, any $x_1$ in bands of $[\hat{a}_{h_1},\hat{b}_{h_1}]$ and $z_2$ away from bands, we have
\[
\theta_{h_1,h_1}\big(\mathcal{F}_{h_1,h_2}(x_1^+,z_2) + \mathcal{F}_{h_1,h_2}(x_1^-,z_2)\big) + \sum_{g \neq h_1} 2\theta_{h_1,g}\,\mathcal{F}_{g,h_2}(x_1,z_2) = - \frac{\delta_{h_1,h_2}}{(x_1 - z_2)^2}.
\]
Third, for an analytic function $f$ near the bands, we have as $\N \rightarrow \infty$
\[
\amsmathbb{E}\big[(\Delta\textnormal{\textsf{Lin}}[f])^2\big] = \sum_{h_1,h_2 = 1}^{H} \oint_{\gamma_{h_1}}\oint_{\gamma_{h_2}} \frac{\dd z_1 \dd z_2}{(2\ii\pi)^2} \,\mathcal{F}_{h_1,h_2}(z_1,z_2)\,f(z_1)f(z_2) + o(1).
\]
where the contour $\gamma_h$ surrounds the $h$-th band. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Lemma 20 (Time extension, causality, and restricted operator norms) of arXiv:2607.10813, '2607.10813'] Let $0<T\le T_0$.  There is a bounded linear extension
\begin{equation}
 \mathfrak E_{T,T_0}:E_T^{2,\sigma}\longrightarrow E_{T_0}^{2,\sigma},
 \qquad
 \mathfrak R_T\mathfrak E_{T,T_0}=I,
\end{equation}
whose norm is bounded by an absolute constant independently of $T$ and $T_0$.
The analogous assertion holds after translating the interval.

Call an operator $\mathcal A$ on $E_{T_0}^{2,\sigma}$ causal if inputs that
agree on $[0,t]$ have outputs that agree on $[0,t]$, for every $t\le T_0$.
For a causal operator, define
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal A_{[0,T]}:=\mathfrak R_T\mathcal A\mathfrak E_{T,T_0}.
\end{equation}
This restriction is independent of the chosen bounded extension.  More
generally, if $I=[t_0,t_1]$ and $w\in E_{I,0}^{2,\sigma}$, extend $w$ by zero on
$[0,t_0]$ and by any bounded extension after $t_1$; the restriction of
$\mathcal A$ to $I$ is again independent of the extension after $t_1$.  We
denote this zero-history operator by $\mathcal A_I$.

\end{equation}

body:
Let Omega in R^n be open and u in L^1_loc(Omega) satisfy integral_Omega u (Laplacian of phi) dx = 0 for every phi in C_c^infinity(Omega). Then u agrees almost everywhere with a function that is harmonic, hence real-analytic, in Omega. More generally, if P is a linear differential operator with smooth coefficients that is elliptic (nonvanishing principal symbol), then every distributional solution of Pu = f with f smooth is smooth; ellipticity, not any a priori regularity of u, is what does the work.
Omega open in R^n
u in L^1_loc(Omega)
integral u times Laplacian of phi vanishes for all phi in C_c^infinity(Omega) (u is harmonic in the sense of distributions)

Then u_eps is smooth and for x in Omega_eps the Laplacian of u_eps at x equals integral u(y) (Laplacian of rho_eps)(x - y) dy = 0 by hypothesis, since y -> rho_eps(x - y) is in C_c^infinity(Omega). So u_eps is harmonic on Omega_eps, hence satisfies the mean value property, hence is reproduced by convolution with any radial mollifier: u_eps convolved with rho_delta = u_eps on Omega_{eps + delta}. Since convolution is commutative and associative, u_eps convolved with rho_delta = u_delta convolved with rho_eps, so u_eps = u_delta convolved with rho_eps on Omega_{eps+delta}. Letting eps tend to 0, u_eps converges to u in L^1_loc, while the right-hand side converges locally uniformly to u_delta; hence u = u_delta a.e. on each compact subset of Omega_delta. Thus u coincides a.e. with the harmonic function u_delta there, and these functions agree on overlaps, giving a single harmonic representative on Omega. Let U subset R^d be an open set and let {K_n}_{n=1}^infinity be an increasing sequence of closed subsets of U with Union_{n} K_n = U, such that for each n there exists an open precompact set K_tilde_n with K_n subset K_tilde_n subset U. Consider the autonomous SDE dX_t = mu(X_t) dt + sigma(X_t) dW_t where mu, sigma are locally Lipschitz on U. If there exists a nonnegative function V in C^2(U) and a constant alpha > 0 such that L V <= alpha * V on U, and inf_{x in U \ K_n} V(x) -> infinity as n -> infinity, then for any initial condition X_0 with P(X_0 in U) = 1, there exists a unique strong solution X_t for all t >= 0, and U is invariant: P(X_t in U for all t >= 0) = 1.
U is an open set in R^d
{K_n} is an exhaustion of U by closed sets with precompact open envelopes
mu, sigma are locally Lipschitz on U
L V <= alpha * V and V blows up at the boundary and infinity

body: Bayes' theorem, named after Thomas Bayes, gives a mathematical rule for inverting conditional probabilities, allowing the probability of a cause to be found given its effect. For example, with Bayes' theorem, the probability that a patient has a disease given that they tested positive for that disease can be found using the probability that the test yields a positive result when the disease is present. The theorem was developed in the 18th century by Bayes and independently by Pierre-Simon Laplace.

  Suppose that on an event $E$, we have that $d^{S}(X, Y) \leq \varepsilon$ almost surely.

  \begin{equation}
    d_{P}^{S}
    \bigl(
      P(X \in \cdot), P(Y \in \cdot)
    \bigr)
    \leq 
    P(E^{c}) + \varepsilon.
  \end{equation}

[Lemma 17 of arXiv:2607.18862, 'Tamed Euler Schemes for Singular SDEs with Multiplicative L\'{e}vy Noise'] Let $K>0$ be a constant and let $B,\widetilde{B}$ be symmetric invertible matrices such that $K^{-1}I\leq B\widetilde{B}^{-1}\leq KI$. Then, for all $x\in\mR^d$, we have the following bound
	\be
	|(p_B-p_{\widetilde{B}})(x)|\leq N\|I-B\widetilde{B}^{-1}\|(p_{\frac{B}{2}}+p_{\frac{\widetilde{B}}{2}})(x)
	\ee 
	where $p_B(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{(2\pi)^d\det{(B)}}}\exp{\bigg(-\frac{1}{2}x^TB^{-1}x\bigg)}$ and $N$ is a constant that depends only on $d,K$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Corollary 5 (Time-uniform probability estimate for the mixed example) of arXiv:2608.17540, 'Pathwise stability for one-dimensional SDEs driven by Brownian motion and a symmetric stab'] In the setting of Proposition~\ref{prop:mixed-brownian-error}, assume $x_0=\wt x_0$ and $\|r\|_{L^2(0,T)}<1$. Then, for every $h>0$,
\[
  \mathbb P\left(\sup_{0\le t\le T}|X_t-\wt X_t|>h\right)
  \le
  \frac{C}{h^{\alpha-1}}
  \|r\|_{L^2(0,T)}^{\frac{2(\alpha\wt\eta-1)}{\alpha\wt\eta-\alpha+2}}.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
  \mathbb P\left(\sup_{0\le t\le T}|X_t-\wt X_t|^{\alpha-1}>h\right)
  \le
  \frac{C}{h}
  \|r\|_{L^2(0,T)}^{\frac{2(\alpha\wt\eta-1)}{\alpha\wt\eta-\alpha+2}}.
\]
The constant is independent of $h$ and $r$; for $0<\lambda<1$ it can be chosen uniformly in $\lambda$.

body:
For iid Exp(1) edge weights on undirected nearest-neighbor Z^2, let T_n be the passage time from (0,0) to (n,0), n>=1, and sigma_n^2=Var(T_n)>0. Enumerate all edges, let F_k be the first-k-edge sigma-field with trivial F_0, M_{n,k}=E[T_n|F_k]-E T_n, D_{n,k}=M_{n,k}-M_{n,k-1}, and Q_{n,k}=sum_{j<=k} D_{n,j}^2. Uniform boundedness of E|T_n-E T_n|^4/sigma_n^4 is equivalent up to factor 81 to uniform boundedness of E Q_{n,k}^2/sigma_n^4 over n,k. If V_{n,k}=sum_{j<=k} E[D_{n,j}^2|F_{j-1}] satisfies E V_{n,k}^2<=a sigma_n^4 and sum_{j<=k} E D_{n,j}^4<=b sigma_n^4 uniformly for finite a,b>=0, then E|T_n-E T_n|^4<=81(sqrt(a)+sqrt(b))^2 sigma_n^4. These lattice estimates are hypotheses, not established facts.
The precise undirected lattice Exp(1) model in the statement
Countable full edge enumeration and corresponding exposure filtration
For the sufficient criterion, the two displayed uniform moment budgets are assumed

Exact remaining lattice condition and a predictable criterion

In the original specialization, T_n is the undirected nearest-neighbor passage time from (0,0) to (n,0) in Z^2 with iid Exp(1) edge weights. Enumerate the countably many edges, let F_k be the sigma-field generated by the first k weights, and set

    M_{n,k}=E[T_n | F_k]-E T_n,
    D_{n,k}=M_{n,k}-M_{n,k-1},
    sigma_n^2=Var(T_n),
    Q_{n,k}=sum_{j<=k} D_{n,j}^2.

Use a trivial F_0. T_n has finite fourth moment, since it is nonnegative and bounded above by the weight of the straight n-edge path. Its variance is positive: the minimum of the four weights incident to the starting vertex is a lower bound with unbounded support, while the straight-path upper bound is finite. Thus T_n cannot be almost surely constant. The endpoint is distinct for n>=1.

The following two conditions are equivalent up to universal constants:

    G: sup_n E|T_n-E T_n|^4 / sigma_n^4 < infinity;
    Q: sup_{n,k} E Q_{n,k}^2 / sigma_n^4 < infinity.

If G holds with constant K, conditional Jensen and the reverse inequality in L6 give Q with constant 81K. If Q holds with constant C, the forward inequality in L6 gives E M_{n,k}^4<=81C sigma_n^4. Moreover M_{n,k} converges to T_n-E T_n in the L^4 norm. To justify this step, cylinder random variables measurable with respect to some F_j are dense in L^4(F_infinity); conditional expectation is an L^4 contraction. Approximating T_n-E T_n by such a variable X gives, for k>=j,

    ||E[T_n-E T_n | F_k]-(T_n-E T_n)||_4
      <= 2 ||X-(T_n-E T_n)||_4.

T_n is F_infinity-measurable because it is an infimum over a countable collection of finite-path sums. The displayed approximation therefore proves the asserted convergence. Taking k to infinity yields G with constant 81C.

For a concrete sufficient criterion put

    v_{n,j}=E[D_{n,j}^2 | F_{j-1}],
    V_{n,k}=sum_{j<=k} v_{n,j}.

Suppose fixed finite constants a,b>=0 satisfy, uniformly in n,k,

    E V_{n,k}^2 <= a sigma_n^4,
    sum_{j<=k} E D_{n,j}^4 <= b sigma_n^4.

Then G holds with constant 81(sqrt(a)+sqrt(b))^2. Proof: the differences D_{n,j}^2-v_{n,j} form an L^2 martingale difference sequence. Orthogonality and conditional expectation give the exact identity

    E(Q_{n,k}-V_{n,k})^2
      = sum_{j<=k} (E D_{n,j}^4-E v_{n,j}^2)
      <= sum_{j<=k} E D_{n,j}^4.

Minkowski now bounds ||Q_{n,k}||_2 by ||V_{n,k}||_2 plus the square root of the jump-fourth-moment sum. Apply L6 and L^4 convergence. All uses of orthogonality concern actual martingale differences; no conditional probabilities are multiplied.

This criterion has not been verified for lattice FPP. The comparison Q<=>G is a reformulation of the missing moment estimate, not a proof that it holds. Unconditional identities E Q_{n,k}=E V_{n,k}=E M_{n,k}^2<=sigma_n^2 are insufficient to bound the required second moments of Q or V. The variance denominator here is that of the full T_n, not that of a truncated martingale.

## Counterexample to replacing the square-function second moment by its mean

Let 0<p<=1, B be Bernoulli(p), and epsilon be an independent symmetric sign. Use F_0 trivial, F_1=sigma(B), F_2=sigma(B,epsilon), and M_0=M_1=0, M_2=B epsilon/sqrt(p). This is a martingale with variance 1. Nonetheless

    Q_2=V_2=B/p,
    E Q_2=E V_2=1,
    E Q_2^2=E V_2^2=E M_2^4=1/p.

Thus the needed bound can fail arbitrarily badly even for two independent input variables and a two-step Doob martingale. Independence of the inputs does not make the conditional variance budget deterministic. [Definition 1 (Progress-aware exploitation score) of arXiv:2608.25116, '\method: Gradient Refinement and Progress-Aware Exploitation for Query-Efficient High-Dime'] Let $\gamma_\bv=\mu_\bv/\sigma_\bv$ denote the standardized directional
mean. The progress-aware exploitation score of direction $\bv$ at $\bx$ is
\begin{align}
\mathcal{P}(\bv) &:= \mathbb{E}\bigl[-\nabla_\bv f(\bx)\mid \nabla_\bv f(\bx)<0\bigr] \notag \\
&= \sigma_\bv\!\left[\frac{\phi(\gamma_\bv)}{\Phi(-\gamma_\bv)} - \gamma_\bv\right],

\end{align}
where $\phi$ and $\Phi$ are the standard normal PDF and CDF.
title: Progress-aware exploitation score

[Lemma prop:geodesics_intersect of arXiv:2512.09219, 'Strong confluence of geodesics in Liouville quantum gravity'] It is almost surely the case that the following is true. Let $P_n\colon [0,T_n]\rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ be a sequence of $D_h$-geodesics converging to some $D_h$-geodesic $P \colon [ 0 , T]\rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ as $n \to \infty$ in the Hausdorff sense with respect to $D_h$. Let $0<s<t<T$. Then, given $\varepsilon>0$, for all $n$ large enough, we have at least one of the following:
  \begin{enumerate}[(a)]
  \item  $d_H^1(P\lvert_{[s,t]},P_n\lvert_{[s,t]})\leq \varepsilon$,
  \item  $P\lvert_{[s,t]}\cap P_n\lvert_{[s,t]} \neq \emptyset$.
  \end{enumerate}
title: Lemma prop:geodesics_intersect of arXiv:2512.09219

[Lemma 2 of arXiv:2608.25221, 'Representing MAX functions using two-hidden-layer ReLU networks'] Fix a natural number $k\geq 1$. For any atom pattern $P$ of degree $k$, there exist $\eta_L, \eta_R \in \Z^N_+$ such that $\|\eta_L\|_1 = \|\eta_R\|_1 = k$ such that $$\mathcal{A}_P(x) = \max\{\langle \eta_L, x\rangle, \langle \eta_R, x\rangle\}$$ for all $x \in \mathcal{C}$. $\eta_L$ and $\eta_R$ are given by the closed-form formulas: $$(\eta_L)_i = \sum_{j=1}^k \mathbf{1}_{\min(p_j) = i} \qquad \forall i = 1, \ldots, N,$$
$$(\eta_R)_i = \sum_{j=1}^k \mathbf{1}_{\min(q_j) = i} \qquad \forall i = 1, \ldots, N,$$ where $\min(p_j)$ and $\min(q_j)$ denote the minimum of the pair of numbers in $p_j$ and $q_j$, respectively.

[Theorem 15 of arXiv:2609.00448, 'Equivariant formality and representation theory'] \textnormal{(\cite[Theorem 1.3]{F2}).} Let $G$ act on a finite CW-complex $X$. Then the following are equivalent. 
\begin{enumerate}
	\item $X$ is an equivariantly formal $G$-space.
	\item The forgetful map $f: K_G^*(X; \mathbb{Q})\to K^*(X; \mathbb{Q})$ is surjective. 
	\item The forgetful map $f$ induces an isomorphism $K_G^*(X; \mathbb{Q})\otimes_{R(G; \mathbb{Q})}\mathbb{Q}\to K^*(X; \mathbb{Q})$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Proposition 28 of arXiv:2605.14206, 'The clumsy coupon collector's problem'] For any $r > 0$, the tail event $\{ T_{m, p} \geq r \}$ has the following
  upper bound:
  \begin{align*}
      \PP(T_{m, p} \geq r)
      &\leq 2 - 2 
      \binom{m\exp(1/r)}{m}^{-1}
      (1-p)^m\\
      &\phantom{{} \leq 2 - 2} \times
      \left[
      1 - \int_0^1 p \, m
      \left(1-x\right)^{m\exp(1/r)-m}
      \left(1-p\,x\right)^{m-1} dx
      \right]^{-1}.
  \end{align*}
  \begin{proof}
    Since $T_{m, p}$ is non-negative,
    we can invoke a common bound from \cite[p.~126]{kallenberg2021probability},
    namely $\PP(T_{m,p} \geq r) \leq 2\left(1 - M_{T_{m,p}}(-1/r)\right)$.
    Substitute Lemma \ref{thm:factored mgf}.
  \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition 28 of arXiv:2605.14206

Own work draft, proof (unaudited); no independent review. For any fixed r>0, ReLU spiked random features with iid unit-sphere (or Gaussian N(0,I_d/d)) bulk rows and per-neuron spike r(v^T x), normalized by 1/sqrt(m), fail the ordinary Montanari-Saeed Gaussian projection condition along theta=1_m/sqrt(m). The projection converges in conditional L2 to h(rG)=E_Z ReLU(Z+rG), which is nonconstant and positive. Matched full Gaussian features have a strictly positive bounded-Lipschitz negative-tail discrepancy. Singleton-readout ERM with that negative-tail loss gives minimum limits 0 and c_r>0. Scope: This refutes only the ordinary Gaussian reduction including this readout direction, not conditional Gaussian equivalence or ridge equivalence. Constant per-neuron spike has norm r sqrt(m), not a bounded-operator spike. No novelty claim for the conditional structure already identified in Cui et al.
d,m,n->infinity
fixed r>0
v deterministic unit vector
x iid N(0,I_d) independent of frozen bulk W
bulk iid uniform unit-sphere or N(0,I_d/d)
feature normalization 1/sqrt(m)
ordinary unconditional matched Gaussian comparison, not the conditional equivalent
title: Draft: ReLU spiked random features fail ordinary Gaussianity along a delocalized mean direction

[Theorem 16 (Full convergence of a fixed anchored finite-time Hopf profile) of arXiv:2609.00501, 'Uniqueness of Finite-Time Varifold Limits for the M\"obius-Invariant Willmore Flow'] Under the hypotheses of Corollary~\ref{cor:hopf}, fix the oriented
normal gauge and the material anchor introduced above, and let
\(\widetilde\gamma_t\) be the anchored constant-speed profile
\eqref{eq:anchored-gauge}.  Set
\begin{equation}
 
 C_{\mathrm g}:=\left(\frac2\pi+64\right)^{1/2}.
\end{equation}
Then, for \(0\leq s<t<T\),
\begin{equation}
 
 \|\widetilde\gamma_t-\widetilde\gamma_s\|_{L^2(\Sph^1)}
 \leq
 \frac{C_{\mathrm g}}{\sqrt\pi}
 \sqrt{(t-s)\bigl(W(s)-W(t)\bigr)} .
\end{equation}
There are an embedded regular constant-speed curve
\(\gamma_T\in W^{2,2}(\Sph^1,\Sph^2)\cap C^1(\Sph^1,\Sph^2)\)
and a number \(L_T\in[\pi,8]\) such that, as \(t\nearrow T\),
\begin{align}
 \widetilde\gamma_t&\rightharpoonup\gamma_T
 &&\text{weakly in }W^{2,2}(\Sph^1,\R^3),\\
 \widetilde\gamma_t&\longrightarrow\gamma_T
 &&\text{strongly in }W^{1,2}(\Sph^1,\R^3),\\
 \widetilde\gamma_t&\longrightarrow\gamma_T
 &&\text{strongly in }C^{1,\alpha}(\Sph^1,\R^3),
   \quad 0<\alpha<\tfrac12,\\
 L(\widetilde\gamma_t)&\longrightarrow L_T=L(\gamma_T),
 \qquad |\partial_x\gamma_T|=L_T .
\end{align}
The trace of \(\gamma_T\) is the embedded \(C^1\) profile
\(\pi(\spt\Var_T)\) of the unique limiting Hopf torus.
title: Full convergence of a fixed anchored finite-time Hopf profile

Suppose one-way functions exist. For any measurement count m>d^0.01, Gupta et al. establish a family of 10-well-modeled distributions over R^d and normalized linear measurement models Y=A X+eta with m measurements, ||A||_op<=1 and independent eta~N(0,beta^2 I_m), beta=Theta(1/(log d)^2), for which (1/10,1/10)-posterior sampling requires superpolynomial time in d. Well-modeled and posterior sampling have exactly the meanings of the two companion definition cards. In particular the approximation guarantee is a typical-measurement coupling guarantee; the shrinking noise parameter is a standard deviation, not a variance. The result supplies priors with efficient approximate smoothed-score representations despite computationally hard posterior sampling. It does not assert this lower bound under a dimension-independent noise level or under log-concavity, and gives no general unit-cost exact-score-oracle lower bound.

Own-work draft. Status: proof (unaudited), C023 v2; independent audit and novelty assessment pending. Gaussian input, unit teacher u, fixed positive outer weights, activation sigma=sqrt(A)He2/sqrt(2)+sqrt(B)He3/sqrt(6), and zero temperature. For d>=4, 1/2<=a<1, 0<=p<1, define n=d-1, ell=1-p, q=1-a^2, J=n(1+a^3)-3aq, D=aJ+q, A=3D/(3D+2dq), B=1-A, s=q/J. The law rho*=p delta_u+ell times the uniform latitude u.w=-a has an attracting basin among axial laws with fixed pole mass p. Put W=-na(1+a^2+4a^3-2a^5)+6a^2q^2, Lf=ell*q*(6BJ/n)*(s-a), Lc=ell*(6B/n)*W, gamma=min(-Lf,-Lc)>0. For initial ring overlap -a+h, set N0=|Eh|+||h-Eh||infinity. If N0<=min((1-a)/2,gamma/(3072ell)), then Nt<=N0 exp(-gamma*t/2), and the spherical laws converge in W2 to rho*. The collective rate Lc includes the changing moment feedback; Lf is only the frozen-field rate. The exact factorization W=-(n-3)a(1+a^2+4a^3-2a^5)-3a[(1-a)^2+4a^3(2-a^2)] proves negativity. A polynomial Frechet remainder gives Dini derivative N'<=-gamma*N+1536ell*N^2. This is a local zero-temperature basin with fixed pole mass. It supplies neither uniform-start reachability nor a noisy escape-time lower bound, and does not assert a local risk minimum in unrestricted W2 topology. Exact algebra checks are supplemental; the Lean attempt is runtime-unverified.

body:
[Proposition prop:4D-cov of arXiv:2507.19554, 'Full extremal process in four-dimensional membrane model'] The covariance of the 4D membrane models $h_v$ satisfies
	\begin{itemize}
		\item
		There exists constant $\alpha_0'$ such that for $u, v \in V_N$, one has
		\bequ
			\begin{aligned}
				\Var\lp h_v^{N} \rp & \leq \frac{8}{\pi^2}\log N + \alpha_0; 		\\
				\mbE\lb \lp h_u^{N} - h_v^{N} \rp^2 \rb & \leq \frac{8}{\pi^2}\lp 2\log \lp 1 + \lv u - v \rv \rp - \lv \Var\lp h_v^{N} \rp - \Var\lp h_u^{N} \rp \rv + 4\alpha_0 \rp.
			\end{aligned}
		\eequ
		\item
		For any $\delta > 0$ there is a constant $\alpha^{\delta} > 0$ such that for all $u, v \in V_N$ with $\min\lp d_N\lp u \rp, d_N\lp v \rp \rp \geq \delta N$, one has
		\bequ
			\lv \Cov\lp h_v^{N}, h_u^{N}\rp - \log\frac{N}{1 + \lv u - v \rv} \rv \leq \alpha^{\delta}.
		\eequ 
	Here	$d_N\lp v \rp := \dist\lp v, \p V_N \rp$
		\item 
		There are a constant $\theta_0 > 0$, a continuous function $f_1: \lp 0, 1 \rp^4
		\rightarrow \mbR $ and a function $f_2: \mbZ^4 \times \mbZ^4 \rightarrow \mbR$
		such that the following holds. For all $L, \epsilon > 0, \theta > \theta_0$ there
		exists $N_0' = N_0'\lp L, \epsilon, \theta \rp$ such that for all
		$x \in \lb 0, 1 \rb^4, N \geq N_0', Nx \in \mbZ^4$ and
		$d\lp x \rp \geq \frac{\lp \log N \rp^{\theta}}{N}$ and for all
		$u, v \in \lb 0, L \rb^4 \cap \mbZ^4$, 
		\bequ
			\lv \Cov\lp h^{N}_{Nx + v}, h^{N}_{Nx + u} \rp - \frac{8}{\pi^2}\log N - f_1\lp x \rp - f_2\lp u, v \rp \rv < \epsilon.
		\eequ
		\item 
		There are a constant $\theta_1 > 0$ and a continuous function $f_3: D^4 \rightarrow \mbR$, where $D^4 := \lbb \lp x, y \rp, x, y \in \lp 0, 1 \rp^4, x \neq y \rbb$ such that the following holds: for all $L, \epsilon > 0, \theta > \theta_1$ there exists $N_1' = N_1'\lp L, \epsilon, \theta \rp$ such for all $x, y \in \lb 0, 1 \rb^4, Nx, Ny \in \mbZ^4$ and $d\lp x \rp \geq \frac{\lp \log N \rp^{\theta}}{N}$, $\min\lp d\lp x \rp, d\lp y \rp \rp \geq \frac{\lp \log N \rp^{\theta}}{N}$ and $\lv x - y \rv \geq \frac{1}{L}$ we have	
		\bequ
			\lv \Cov\lp  h^{N}_{Nx},  h^{N}_{Ny} \rp - f_3\lp x, y \rp \rv < \epsilon.
		\eequ
	\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Covariance of 4D membrane models \cite{schweiger2020maximum}

[Proposition 11 (Biorthogonal systems) of arXiv:2608.30722, 'Intermediate Singular Values of Random Matrices\\ under Second-Moment and Anti-Concentrati'] \hfill
\begin{enumerate}
  \item[\textnormal{(1)}] Let $D$ be an invertible $n \times n$ matrix with columns $v_k = De_k$. Define $v_k^* = (D^{-1})^* e_k$. Then
  $(v_k, v_k^*)_{k=1}^n$ is a complete biorthogonal system in
  $\mathbb{R}^n$.
  \item[\textnormal{(2)}] Every linearly independent system $(v_k)_{k=1}^n$
  in an $n$-dimensional Hilbert space $H$ admits a unique dual system
  $(v_k^*)_{k=1}^n$ such that $(v_k, v_k^*)$ is a complete biorthogonal
  system.
  \item[\textnormal{(3)}] In a complete biorthogonal system, $\|v_k^*\|_2 = 1/\dist(v_k, \Span(v_j:j \neq k))$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma judge the singular numbers of arXiv:2412.05999, 'Non-Archimedean GUE corners and Hecke modules'] Let $D\in\Alt_{2k-1}(F)$, and $\alpha_1=(c_{1,1},\ldots,c_{(2k-1),1})^t,\alpha_2=(c_{1,2},\ldots,c_{(2k-1),2})^t\in M_{(2k-1)\times 1}(F)$. Also, let 

$$D_1=\begin{pmatrix}0 & \alpha_1^t\\ -\alpha_1 & D\end{pmatrix},D_2=\begin{pmatrix}0 & \alpha_2^t\\ -\alpha_2 & D\end{pmatrix},D_{12}=\begin{pmatrix}0 & \alpha_1^t+\alpha_2^t\\ -\alpha_1-\alpha_2 & D\end{pmatrix}$$

Then $\det (D_{12})=\det D_1+\det D_2\pm2\sqrt{\det D_1\det D_2}$. Here $\pm\sqrt{\det D_1\det D_2}$ is one of two elements in $F$ such that its square equals $\det D_1\det D_2$.

body: FIRES WHEN a paper states a clean iff and credits it to an earlier short note, especially one in another language, and you are about to record the problem as resolved in the literature. WHAT HAPPENED: Ganikhodjaev and Zanin, arXiv:1205.3841 (2012, Russian), state as Theorem 1 that the Volterra operator on S^2 is non-ergodic if and only if a, b, c are nonzero and of one sign, attributing the condition to their 2004 note (Russian Math. Surveys 59:3, 571-572) whose TITLE announces only a necessary condition. An intermediate pass of this campaign recorded the problem as RESOLVED IN THE LITERATURE on that basis. Reading the 2004 note in full (Mathnet) shows it proves ONLY the necessary condition; the sufficiency was not there and had to be proved - see the E0061 result node. CONDITION OF FAILURE: an attribution chain read from the citing paper rather than from the cited one. The circumstantial warning was already visible and was not acted on: the 2009 source POSED the question five years AFTER the note it is attributed to, which is close to impossible if the note contained the answer.

[Lem FT_of_const._1_fn of arXiv:2606.29829, ''] Recall that $\widehat{G}$ is the set of equivalence classes of irreducible representations of the finite group $G$. Let $\mathbf{1}:G\rightarrow\{0,1\}$ be defined by $\mathbf{1}(g)=1$ for all $g\in G$, and $\delta_{*,*}$ denotes the Kronecker delta. Then
	\[\widehat{\mathbf{1}}(\sigma)=\frac{|G|}{d_{\sigma}}\;\delta_{\sigma,\trivial}\;I_{\sigma},\quad\sigma\in\widehat{G}.\]
	Here, $I_{\sigma}$ denotes the identity operator on the irreducible $G$-module indexed by $\sigma$, and $d_{\sigma}$ denotes its dimension.

body:
[Theorem 27 of arXiv:2511.06414, 'Non-uniform Edgeworth expansions for weakly dependent random variables and their applicati'] (i) Suppose that $\|f_n\|_{L^\infty}=O(n^{-\be})$ for some $\be\in(0,1/2)$. Then  Assumption \ref{DerAss} holds true when $r:=m-2<\frac1{1-2\be}$, and therefore the  non-uniform Edgeworth expansions of order $r$ and the  Edgeworth expansions in transport distances of order $r$ (as in Theorems \ref{Edge2} and \ref{Edge1}) and the expansions of the expectations as in Corollary \ref{Cor} (ii) hold true (with such $m$). In particular, if $\|f_n\|_{L^\infty}=O(n^{-1/2})$ then $S_n$ obeys expansions of all orders (in all of the above senses).

Moreover, the condition $r=m-2<\frac1{1-2\be}$ is optimal even for independent summands.
\vskip0.12cm
(ii) Suppose that $\cX$ is a compact Riemannian manifold, and that $f_n$ are uniformly H\"older continuous with some exponent $\al$. Additionally, assume that all the measures $\mathfrak{m_j}$ coincide with the volume measure and the transition densities $p_j$ which are (uniformly) bounded and bounded away from the origin. Then the non-uniform Edgeworth expansions of order $r=m-2$, 
the Edgeworth expansions in transport distances of order $r$, and the  expansions of the expectations as in Corollary \ref{Cor}(ii) hold true for every $m$ so that $r=m-2<\frac{1+\al}{1-\al}$, where for $\al=1$ we set $\frac{1+\al}{1-\al}=\infty$ (in particular, for Lipschitz continuous functions we get expansions of all orders in all of the above senses).

Moreover, the condition $r=m-2<\frac{1+\al}{1-\al}$ is optimal even in the iid case.

[Lem 2 of arXiv:2608.30763, 'Ultracontractivity of heat semigroups with non-local Robin boundary conditions via two-sid'] The boundary operator $C$ is  $\mathrm{L}^{\infty}$-continuous with 
$$
\left\| C \right\|_{\mathrm{L}^{\infty} \to \mathrm{L}^{\infty}} \ = \ \left\| C {\bf 1}\right\|_{\mathrm{L}^{\infty}(\partial \Omega)}.
$$
In particular, 
$$
\left| Cu \right| \ \leq \ \left\| u \right\|_{\mathrm{L}^{\infty}(\partial \Omega)} C {\bf 1}
$$ 
holds pointwise almost everywhere in $\partial \Omega$ for every $u \in \mathrm{L}^{\infty}(\partial \Omega)$. Furthermore
$C$ acts boundedly on $\mathrm{L}^{p}(\partial \Omega)$ for every $p \in [2,\infty)$ with
$$
\left\| C \right\|_{\mathrm{L}^{p} \to \mathrm{L}^{p}} \ \leq \ 
\max\left\{ \left\| C \right\|_{\mathrm{L}^{2} \to \mathrm{L}^{2}}, \left\| C {\bf 1}\right\|_{\mathrm{L}^{\infty}(\partial \Omega)} 
\right\} 
$$

[Corollary 8 of arXiv:2607.20373, 'Embedding martingale diffusions as binary posteriors in sequential inference'] $P$ is a C-S posterior if and only if there exist $\kappa\in\mathbb R$ and
$h\in C^2(J;(0,\infty))$ with $\delta=h'/h$ such that
$\widehat h(t,x):=e^{\kappa t/2}h(x)$ is space-time harmonic for $\mathcal L_0$.
In this case, the local likelihood-ratio process is $L_t=\widehat h(t,X_t)/\widehat h(0,x_0)$ for $t<\zeta$.

body: In probability theory, statistics and related fields, a Poisson point process is a type of mathematical object that consists of points randomly located on a mathematical space with the essential feature that the points occur independently of one another. The process's name derives from the fact that the number of points in any given finite region follows a Poisson distribution. The process and the distribution are named after French mathematician Siméon Denis Poisson. The process itself was discovered independently and repeatedly in several settings, including experiments on radioactive decay, telephone call arrivals and actuarial science.
title: Poisson point process

body: [Lemma 68 of arXiv:2608.20252, '2608.20252'] In a Hilbert space, if $x_n\rightarrow x$ weakly, there is a convex combination of the $\{x_1,x_2,\ldots, x_n\}$ which converges strongly to $x$, that is $\|x_n -x\|\rightarrow 0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 1 (The $5/8$ bound) of arXiv:2608.17743, 'A $5/8$ Lower Bound on the Banach-Mazur Distance to the Cross-Polytope'] There exist universal constants $c,C>0$ such that, for all sufficiently large $n$,
$$
\p\left\{d_{\mathrm{BM}}(G_m,B_1^n)\ge c n^{5/8}(\log n)^{-1/4}\right\} \ge 1-\frac{C}{n}.
$$
Consequently,
$$
R_1(n)\ge c n^{5/8}(\log n)^{-1/4}.
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition def:BST of arXiv:2608.19050, 'Online Permutation Embedding: \\ Optimal Stopping and Scaling Laws'] Let $\pi \in \Pi_k$ be a permutation. The binary search tree 
$\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{BST},\pi}$ is constructed by inserting nodes labeled $1,\dots,k$ (containing keys
$\pi(1),\pi(2),\dots,\pi(k)$, respectively) sequentially into an initially empty binary search tree. The first node, labeled 1, is inserted as the root. Each remaining node $i$ is sequentially inserted as follows. Start at the root; descend to the left if the key $\pi(i)$ is smaller 
than the key of the current node, and descend to the right otherwise. Repeat this descent until an empty position is reached, and insert the current node at this empty position. If $\pi$ was drawn uniformly at random from $\Pi_k$, then we further say that $\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{BST},\pi}$ is a \textit{random} BST on $[k]$.

[Definition 13 (Potential of the $n$-atomic $q$-Bass map) of arXiv:2607.15872, 'Existence of $q$-Bass martingales in the semidiscrete setting'] Let $\nu, q \in \Prob(\RR)$ satisfy Assumption~\ref{ass:technical-assumptions}, and set $D := [0,\diam(\supp(q)))^{n-1}$. Let $f : D \to \RR^{n-1}$ be the corresponding $n$-atomic $q$-Bass map. Define $v : D \times \RR \to \RR$ by $v(h,z) := U_\nu\big(g(h,z)\big)$ and $V : D \to \RR$ by 
\[
V(h) := \int_\RR v(h,z)\,dz.
\]
We call $V$ the \emph{potential} of the $n$-atomic $q$-Bass map $f$.
title: Potential of the $n$-atomic $q$-Bass map

[Lemma lem:scalar-solver-detailed of arXiv:2609.00556, 'Higgs--Demailly System and Positivity of Higgs Bundles'] Fix a bounded subset of triples $(f,u,t)$ such that $u$ is trace-free
Hermitian and, for some $\delta>0$ independent of the triple,
\begin{equation}
 \left(\frac\beta r+\Delta_\omega^{\mathbb C} f+(1-t)\alpha\right)\operatorname{Id}_E
 -e^f u\geq\delta\operatorname{Id}_E.
\end{equation}
Then the equation
\begin{equation}
 \det\left[
  \left(\frac\beta r+\Delta_\omega^{\mathbb C} U+(1-t)\alpha\right)\operatorname{Id}_E
  -e^f u
 \right]=e^{\lambda U}a_0
\end{equation}
has a unique admissible solution $U\in C^{2,\gamma}(M,\mathbb R)$.  On
bounded subsets satisfying (equation eq:scalar-margin of the paper),
$U$ is bounded in $C^{4,\gamma}$ and depends smoothly on $(f,u,t)$
in the corresponding Banach spaces.

[Definition 2 of arXiv:2605.03851, 'The Relay Random Tree:\\A stochastic geometry approach of multihop relay in an urban visib'] \textbf{Blockage.}

    For $\landsc$ a landscape and $(x, y)\in \Half$ a point, we call (first) blocking building of $(x, y)$ in $\landsc$ the following quantity when it is well defined:
    \[\tau(x, y, \landsc) = (x_b, y_b) := \underset{\substack{(a, b) \in \landsc \\a>x}}{\text{argmax}} \frac{b-y}{a-x}.\]
    When the blocking building of $(x, y)$ is well defined, we further introduce its blockage angle as:
    \[\theta(x, y, \landsc): = \arctan\left(\frac{y_b - y}{x_b-x}\right).\]
    In the following, when the involved landscape is unequivocal, we will simply write $\tau(x, y)$.

Let R be a commutative Noetherian ring and f an element of R that is neither a unit nor a zero-divisor. If p is a minimal prime ideal containing the principal ideal (f), then the height of p is 1 (height(p) = 1). Geometrically, cutting an irreducible affine variety of dimension d by a single hypersurface not containing it results in components of dimension d - 1.

[Prop 54 of arXiv:2507.00346, 'The strong convergence phenomenon'] Let $\Gamma$ be a finitely generated group with generating set
$\boldsymbol{g}=(g_1,\ldots,g_r)$, and let
$\rho_1:\Gamma\to B(H_1)$ and
$\rho_2:\Gamma\to B(H_2)$ be unitary representations.
Then the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[1.]
\itemsep\smallskipamount
\item
$\rho_1$ and $\rho_2$ are weakly equivalent.
\item
$\|P(\rho_1(\boldsymbol{g}),\rho_1(\boldsymbol{g})^*)\|=
\|P(\rho_2(\boldsymbol{g}),\rho_2(\boldsymbol{g})^*)\|$
for all $P\in\mathbb{C}\langle x_1,\ldots,x_{2r}\rangle$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

\geq
C_p n\log n-c_p n.

[Theorem thm:extremal of arXiv:2609.03904, 'Extremal Families for Matchings in Permutations'] Let $n\geq s\geq2$, and let $\mathcal F\subseteq S_n$ satisfy
$\nu(\mathcal F)<s$.  Then
\[
   |\mathcal F|\leq(s-1)(n-1)!.
\]
Equality holds if and only if one of the following holds:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item there are $i\in[n]$ and $J\subseteq[n]$, with $|J|=s-1$, such that
$
   \mathcal F=\{\sigma\in S_n:\sigma(i)\in J\};
$
\item there are $j\in[n]$ and $I\subseteq[n]$, with $|I|=s-1$, such that
$
   \mathcal F=\{\sigma\in S_n:\sigma^{-1}(j)\in I\}.
$
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm:extremal of arXiv:2609.03904

Let X,Y be real random variables defined on the same probability space, and let a<=b be finite real numbers. With d_TV(mu,nu)=sup_A|mu(A)-nu(A)|, P(a<=X<=b)<=0.5*(1+P(|X-Y|<=b-a)+d_TV(Law(X),Law(Y))). In particular a coupling can bound interval concentration away from one if its marginals are close in total variation but it has a positive probability of a separation larger than the interval length. Source: A general method for lower bounds on fluctuations of random variables, Lemma 1.2 and its proof, pp.3-4.

[Lemma 11 of arXiv:2609.03819, 'Stochastic damped wave and Euler-Bernoulli equations with singular locally H\"older contin'] Assume \ref{H0}, \ref{H1} and \ref{H3} hold. Hence, there exist constants $M_0\geq 1$ and $b>0$, independent of $t\in(0,\infty)$ and $n\in\N$, such that, for every $n\in\N$ and $t\in (0,\infty)$, we have 
\begin{align}
&\|e^{tA_n}\mathcal{V}_n\|_{\mathcal{L}(U,H_n)}\leq \frac{M_0e^{-b\zeta t}}{t^{\gamma_1}},\\
&\|\Gamma_{t,n}\mathcal{V}_n\|_{\mathcal{L}(U,H_n)}\leq \frac{M_0}{t^{\gamma_2}},\\
&\|\Gamma_{t,n}\mathcal{G}_n\|_{\mathcal{L}(U,H_n)}\leq \frac{M_0}{t^{1/2}},\\
&\|\Gamma_{t,n}\|_{\mathcal{L}(H_n)}\leq \frac{M_0}{t^{\gamma_3}},
\end{align}
where, if $\alpha\in\left(0,\frac12\right]$, then $\zeta=\mu_1^\alpha$ and 
\begin{align}
&\gamma_1= \frac{\beta}{\alpha},
\\
&\gamma_2=\frac12+\frac{\beta+\delta}{\alpha},\\
&\gamma_3=\frac12+\max\left\{\frac\delta\alpha, 1\right\}, 
\end{align}
while, if $\alpha\in\left[\frac12,1\right)$, then $\zeta=\mu_1^{1-\alpha}$ and
\begin{align}
&\gamma_1= 
\max\left\{\frac{\beta}{\alpha},\frac{\beta+\frac12-\alpha}{1-\alpha}\right\}, 
\\
&\gamma_2=\frac12+\frac{\beta+\delta}{1-\alpha},\\
&\gamma_3=\frac12+\max\left\{\frac{\delta+\alpha-\frac12}{1-\alpha}, 1\right\}, 
\end{align}

body: In mathematics, Schur's lemma is an elementary but useful statement in representation theory of groups and algebras. In the group case it says that if M and N are two finite-dimensional irreducible representations of a group G and φ is a linear map from M to N that commutes with the action of the group, then either φ is invertible, or φ = 0. An important special case occurs when M = N, i.e. φ is a self-map; in particular, for representations over an algebraically closed field, any element of the center of a group must act as a scalar operator on M. The lemma is named after Issai Schur who used it to prove the Schur orthogonality relations and develop the basics of the representation theory of finite groups. Schur's lemma admits generalisations to Lie groups and Lie algebras, the most common of which are due to Jacques Dixmier and Daniel Quillen.
title: Schur's lemma

        \item For all $0 \leq \rho \leq 1$, there exists a universal constant $C>0$ such that for all $z \geq 1$

         R_z(\rho) \leq Cz \cdot \exp \left( \frac{z^2\rho}{1+\rho} \right).
        \]

[Lemma lem:ODE_with_critical_driving_term of arXiv:2508.18807, '{\bf Critical long-range percolation I: High effective dimension}'] Let $a>0$, let $h$ be a positive, measurable, regulary varying function of index $a$, and suppose that $f$ is a  positive, differentiable function such that
\[
f'(r) =\frac{(1-\delta_{1,r}) af(r)+(1-\delta_{2,r})h(r)}{r}
\]
where $\delta_{1,r}$ is a logarithmically integrable error function. If $r^{-a} h(r)$ is \emph{not} logarithmically integrable, then
\[
f(r) \sim r^{a} \int_{r_0}^r \frac{h(s)}{s^{a+1}} \dif s
\]
as $r\to\infty$, where $r_0$ is sufficiently large that $h$ is locally bounded on $[r_0,\infty)$. Otherwise, if $r^{-a}h(r)$ is logarithmically integrable, then there exists a constant $A>0$ such that $f(r)\sim Ar^{a}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition 18 (Uniform BMO--Girsanov package) of arXiv:2608.06393, 'Intrinsic Tangential Hadamard Differentiability of Rough-BSDE Solution Maps'] Let \(\{N^\theta\}_{\theta\in\Theta}\) be continuous martingales on \(I\)
such that
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}
 \|N^\theta\|_{\mathrm{BMO}_2(\mathbb P;I)}\leq n_*.
\]
For \(u\leq t\leq v\), set
\[
 L_t^\theta
 :=\exp\left(
  N_t^\theta-N_u^\theta
  -\frac12(\langle N^\theta\rangle_t-
              \langle N^\theta\rangle_u)
 \right),
\]
so that \(L_u^\theta=1\), and define
\(d\mathbb Q^\theta/d\mathbb P=L_v^\theta\) on \(\mathcal F_v\).
There exist exponents \(r_+,r_->1\) and constants
\(C_+,C_-,C_{\mathrm{eq}}<\infty\), depending only on \(n_*\), such that,
uniformly in \(\theta\) and \(\tau\in\mathcal T_I\),
\begin{align}
 \mathbb E_\tau^{\mathbb P}
 \left[\left(\frac{L_v^\theta}{L_\tau^\theta}\right)^{r_+}\right]
 &\leq C_+,
 \\
 \mathbb E_\tau^{\mathbb Q^\theta}
 \left[\left(\frac{L_\tau^\theta}{L_v^\theta}\right)^{r_-}\right]
 &\leq C_-.
 
\end{align}
Moreover, if \(X\) is a continuous \(\mathbb P\)-local martingale and
\[
 \widetilde X^\theta
 :=X-\langle X,N^\theta\rangle,
\]
then
\begin{equation}
 C_{\mathrm{eq}}^{-1}\|X\|_{\mathrm{BMO}_2(\mathbb P;I)}
 \leq
 \|\widetilde X^\theta\|_{\mathrm{BMO}_2(\mathbb Q^\theta;I)}
 \leq
 C_{\mathrm{eq}}\|X\|_{\mathrm{BMO}_2(\mathbb P;I)}.
 
\end{equation}
The exponents are selected after the budget \(n_*\) is fixed.  The
proposition does not assert \(r_+=r_-=2\), nor does it prescribe the same
exponent under the two measures. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Uniform BMO--Girsanov package

Method: Optimal Glauber mixing near the coloring degree threshold explicit structural calculation Result: The elementary Hamming path coupling stops at q>2*Delta. For configurations differing at one vertex, updating that vertex removes the disagreement. Updating one of its at most Delta neighbors creates disagreement with probability at most1/(q-Delta), by maximally coupling the two uniform available-color sets. Therefore E[H_next]<=1-1/N+Delta/[N*(q-Delta)], which contracts precisely when q>2*Delta. Check: The two available-color sets differ by at most one exchanged color, each has at least q-Delta elements, and their uniform laws have total variation at most1/(q-Delta). Iterating the path coupling yields an N*log N bound with constant proportional to(q-Delta)/(q-2*Delta). Obstruction: The denominator degenerates before the source threshold. Exploiting local color availability or multi-vertex moves is necessary; the failed bound is not a counterexample to rapid mixing.

If sqrt(n) (T_n - theta) converges in distribution to N(0, sigma^2) and g is differentiable at theta with g'(theta) nonzero, then sqrt(n) (g(T_n) - g(theta)) converges in distribution to N(0, g'(theta)^2 sigma^2). When g'(theta) = 0 and g''(theta) exists nonzero, the rate improves to n with a scaled chi-squared limit (second-order delta method).

[Conjecture conj:global of arXiv:2607.10717, 'Separatrix structure and the geometry of reset distributions'] Under assumptions \textnormal{(S1)--(S4)}, the sign of
$\partial_\gamma C(\pi,\gamma)$ is globally determined by
\[
\operatorname{sgn}\bigl(\partial_\gamma C(\pi,\gamma)\bigr)
= \operatorname{sgn}\langle\pi - \pi^*, \psi(\gamma)\rangle
\]
for all $\pi\in\Delta_{m-1}^\circ$ and all $\gamma\in(0,1)$.
In particular, $\Sigma$ acts as a global orientation boundary
for the reset response: every distribution on one side of
$\Sigma$ responds monotonically to changes in $\gamma$, with
the sign determined by the side. (Stated as a conjecture by the paper; open unless the paper says otherwise.)
title: Global orientation principle

body:
Let m,n,r be positive integers, lambda>=0, and let Lhat:R^(m by n)->[0,infinity) be the convex C2 empirical loss in the NTK formulation. Assume Lhat(D)+lambda*||D||_* attains a global minimum. Let P be a nonzero positive-semidefinite symmetric (m+n)-by-(m+n) matrix. For U in R^(m by r), V in R^(n by r), put Q=[U;V] and g(U,V)=Lhat(UV^T)+(lambda/2)(||U||_F^2+||V||_F^2)+tr(P QQ^T). If Q is a second-order stationary point of g (Euclidean gradient zero and Hessian positive semidefinite in every factor direction) and rank(Q)<r, then Q globally minimizes g over all factors of these dimensions. This is the fixed-P rank-deficient lemma; it requires no probability law for P and no NTK sample-size rank threshold.
m,n,r positive integers; lambda>=0
Lhat nonnegative, convex and C2; its nuclear-regularized objective attains a minimum
P is nonzero symmetric positive semidefinite
The unconstrained factor Q is rank deficient and satisfies both first- and second-order stationarity
title: Jang--Lee--Ryu Lemma 4.4: rank-deficient SOSPs of the perturbed LoRA NTK loss are global

[Lemma lem:rn_derivative of arXiv:2507.15589, 'Tightness of approximations to metrics on non-simple conformal loop ensemble gaskets'] Fix $M > 0$ and let $h$ (resp.\ $h_0$) be a GFF on $\mathbf{D}$ with boundary conditions bounded by $M$ (resp.\ zero boundary conditions).  Fix $r \in (0,1)$ and let $\mathcal {Z}_r$ be the Radon-Nikodym derivative of the law of $h|_{B(0,r)}$ with respect to $h_0|_{B(0,r)}$.  For each $q \in \mathbf{R}$ there exists a constant $C \in (0,\infty)$ depending only on $q$, $r$, and $M$ so that
\[ \mathbf{E}[ \mathcal {Z}_r^q] \leq C.\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma lem:rn_derivative of arXiv:2507.15589

body: [campaign status: author_checked_candidate - author-checked, unrefereed] Agresti and Veraar (journal version 2025, p. 130), Problem 5 asks: if u_0^n tends to u_0 in L^2(Omega; H), does u^n tend to u in L^2(Omega; L^2(0,T;V) intersect C([0,T];H))? Our result (id P0267, 2026-09-08): NO, from the same critical Allen-Cahn example as P0266. Take u_0^n = 1/n tending to 0; the limit solution is identically zero, and convergence in L^2(Omega; C([0,T];H)) would require E sup ||u^n||^2 to tend to 0, but that quantity is infinite for every n by the P0266 result (the constant-data solution's supremum has tail index one, coming from a four-dimensional Bessel process's capacity estimate). Verification as the source words it: uses the same construction and checks as Problem 4; of the six problems attacked in that session the memo states these two have the best odds of being genuinely new, since the source is a year old. Prior art not cleared. Allen-Cahn on the 1-d torus with 1-d quadratic noise, critical gamma^2 = 2 u_0^n = 1/n tending to 0

[Lemma 8 of arXiv:2609.03506, 'Divergence of decreasing rearranged Fourier series\\ on every infinite compact abelian gro'] With the coefficients \(a_v\) defined above, let
\[
 \tau=\min\{\ell\in\{1,\ldots,N\}:|S_\ell|>\beta-1\},
 \qquad \min\varnothing=\infty,
\]
at each point of the underlying product group. Then
\[
 \sum_{v\in\T_N}a_vh_v=S_{\tau\wedge N}
\]
and, at every point,
\begin{equation}
 \left|\sum_{v\in\T_N}a_vh_v\right|\leq \beta.
\end{equation}

 =S_{\tau\wedge N},
\]

[Theorem 14 of arXiv:2604.01701, '\bf Chung-type laws of the iterated logarithm for $m$-fold weighted integrated fractional '] Let $m\ge 0$, $\gamma\ge 0$, $\alpha_1+\cdots+\alpha_i<H+i+\gamma$, $i=1,\ldots,m$,  $\tau=H+m+\gamma$. Suppose  $q\ge 1$, $\frac{1}{r}=H+m+\gamma+\frac{1}{q}$, and  $\|w\|_{r,\tau,q}<\infty$. Then
\begin{align}
 &\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}  \epsilon^{1/\tau}\log \pr\left(\left\|w(t)t^{\alpha_1+\cdots+\alpha_m}  J_{m,\bm\alpha}(I_{\gamma}B_H)(t) \right\|_{L^q(0,\infty)}<a_H \epsilon\right)\nonumber\\
 =&\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}  \epsilon^{1/\tau}\log \pr\left(\left\|w(t)t^{\alpha_1+\cdots+\alpha_m}  J_{m,\bm\alpha}(W_{H+\gamma})(t) \right\|_{L^q(0,\infty)}< \epsilon\right)\nonumber\\
=& \lim_{\epsilon\to 0} \epsilon^{1/\tau}\log \pr\left(\left\|wW_{\tau}\right\|_{L^q(0,\infty)}< \epsilon\right) 
= -\kappa(\tau,q)\|w\|_{L^r(0,\infty)}^{1/\tau}, 
\end{align}
where $\kappa(\lambda,q)$ is defined as \eqref{eq:constant:2}.  When $q=\infty$, we assume that $w$  is almost everywhere continuous. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 14 of arXiv:2604.01701

[Definition def:flow of arXiv:2606.12143, 'Continuous stochastic flows driven by white noise and their duals'] A \textbf{stochastic flow} driven by $\mathcal W$ is a family of processes 
$$
\mathcal S = \left\{\bigl(\mathcal S_{r,x}(a),\, x \ge r\bigr)\right\}_{(a,r) \in {\mathbb R}^2}
$$
such that, for each $(a,r) \in {\mathbb R}^2$, the process $(\mathcal S_{r,x}(a),\, x \ge r)$ is the almost sure unique strong solution to~(equation eq:SDE_gener of the paper), and the following properties hold almost surely:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textnormal{(R\arabic*)}, nosep]
    \item $\mathcal S_{r,r}(a) = a$ for all $(a,r) \in {\mathbb R}^2$. 
    \item For every $r \le x$, $a \mapsto \mathcal S_{r,x}(a)$ is c\`adl\`ag. 
    \item For any $(a_1,r_1), (a_2,r_2) \in {\mathbb R}^2$ and any $z \ge y \ge \max\{r_1,r_2\}$,
    $$
        \mathcal S_{r_1,y}(a_1) < \mathcal S_{r_2,y}(a_2) 
        \ \Longrightarrow\ 
        \mathcal S_{r_1,z}(a_1) \le \mathcal S_{r_2,z}(a_2).
    $$ 
\end{enumerate}

\vspace{-1.2em} 
A stochastic flow is said to be \textbf{continuous} if, almost surely, all flow lines are continuous. 
It is said to be \textbf{unique} if any other stochastic flow associated with~(equation eq:SDE_gener of the paper) satisfying the above properties is equal to $\mathcal S$ almost surely.
title: Definition def:flow of arXiv:2606.12143

Let P be an input probability law on X and let f,g:X->R be measurable functions with finite means E_P[f] and E_P[g]. Define c_P(f,g;x)=(f(x)-E_P[f])*(g(x)-E_P[g]) and L_cov(f,g;x,P)=max{0,1-c_P(f,g;x)}. Both centers use the same law P. In a curriculum, changing the sampling law therefore changes these centers. This is the population-centered covariance-loss definition used by Cornacchia-Mossel; their Remark1 describes estimating the two inner expectations and gradients with batches.
The input law P and both finite function means are specified.
For a finite Boolean input space, all real-valued network functions have finite means.
title: Cornacchia-Mossel covariance loss: population-centered product inside a hinge
