body:
There is NO inclusion between L^p and L^q on a general measure space, and the two familiar inclusions run in OPPOSITE directions. (a) Finite measure (mu(X) < infinity), p < q: L^q is contained in L^p, with ||f||_p <= mu(X)^{1/p - 1/q} ||f||_q; the inclusion is strict, e.g. on [0,1], f(x) = x^{-1/2} is in L^1 but not L^2. (b) Counting measure, p < q: l^p is contained in l^q, with ||a||_q <= ||a||_p - the reverse containment; strictness: a_n = 1/n is in l^2 but not l^1. (c) Lebesgue measure on R^n: NEITHER containment holds. On R, |x|^{-1/2} 1_{{|x|<1}} is in L^1 but not L^2, while (1 + |x|)^{-1} is in L^2 but not L^1 - the first fails by a local singularity, the second by slow decay at infinity. What IS always true is the interpolation statement: for p_0 < p < p_1, L^{p_0} intersect L^{p_1} is contained in L^p, with ||f||_p <= ||f||_{p_0}^{1-theta} ||f||_{p_1}^{theta}. So a step 'f in L^2 hence f in L^1' is only legitimate after the measure has been declared finite (with the factor mu(X)^{1/2} exhibited), and 'f in L^1 hence f in L^2' only on an atomic space with atoms bounded below.
all examples are for Lebesgue measure on [0,1] or R, and counting measure on N
title: Pitfall: L^p inclusions depend on the measure, and point in opposite directions for finite measures and for counting measure

[Lemma lem:sufficient of arXiv:2411.11415, 'The ballistic limit of the log-Sobolev constant equals the Polyak--\L{}ojasiewicz constant'] Suppose that there exists a Lyapunov function $W \colon \R^d \to \R$ with
$W \geqslant 1$, and a set $K \subseteq \R^d$, such that the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item[1.] The restricted measure $\mu|_K$ satisfies a Poincar\'e inequality with constant
    $C_K$, so that $C_{\msf{P}}(\mu|_K) \leqslant C_K$.
    \item[2.] There are constants $b, \lambda > 0$ such that
    for almost every 
    $x \in \R^d$:
    $$
    -\frac{\mathcal{L}_\mu W(x)}{W(x)} \geqslant \lambda\,(1 - b\mathbbold{1}_K(x))\,,
    $$ where $\mathcal{L}_\mu$ is the generator for $\mu$,
    namely $\mathcal{L}_\mu  \deq  \Delta + \langle \nabla \log \mu, \nabla \cdot \rangle$.
\end{enumerate}
Then,
$$
C_{\msf{P}}(\mu) \leqslant \lambda^{-1} + bC_K\,.
$$

[Definition 6 (Hyperbolic and de Sitter horocyclic evolutes \cite{CIT2024}) of arXiv:2608.26823, 'Evolutes, involutes and parallels of Legendre curves in hyperbolic and de Sitter 2-spaces '] \rm
Let $(\bgamma_h,\bgamma_h^d):I\rightarrow\Delta_1$ be a spacelike Legendre curve  with curvature $(m_h,n_h)$. Suppose that there exists a smooth function $f:I\rightarrow\R  $ such that $m_h(t)+f(t)n_h(t)=0$ for all $t\in I$. 
Then the \textit{hyperbolic horocyclic evolute}   $\mathcal{HE}^\pm(\bgamma_h,\bgamma_h^d):I\rightarrow H^2$  of $(\bgamma_h,\bgamma_h^d)$   is defined as  
\begin{equation}\notag
\mathcal{HE}^\pm(\bgamma_h,\bgamma_h^d)(t)=\bgamma_h(t)+f(t)\bgamma_h^d(t)+\frac{f^2(t)}{2}(\bgamma_h(t)\pm\bgamma_h^s(t)).
\end{equation} 
The \textit{de Sitter horocyclic evolute}   $\mathcal{DE}^\pm(\bgamma_h,\bgamma_h^d):I\rightarrow S_1^2$    of $(\bgamma_h,\bgamma_h^d)$   is defined as  
\begin{equation}\notag
\mathcal{DE}^\pm(\bgamma_h,\bgamma_h^d)(t)=\mp\frac{f^2(t)}{2}\bgamma_h(t)\mp f(t)\bgamma_h^d(t)+ \left(1-\frac{f^2(t)}{2}\right)\bgamma_h^s(t).
\end{equation}
title: Hyperbolic and de Sitter horocyclic evolutes \cite{CIT2024}

[Definition def:regular-markovian-2bsde of arXiv:2608.16119, 'Fully nonlinear parabolic equations under a fixed reference diffusion: weighted \texorpdfs'] Fix $0\leq\alpha<1$ and $\psi\in H^2(\mu_T)$.  For the purposes of this paper,
a regular fixed-reference Markovian 2BSDE solution consists of Borel fields
$(u,p,H):Q\to\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d\times\mathsf{S}^d$ and a process
$\mathfrak A\in\mathbb V^2(\mathbb R^d)$ with $\mathfrak A_0=0$.  The field
compositions must admit representatives
\begin{equation*}
 Y=u(\cdot,X),\qquad P=p(\cdot,X),\qquad \mathsf H=H(\cdot,X).
\end{equation*}
These representatives satisfy
\begin{equation*}
 Y\in\mathbb S^2(\mathbb R),\qquad
 P\in\mathbb S^2(\mathbb R^d),\qquad
 P^\top\in\mathbb H^2(\mathsf M^X;\mathbb R),\qquad
 \mathsf H\in\mathbb H^2(\mathsf M^X;\mathbb R^d),
\end{equation*}
and the fields must satisfy the regularity condition
\begin{equation*}
 F[u,p,H]\in H_{x,\alpha}^1,
\end{equation*}
as well as the following dynamics:
\begin{align}
 Y_t&=\psi(X_T)+\int_t^TF[u,p,H](s,X_s)\,\mathrm d s
          -\int_t^TP_s^\top\,\mathrm d\mathsf M_s^X,
 \\
 P_t&=P_0+\mathfrak A_t+\int_0^t\mathsf H_s\,\mathrm d\mathsf M_s^X,
 \qquad P_T=D_x\psi(X_T).
 
\end{align}
The identities $p=D_xu$ and $H=D_x^2u$, as well as absolute continuity of
$\mathfrak A$, are not imposed in this definition.
title: Definition def:regular-markovian-2bsde of arXiv:2608.16119

[Lemma 23 of arXiv:2512.04544, 'On the diameter of random uniform hypergraphs in dense regime'] Let $t,c,d,n,p$ and  $N$ be in Assumption \ref{ass main}.
Set
\[
\eta_k: = \exp \left( \sum\limits_{l=1}^{k} \epsilon_l \right) -1,
\]
where $\epsilon_1,\ldots, \epsilon_k$ are as defined in \Cref{lemma 18}. Define, for $1\le k\le d-1$, 
\begin{equation} 
	\Omega_{k,x}^*:=	\{\mathcal H\in \mathscr H[n]\suchthat \left\vert \vert \Gamma_{l}(x)\vert -  (t-1)^{l} N^l p^l  \right\vert \leq \eta_l (t-1)^{l} N^l p^l ,\forall \; 1 \leq l \leq k\} ,
\end{equation}
Then we have $\Prob(\Omega_{k,x}^*)\ge 1- 3kn^{-10}$  for large $n$.

	$$
	N_t=N_0+\int_{0}^{t} Z_s dB_s+\int_{0}^{t} U_s d M_s,\quad t \in [0,T].
	$$
	Moreover, if $N$ is square integrable, then 
	$$
	\mathbb{E}\int_{0}^{T}\left( \left| Z_s \right|^2 + \left|U_s\right|^2 \gamma_s\right) ds <\infty.
	$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Proposition prop:real-zero-family of arXiv:2607.25616, 'Stealthy point processes and lattice induction'] For some $\varepsilon>0$, the following assertions hold.

For every $z\in Z$, all zeros of $F_z$ are real and simple, and
its zero set
\[
    P_z:=\{x\in\mathbb R:F_z(x)=0\}
\]
is uniformly Delone. More precisely, there is $\delta>0$ such
that
\[
    P_z=\{p_\lambda(z):\lambda\in\Lambda\},
    \qquad
    |p_\lambda(z)-\lambda|<\delta
\]
for every $\lambda\in\Lambda$ and $z\in Z$.

The map
\[
    z\longmapsto\delta_{P_z}
\]
is Borel, and
\[
    P_{Tz}=P_z-1
    \qquad
    (z\in Z).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Theorem thm:LD-DG of arXiv:2509.04333, 'The limiting law of the Discrete Gaussian level lines'] {LMS16}}]
		There exist constants $\beta_0>0$ and $c>c'>0$ so that the following holds for every $\beta\geq \beta_0$ and integer $h\geq 2$. Let $V \subset \mathbb Z^2$ be a region containing $\ensuremath{\mathcal B}_r(o)$, the ball of radius $r=\lceil 2c h/\log h\rceil $ centered at the origin $o$, as well as $\ensuremath{\mathcal B}_{r+1}(z)$ for a site $z\in V$. Then
		\begin{align}
			\exp\Big(-c\beta \frac{h}{\log h}\Big) \leq &\;\frac{{\widehat\pi}_V^0(\phi_o = h)}{{\widehat\pi}_V^0(\phi_o = h-1)} \leq 
			\exp\Big(-c'\beta \frac{h}{\log h}\Big)
			\,,\\
			\exp\Big(-2\pi\beta\frac{h^2}{\log h} - c \beta \frac{h^2}{\log^2h}\Big)
			\leq  &\quad\;\;{\widehat\pi}_V^0(\phi_o = h)\!\!\!\!\quad\;\leq \exp\Big(-2\pi\beta\frac{h^2}{\log h} + c \beta\frac{h^2}{\log^2h}\Big)\,,\\
			&\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!
			{\widehat\pi}_V^0(\phi_z = h \mid \phi_o = h) \leq \exp\Big(-c \beta \frac{h^2}{\log^2h}\Big)\,.
		\end{align}

	    \mbox{and}\quad\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{\log\phi(n)}\sum_{h=0}^n(1-\pi_h)=\nu;\\ &\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1-f_n(\pi_n)}{L(n)-L(n-1)}=\nu;\\ &

	    \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\sum_{j=n_0+1}^n(1-q_j^{(0)})^2}{L(n)}=0\quad\mbox{for every integer}\ n_0;\\ & 
	    
         \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{L(n)}\sum_{j=n_0+1}^n(1-\pi_j)^2=0;\\ &

body:
[Lemma 19 of arXiv:2607.16502, 'Asymptotic Behavior of Path Functionals for Vector-Valued Gaussian Processes at High Level'] Let \(L>0\), let \(G:\R^d\to\R_+\) be continuous and coordinatewise
non-decreasing, and let
\(\mu\) be a regular finite capacity satisfying the support-intersection
property on \(E\), with \(\mu(E)>0\). Define
\[
  \Gamma(\bm f)=\int_0^\infty \mu\{t\in E:G(\bm f(t))>s\}\,ds-L .
\]
\begin{enumerate}[a)]
  \item 
  If
  \begin{equation}
    
    G(\bm y)>0,\quad \bm z\succ\bm y
    \quad\Longrightarrow\quad G(\bm z)>G(\bm y),
  \end{equation}
  then \(\Gamma\) satisfies condition~\ref{F2}.
  \item 
  If \(\mu\) is convex, \(\supp\mu\) is connected,
  \(\mu(\supp\mu)=\mu(E)\), and \(L/\mu(E)\) is not a plateau level of \(G\),
  then \(\Gamma\) satisfies condition~\ref{F2}.
\end{enumerate}

[Lemma 26 (Energy-localized saddle ansatz) of arXiv:2607.20882, 'An Eyring--Kramers Law for the Hypoelliptic Third-Order\\ Langevin Diffusion'] Let $\rho_\eps=\delta_\eps^3$.  There is
$G_\eps\in C_c^\infty(\R^{3d};[0,1])$ such that
\begin{equation}

G_\eps=1\ \hbox{ on }\{H\le U(\sigma)+a_\eps/2\},\qquad
G_\eps=0\ \hbox{ on }\{H\ge U(\sigma)+5a_\eps/6\},
\end{equation}
and $|\partial^\alpha G_\eps|\le C_\alpha\rho_\eps^{-|\alpha|}$.
Writing $j_\eps=\Phi_\sigma(\Lambda_\sigma/\sqrt\eps)$, for every $\vartheta>0$
there is an admissible $f_{\eps,\vartheta}\in C_c^2(\R^{3d};[0,1])$ which equals
$G_\eps j_\eps$ on $\mathcal K_\eps$, $G_\eps$ on the part of $J_\eps^m$
outside the $m$-side layer, and zero on the part of $J_\eps^s$ outside the
$s$-side layer.  Across the two physical faces it is
\begin{equation}

f_{\eps,\vartheta}=
\begin{cases}
G_\eps\{j_\eps+\chi_{\eps,\vartheta}^-(1-j_\eps)\},&m\text{-side layer},\\
G_\eps j_\eps,&\mathcal K_\eps,\\
G_\eps(1-\chi_{\eps,\vartheta}^+)j_\eps,&s\text{-side layer},\\
G_\eps,&J_\eps^m\text{ away from the layer},\\
0,&J_\eps^s\text{ away from the layer or }J_\eps^c,
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
where $\chi_{\eps,\vartheta}^\pm$ are flat at both ends, equal to one at the
outer end and zero at the inner end.
Every derivative not contained in the
logarithmic saddle box $\mathcal K_\eps$ in
\eqref{eq:logarithmic-saddle-box} or a physical side layer
$\mathcal A_{\eps,\vartheta}^\pm$ in \eqref{eq:physical-side-layers} is supported in
$\{H\ge U(\sigma)+a_\eps/2\}$.

body: Let X_n, X be random variables or vectors with X_n -> X in distribution as n -> infinity, and let Y_n -> c in probability for a constant c. Then X_n + Y_n -> X + c in distribution, X_n Y_n -> c X in distribution, and, provided c is not 0, X_n / Y_n -> X / c in distribution. More generally, if g(x,y) is continuous at every point (x,c), then g(X_n,Y_n) -> g(X,c) in distribution. Slutsky's theorem lets one combine a distributional limit with a probability limit as though the latter were a genuine constant. Due to Eugen Slutsky.

Let (M, g) be a complete Riemannian manifold of dimension n whose Ricci curvature satisfies Ric >= (n - 1) K g for a constant K, and let V_K(r) denote the volume of a geodesic ball of radius r in the simply connected complete space of constant curvature K (the sphere of radius 1/sqrt(K) for K > 0, Euclidean space for K = 0, hyperbolic space of curvature K for K < 0; for K > 0 take r <= pi / sqrt(K)). Then for every point p in M the function r |-> vol(B(p, r)) / V_K(r) is nonincreasing on (0, infinity) (on (0, pi/sqrt(K)] if K > 0) and tends to 1 as r -> 0. Consequently vol(B(p, r)) <= V_K(r) for all r (Bishop's inequality); for K = 0, vol(B(p, r)) <= omega_n r^n, volume grows at most Euclideanly and the limit vol(B(p, r)) / (omega_n r^n) as r -> infinity (the asymptotic volume ratio) exists and is at most 1; and vol(B(p, R)) / vol(B(p, r)) <= V_K(R) / V_K(r) for r <= R, which is the doubling-type estimate behind Gromov's precompactness theorem, Milnor's polynomial growth of the fundamental group under Ric >= 0, and Cheng's maximal diameter theorem (equality in the diameter bound pi/sqrt(K) forces the round sphere).
(M, g) complete, dimension n >= 2, Ric >= (n - 1) K
for K > 0 the radii are restricted to r <= pi/sqrt(K) (Myers' theorem bounds the diameter by this)
balls are metric balls; the comparison is with the constant-curvature space form of the same dimension

[Theorem main2 of arXiv:2412.00865, 'On the spectral problem and fractional diffusion limit for Fokker-Planck with(-out) drift '] Assume (a1 of the paper)--(a5 of the paper) and assume that  $f_0$ is a non-negative function in  $ L^2_{F^{-1}}(\mathbb{R}^{2d})\cap L^\infty_{F^{-1}}(\mathbb{R}^{2d})$. Let $f^\varepsilon$ be the solution of (equation fp-theta of the paper) in $Y$ with initial data $f_0$ and $\theta(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon^{\alpha} $. Let $ \kappa$ be the constant given by (equation def kappa of the paper). Then, $f^\varepsilon$ converges weakly star in $L^\infty\big([0,T]; L^2_{F^{-1}}(\mathbb{R}^{2d})\big)$ towards $\rho(t,x) F(v)$, where $\rho$ is the unique solution to

[Theorem thm:class5 of arXiv:2608.28007, 'Exact Risk Ratios for Weighted Data Selection in Linear Regression'] Let $B=\{b_1,\dots,b_5\}$ be a positive basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$. Up to renumbering,
independent positive rescaling of each vector, and an invertible linear map,
\[
b_1=e_1,\quad b_2=e_2,\quad b_3=-e_1-e_2,\quad
b_4=e_3-\tfrac\kappa2e_1,\quad b_5=-e_3-\tfrac\kappa2e_1,
\]
for some $\kappa\ge0$; equivalently
\begin{equation}
b_1+b_2+b_3=0,\qquad \kappa b_1+b_4+b_5=0 .
\end{equation}
For $\kappa=0$ the basis splits into a rank-$2$ triangle circuit and an
antipodal pair; all $\kappa>0$ form one orbit, in which two rank-$2$
triangle circuits share the vector $b_1$.

where $m^2\ge 0$ and $A$ is  a densely defined self-adjoint infinitesimal
generator  on $L^2(S,\pi)$ of a strongly continuous semigroup
for an ergodic invariant probability $\pi$
such
that $ A^{-1}$ is a bounded linear operator on the range
$\mathcal{R}(A)=1_\pi^\perp$.
 Define a bounded linear transformation $T:1_\pi^\perp\to 1_\pi^\perp$ 
by
\begin{equation}
Tf = 
(-A)^{\frac{1}{2}}(A-m^2)^{-\frac{1}{2}}f, \quad f\in 1_\pi^\perp.
\end{equation}
Let $Z$ denote the Stationary UGRF obtained
by a Lamperti transformation with dissipative 
operator $\Gamma={\mathbf I}$ 
and with covariance operator $C = -2A^{-1}$.
Then the linearly transformed Stationary UGRF
 $Z$ defined by $TZ$
 is It\^o's $OU\mathcal{L}(1_\pi^\perp)$-process  with 
parameters
$C=-(A-m^2)^{-1}$ and
and characteristic operator $\Gamma = {\bf I}$. 
In particular,  $Q=C$.

body:
[Definition 2 of arXiv:2608.29086, '2608.29086'] [$M_1 \subset M_2$]
Given two triangular meshes $S$ and $M$. $S$ is called a \textit{submesh} of $M$ if
\begin{align*} 
Tri(S) &\subset Tri(M), \\
Edge(S)&:=\{ ab \in Edge(M)\ |\ \exists c \in Ver(M) \text{ such that } abc \in Tri(S) \}, \\
Ver(S)&:=\{ a \in Ver(M) \ |\  \exists b \in Ver(M) \text{ such that } ab \in Edge(S) \}.
\end{align*}
$SUBMESH(M)$ denotes the collection of all submeshes of $M$. Given $M_1, M_2 \in SUBMESH(M)$. \underline{We write $M_1 \subset M_2$ if $M_1 \in SUBMESH(M_2)$}.
title: Definition 2 of arXiv:2608.29086

body:
[Lemma 14 (Joint compactness through the endpoints) of arXiv:2608.30211, '2608.30211'] Let $D_n$ be a uniformly $C^{2,\gamma}$ sequence converging locally in
$C^{2,\gamma'}$, for some $\gamma'<\gamma$, to a domain $D_\infty$.  Let
$\varrho_n\to\varrho_\infty\in[0,1]$, and suppose
$u_n\in C^2(D_n)\cap C^1(\overline{D_n})$ satisfies
\begin{equation}
 0\leq u_n\leq1,\qquad -\Delta u_n=f(u_n)\ \text{in }D_n,
 \qquad \cN_{\varrho_n}u_n=0\ \text{on }\partial D_n.
\end{equation}
After passage to a subsequence, $u_n$ converges locally uniformly on the
closure of each component that persists under this local smooth convergence
to a function $u_\infty$ satisfying
\begin{equation}
 -\Delta u_\infty=f(u_\infty)\ \text{in }D_\infty,
 \qquad \cN_{\varrho_\infty}u_\infty=0\ \text{on }\partial D_\infty.
\end{equation}

body:
Let $G_1,\dots,G_p$ be independent $n \times n$ matrices with i.i.d. $\mathcal{N}(0,1/n)$ entries. The limiting singular value distribution of the product $G_p \cdots G_1$ is the Fuss-Catalan law of order $p$, whose upper edge is $(p+1)^{(p+1)/2}p^{-p/2}$. For $p=1$ this is $2$, recovering the square Gaussian case; for $p=2$ it is $3^{3/2}/2=\sqrt{27/4}=2.5980\ldots$; for $p=3$ it is $3.0792\ldots$. Moreover the largest singular value itself converges to that edge, not merely the bulk. This last point matters and is strictly stronger: convergence of the spectral distribution locates the edge but by itself does not exclude an outlier above it, so a bound that needs no outlier cannot be justified by the Fuss-Catalan law alone.

entries i.i.d. centered Gaussian, variance 1/n
square factors of equal dimension

[Proposition 50 (Saturation of the Toeplitz quadratic form) of arXiv:2602.14618, 'Finitary coding and Gaussian concentration\\ for random fields'] Let $b=(b_m)_{m\in\mathbb Z^d}$ be a nonnegative, absolutely summable kernel on $\mathbb Z^d$, with
\[
\|b\|_1 := \sum_{m\in\mathbb Z^d} b_m < \infty.
\]
For any finitely supported vector $\delta=(\delta_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}$, define the quadratic form
\[
Q(\delta) := \sum_{k,\ell\in\mathbb Z^d} \delta_k\,\delta_\ell\, b_{\ell-k}.
\]
Then
\[
\sup_{\delta\neq 0} \frac{Q(\delta)}{\|\delta\|_2^2} = \|b\|_1.
\]
Moreover, this supremum is asymptotically attained by block indicators:
if $\delta^{(L)}_k := \1_{\{k\in\Lambda_L\}}$ with $\Lambda_L := [-L,L]^d\cap\mathbb Z^d$, then
\[
\lim_{L\to\infty} \frac{Q(\delta^{(L)})}{\|\delta^{(L)}\|_2^2} = \|b\|_1.
\]

body:
Let $Y_n = X_n + \sigma Z_n$ where $Y_n$ is $m \times n$ with $m/n \to \beta \in (0, 1]$, $Z_n$ has i.i.d. entries of mean zero, variance one and finite fourth moment, and $X_n$ has fixed rank $r$ with singular values $\sigma\sqrt{n}\, x_1, \dots, \sigma\sqrt{n}\, x_r$ (so the $x_k$ are the signal singular values on the scale of the noise, $x_k > 0$ fixed). Write the singular values of $Y_n$ on the same scale, $y_k := s_k(Y_n) / (\sigma \sqrt{n})$. THEOREM (Gavish and Donoho, 2017). (i) For each $k \le r$: if $x_k > \beta^{1/4}$ then $y_k \to \sqrt{(x_k^2 + 1)(x_k^2 + \beta)} / x_k$, and if $x_k \le \beta^{1/4}$ then $y_k \to 1 + \sqrt\beta$ (the bulk edge); every other singular value of $Y_n$ converges to the bulk. (ii) Among all estimators of the form $\hat X = \sum_k \eta(y_k)\, \sigma\sqrt{n}\; \hat u_k \hat v_k^T$ that keep the sample singular vectors and replace each singular value by a function $\eta$ of it, the one minimizing the asymptotic Frobenius loss $\lim \|\hat X - X_n\|_F^2 / (\sigma^2 n)$ is $$\eta^*(y) = \frac{1}{y}\sqrt{(y^2 - \beta - 1)^2 - 4\beta} \quad \text{for } y \ge 1 + \sqrt\beta, \qquad \eta^*(y) = 0 \quad \text{for } y < 1 + \sqrt\beta.$$ (iii) The asymptotic loss of $\eta^*$ is strictly smaller than that of hard thresholding at any threshold and of soft thresholding at any threshold whenever some $x_k > \beta^{1/4}$; on a pure-noise matrix ($r = 0$) $\eta^*$ returns the zero matrix. The rule selects the rank (the number of $y_k$ above the edge $1 + \sqrt\beta$) and the amount of shrinkage of each retained component from the data, without cross-validation; with $\sigma$ unknown it is combined with the median estimate $\hat\sigma = y_{\mathrm{med}}/\sqrt{n \mu_\beta}$.

[Corollary 13 of arXiv:2608.23450, 'The Oldest Allele in a Moran Model'] Let $g_0$ be defined as in Proposition \ref{prop:expected_hitting_time} there exist positive constants $c_1, c_2, c_3$ such that for all $x \in (0, 1)$:
\begin{align}
    0 < g_0'(x) &\le c_1(1 - \ln x),  \\
    |g_0''(x)| &\le c_2 x^{-1},  \\
    |g_0'''(x)| &\le c_3 x^{-2}. 
\end{align}
Furthermore, there exists a neighborhood $(0, \delta)$ near the absorbing boundary $0$ such that $g_0''(x) < 0$, making $g_0$ strictly concave there.

body:
[Lemma lem:a1 of arXiv:2607.24164, 'The KLS constant is $O(\log^{1/4} n)$'] Let $X \sim \mu$ be an isotropic log-concave random vector in $\mathbb{R}^n$. To prove (thm:1.2 of the paper), it is enough to consider measures of the form
\[
  \,\mathrm{d}\mu(x)
  =\rho(x)\,\,\mathrm{d} x
  =e^{-V(x)}\mathbf{1}_{K}(x)\,\,\mathrm{d} x,
\]
where $K\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ is bounded, open, and convex, and $V$ is smooth and
convex on an open neighborhood of $\overline K$. There are isotropic
log-concave measures $\mu_\varepsilon$ of this form such that
\[
  \mathbb{E}_{X\sim\mu_\varepsilon}p(X)
  \longrightarrow
  \mathbb{E}_{X\sim\mu}p(X)
\]
for every polynomial $p$ of degree at most four as
$\varepsilon\downarrow0$.

body: [Definition 1 (Distribution--kernel pair) of arXiv:2604.20634, 'Distributional Statistical Models:\\ \large Weak Moments, Cumulants, and a Central Limit T'] A \emph{distribution--kernel pair} is a tuple $(T,\varphi)$ with $T \in \mathcal{S}'(\R^d)$ and $\varphi \in \mathcal{S}(\R^d)$. [Theorem 4 of arXiv:2605.20026, 'Quasihelix properties\\ of selected Volterra Gaussian processes'] Let $\gamma\in[0,1)$. Then the following assertions hold.
\begin{enumerate}[1)]
\item Let $\alpha\in(-1/2+\gamma/2,1/2+\gamma/2)$. Then 
\begin{enumerate}
    \item[$(i)$]
There exists a constant $C(\alpha,\gamma)>0$ such that, for any $0\le s<t$,
\[
\ex\big(U^{(2)}(t)-U^{(2)}(s)\big)^2
\le C(\alpha,\gamma)(t-s)^{2\alpha+1-\gamma}.
\]

\item[$(ii)$]
The process $U^{(2)}$ is a local
$(\alpha+\frac12,\alpha+\frac{1-\gamma}{2},0,T)$-generalized quasihelix for any $T>0$.
\end{enumerate}

\item If $\alpha\in[1/2+\gamma/2,1)$, then the process $U^{(2)}$ is a local
$(\alpha+\frac12,\alpha,0,T)$-generalized quasihelix for any $T>0$.

\item If $\alpha\ge1$, then the process $U^{(2)}$ is a local
$(\alpha+\frac12,1,0,T)$-generalized quasihelix for any $T>0$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 4 of arXiv:2605.20026

Let Y be uniform on {-1,+1} and X|Y=y have law N(y mu,Sigma), with Sigma positive definite. For a closed l2 adversarial ball of radius epsilon>=0, define d=min_{||z||_2<=epsilon} sqrt((mu-z)^T Sigma^{-1}(mu-z)). The maximum robust classification accuracy over all measurable classifiers is Phi(d), where Phi is the standard normal CDF. If epsilon<||mu||, a minimizing z yields the optimal centered halfspace with normal Sigma^{-1}(mu-z). If epsilon>=||mu||, d=0 and a constant classifier attains accuracy 1/2. For Sigma=sigma^2 I the answer is Phi((||mu||-epsilon)_+/sigma). This optimum is known from Bhagoji, Cullina and Mittal and is restated by Dan, Wei and Ravikumar, Theorem 2.1, arXiv:2006.16384v1, printed p.5.

body:
[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] Consider the hyperoctahedral group $H_N$, which appears as the symmetry group of the $N$-cube, or the symmetry group of the $N$ coordinate axes of $\mathbb R^N$:
$$S_N\subset H_N\subset O_N$$
In matrix terms, $H_N$ consists of the permutation-type matrices having $\pm1$ as nonzero entries, and we have a wreath product decomposition as follows:
$$H_N=\mathbb Z_2\wr S_N$$
In this picture, the main character counts the signed number of fixed points, among the coordinate axes, and its truncations count the truncations of such numbers.

[Proposition of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] We have polar coordinates in $2$ dimensions,
$$\begin{cases}

[Propositio generalH of arXiv:2609.00108, 'The double sphere solution in the liquid drop model'] Let $\Sigma\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a smooth oriented surface with metric $g$,
		second fundamental form $A$, unit normal $\nu$, and mean curvature
		$H=\operatorname{tr}_g A$, with the convention
		\[
		\nabla_i\nu=A_i{}^j e_j.
		\]
		For $h\in C^2(\Sigma)$ sufficiently small in the sense that
		\[
		|A||h|+|\nabla_\Sigma h|\le \delta
		\]
		for some $\delta>0$ sufficiently small, the mean curvature of the normal graph
		\[
		\Sigma_h
		=
		\{x+h(x)\nu(x):x\in\Sigma\}
		\]
		can be written as
		\[
		H_{\Sigma_h}
		=
		H
		+
		\Delta_\Sigma h
		+
		|A|^2 h
		+
		\mathcal Q_\Sigma[h],
		\]
		where $\mathcal Q_\Sigma[h]$ satisfies
		\begin{equation}
			\begin{aligned}
				|\mathcal Q_\Sigma[h]|
				\le {}&
				C
				\Big(
				|A||h|
				+
				|\nabla_\Sigma h|^2
				\Big)
				|\nabla_\Sigma^2h|
				\\
				&+
				C
				\Big(
				|A|^3|h|^2
				+
				|A||\nabla_\Sigma h|^2
				+
				|h||\nabla_\Sigma A||\nabla_\Sigma h|
				\Big).
			\end{aligned}
		\end{equation}
		Here and below all contractions are taken with respect to the metric $g$.
		
		Moreover, let $h_1,h_2\in C^2(\Sigma)$ satisfy \[ |A||h_i|+|\nabla_\Sigma h_i|\le \delta, \qquad i=1,2, \] for $\delta>0$ sufficiently small, and set \[ w=h_1-h_2. \] Then one has the pointwise estimate \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} &|\mathcal Q_\Sigma[h_1]-\mathcal Q_\Sigma[h_2]| \le {} C \Big( |A|(|h_1|+|h_2|) + |\nabla_\Sigma h_1|^2 + |\nabla_\Sigma h_2|^2 \Big) |\nabla_\Sigma^2 w| \\ &+ C|A| \Big( |\nabla_\Sigma^2 h_1| + |\nabla_\Sigma^2 h_2| \Big) |w| + C \Big( |\nabla_\Sigma h_1|
				+ |\nabla_\Sigma h_2| \Big) \Big( |\nabla_\Sigma^2 h_1| + |\nabla_\Sigma^2 h_2| \Big) |\nabla_\Sigma w| \\ &+ C|A|^3 \Big( |h_1|+|h_2| \Big) |w| + C|A| \Big( |\nabla_\Sigma h_1| + |\nabla_\Sigma h_2| \Big) |\nabla_\Sigma w| \\ &+ C|\nabla_\Sigma A| \Big[ \Big( |\nabla_\Sigma h_1| + |\nabla_\Sigma h_2| \Big) |w| + \Big( |h_1|+|h_2| \Big) |\nabla_\Sigma w| \Big]. \end{aligned} \end{equation} In particular, the difference estimate is quadratic in the sense that every term on the right-hand side contains one factor measuring the size of $h_1$ or $h_2$ and one factor measuring the size of $h_1-h_2$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Propositio generalH of arXiv:2609.00108

[Lemma Lstar-d of arXiv:2507.01406, '{\Large On Iterated Lorenz Curves with Applications: The Multivariate Case }'] Let $\{L_{n}\}_{n\geq 0}$ be the sequence generated by (\ref
{941b}). Then for every sequence of indices $n_{k}\rightarrow \infty $ there
exists a subsequence (still denoted $n_{k}$) and a distribution function $
L^{\ast }$ on $[0,1]^{d}$ such that 
\begin{equation}
\sup_{x\in \lbrack 0,1]^{d}}\left\vert L_{n_{k}}(x)-L^{\ast }(x)\right\vert
\rightarrow 0\quad \text{as }k\rightarrow \infty ,  
\end{equation}
and the marginals $L_{i}^{n_{k}}$ converge uniformly to the marginals $
L_{i}^{\ast }$ of $L^{\ast }$, with inverses $T_{i}^{n_{k}}\rightarrow
T_{i}^{\ast }=(L_{i}^{\ast })^{-1}$ uniformly on $[0,1]$.\hfill\ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem thm: thinning application of arXiv:2411.02917, '\hspace*{2mm}\\[-16mm] Stein's Method for Spatial Random Graphs'] For $\mathcal{X} \subset \R^d$ compact, let $\Xi$ be a point process on $\mathcal{X}_{1/q} = \tau_q^{-1}(\mathcal{X})$ fulfilling Condition~(equation eq:condsigma of the paper). Choose $r_* \geq 0$ such that $\Prob(R \geq r_*) > 0$ (to rule out a trivial case) and denote  by $P_{r_*,q} \otimes Q_{r_*,q}$ the distribution of the percolation graph $(\Xi_{r_*,q}, \Sigma_{r_*,q})$ of the Boolean model based on $\hat{R}_i$ after thinning and rescaling. \\
Let $\lambda > 0$ and $t = q^{1/d} \hat{r}_*$. Furthermore, denote by $P^\lambda$ the homogeneous Poisson process distribution with intensity $\lambda$ and set $\kappa_{t}(x,y) = \1_{\{\norm{x-y} \leq 2t\}}$. \\
Then we have
\begin{align*}
    W_{\mathbb{G},i} \bigl(P_{r_*,q} \otimes Q_{r_*,q} \hspace*{1.5pt} , \, P^{\lambda} \otimes Q^{\kappa_{t}}\bigr) 
    &\leq c_V(\lambda)\, \E\bigl(\bignorm{\lambda\,\text{Leb}^{d}(\diff x) - p(r_*) \hspace*{1.5pt} \E \bigl( L(\tau_{q}^{-1}(\cdot) \,|\, \Xi\tau_q^{-1}) \bigm| \Xi_{r_*,q} \bigr) }_{\text{TV}} \bigr) \\[0.5mm]
    &\hspace{6mm}  {}+c_E(\lambda) \, \lambda\, c_d\, p(r_*) \, q \, \E\Xi(\mathcal{X}_{1/q}) \,
    d \, 2^d \E\bigl[(\hat{R}-\hat{r}_*) \hat{R}^{d-1} \bigm| R \geq r_* \bigr],
\end{align*}
where $c_d = \frac{\pi^{d/2}}{\Gamma(d/2 +1)}$ is the volume of the unit ball in $\R^d$ and $c_V(\lambda)$, $c_E(\lambda)$ are defined in Equations~(equation eq: SteinPoissonV of the paper) and~(equation eq: SteinPoissonE of the paper).
title: Approximation of Boolean percolation graph by random geometric graph

[Definition 14 (Admissible spectral cutoffs) of arXiv:2607.10813, '2607.10813'] A family $(\pi_\Lambda)_{\Lambda\ge1}$ is called admissible if
$\pi_\Lambda=m_\Lambda(D)$, where $m_\Lambda\in C_c^\infty(\R^3)$ is real and
even, and there exist constants $0<c_0<C_0<\infty$ such that
\begin{equation}
  m_\Lambda(\xi)=1\quad\text{for }|\xi|\le c_0\Lambda,
  \qquad
  \operatorname{supp}m_\Lambda\subset\{|\xi|\le C_0\Lambda\}.
\end{equation}
Moreover,
\begin{equation}
  \sup_{\Lambda\ge1}\Lambda^{|\alpha|}
  \|\partial^\alpha m_\Lambda\|_{L^\infty}<\infty
  \quad\text{for every multi-index }\alpha,
  \qquad
  m_\Lambda(\xi)\longrightarrow1
  \quad(\xi\in\R^3).
\end{equation}
No radiality, monotonicity, or nesting is imposed.  A fixed-profile family is
given by $m_\Lambda(\xi)=m(\xi/\Lambda)$ for a real even
$m\in C_c^\infty(\R^3)$ that equals one near the origin.  A dyadic
fixed-profile family is indexed by $\Lambda=2^n$, $n\in\N$.  An \emph{admissible cofinal cutoff sequence} is a sequence
$(\pi_{\Lambda_n})_{n\ge1}$ drawn from an admissible family, with
$\Lambda_n\to\infty$.  Statements for a continuous cutoff parameter are
understood sequentially along every admissible cofinal sequence.
title: Admissible spectral cutoffs

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:fd30636d90c2d8612389f68694b6b69959f107b882736340e33392c3e44bf8c4","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/fd/fd30636d90c2d8612389f68694b6b69959f107b882736340e33392c3e44bf8c4.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:bf9d60fd295110c837acc17ffc46fa35cc67c9fc39712881ce89a999e711bd00","bundle_entry_key":"claim-016","bundle_id":"population.adam-corrected-backward-witness-fullrank-mixed-spectrum-006","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"discrete dynamical systems and adaptive optimization","draft":"w706/bundle_006.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:optimization.adam:adam-p-equals-one-fullrank-mixed-spectrum-active-curvature-nontracking","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"T421-W706-016 v3; target1; kind narrowed; proof (unaudited).

STATEMENT
Put lambda_star=13673160/358811. Fix compact intervals

 lambda_h in[H0,H1], lambda_l in[L0,L1],
 lambda_star<H0<=H1<infinity, 0<L0<=L1<38.

There exists delta>0, depending only on these intervals, such that
for EACH fixed eigenvalue pair in these intervals and EACH eta>0,
ordinary separately bias-corrected Adam with beta1=.9,beta2=.999,
epsilon=eta outside sqrt and standard zero moments satisfies

 limsup_t |eta*C_active,t-38|>=delta                     (1)

for Lebesgue-almost every initial position in R^2. The exceptional
null set may depend on the eigenvalues and eta. For fixed eigenvalues,
the conclusion holds simultaneously along any specified countable
eta sequence under any absolutely continuous joint initialization law;
coordinate independence is not assumed.

Hence generic p=1 nontracking holds for EVERY fixed pair
lambda_h>lambda_star and0<lambda_l<38. This extends016v2's fixed
[2000,3000]x[10,20] windows to the entire strict mixed unstable/subcritical
range. It does NOT include lambda_l=38, the neutral high boundary,
or the regime38<lambda_l<lambda_star. No attracting dynamics or time
average is identified. The delta is existential, not computed.

AUDIT / HARDEST PIECE
This is UNAUDITED. It uses012v2's low-cap convergence,015v3's corrected
scalar countable cycle basin and uniform local capture,023v1's direct
zero-work full-path classification, and025v1's Green origin decay.
The difficult standard-initialization cycle countability in015v3
remains an independent audit burden. Unlike021's singular-floor proof,
this proof needs no source potential or closed-relation singular lift:
the scalar high floor rho=1/lambda_h stays strictly positive.

1. NORMALIZATION, BOUNDEDNESS AND THE LOW COORDINATE
For either coordinate let X=x/eta,M=m/(eta*lambda),
V=v/(eta*lambda)^2,rho=1/lambda. The raw scalar map is

 M'=bM+(1-b)X, V'=dV+(1-d)X^2,
 X'=X-M'/(sqrt(V')+rho).                                (2)

Corrected maps have their ordinary separate clock factors. The
elementary absorbing argument in033 Section1 gives uniform tail
bounds |X|,|M|<=802,V<=802^2, after a start-dependent burn-in.
For high rho in[1/H1,1/H0], the corrected maps converge uniformly
on this compact physical box to the continuous map F_rho in(2).
Claim012v2 gives X_l,M_l,V_l->0 since lambda_l<38, regardless of its
standard initial position.

2. A NARROW ACTIVE BAND IMPOSES A CLOSED SCALAR BAND ON THE OMEGA SET
Suppose limsup |A_t-38|<delta, A_t=eta*C_active,t. Eventually its
defined values lie within delta. Multiply this inequality by the
nonnegative active denominator sum_i g_i^2/P_i. At exact zero gradient
times both extended sides are zero. All coefficients are bounded;
the low coordinate vanishes. For any point (X,M,V) of the high
omega-limit K, taking an adjacent-state limit therefore gives

 X^2*|kappa_rho(X,V)-38|<=delta*X^2,
 kappa_rho(X,V)=1/(sqrt(dV+(1-d)X^2)+rho).                (3)

The harmless positive factor1/(sqrt(V')+rho) was canceled when X!=0;
when X=0 both sides of(3) are zero. Thus(3) remains a closed constraint
at zero positions. K is nonempty compact, F_rho(K)=K, and internally
chain transitive for F_rho. To see the latter, follow a late actual
segment between visits near prescribed x,y in K. Actual tail distance
to K and corrected-map distance to F_rho tend to zero. Project each
segment node into K. Uniform continuity of F_rho bounds each chain
error separately, independently of the segment length.

3. UNIFORM SMALL-BAND REDUCTION TO CRITICAL NEIGHBORHOODS
For delta=0, EVERY full F_rho-path in a compact invariant K satisfying
(3) is a bounded full scalar zero-work path. By023 it is an origin or
cycle path, with a=1/38-rho>0. Hence K is contained in the three
critical states; internal chain transitivity forces one critical orbit.

This exact statement gives a uniform near-critical statement on the
compact rho interval. Fix sufficiently small neighborhoods of the
origin and of the two cycle phases, centered continuously in rho.
For all sufficiently small delta, EVERY compact fully invariant
internally chain-transitive K satisfying(3) lies in their union.
Otherwise take delta_n->0, rho_n converging, and offending K_n. A
Hausdorff subsequence gives K in the common physical compact box.
Uniform convergence F_rho_n->F_rho passes full invariance and(3)
to the limit. It also passes internal chain transitivity: project
the nodes of an arbitrarily fine F_rho_n-chain into K and use uniform
continuity to control each new jump, without accumulating errors.
Thus K is one critical orbit. A selected point outside the chosen
neighborhoods persists outside at the limit, a contradiction.

Choose OUTER neighborhoods first, with these properties uniformly
over rho: they are disjoint; a corrected late step with both ends in
their union cannot change orbit groups or select a wrong cycle phase;
cycle neighborhoods are within015v3's uniform physical capture region;
the origin neighborhood is small enough for the uniform Green estimate
in Section4. Uniform continuity at the separated critical states and
compactness give the nonjump conditions. Use INNER half-radius
neighborhoods for the preceding compactness reduction. For delta small
enough, K lies in the inner union; hence the actual tail lies in the
outer union. Nonjump separation makes it eventually stay in the
origin group or the alternating cycle group.

4. THE ORIGIN ALTERNATIVE CONTRADICTS THE ACTIVE BAND
For high lambda in[H0,H1], the limiting position-pair matrix

 A_h=[[1+b-(1-b)*lambda_h,-b],[1,0]]

has real roots -b<r_s<0,r_u<-1. Their gaps from b and the unit circle
are uniform on the compact high interval. Choose
sup |r_s|<q<nu<b. Eigenbases and inverses are uniformly bounded.
The origin neighborhood and late clocks can be chosen so the actual
position-pair coefficients, throughout that neighborhood, are close
enough to A_h for BOTH Green contractions in036 Section2 (weighted
q and bounded weight1). This argument requires only boundedness and
small coefficient perturbations, NOT prior origin convergence.
Consequently a high-coordinate tail staying in this neighborhood has
|X_h,t|<=C*q^t. Stable raw moment and variance recursions then imply
M_h,V_h->0 as well. Thus both coordinates actually approach their origins.

If the standard low initial position is nonzero,025 gives a subsequence
of active sharpness tending to lambda_l<=L1<38. This is incompatible
with an eventual band delta<(38-L1)/2. We may remove the line x_l,0=0
as a null exceptional set; no assertion on that line is needed here.
Thus the origin alternative is excluded for almost every start.

For clarity, the low-coordinate lower-rate estimate can be chosen
uniformly too: the explicit matrix Q in036 Eq10 is positive definite
for fixed nu<b and every low trace T with |T|<=1+b. It obeys
A_l^T Q A_l=nu^2 Q+A_l^T A_l. On compact low parameters its strict
gain margin is uniform, and actual coefficients approach A_l once
the low coordinate decays. This confirms the rate comparison across
the whole stated low interval, including repeated-root parameters.

5. THE CYCLE ALTERNATIVE HAS A NULL STANDARD-INITIALIZATION SET
If the actual high tail stays in the alternating cycle neighborhoods,
015v3's corrected local capture gives convergence to that scalar cycle.
Here rho<=1/H0<rho_star, and015v3 applies uniformly on this compact
range. For fixed eta and lambda_h, its standard initial positions
converging to this corrected cycle form a countable set. Thus full
initial positions reaching this alternative lie on countably many
vertical lines. Together with the removed low-zero line they have
Lebesgue measure zero. No product law or coordinate independence is
needed. Outside this exceptional set, the assumed strict limsup band
is impossible, proving(1).

Active quotients at finite zero-gradient times can be treated either
by the zero extension used in Section2 or by removing their null
initial lines. For fixed finite time, a nonzero scalar standard initial
position maps analytically to its position on either sign half-line:
positive raw variance after the first update makes all subsequent
square roots analytic. The bounded-increment properness estimate
prevents that analytic function from being identically zero. Its
zeros are countable. Hence the countable union of finite-time zero
events is null, and generic trajectories have all their quotients
defined. Along any specified countable eta sequence, union the null
exceptional sets; an absolutely continuous joint law still assigns
zero mass. This gives the stated simultaneous conclusion.

[Defi 24 of arXiv:2608.02103, '$p$-Adic Diffusion and Random Walks on $[0,1]$'] For a step function $w:[0,1] \times [0,1] \rightarrow [0,1]$ define the cut norm as
\[||w||_{\Box}=\sup_{S,T\subset \mathcal{M}([0,1])}\iint_{S\times T} w(x,y)dxdy,\]
Where $\mathcal{M}([0,1])$ denotes the measurable sets of $[0,1]$. The following relations with the $L^{p},L^2$ and $L^{\infty}$norm holds true
\[||w||_{\Box}\leq||w||_{1}\leq||w||_{2}\leq||w||_{\infty} \]
The cut metric is then defined as 
\[\delta_{\Box}(w,u)=\inf_{\phi\in\mathcal{L}}||u(\phi(x),\phi(y))-w(x,y)||_{\Box}\]
where, $\mathcal{L}$ is the space of Lebesgue measurable bijections on the unit interval.

\begin{equation}

[Theorem thm: quadratic interaction random of arXiv:2503.24372, 'A criterion on the free energy for log-Sobolev inequalities in mean-field particle systems'] Let $V(x)=\frac{x^4}{4}-\lambda \frac{x^2}{2}$ ($\lambda\in\R$) or more generally suppose that $V$ satisfies Assumption~(ass_doublewell of the paper). 
Let $T_c$ denote the critical temperature (equation eq_def_beta_c of the paper) of the fully connected mean-field-model $m^{N}_T$ with $W (x,y) = - x y$. 
Let $\bbP_N$ be the uniform measure on random regular graphs $G_N$ in $\{1, \dots , N\}$ with fixed degree $d_N$ at each site or the measure of Erd\"os-R\'enyi graphs with mean degree $d_N$.

Assume either that $\lim_{N\to\infty} d_N=\infty$ in the random regular graph case, 
or that $\lim_{N\to\infty} d_N/\log N= \infty$ in the Erd\"os-R\'enyi case.
Then:

\begin{itemize}
	\item[(i)]
For $T>T_c$, there is a constant $\gamma_T>0$ such that
\begin{align}

&+ (\theta - 1) \int_y^1 {\mathcal B eta}(\mathrm{d}\zeta; 1/2, \theta - 3/2) \left\{ \int_{\sqrt{y/\zeta}}^1 (\zeta x^2 - y)^{\alpha} \mathsf{G}(\mathrm{d} x) + e^{i\alpha\pi} \int_0^{\sqrt{y/\zeta}} (y - \zeta x^2)^{\alpha}

[Definition 3 of arXiv:2605.30560, 'Projected McKean--Vlasov Dynamics for Entropic Weak Optimal Transport'] A map $F:\mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R}^d)\to\mathbb{R}$ admits a
\emph{linear functional derivative} $\delta_m F$ if
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), ref=(\roman*)]
    \item $\delta_m F:\mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R}^d)\times\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ is continuous, and for every $R>0$ there exists $C_R>0$ such that whenever $\int |x|^2 \, \rho(dx) \leq R$
    \begin{align*}
       | \delta_m F(\rho, y)| \leq C_R(1+|y|^2).
    \end{align*}
\item  It satisfies the normalization $\int\delta_m F(\rho)(y)\rho(dy)=0$, \, $\forall \, \rho \in \Pc_2(\R^d)$. 
\item For any $\rho,\rho' \in \Pc(\R^d)$, it holds that
\[
F(\rho')-F(\rho)
\;=\;
\int_0^1\!\!\int \delta_m F\big((1-t)\rho+t\rho'\big)(y)\,(\rho'-\rho)(dy)\,dt.
\]
\end{enumerate}

\[
  H_{2\ell(w_D)+j+1}(\BK_{\mathcal K}(W);\Z).

body:
[Corollary 3 of arXiv:2608.03771, '\vspace{-5ex}\bfseries\scshape{Local law and delocalization for the Sachdev--Ye--Kitaev mo'] Let $\varepsilon_0>0$, $\delta\in(0,\frac{4}{5})$, and let $q$ be even with $2\leqslant q\leqslant N^{\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon_0}.$
For $\tau\in\{\text{Full},+,-\}$, define the spectral form factor
\[
K_{N,\tau}(t)
=
\Eds\left[
\left|
\tr_\tau(\e^{-\i tH_q})
\right|^2
\right].
\]
Let $T$ satisfy $1\leqslant T\leqslant\sqrt{\left(\frac{4}{5}-\delta\right)\log\left(\frac{N}{q^2}\right)}.$
Then there exists $C>0$ such that
\begin{equation}

\sup_{|t|\leqslant T}
\left|
K_{N,\tau}(t)-\e^{-t^2}
\right|
\leqslant
C\left[
\left(
\alpha_{N,q}T^2(1+\log T)
\right)^{\frac{4}{5}}
+
\frac{T^2}{M}
\right]\leqslant
C\left(\frac{q^2}{N}T^2(1+\log T)\right)^{\frac{4}{5}}.
\end{equation}
In particular,
\begin{equation}

\sup_{|t|\leqslant T}
\left|
\frac{K_{N,\tau}(t)}{\e^{-t^2}}-1
\right|
\xrightarrow[N\to\infty]{}0.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Corollary 21 of arXiv:2605.05864, 'Classification and Metrization of Classes of Smooth measures'] Assume that the Dirichlet form $(\form, \dom)$ is transient. The following hold$:$
\begin{itemize}
\item[\sf (1)]
If a smooth measure $\mu$ satisfies $R\mu \in L^\infty(E;m)$ and $\mu(E)<\infty$, then $\mu$ belongs to ${\cal S}_0^{(0)}$.

\item[\sf (2)] {\rm({\it cf.} \cite[Theorem 2.4.2]{FOT11})}
 If $\mu$ is a smooth measure such that $R\mu \in L^\infty(E;m)$, then
$$
\int_E \tilde{u}(x)^2 \mu(dx) \le \| R\mu\|_\infty \form(u,u)<\infty, \quad u \in \dom_e.
$$
In particular, this implies that the embedding $\tilde{\dom}_e \subset L^2(E;\mu)$ is continuous, where $\tilde{\dom}_e$ is the set of all quasi-continuous modifications of functions 
in $\dom_e$.

\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 7 (Baker) of arXiv:2609.02478, 'Improved Weyl bounds on short intervals'] Let $k\ge3$, and suppose that there are integers $r,v_2,\ldots,v_k$ satisfying
\[
  \gcd(r,v_2,\ldots,v_k)=1
\]
and
\begin{equation}
  |r\alpha_j-v_j|
  \le \frac{N^{1-j}}{4k^4}
  \qquad(2\le j\le k).
\end{equation}
If, for some $\eta>0$,
\begin{equation}
  |g_k(\boldsymbol\alpha;N)|\ge A
  >r^{1-1/k}N^\eta,
\end{equation}
then there is an integer $t$ with $1\le t\le2k^2$ such that
\begin{align}
  tr&\le (NA^{-1})^kN^\eta,\\
  t|r\alpha_j-v_j|
  &\le (NA^{-1})^kN^{-j+\eta}
  \qquad(2\le j\le k),\\
  \|tr\alpha_1\|
  &\le (NA^{-1})N^{-1+\eta}.
  
\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lem 22 of arXiv:2608.20552, 'One-point fluctuations for exponential last passage percolation under upper-tail condition'] We call $(\ff_L)_{L>0}$ a \emph{modified Gaussian family} if
\beqq
        \ff_L(z)=e^{L\GG(z)+L^{2/3}\HH(z)+L^{1/3}\KK(z)+\EE_L(z)},
\eeqq
where $\GG$ is the leading phase of a Gaussian family in one of Cases~\textnormal{(a)}-\textnormal{(c)}, $\HH$ and $\KK$ are fixed functions of the form $c_1\log(z+1)+c_2\log z+c_3z$, and $\EE_L$ is as in \eqref{eq:Gaph}. Let $\cp$ be a regular critical point of $\GG$. Then, for every $\epsilon\in(0,1/2)$, there exists $L_0>0$ such that, for all $L>L_0$ and $|w|\le L^{\epsilon/3}$,
\beq
        \ff_L(\cp+wL^{-1/2})=\ff_L(\cp)e^{\frac12\GG''(\cp)w^2+\HH'(\cp)wL^{1/6}}\bigl(1+O(L^{-1/6+\epsilon/3})\bigr).
\eeq
If $\HH'(\cp)=0$ for $\cp=\cp^-$ or $\cp=\cp^+$, the corresponding decay and $L^1$ estimates in Lemma~\ref{lem:asymptotics_f2} remain valid without change. If $\HH'(\cp)\ne0$, then, for every $b\in\R$, the corresponding $L^1$ estimate is replaced by the appropriate bound below:
\beqq
        \|\ff_L\|_{L^1(\cont_-^L(\cp^-+bL^{-1/2}))}\le\frac{Ce^{CL^{1/3}}}{L^{1/2}}|\ff_L(\cp^-)|,\qquad \left\|\frac1{\ff_L}\right\|_{L^1(\cont_+^L(\cp^++bL^{-1/2}))}\le\frac{Ce^{CL^{1/3}}}{L^{1/2}|\ff_L(\cp^+)|}.
\eeqq
The constants may be chosen uniformly when $b$ ranges over a fixed bounded set.

[Proposition prop:twodir of arXiv:2608.30254, 'Exact Recovery Thresholds for Weighted Data Selection\\ in Vector-Valued Linear Regression'] Suppose the atoms take exactly two directions. Then the directions are
antipodal, each class has total weight $\frac12$ and zero conditional mean,
and $C(q)=\frac12(|m_+|^2+|m_-|^2)$ where $m_\pm$ are the conditional means
of the selected weights. Consequently
\[
  \inf_{|\operatorname{supp} q|\le4}C\le\frac E4,\qquad
  \inf_{|\operatorname{supp} q|\le3}C\le\frac{5E}8 ,
\]
and both constants are attained: for six equally weighted atoms with
$z$-values the cube roots of unity over each direction, the three-point
optimum is exactly $\frac{5E}8$ and the four-point optimum exactly
$\frac E4$. Equality at $\frac{5E}8$ forces both classes to have equal
energy, conditional weights $\frac13$ each, and equilateral $z$-triangles of
equal radius. Furthermore, for five-atom two-direction systems the sharp
constant at three points is $\frac47<\frac58$ (attained by an equilateral
triple against an antipodal pair with energy ratio $4{:}3$).

[Definition def:MP-basis of arXiv:2608.12415, 'Sharp Phase Transition for Ellipsoid Fitting'] Fix \(0<\gamma<1\). Let \(\{\mathfrak \mathfrak q_t^{(\gamma)}\}_{t\ge0}\) be the polynomial sequence defined by
\[
    \mathfrak q_0^{(\gamma)}(x)=1,
    \qquad
   \mathfrak q_1^{(\gamma)}(x)=x-1,
\]
and, for \(t\ge1\),
\[
    \mathfrak q_{t+1}^{(\gamma)}(x)
    =
    \bigl(x-(1+\gamma)\bigr)\mathfrak q_t^{(\gamma)}(x)
    -
    \gamma \cdot \mathfrak q_{t-1}^{(\gamma)}(x).
\]
When the dependence on \(\gamma\) is clear, we write \(\mathfrak q_t=\mathfrak q_t^{(\gamma)}\).
title: MP Polynomial Basis

[Theorem 2 of arXiv:2607.26254, 'A Simple Model of Sea Spray'] The sea spray process $\mathcal{S}_t(z)$ is a stationary stochastic process with mean value function,
\begin{align*}
m(z) & = E\left[\mathcal{S}_t(z)\right]\\
& =\tfrac{4}{3}\pi\rho   \int_0^\infty \negthickspace \int_0^\infty r^3_s\, 1_{(0,z]}(z_s(r))\mathcal{F}(dr) ds,
\end{align*}

and covariance function,
\begin{align*}
& \sigma^2(t,z; s, w)  = E(\,[\mathcal{S}_t(z)-m(z)]\cdot [\mathcal{S}_s(w)-m(w]\,)\\
& = \tfrac{16}{9}\pi^2\rho^2 \int_0^\infty \int_0^\infty r^3_{t -s\land t +u} r^3_{s -s\land t +u}\, 1_{(0, z]}(z_{t -s\land t +u}(r))\,1_{(0, w]}(z_{s-s\land t +u}(r))\mathcal{F}(dr) du,
\end{align*}
where $a\land b$ is the smaller of $a$ and $b$ and $1_A$ is the indicator function of the set $A.$ In particular, the equal-time covariance is,
$$
\sigma^2(z,t; w,t) = \tfrac{16}{9}\pi^2\rho^2 \int_0^\infty \int_0^\infty r^6_u\, 1_{(0, z\land w]}(z_u(r))\mathcal{F}(dr) du.
$$

[Proposition 29 of arXiv:2604.03213, 'Asymptotic expansion for transport maps \\ between laws of multimatrix models'] Given the following objects,
	\begin{itemize}
        \item $\cU$ and $\cV$ bases of Hilbert spaces $H_{\cU}$ and $H_{\cV}$,
		\item $Z^N = (Z_i^N)_{1\leq i\leq d}$ deterministic matrices of size $N$,
		\item $X^N = (X_e^N)_{e\in \cU}$ independent GUE random matrices of size $N$,
		\item $x = (x_e)_{e\in \cV}$ free semicircular variables,
		\item $f\in \cL^k(\cB)$ with $\cB$ the basis of $\C^d\oplus H_{\cU}\oplus H_{\cV}$.
	\end{itemize}
	Then if our weights satisfy Assumption \ref{Assum:weight}, with $\cA_N$ the free product of $\M_N(\C)$ and the von Neumann algebra generated by $x$,
    $$ \limsup_{N\to\infty} \E\left[\norm{(Z^N,X^N,x)}_{\cA_N,c}\right] <\infty,$$
    and almost surely $R_N=\norm{(Z^N,X^N,x)}_{\cA_N,c}$ is finite. Finally, for all $M\geq 0$ and $K>0$, there exists a constant $C_{M,K}$ such that for $N>2K$,
    \begin{equation}
        
        \E\left[\norm{f}_{\cC^k,R_N+M}\right] \leq C_{M,K} e^{K\sup_i \norm{Z_i^N}^2} \norm{f}_{\cL^k,K}.
    \end{equation}
title: Proposition 29 of arXiv:2604.03213

[Theorem 4 (\textsf{Simultaneous fixed-chaos martingale core}) of arXiv:2607.28742, '2607.28742'] Fix $p\in[2,\infty)$ and let
\[
  F_j=I_{q_j}(f_j)\in L^p(\Omega),
  \qquad j=1,\ldots,d,
\]
where $d\geq1$, $q_j\geq1$, and
$f_j\in L_s^2(\mu^{q_j})$.  There exist increasing finite-dimensional
subspaces $H_n\subset L^2(\mu)$, their orthogonal projections $P_n$,
and increasing $\s$-algebras
\begin{align}
  \cG_n
  =\sigma\big\{ \eta(A_{n,1}),\ldots,\eta(A_{n,m_n})\big\},
  
\end{align}
where the sets $\{A_{n,k}: 1\leq k \leq m_n\}$ are pairwise disjoint 
with $\mu( A_{n,k})\in(0, \infty)$
such that
\begin{align}
  F_{j,n}
  :=\E[F_j|\cG_n]
  =I_{q_j}\bigl(P_n^{\otimes q_j}f_j\bigr)
  \in\fin_{q_j}.
  
\end{align}
Moreover, for any $j\in\{1, ...,d\}$,
we have
\begin{align}
  F_{j,n}\xrightarrow[\text{in }L^p(\Omega)]{n\to+\infty} F_j.
  
\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: \textsf{Simultaneous fixed-chaos martingale core}

body:
Let F be a probability law on R^d that is n-completely mixable: some coupling X_1,...,X_n of F satisfies X_1+...+X_n=K almost surely for a fixed vector K. For every linear subspace V of R^d, the law of the orthogonal projection P_V X_1 is n-completely mixable on V; its coupling has constant sum P_V K. In particular every one-dimensional projection of a completely mixable vector law is completely mixable. Source: Ruodu Wang, Current Open Questions in Complete Mixability, Proposition 6, Section 2.5, p.16.
d and n are positive integers
F is n-completely mixable on R^d
V is a linear subspace of R^d

[Theorem thm:purestates of arXiv:2602.12595, '\textbf{Michel Talagrand and the Rigorous Theory of Mean Field Spin Glasses}'] Assume the extended Ghirlanda--Guerra identities hold and the limiting overlap distribution \(\pi\) has an atom
\(\pi(\{q^{\ast}\})=a>0\) at its maximal point \(q^{\ast}\).
Then there exist disjoint random sets \(A_1,A_2,\dots\subset \Sigma_N\) such that:
\begin{enumerate}
\item The weight sequence \(\big(G_N(A_k)\big)_{k\ge 1}\) converges in distribution to a Poisson--Dirichlet law \(\mathrm{PD}(1-a)\).
\item Within each \(A_k\), overlaps concentrate near \(q^{\ast}\): for every \(\varepsilon>0\), for large \(N\), with high probability,
\[
\int_{A_k\times A_k} |R_{1,2}-q^{\ast}|\,\,\mathrm{d} G_N(\sigma^1)\,\mathrm{d} G_N(\sigma^2)
\le \varepsilon\,G_N(A_k)^2.
\]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Lemma 34 (Finite-dimensional inverse for the negative raw branch) of arXiv:2607.04138, 'Hives from deformed GUE minor processes'] \lab{lem:double-moment-inverse}
Let \(X,Y,Z,W>0\) satisfy
\begin{equation}\lab{eq:inverse-moment-region}
 X+Y+Z<W<(\sqrt X+\sqrt Y+\sqrt Z)^2.
\end{equation}
There are unique \(S,A,B,D>0\) such that
\begin{align}
 X&=A+\frac{A^2}{S},&
 Y&=B+\frac{B^2}{S},&
 Z&=D+\frac{D^2}{S},\lab{eq:inverse-three-moments}\\
 W&=A+B+D+\frac{(A+B+D)^2}{S}.\lab{eq:inverse-fourth-moment}
\end{align}
Consequently, \(T=-S\) and \(F=-(S+A+B+D)\) give the unique solution
of these moment equations in the raw-parameter branch \(T<0\), \(F<0\).
The scalar equation determining \(S\) has a nonvanishing derivative at its
root.

Moreover, let \(w,w'>0\), let \(u,u'>0\), and suppose
\[
 a^2=w^2+u^2,\qquad b^2=(w')^2+(u')^2,\qquad
 \theta=\frac{u}{w^2}=\frac{u'}{(w')^2}.
\]
If
\begin{align*}
 X_n&=a^2n,&Y_n&=b^2n,\\
 Q_n&=n^{21}+O(n^{20}),\\

[Definition def:sections of arXiv:2411.07157, 'Rough differential equations in the flow approach'] Given $\tau \in \mathfrak{T}$, we define $\text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\tau] \subset \prod_{\underline{\tau} \in \tau} \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\underline{\tau}]$ 
by setting 
\begin{equs}
\text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\tau]
\eqdef
\big\{ 
\big(F_{\underline{\tau}}\in \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\underline{\tau}] : \underline{\tau} \in \tau\big): \enskip 
\forall \underline{\tau}, \underline{\tau}' \in \tau\;\text{and}\; f \in \mathrm{Iso}(\underline{\tau},\underline{\tau}')\,,\; \mathbf{f} F_{\underline{\tau}} =  F_{\underline{\tau}'}
\big\}\,.
\end{equs}
We define $\text{${\mcb{C}}$}[\tau]\subset \prod_{\underline{\tau} \in \tau} \text{${\mcb{C}}$}[\underline{\tau}]$ analogously. 

Moreover, for $\underline{\tau} \in \tau \in \mathfrak{T}$, let $\iota_{\tau,\underline{\tau}}: \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\tau] \rightarrow \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\underline{\tau}]$ be the ``fiber'' map $\big(F_{\underline{\tau}'}\in\mathcal{H}^{\underline{\tau}'} : \underline{\tau}' \in \tau\big) \mapsto F_{\underline{\tau}}$. 
Observe that $\iota_{\tau,\underline{\tau}}$ has a left inverse given by the ``section'' map $\pi_{\tau,\underline{\tau}}: \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\underline{\tau}] \rightarrow \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\tau]$ defined by setting
\[
\text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\underline{\tau}]\ni F_{\underline{\tau}}\mapsto\pi_{\tau,\underline{\tau}}F_{\underline{\tau}}\eqdef\Big(\frac{1}{|\mathrm{Iso}(\underline{\tau},\underline{\tau}')|}
\sum_{f \in \mathrm{Iso}(\underline{\tau},\underline{\tau}')} \text{$\mathbf{f}$} F_{\underline{\tau}} : \underline{\tau}'\in\tau\Big)\in \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\tau]
\,.
\] 
We use the same notation for the analogous maps between $\text{${\mcb{C}}$}[\underline{\tau}]$ and $\text{${\mcb{C}}$}[\tau]$. 

Note that $|\mathrm{Iso}(\underline{\tau},\underline{\tau}')|$ actually does not depend on the choice of $\underline{\tau},\underline{\tau}'\in\tau$. In the sequel, we therefore just write $|\mathrm{Aut}(\tau)|\eqdef |\mathrm{Aut}(\underline{\tau})|$ for any $\underline{\tau}\in\tau$.

Finally, for $\underline{\tau} \in \tau$ we sometimes write $\iota_{\underline{\tau}} \eqdef \iota_{\tau,\underline{\tau}}$ and $\pi_{\underline{\tau}} \eqdef \pi_{\tau,\underline{\tau}}$ to lighten subscripts.

[Proposition 8 of arXiv:2607.21062, 'A new probabilistic approach for\\ mean field games of optimal stopping'] Suppose that Assumptions \ref{assumption:1A} and \ref{assumption:1B} hold. Let $L,L'\in\mathcal V$. Consider the corresponding solutions $X,X'\in\mathbb S^2$ of equation \eqref{MFG SDE} and $(Y,Z,A),$ $(Y',Z',A')\in\mathbb S^2\times\mathbb H^2\times\mathbb A^2$ of equation \eqref{RBSDE}, respectively. Then, there exists a constant $c$, depending only on $X_0$, $T$, $K$, $\phi$, such that
    \begin{align}
    &\mathbb E\bigg[\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}|\Delta Y_t|^2 + \int_0^T |\Delta Z_t|^2dt + \sup_{0\leq t\leq T}|\Delta A_t|^2\bigg] \notag \\
    &\leq c\,\mathbb E\bigg[\int_0^T\big|f(t,X_t,\mathbb E[\bar f(t,X_t)L_t]) - f(t,X_t',\mathbb E[\bar f(t,X_t)L_t])\big|^2dt\bigg] \\
    &\quad+ c\int_0^T\big|\mathbb E[\bar f(t,X_t)L_t] - \mathbb E[\bar f(t,X_t')L_t']\big|^2dt + c\,\mathbb E\big[|\xi_T-\tilde\xi_T'|^2\big] + c\sqrt{\mathbb E\Big[\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}|\xi_t-\tilde\xi_t'|^2\Big]} \notag \\
    &\quad+ c\bigg|\mathbb E\bigg[\int_{0^-}^T\phi(T-s)dL_s\bigg] - \mathbb E\bigg[\int_{0^-}^T\phi(T-s)dL_s'\bigg]\bigg|^2 \notag \\
    &\quad+ c\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}\bigg|\mathbb E\bigg[\int_{0^-}^T\phi(t-s)dL_s\bigg] - \mathbb E\bigg[\int_{0^-}^T\phi(t-s)dL_s'\bigg]\bigg|, \notag
    \end{align}
    where $\Delta Y_t=Y_t-Y_t'$, $\Delta Z_t=Z_t-Z_t'$, $\Delta A_t=A_t-A_t'$, $\xi_t=h(t,X_t,\mathbb E[\int_{0^-}^T\phi(t-s)dL_s])$, $\tilde\xi_t'=h(t,X_t',\mathbb E[\int_{0^-}^T\phi(t-s)dL_s])$, for every $t\in[0,T]$.

body: In mathematical analysis, Lipschitz continuity is a regularity property of functions between metric spaces that is stronger than uniform continuity, and hence also stronger than continuity. Intuitively, a Lipschitz continuous function is limited in how fast it can change: there exists a real number such that, for every pair of points on the graph of this function, the absolute value of the slope of the line connecting them is not greater than this real number; the smallest such bound is called the Lipschitz constant of the function. For instance, every function that is defined on an interval and has a bounded first derivative is Lipschitz continuous.

body:
Own work, proof draft UNAUDITED; novelty unestablished. Let N,P>=2 and M>=1 be integers. Independent factor arrays U and V
have iid centered real entries of variance one within each array,
with finite fourth moments u4=E u^4 and v4=E v^4. No symmetry or
vanishing third moment is assumed. Let Z be independent standard
Gaussian noise, X=UV^T/sqrt(N), Y=sqrt(s)X+Z, and d=NP. Define

 beta=M/N, c=(N-1)(P-1)/N^2,
 a=(N+u4-3)/N, b=(P+v4-3)/N, v(s)=1+beta s,
 Q(s)=v(s)^3+beta(a+b)v(s)s^2+beta*a*b*s^3,
 D(s)=v(s)^2 Q(s),
 i_N(s)=I(X;Y)/d, B_N(s)=log(v(s))/2-i_N(s),
 m_N(s)=E||X-E[X|Y]||F^2/d, g(s)=beta/v(s).

Since u4,v4>=1, a,b>=0. For every s>=0,

 g(s)-m_N(s)>=beta^2 c s^3/D(s),                      (1)
 B_N(s)>=(beta^2 c/2) integral_0^s t^3/D(t) dt
       >=beta^2 c s^4/[8 D(s)].                      (2)

An explicit one-sided quartic remainder, for 0<=s<=1, is

 B_N(s)>=beta^2 c s^4/8-beta^2 c C_N s^5/10,
 C_N=D(1)-1.                                         (3)

These are finite-dimensional inequalities, not formal expansions.
With bounded positive aspect ratios, C_N is bounded uniformly for
fixed factor fourth moments. If P/N->alpha>0, M/N->beta0>0, then
every limiting information function satisfies

 log(1+beta0 s)/2-i(s)
 >=alpha beta0^2 s^4/[8 D_infty(s)],
 D_infty(s)=(1+beta0 s)^2[(1+beta0 s)^3
       +beta0(1+alpha)(1+beta0 s)s^2+beta0 alpha s^3].  (4)

Consequently the lower limiting quartic coefficient is at least
alpha beta0^2/8. No matching upper coefficient is proved here.

Claim w718-T287-038 v2, Target1 partial result, proof (unaudited).
Novelty unestablished. This proves the one-sided quartic bound, not
the requested sharp two-sided quartic expansion.

Prior-work scope: Semerjian, arXiv:2402.16719v2, abstract, treats
symmetric orthogonally invariant matrix denoising and conjectures
an extension beyond that class. Its Eq(108) gives scalar cubic
polynomial-estimator normal equations. Polynomial least squares
is therefore not a new method here. The finite-N rectangular UV^T
identity and its conditioned-mixture KL consequence are written
out separately below; absence of an identical literature bound
has not been established.

## 1. Statement and exact finite-size constants

Let N,P>=2 and M>=1 be integers. Independent factor arrays U and V
have iid centered real entries of variance one within each array,
with finite fourth moments u4=E u^4 and v4=E v^4. No symmetry or
vanishing third moment is assumed. Let Z be independent standard
Gaussian noise, X=UV^T/sqrt(N), Y=sqrt(s)X+Z, and d=NP. Define

 beta=M/N, c=(N-1)(P-1)/N^2,
 a=(N+u4-3)/N, b=(P+v4-3)/N, v(s)=1+beta s,
 Q(s)=v(s)^3+beta(a+b)v(s)s^2+beta*a*b*s^3,
 D(s)=v(s)^2 Q(s),
 i_N(s)=I(X;Y)/d, B_N(s)=log(v(s))/2-i_N(s),
 m_N(s)=E||X-E[X|Y]||F^2/d, g(s)=beta/v(s).

Since u4,v4>=1, a,b>=0. For every s>=0,

 g(s)-m_N(s)>=beta^2 c s^3/D(s),                      (1)
 B_N(s)>=(beta^2 c/2) integral_0^s t^3/D(t) dt
       >=beta^2 c s^4/[8 D(s)].                      (2)

An explicit one-sided quartic remainder, for 0<=s<=1, is

 B_N(s)>=beta^2 c s^4/8-beta^2 c C_N s^5/10,
 C_N=D(1)-1.                                         (3)

These are finite-dimensional inequalities, not formal expansions.
With bounded positive aspect ratios, C_N is bounded uniformly for
fixed factor fourth moments. If P/N->alpha>0, M/N->beta0>0, then
every limiting information function satisfies

 log(1+beta0 s)/2-i(s)
 >=alpha beta0^2 s^4/[8 D_infty(s)],
 D_infty(s)=(1+beta0 s)^2[(1+beta0 s)^3
       +beta0(1+alpha)(1+beta0 s)s^2+beta0 alpha s^3].  (4)

Consequently the lower limiting quartic coefficient is at least
alpha beta0^2/8. No matching upper coefficient is proved here.

## 2. A leave-one-out cubic statistic and its exact norm

For a matrix y define

 tau_ij(y)=(1/N) sum_(k!=i,l!=j) y_il y_kj y_kl.

The omitted row/column coincidences ensure
partial_(y_ij) tau_ij=0, hence div tau=0. All terms in
E||tau(Y)||^2 have at most fourth powers of any individual factor
entry: across two three-edge L-shapes every row and column occurs
at most four times. Thus finite fourth moments, not sixth moments
of u or v, suffice for the integrations below.

The exact sixth mixed-moment identity is

 E||tau(Y)||^2/d=c Q(s).                              (5)

Here is a direct derivation. Fix i,j, and classify the two triples
in tau_ij^2 according to whether k=k' and l=l'. Divide their counts
by (N-1)(P-1). The relative counts are respectively

 1, P-2, N-2, (N-2)(P-2).

For the pure-signal sixfold products in these four cases, the
expectations are, in the same order,

 beta^3+beta^2(u4+v4-2)/N+beta(u4-1)(v4-1)/N^2,
 beta^2/N+beta(u4-1)/N^2,
 beta^2/N+beta(v4-1)/N^2,
 beta/N^2.                                           (6)

To verify each expression, expand hidden indices, partition the six
positions according to their equal hidden index, and use independence
of factor entries. A block with a singleton row or column vanishes
by centering. Every surviving row/column multiplicity is two or four;
the number of assignments to r distinct hidden blocks is (M)_r.
This proves (6) without presuming Gaussian or symmetric entries.

For mixed Gaussian-noise terms, only identical matrix positions can
pair, and each position occurs at most twice. The coefficients of
s^0,s^1,s^2,s^3 in (5), after division by c, are respectively

 1,
 3 beta,
 3 beta^2+beta(a+b),
 beta(beta+a)(beta+b).

The last line follows from (6); the s^2 line also includes one
noise pair times the four-corner rectangle moment beta/N in the
same-k/different-l and different-k/same-l cases. Expanding Q gives
exactly these four coefficients.

The independent finite verifier enumerates all hidden-index
partitions and all eligible Gaussian noise pairings, then clears
denominators by N^5 and compares every integer polynomial
coefficient in N,P,M,u4,v4. This is a formal coefficient identity,
not evidence from substitutions. See scripts/certify_rectangle_sixth_moment.py
and logs/rectangle_sixth_moment_certificate.json. It certifies only
the finite moment algebra.

## 3. Direct polynomial-estimator proof of the risk bound

The initially derived score projection has an equivalent elementary
proof that removes any need for score integration by parts. The
centered output covariance is v(s) I_d. Put

 l(Y)=sqrt(s)beta Y/v(s).

Its risk is g(s). The exact four-corner rectangle moments give

 E[X dot tau(Y)]/d=beta c s^(3/2),
 E[Y dot tau(Y)]/d=beta c s^2,
 E[(X-l(Y)) dot tau(Y)]/d=beta c s^(3/2)/v(s).         (7)

Indeed for distinct i,k and j,l,
E[X_ij X_il X_kj X_kl]=beta/N. The four factors use each row
and each column twice, so only a common hidden index survives.
In the first line of (7), all three Y factors must supply their
signal part; in the second line all four must do so. Noise terms
vanish because the matrix positions are distinct. These are finite
sums of absolutely integrable terms; no Fubini or limiting argument
is required. Cauchy-Schwarz also gives integrability directly from
the finite second moments of X,Y and the finite norm (5).

Consider the explicit degree-three estimator

 Xhat(Y)=l(Y)+b_s tau(Y),
 b_s=beta s^(3/2)/[v(s)Q(s)].

Expanding its squared error using (5) and (7) yields exactly

 E||X-Xhat(Y)||^2/d=g(s)-beta^2 c s^3/D(s).            (8)

The Bayes conditional mean minimizes squared error among measurable
estimators. Therefore m_N(s) is at most (8), proving (1). This
direction supplies a KL lower bound after I-MMSE; it cannot give
the matching upper bound. No regularity theorem for a Gaussian
mixture density is used in this direct proof.

## 4. Integrating the risk improvement with an explicit remainder

I-MMSE for finite-second-moment inputs gives
B_N'(s)=[g(s)-m_N(s)]/2 and B_N(0)=0. Integrating (1) proves the
first bound in (2). D has nonnegative polynomial coefficients and
D(0)=1, so D(t)<=D(s) for 0<=t<=s. This proves the second bound.

For 0<=t<=1, D(t)-1<=t[D(1)-1]=C_N t. Since D(t)>=1,
1/D(t)>=1-[D(t)-1]>=1-C_N t. Integrate t^3(1-C_N t) to obtain
(3), including its denominators8 and10. No inequality involving
the derivative of a pointwise information bound is being asserted.

For convergent positive aspects, a->1,b->alpha,c->alpha. Passing
through the explicit finite inequalities gives (4), without
interchanging SNR differentiation with the dimension limit.

## 5. The conditioned Gaussian mixture requested in NEXT

Specialize to sub-Gaussian U and Gaussian V as in034. Condition U
on E={||U||op<=L sqrt(N)} and call the resulting output density p_E.
Let q_v=N(0,v(s)I_d). Define the normalized conditioned KL
K_E,N(s)=D(p_E||q_v)/d. Retain034's explicit q_N,J,delta_N and set

 H_N(s)=sqrt(s)delta_N+s[beta_*q_N+J sqrt(q_N)]/v(s).

The exact conditional trace/entropy identity and034's paid coupling
and energy errors give

 |K_E,N(s)-B_N(s)|<=H_N(s).

Therefore (2) gives the explicit conditioned-mixture lower bound

 K_E,N(s)>=beta^2 c s^4/[8D(s)]-H_N(s).              (9)

Meanwhile034 gives only K_E,N(s)<=A s^4+2q_N/(NP). Thus the
lower coefficient in the limiting mixture is alpha beta0^2/8;
the upper coefficient is not yet matched. The conditioning error
vanishes exponentially with N at each fixed positive SNR and was
not discarded as a mere small event probability.

## 6. Exact remaining obstruction: a nonlinear projection residual

Let l(Y)=sqrt(s)beta Y/v(s) and

 b_s=beta s^(3/2)/[v(s)Q(s)],
 R_N(s)=E||E[X|Y]-l(Y)-b_s tau(Y)||^2/d.

Equation(7) implies that the bracketed residual is orthogonal to
tau in L^2. Consequently, for s>0, the exact decomposition is

 g(s)-m_N(s)=beta^2 c s^3/D(s)+R_N(s), R_N(s)>=0,
 B_N(s)=(beta^2 c/2) integral_0^s t^3/D(t)dt
                  +(1/2) integral_0^s R_N(t)dt.      (10)

No claim is made that tau is itself orthogonal to the linear
observations. Orthogonality to tau in this single projection is
enough for (10); the residual includes any needed linear cancellation.

To finish a limiting sharp quartic expansion one must additionally
prove that the limiting upper envelope of the integrated residual
is o(s^4). For an explicit O(s^5) remainder, a sufficient NEW input
would be R_N(t)<=epsilon_N t^2+C t^4 for a dimension-independent C
and epsilon_N->0, on a fixed SNR interval. Neither034's second
moment bound nor032's nonuniform finite Taylor bound proves this.
This residual estimate is the FIRST unproved step in extending
the present argument to the full requested quartic expansion.

Least trusted new steps for independent review: the sixth mixed
moment algebra and its finite-fourth-moment scope, followed by the
conditioning transfer in (9). The direct proof needs no score
integration by parts. All analytic steps remain independently

body: [Abstract of arXiv:2609.03532, 'Airy limit for the Jack process and topological expansion'] For every $\beta>0$, we establish multi-time soft-edge moment convergence for the Jack--Plancherel process, a discrete $\beta$-analogue of Dyson Brownian motion. The limiting moments admit an absolutely convergent expansion in terms of nonnegative Brownian bridges decorated by pairs of equal and opposite jumps. At equal times, we identify this limit with the joint Laplace statistics of the Airy$_\beta$ process for $\beta\geq1$. The same Brownian expansion yields an asymptotic $\beta$-topological expansion of the marginal $b$-conjecture and, at $\beta=2$, an explicit nonnegative formula for the Witten--Kontsevich intersection numbers.
title: Abstract of arXiv:2609.03532: Airy limit for the Jack process and topological expansion

		$c,C>0$ and $t_0<\infty$, depending only on
		$d,\nu_0,\theta_0,K_0$, such that every mean-zero i.i.d.\ field satisfying
		\[
			\Var(\zeta(0))\geq\nu_0^2,
			\qquad
			\mathbb{E} e^{\theta_0|\zeta(0)|}\leq K_0
		\]
		satisfies, for every $t\geq t_0$,
		\begin{equation}
			\mathbb{E} u_t(0)\geq c(\log t)^{2/d}.

			Moreover, for every $x\in\mathbb{Z}^d$, $t\geq0$, and $s\geq0$,
			\begin{equation}
				\mathbb{P}\left(|u_t(x)-\mathbb{E} u_t(0)|\geq s\right)
				\leq C\exp\{-c\min(s^2,s)\}\, .
			\end{equation}
			Consequently, for every fixed $x\in\mathbb{Z}^d$,
			\[
				\frac{u_t(x)}{\mathbb{E} u_t(0)}\longrightarrow1
				\qquad\textup{in $L^2$ and almost surely}\, .
			\]

[Theo 10 (Marton's Gaussian concentration bound) of arXiv:2602.14618, 'Finitary coding and Gaussian concentration\\ for random fields'] \leavevmode\\
Let $X=(X_i)_{i\in\Zd}$ be an i.i.d. random field where the $X_i$ take values in a standard Borel space $A$. 
Let $g:A^{\Zd}\to\mathbb{R}$ be a local function.
Assume there are measurable functions $c_i:A^{\dep(g)}\to [0,+\infty)$, $i\in\dep(g)$, such that for all $x,x'\in A^{\Zd}$
\begin{equation}
\big|\, g(x)-g(x')\big|\leq \sum_{i\,\in\dep(g)} c_i(x)\, \1_{\{x_i\neq x'_i\}}.
\end{equation}
Then  
\begin{equation}
\log\E\!\left[\e^{\lambda (g(X)-\E[g(X)])}\right]\leq 
\frac{\lambda^2}{2} \sum_{i\in\dep(g)} \E\big( c_i^2(X)\big),
\quad\forall \lambda>0.    
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Marton's Gaussian concentration bound

body: For observed data x under two hypotheses, the likelihood ratio is Lambda(x) = L(theta_0; x) / L(theta_1; x), the ratio of the likelihood under the null to that under the alternative. The Neyman-Pearson lemma shows that the most powerful test of a simple null against a simple alternative at a given size rejects exactly when Lambda is below a threshold. A family with monotone likelihood ratio in a statistic T admits uniformly most powerful one-sided tests, and the generalized likelihood-ratio statistic -2 log Lambda has an asymptotic chi-squared distribution (Wilks' theorem).
title: Likelihood Ratio

body:
[Theorem thm:backward_flow_SDE of arXiv:2606.12143, 'Continuous stochastic flows driven by white noise and their duals'] Suppose that $(\sigma,b)$ satisfy Assumption~(assu:H of the paper) and conditions~(item:1a of the paper)--(item:1d of the paper), and let $\mathcal S$ be the associated stochastic flow. Then, for any $(a,r) \in {\mathbb R}^2$, $\mathcal S^*_{-r,-\cdot}(a)$ is the almost sure unique strong solution to
\begin{align}
    \nonumber \mathcal S^*_{-r,-x}(a) 
    = a 
  &- \int_r^x\!\! \int_{{\mathbb R}} \sigma\big( \mathcal S^*_{-r,-u}(a), -u, s \big) \mathcal W^*(\ensuremath{\mathrm{d}} s, \ensuremath{\mathrm{d}} u) 
  - \int_r^x b\big( \mathcal S^*_{-r,-u}(a), -u \big) \ensuremath{\mathrm{d}} u \\
  &
  + \frac{1}{2} \int_r^x 
   \partial_x \bar\sigma \big( \mathcal S^*_{-r,-u}(a), -u \big) \ensuremath{\mathrm{d}} u, 
  \qquad x \ge r,
\end{align}
where $\mathcal W^*$ is the image of $\mathcal W$ under the map $(a, r) \mapsto(a,-r)$. Moreover, the collection
$\{(\mathcal S^*_{-r,-x}(a),\, x \ge r)\}_{(a,r) \in {\mathbb R}^2}$ forms a stochastic flow. In particular, $(\mathcal S^*)^*=\mathcal S$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm:backward_flow_SDE of arXiv:2606.12143

$$
\alpha_i(s) = \mathrm E[\alpha^-(x,K)|S=s] = \sum_{k=0}^n \alpha^-(x,k)\pi_K'(k|s).
$$
If $s_i=1$, then $x\in\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}$ and
$$
\alpha_i(s) = \mathrm E[\alpha^+(x,K)|S=s] = \sum_{k=0}^n \alpha^+(x,k)\pi_K'(k|s).
$$

[Definition of arXiv:2411.10296, 'Parking on a random rooted binary tree'] We say that a subset $t \subseteq \mathds{V}$ is a \emph{rooted binary tree} if
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $\emptyset \in t$
        \item $v \in t \implies p(v) \in t$
        \item for every $v \in t$, there exists $0 \leq c(v) \leq 2$ such that if $c(v)= 0$ then $v1, v2 \notin t$, and if $c(v) > 0$ then $vi \in t$ if and only if $1 \leq i \leq c(v)$.
    \end{enumerate}
We take the edges of $t$ to be directed from $v$ to $p(v)$.
title: Unnumbered definition of arXiv:2411.10296, 'Parking on a random rooted binary tree'

[Lemma 11 of arXiv:2609.02826, '2609.02826'] Let $R$ be a discrete valuation ring and let $S=\Spec R$.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item A separated group algebraic space locally of finite presentation over
  $S$ is a scheme.  If it is proper and flat over $S$, then it is projective
  over $S$.
  \item A flat finitely presented $S$-group scheme is Cohen--Macaulay.
\end{enumerate}

CAMPAIGN RESULT [independently checked proof; E0095-BIP v1; no novelty claim]. Let G be a finite connected bipartite unweighted d-regular graph, d>=2, with both bipartition classes of even size and lambda_2(L_G)>=2. Among perfect matchings of new edges, the optimal non-lazy absolute SRW gap on the (d+1)-regular augmentation is 2/(d+1). A matching attains it if and only if every matching edge lies within a bipartition class. This includes Q_d for d>=2 and K_{m,m} for even m>=2. It does not assert total-variation mixing-time optimality, and the spectral threshold is needed for the sufficiency argument.

[Lemma dyson_bm_monotonic of arXiv:2411.17827, 'Ordered random walks and the Airy line ensemble'] Suppose $(Y_1, \ldots, Y_d)$ and $(Z_1, \ldots, Z_d)$
are coupled Dyson Brownian motions run with the same Brownian motions as described above started from $y_1 \leq \ldots \leq y_d$ and $z_1 \leq \ldots \leq z_d$ respectively.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item Suppose that $y_j \geq z_j$ for all $ j = 1, \ldots, d$. 
Then, for all $t \geq 0$ we have that $Y_j(t)\geq Z_j(t)$ for all $j = 1, \ldots, d$.
    \item Suppose that $y_j - y_i \geq z_j - z_i$ for all $1 \leq i < j \leq d$. 
Then, for all $t \geq 0$ we have that $Y_j(t) - Y_i(t) \geq Z_j(t) - Z_i(t)$ for all $1 \leq i < j \leq d.$
\end{enumerate}

body:
Consider i.i.d. first-passage percolation on Z^d with weight law F. EXISTENCE of a finite geodesic between every pair of vertices, almost surely and simultaneously over all pairs, is known in each of the following cases, and the case division matters. (a) d = 2 and F ARBITRARY: Wierman and Reh proved that for any passage time distribution, with probability one there is a geodesic between any two points of Z^2. (b) Any d, with F(0) < p_c(d): existence follows from standard subcritical estimates. (c) Any d, with F(0) > p_c(d) and E[tau_e] < infinity: existence was proved by Zhang. (d) The remaining case F(0) = p_c(d) with d > 2 is STILL UNRESOLVED in general, though existence is known for distributions with F(0) = F(delta) = p_c for some delta > 0 in sufficiently high dimensions. So it is WRONG to say that geodesics need F(0) < p_c; that condition is sufficient and convenient, not necessary, and supercritical zero-weight percolation does not by itself destroy existence. UNIQUENESS is a separate matter: a continuous F is a SUFFICIENT condition for the model to be uniquely geodesic, since two distinct finite paths then have equal passage time with probability zero and there are countably many pairs of paths. With atoms - a two-valued weight law, say - ties are genuine and multiple geodesics occur with positive probability. All of the above is about FINITE geodesics; the existence, direction, uniqueness and coalescence of semi-infinite geodesics is a separate and largely open subject whose known results require differentiability or curvature assumptions on the limit shape. [Wierman and Reh (1978); Kesten, Aspects of First Passage Percolation, (9.23); Zhang; verified against Auffinger, Damron and Hanson, 50 Years of First-Passage Percolation, Section 4.1]
i.i.d. nonnegative weights on Z^d
existence holds in case (a) d=2 with no hypothesis, case (b) F(0) < p_c, case (c) F(0) > p_c with E tau_e < infinity; case (d) F(0) = p_c with d > 2 is OPEN
F continuous is a SUFFICIENT condition for uniqueness
the statement is about FINITE geodesics only

body:
[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] Given a graph $X$, with adjacency matrix $d\in M_N(0,1)$, and with a distinguished vertex $*$, the number $L_k$ of loops of length $k$ based at $*$ is given by:
$$L_k=(d^k)_{**}$$
When writing $d=U\lambda U^{-1}$ with $U\in O_N$ and $\lambda=diag(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_N)$ with $\lambda_i\in\mathbb R$, we have
$$L_k=\sum_iU_{*i}^2\lambda_i^k$$
and the real probability measure $\mu$ having these numbers as moments is given by
$$\mu=\sum_iU_{*i}^2\delta_{\lambda_i}$$
with the delta symbols standing as usual for Dirac masses.

[Definition 1 (Fractional Sobolev spaces, \cite{MR1893308}) of arXiv:2607.23548, '\textbf{A CIR-Type Diffusion Driven by Hermite Processes:\\ Well-Posedness, Positivity and'] Let $\alpha \in \bigl(0, \tfrac{1}{2}\bigr)$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
  \item $W_1^\alpha(0,T;\mathbb{R})$ is the space of measurable
        functions $f:[0,T]\to\mathbb{R}$ with
        \[
        \|f\|_{\alpha,1}
        := \sup_{t\in[0,T]}\!\left(|f(t)|
        + \int_0^t \frac{|f(t)-f(s)|}{|t-s|^{\alpha+1}}\,ds\right)
        < \infty.
        \]

  \item $W_2^{1-\alpha}(0,T;\mathbb{R})$ is the space of measurable
        functions $\varphi:[0,T]\to\mathbb{R}$ with
        \[
        \|\varphi\|_{1-\alpha,2}
        := \sup_{0\le s<t\le T}\!\left(
        \frac{|\varphi(t)-\varphi(s)|}{(t-s)^{1-\alpha}}
        + \int_s^t \frac{|\varphi(\tau)-\varphi(s)|}{(\tau-s)^{2-\alpha}}
        \,d\tau\right) < \infty.
        \]
\end{enumerate}
There hold the continuous embeddings, for every
$\beta\in(0,H-\tfrac{1}{2})$ and $\gamma\in(0,\beta)$,
\[
C^{H-\beta+\gamma}(0,T;\mathbb{R})
\subset W_2^{H-\beta}(0,T;\mathbb{R})
\subset C^{H-\beta}(0,T;\mathbb{R}).
\]
title: Fractional Sobolev spaces, \cite{MR1893308}

[Lemma lem:expectation-taylor of arXiv:2608.23742, 'Second-order fusion asymptotics for $\Sine_\beta$ correlation functions'] Let $d\ge1$, $\gamma>0$, and put $D=d\gamma$. Let $K\subset\mathbb R^d$ be compact. Suppose that real random variables $X,Y,M$ satisfy, for some $p,q$,
\begin{equation}
p>\max\{2,D\},\qquad q>\max\{1,D\},\qquad
2q\left(1-\frac1p\right)>1,
\end{equation}
and $X\in L^p$, $Y,M\in L^q$. Suppose, uniformly for $b\in K$ and $1\le j\le d$,
\begin{equation}
U_j(t,b)=tb_jX+\frac{t^2b_j^2}{2}Y+R_j(t,b),
\qquad |R_j(t,b)|\le C_K|t|^3M.
\end{equation}
Then, with
\[
F(u):=\prod_{j=1}^d|1+u_j|^\gamma,
\qquad A(b):=\sum_jb_j,
\qquad B(b):=\sum_jb_j^2,
\]
one has, uniformly for $b\in K$,
\begin{align}
\mathbb E F(U(t,b))
&=1+\gamma tA(b)\mathbb E X\\
&\quad+\frac{t^2}{2}\left\{\gamma B(b)\mathbb E Y+
\left[\gamma(\gamma-1)B(b)+\gamma^2(A(b)^2-B(b))\right]\mathbb E X^2\right\}
+o(t^2).\notag

body:
[Lemma 23 (Cone of influence; pathwise echo decay) of arXiv:2608.15987, 'Threshold cascades of interacting diffusions on unimodular random trees: a conditional bra'] Assume the saturated regime and $\kappa<1$. Couple the true system $s$ and the directed system $\tilde s$ (all back-reaction and non-genealogical couplings replaced by their saturated idealisations) synchronously, edge by edge, using the same Brownian motions. Let $D^{(v)}_t:=s^{(v)}_t-\tilde s^{(v)}_t$. Then, pathwise,
\[
\sup_{t\le\tau}\big|D^{(v)}_t\big|\le\frac{\gamma_{\max}\,\varepsilon(\delta)}{\alpha_{\min}(1-\kappa)}\sum_{u\in S_\tau}\kappa^{d(u,v)},
\]
where $S_\tau$ is the set of vertices failed by time $\tau$ and $d(\cdot,\cdot)$ is graph distance: the influence of an echo source decays geometrically, at rate $\kappa$, in graph distance.
