body:
[Proposition 27 of arXiv:2609.02416, '2609.02416'] Let $\mathcal L\subset(0,\infty)$ be open and assume $\mathrm{(A_{an})}$. Then $\lambda_p(L)=\Lp(\cA_L)$ is real analytic on $\mathcal L$. More precisely, if $v_L(\xi)=\phi_L(L\xi),\qquad -1\le\xi\le1$,
and $v_L(0)=1$, then $L\mapsto v_L$ is real analytic from $\mathcal L$ into $C^1([-1,1])$. After pull-back and a fixed nonzero normalization, the adjoint eigenfunction depends real analytically on $L$ as well.

At every $L_0\in\mathcal L$, writing $h=L-L_0$, one has convergent expansions
\[
\mathscr A_{L_0+h}=\sum_{n=0}^\infty h^n\mathscr A_n,\qquad
\lambda_p(L_0+h)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty h^n\lambda_n,\qquad
v_{L_0+h}=\sum_{n=0}^\infty h^nv_n
\]
in $\mathcal L(C^1,C)$, $\R$ and $C^1([-1,1])$, respectively. The coefficients are determined recursively by
\[
(\mathscr A_0+\lambda_0)v_n+\lambda_nv_0
=-\sum_{k=1}^n\mathscr A_kv_{n-k}
-\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\lambda_kv_{n-k},
\qquad v_n(0)=0,
\]
for $n\ge1$. If $v_0^*$ is the adjoint eigenfunction normalized by $\int_{-1}^{1}v_0v_0^*=1$, then
\[
\lambda_n=-\int_{-1}^{1}v_0^*(\xi)
\left(
\sum_{k=1}^n\mathscr A_kv_{n-k}
+\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\lambda_kv_{n-k}
\right)(\xi)\,d\xi.
\]

body:
[Corollary cor:tailrl-binary-recovery of arXiv:2609.02987, 'Tail Likelihood Reinforcement Learning'] Suppose $r_i\in\{0,1\}$ and let
$M:=\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbf 1\{r_i=1\}$. If $M>0$, then every successful
rollout receives weight $1/M$ and every unsuccessful rollout receives weight
zero. Hence the uncentered TailRL{} estimator reduces to
\begin{equation}
g_{\mathrm{TailRL}}^{(N)}(x)
=
\frac{1}{M}
\sum_{i:r_i=1}S_i,

\end{equation}
which is the MaxRL estimator. After mean-centering, successful rollouts have
weight $1/M-1/N$ and unsuccessful rollouts have weight $-1/N$. If $M=0$,
all uncentered and centered weights are zero.

[Prop w0exist3 of arXiv:2608.30777, 'Inhomogeneous nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation \\ in Fourier-Lebesgue and modulation space'] Let $\phi_{0} \in L^2, \psi\in \widehat{L}^{r}$ and $X_{1}(T)$ be as in  (equation X1(T) of the paper). Denote by  $v_{0}$  the $L^2-$global solution  (as in (equation gwpl2 of the paper)) for initial value $\phi_{0}$.
Then  there exists  a constant $C=C(\alpha,b)>0$ such that  integral equation $$w_{0}= i \mu \int_{0}^{t} e^{i(t-\tau)\partial_x^2}|x|^{-b} G(v_{0} + e^{i\tau\partial_x^2}\psi_{0}, w_{0},0) \, d\tau +  i \mu \int_{0}^{t} e^{i(t-\tau)\partial_x^2}|x|^{-b} G(v_{0}, e^{i\tau\partial_x^2}\psi_{0},0) \, d\tau$$ has a unique solution  $w_{0} \in X_{1}(T)$   provided $T$ satisfying
\begin{align}
    T &\leq 1 \\
    T &\leq C \left( \|\phi_{0}\|_{L^{2}} + \|\psi_{0}\|_{{\widehat{L}^{r}}} \right)^{-\frac{\alpha-1}{\frac{5-\alpha}{4} - \frac{1}{\nu}}} \\
   T &\leq C \left( \|\psi_{0}\|_{\widehat{L}^{r}} \right)^{-\frac{\alpha-1}{\frac{5-\alpha}{4} - \frac{1}{\nu} + \frac{\alpha-1}{q(r)}}}.

body:
[Theorem thm.scfc of arXiv:2606.30517, '\textsc{Convergence towards Ideal Poisson--Voronoi tessellations with a focus on Diestel--'] Let $(E,\mathbf{o},\mu)$ be a proper pointed measured metric space and, for $\lambda >0$, let $X^{(\lambda)}$ be a Poisson point process with intensity measure $\lambda\mu$. Then, $X^{(\lambda)}$ converges weakly (after a suitable shift) to a nontrivial point process $(\Theta_i,\Delta_i)_{i\geq 1}$ in the extended boundary if and only if:
		\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
			\item  the volume function $F$ is log-regularly-varying with positive index (say $b$), and
			\item  the probability measure $F(r)^{-1} \restrict{\mu}{B_r(\mathbf{o})}$, regarded as a probability measure on $\bar E$, converges weakly to a probability measure on $\partial E$ (say $\nu_0$) as $r\to\infty$. 
		\end{enumerate}  
		
		If these conditions hold, then $(\Theta_i)_{i\geq 1}$ are i.i.d.~points on $\partial E$ with distribution $\nu_0$ and $(\Delta_i)_{i\geq 1}$ is an independent Poisson point process on $\mathbb R$ with intensity measure proportional to the measure $\beta$ defined by $\beta((-\infty,r])\coloneqq e^{br}$. If, in addition, the nondegeneracy condition provided just after (def:voronoi of the paper) holds a.s., then the corresponding Poisson--Voronoi diagrams also converge to the Poisson--Voronoi diagram of $(\Theta_i,\Delta_i)_{i\geq 1}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: \textsc{Full Convergence of Nuclei}

[Lemma lem:sector of arXiv:2605.03896, 'Dimer models on astroidal zig-zag graphs'] Let $e\in E(N)$, $\mathsf b\in B(\mathsf G_{c, \mathsf f_0})$ and $\mathsf w\in W(\mathsf G_{c, \mathsf f_0})$.
Assume that one of the following holds:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\operatorname{sign}_{{\mathsf{R}}_\mathsf b}(e)=+$ and $\operatorname{sign}_{{\mathsf{R}}_\mathsf w}(e)=-$.
\item $\operatorname{sign}_{{\mathsf{R}}_\mathsf w}(e)=-$ and $\mathsf b$ lies on $\beta_e$.
\item $\operatorname{sign}_{{\mathsf{R}}_\mathsf b}(e)=+$ and $\mathsf w$ lies on $\beta_e$.
\end{enumerate}
Then $e\subset \mathfrak{N}_{\mathsf b,\mathsf w}$.

[Proposition 8 of arXiv:2607.21374, 'Local structure at the maximum and sharp persistence asymptotics of rough fractional Brown'] Let \(a_n\to\infty\) be any deterministic sequence of positive real numbers.
There exist deterministic dyadic numbers \(h_n\downarrow0\), with
\(h_n\leq a_n\), such that, with
\begin{equation}
  \Delta_n:=\frac{h_n}{a_n},\qquad
  M_n:=\left\lfloor\frac{a_n}{h_n}\right\rfloor,
  \qquad
  \mathcal G_n:=\{j\Delta_n:0\leq j\leq M_n\},
  
\end{equation}
the following holds.  If \(K_n\) is the maximising index of \(B\) on
\(\mathcal G_n\), \(\tau_n=K_n\Delta_n\), and
\begin{equation}
  \Xi_n^{\mathrm{grid}}(t)
  :=a_n^H\bigl(B_{\tau_n+t/a_n}-B_{\tau_n}\bigr),
  
\end{equation}
then
\begin{equation}
  d_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Xi_n^{\mathrm{grid}},\Xi_{a_n})\longrightarrow0
  \quad\text{almost surely}.
  
\end{equation}
Moreover, writing \(T_n=M_n\Delta_n\),
\begin{equation}
  a_n\tau_n\longrightarrow\infty,
  \qquad
  a_n(T_n-\tau_n)\longrightarrow\infty
  \quad\text{almost surely}.
  
\end{equation}

support is $G_r$.  Relative to declared native readers, it is
\emph{coefficient-pure} if the total pushed-forward kernel lies in
\[
 G_r\otimes E_r\otimes\mathbf k\tau_r
\]
for a finite-dimensional label space $E_r$.  A window-pure family is defined
by replacing $D_\infty$ by finite truncations which reproduce the same
singular values on every prescribed finite output window.

[Lemma equivalence des normes of arXiv:2412.00865, 'On the spectral problem and fractional diffusion limit for Fokker-Planck with(-out) drift '] The two norms $\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal{H}_0}$ and $\|\cdot\|_*$ defined by
$$ \| \psi \|_{{\mathcal{H}}_0}^2 := \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \bigg|\nabla_v\bigg(\frac{\psi}{M}\bigg) M \bigg|^2 + \frac{|\psi|^2}{\langle v \rangle^2} \ \mathrm{d} v   \quad \mbox{ and } \quad   \|\psi\|_*^2 := \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \bigg|\nabla_v\bigg(\frac{\psi}{M}\bigg) M \bigg|^2 + V|\psi|^2 \ \mathrm{d} v$$
are equivalent, i.e., there are two positive constants $C_1$ and $C_2$ such that
$$ C_1 \| \psi \|_{\mathcal{H}_0} \leqslant \| \psi \|_* \leqslant C_2 \| \psi \|_{\mathcal{H}_0} , \quad \forall \psi \in \mathcal{H}_0 . $$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

UNPROVED SUFFICIENT INPUT, not a theorem about FPP. For iid Uniform[1,2] undirected nearest-neighbour Z^2 passage times from 0 to n e1, restrict to the exact finite box [-2n,2n]^2. Let H_n and L_n be the threshold kernel and its first-order floor from the finite-product identity. A sufficient route to variance of order n^(2/3) would prove, uniformly in integer n>=1: L_n<=C n^(2/3); H_n(t)-L_n<=C n F(n^(1/3)t) for all t>=0 with nonnegative integrable F; and H_n(t)>=c n for 0<=t<=c' n^(-1/3), for positive constants independent of n. Upper and lower integral bounds then follow by substitution and persistence. All quantitative inputs remain unproved. A qualitative chaos statement, a kernel value only at t=0, or an assumed variance-growth ratio does not supply them. Current full-target openness is UNKNOWN as of this draft.
Exact finite-box reduction for positive bounded edge weights
The named normalized variance identity
Quantitative inputs are a proposed proof obligation, not established hypotheses of the actual model

[Lemma JJKLSX2.3 of arXiv:2506.10448, 'Hitting probabilities and the Ekstr\"om--Persson conjecture'] Let $(X,\rho)$ be a compact $d$-Ahlfors regular metric space. Then, for any $u>0$, there
exists a probability space $(\Xi,\Gamma,\widetilde{\mathbb{P}})$ and, for each $\xi\in\Xi$, a 
compact set $A(\xi)\subseteq X$ such that, for any analytic set $E\subseteq X$, 
\[
\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}(\{\xi\in\Xi\mid A(\xi)\cap E=\emptyset \})=1
\]
if $\dimh E<u$, and 
\[
\Vert \dimh (A(\xi)\cap E) \Vert_{L^{\infty}(\widetilde{\mathbb{P}})}=\dimh E-u
\]
if $\dimh E\geq u$.

body:
For $u_t+Lu\le0$ with $Lu=-a^{ij}u_{x_ix_j}+b^iu_{x_i}+cu$, the identity $\max_{\overline{U_T}}u=\max_{\Gamma_T}u$ requires $c\equiv0$; with $c\ge0$ only the weaker $\max_{\overline{U_T}}u\le\max_{\Gamma_T}u^+$ survives; with $c$ of arbitrary sign even that fails. (a) $c<0$ destroys everything: on $U=(0,\pi)$, $u(x,t)=e^t\sin x$ satisfies $u_t-u_{xx}-2u=0$ (so $c=-2$), has $u=0$ on the lateral sides and $u=\sin x\le1$ at $t=0$, hence $\max_{\Gamma_T}u=1$, yet $u(\pi/2,T)=e^T$ is arbitrarily large. (b) $c\ge0$ genuinely needs the positive part: on $U=(0,\pi)$ let $u$ solve $u_t-u_{xx}+u=0$ with $u\equiv-1$ on $\Gamma_T$ (initial and lateral data $-1$). Then $w=u+1$ solves $w_t-w_{xx}+w=1$ with $w=0$ on $\Gamma_T$, so $w\ge0$ by the $c\ge0$ principle and $w\not\equiv0$; hence $\max_{\overline{U_T}}u>-1=\max_{\Gamma_T}u$, while indeed $\max u\le0=\max_{\Gamma_T}u^+$. (c) What always survives for bounded $c$ of any sign is the comparison principle: $u_t+Lu\le0$ and $u\le0$ on $\Gamma_T$ imply $u\le0$, because $v=e^{-\gamma t}u$ solves an inequality with zeroth-order coefficient $c+\gamma\ge0$ for $\gamma\ge\|c^-\|_\infty$. Uniqueness for the initial-boundary value problem therefore holds for any bounded $c$; it is only the location of extrema that needs the sign condition. Auditor's check: whenever a proof cites 'the maximum principle' for an equation with a reaction term, ask which of (a), (b), (c) is actually being used, and note that the sign convention depends on whether the operator is written $u_t-\Delta u+cu$ or $u_t-\Delta u-cu$.
Sign convention: L u = -a^{ij} u_{x_i x_j} + b^i u_{x_i} + c u, subsolution means u_t + Lu <= 0
c identically zero for the full maximum principle
c >= 0 for the version with the positive part
bounded c of any sign for the comparison (sign) principle only
title: Pitfall: The Parabolic Maximum Principle needs a sign condition on the zeroth-order coefficient

[Lemma lb spread of arXiv:2509.02432, 'A threshold for online balancing of sparse i.i.d. vectors'] Let $C_{\text{\tiny{(lemma:lb spread of the paper)}}} := 3$. Fix any choice of online algorithm $\sigma$, let $1\leq q\leq \frac{\log\log n}{2\log C_{\text{\tiny{(lemma:lb spread of the paper)}}}}$, and define
$$
k:=\sum_{u=1}^q \Big\lceil\frac{n}{(\log n)^{e^u}}\Big\rceil.
$$
Then with probability at least $1-\frac{q}{\log n}$ there are
$\ell\leq 0\leq r$ with $r-\ell\geq q$ such that 
$(A,\sigma)$ contains an $(\ell,r)$--spread
of size at least $\frac{n}{(\log n)^{C_{\text{\tiny{(lemma:lb spread of the paper)}}}^q}}$ at time $k$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma lb spread of arXiv:2509.02432

body: [Lemma projective represent of arXiv:2609.04023, 'Characterizing Contractions and Weighted Blowdowns'] Let $f:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow \mathcal{Z}$ be a representable morphism of separated Deligne-Mumford stacks with respective coarse spaces $\pi_\mathcal{X}:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow X$ and $\pi_\mathcal{Z}:\mathcal{Z}\rightarrow Z$. If the induced map $\overline{f}:X\rightarrow Z$ is projective, then so is $f:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow \mathcal{Z}$. Furthermore, $f$ is representable by schemes.

    \[

    \]
    If $V$ is a stationary rectifiable $p$-varifold in $M$, for $1 \leq p \leq n$, and $\partial_\infty \spt V \subseteq S$, then
    \[
        \spt V \subseteq \mathcal{H}(S).
    \] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

\]
then $x_{\epsilon}\left(  t\right)  $ converges in probability, uniformly in
$t\in\left[  0,T\right]  $, to the solution $x^{\alpha}\left(  t\right)  $ of
the stochastic equation in Stratonovich form (see Section 2.1)
\[\left\{\begin{array}{l}

t\right)  \right)  dt+\sum_{k\in K}\xi_{k}\left(  x^{\alpha}\left(  t\right)

t\right)  \right)  dt}\\[10pt]
\ds{x^{\alpha}\left(  0\right)     =x_{0}}
\end{array}\right.\]
where
\begin{equation}

x\right)  +\alpha}\left(\,  \sum_{k\in K}D\xi_{k}\left(  x\right)  \xi
_{k}\left(  x\right)  +C\left(  x\right)  c_{0}^{-1}\nabla\log k_{T}\left(
x\right)  \right)  
\end{equation}
and where the matrix $C\left(  x\right)  $ is given by 
\[C\left(  x\right)
=\sum_{k\in K}\xi_{k}\left(  x\right)  \otimes\xi_{k}\left(  x\right).\]

[Lemma Lem E eps 1 eps 2 bound v of arXiv:2604.15146, 'Renormalised two-point functions of CLE$_4$ gaskets'] Let $z_1\neq z_2\in D$
and $r_0>0$ such that the disks
$\overline{\mathbb{D}(z_1,r_0)}$ and $\overline{\mathbb{D}(z_2,r_0)}$
are disjoint and contained in $D$.
There is a constant
$c=c(D,z_1,z_2,r_0)>0$ 
(depending on $D$, $z_1$, $z_2$ and $r_0$),
such that for every $v\in\mathbb{R}$,
and for every $\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2\in (0,r_0]$,
$$
\mathbb{P}(E_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}^v)
\leq
\mathbb{P}(E_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}^0)
e^{-c v^2}.
$$

In particular, let $\mathcal{V}$ be a countable subset of $\mathbb{R}$ and 
$a:\mathcal{V}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$.
Then assuming that for every $b>0$,
$$
\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}
\vert a(v)\vert e^{-b v^2}
<+\infty,
$$
we have that as $\max(\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2)\to 0$,
$$
\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}
a(v)\mathbb{P}(E_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}^v)
=
\varepsilon_1^{1/8}
\varepsilon_2^{1/8}
(\mathbf{C}_{\rm{SLE}4}^{\rm loop})^2
\,
\sigma_{\rm tw}^D(z_1,z_2)
\,
\Big(
\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}a(v)
e^{-v^2 \mathcal{M}_D(z_1,z_2)}
\Big)
(1+o(1)).
$$
title: Lemma Lem E eps 1 eps 2 bound v of arXiv:2604.15146

[Definition 17 (T-chain) of arXiv:2607.20838, 'Long-memory Markov chains with power-law intensities'] Let $a$ be a sampling distribution over the non-negative integers $\mathbb{Z}_+$
	and there exists a substochastic transition kernel $T$ such that
	$$
	K_a(x, B) := \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a(k) P^k(x, B) \geq T(x, B), \quad x \in \mathcal X, B \in \mathcal B(\mathcal X)
	$$
	where $T(\cdot, B)$ is a lower semicontinuous for any $B \in \mathcal B(\mathcal X)$.
	Then $T$ is called a continuous component of $K_a$.
	If $\{X_n\}$ is a Markov chain for which there exists a sampling distribution $a$ such that $K_a$ possesses a continuous component $T$ with $T(x, \mathcal X) > 0$ for all $x$, then $\{X_n\}$ is called a T-chain.
title: T-chain

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Weak concentration of nearest-unvisited walks under exponential edge noise structural calculation Result: A standard bounded-difference proof faces a real discontinuity. On the line with vertices A=0,B=1,D=3,C=-1-epsilon, start at A. For epsilon>0 small, the NUV order is A,B,D,C and length7+epsilon. With C=-1+epsilon, the order is A,C,B,D and length5-2epsilon. An arbitrarily small point perturbation changes the route length by nearly2. Thus NUV length lacks the elementary geometric Lipschitz property available for optimized MST or TSP costs. Check: Both examples use true Euclidean shortest-path distances and strict choices for positive epsilon. The discontinuity comes from a tie limit, not a violation of the triangle inequality. It is a deterministic methodological obstruction, not a random-exponential concentration counterexample. Obstruction: One needs probabilistic control of near-tie cascades or stabilization, rather than a uniform deterministic one-coordinate Lipschitz estimate. The no-macroscopic-edge hypothesis alone has not been shown sufficient here.

body: [Lem 8 of arXiv:2511.18861, 'Correlation Decay for Maximum Weight Matchings on Sparse Graphs'] Let $G$ be a finite weighted graph and let $M$ be a matching of $G$. Then $M$ is a MWM if and only if there is no augmenting path for $M$.

Then 
\[
(M \setminus (M \cap P)) \cup (M^c \cap P)
\]
is a matching whose weight is strictly larger than that of $M$, so $M$ cannot be a MWM.

Conversely, suppose that $M$ is not a MWM.  
Then there exists a matching $M'$ of $G$ such that $w_{M'} > w_M$.  
Note that $M \triangle M'$ is a disjoint union of paths and cycles.  
Clearly, at least one such path or cycle $P$ must satisfy
\[
\sum_{e \in P \cap M} w_e \;<\; \sum_{e \in P \cap M^c} w_e.

[Theorem 15 of arXiv:2607.22441, 'The martingale representation theorem for cylindrical martingale valued measures'] [Martingale representation theorem]

Let $M=(M(t, A): t \geq 0, A \in \calA)$ be an orthogonal C.M.V.M. on $X^*$ with continuous paths and which possesses a unique quadratic variation.  
Assume that the operator-valued quadratic variation of $M$ is given by 
\begin{equation}
 \Gamma_{M}([0,t] \times A) = \int_0^t \int_A\; \Phi (r,u) Q\Phi^*(r,u)\; \lambda(du) dr, 
\end{equation}
where $Q$ is a bounded, non-negative, self-adjoint operator on $H$ with  representation  \eqref{representationCovariaQDefiCylinWhineNoiseMeasure}, $\lambda$ is a $\sigma$-finite measure on $U$, which is finite on the sets in $\mathcal{A}$, and $\Phi: \Omega \times[0,T] \times U \rightarrow \mathcal{L}(H,X)$ is $ (\omega,t,u) \mapsto \Phi(\omega,t,u)h$ 
is $\mathcal{P}_{T}\otimes \mathcal{B}(U)/\mathcal{B}(X)$-measurable for every $h \in H$ and such that for $\Psi(\omega,t,u)=\Phi(\omega,t,u) Q^{1/2}$, we have $\Psi(\omega,t,u) \Psi^{*}(\omega,t,u) \in \mathcal{K}^{+}(X)$.

Then there exists a 
cylindrical $Q$-white noise measure $W=(W(t, A): t \geq 0, A \in \calA)$ on $H$ based on $\left(\mathbb{R}_{+} \times U, \mathcal{B}\left(\mathbb{R}_{+}\right) \otimes \mathcal{B}(U),Leb \otimes \lambda\right)$  defined with respect to an extended probability space $(\Omega \times \widetilde{\Omega}, \mathcal{F} \times \widetilde{\mathcal{F}}, \Prob \times \widetilde{\Prob})$ adapted to the filtration $\{\mathcal{F}_{t} \times \widetilde{\mathcal{F}}_{t}\}$, such that 
 $$
M(t,A)(\omega)= \int_0^t\int_A \Phi(\omega,r,u)W(dr,du)(\omega, \widetilde{\omega}),
$$ 
where the last equality must be interpreted as cylindrical random variables. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition def:auxiliary of arXiv:2605.00657, 'Spectral Duality and Reset-Neutral Distributions\\ in Random Walks with Multi-Site Geometr'] For $z\in\{1,\dots,a-1\}$, let $T_{\mathrm{reset}}$ be the first reset time
(geometric with parameter $gamma$, so $\mathbb{P}(T_{\mathrm{reset}}>k)=(1-gamma)^k$
for $k\geq 0$). Define:
\begin{align}
u(z) &:= \mathbb{P}_z(\tau_0<\tau_a,\;\tau_0<T_{\mathrm{reset}})
       = \mathbb{E}_z\!\bigl[(1-gamma)^{\tau_0}\mathbf{1}_{\{\tau_0<\tau_a\}}\bigr],
\\
s(z) &:= \mathbb{P}_z(\tau<T_{\mathrm{reset}})
       = \mathbb{E}_z\!\bigl[(1-gamma)^{\tau}\bigr],

\end{align}
where $\tau=\min\{\tau_0,\tau_a\}$. The rightmost equalities follow from
the independence of $T_{\mathrm{reset}}$ and $\{\xi_n\}$ via
\[
u(z) = \sum_{k=1}^\infty \mathbb{P}_z(\tau_0=k,\,\tau_0<\tau_a)\,\mathbb{P}(T_{\mathrm{reset}}>k)
     = \sum_{k=1}^\infty \mathbb{P}_z(\tau_0=k,\,\tau_0<\tau_a)(1-gamma)^k,
\]
and analogously for $s(z)$.

[Corollary 2 (Rectangular matrices) of arXiv:2606.25204, 'Exponential Rank Bounds for Random Matrices'] Fix \(b\in(0,1)\).  Let \(A\) be an \(m\times n\) random matrix with
independent real entries such that
\[
   \sup_{x\in\R}\PP\{A_{ij}=x\}\leq b<1
   \qquad (1\leq i\leq m,\ 1\leq j\leq n),
\]
and set \(d=\min(m,n)\).  Then for all \(1\leq k\leq d\),
\begin{equation}
   \PP\{\rank A\leq d-k\}\leq \exp(-c_{1.1}dk).
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

CAMPAIGN RESULT [independently checked proof; E0095-SENS v2; no novelty claim]. Let a connected d-regular graph have simple ordinary SRW gap gamma=lambda_2(L)/d, with unit Euclidean Fiedler vector phi. Add absent edge uv with weight t. The gap derivative at t=0 is [(phi_u-phi_v)^2-gamma(phi_u^2+phi_v^2)]/d; the half-lazy derivative is half this expression. With b=e_u-e_v, C=e_u e_u^T+e_v e_v^T and U=[e_u,e_v], for g outside the spectrum of L/d the exact determinant is det(L+tbb^T-g(dI+tC))=det(L-gdI)det(I_2+tH(g)U^T(L-gdI)^(-1)U), H(g)=[[1-g,-1],[-1,1-g]]. Excluded poles require checks in the original pencil. This unadjusted edge variant changes stationary law and differs from Diaconis's stationary-preserving Metropolis variation.

body: In number theory, the Chevalley–Warning theorem implies that certain polynomial equations in sufficiently many variables over a finite field have solutions. It was proved by Ewald Warning and a slightly weaker form of the theorem, known as Chevalley's theorem, was proved by Chevalley. Chevalley's theorem implied Artin's and Dickson's conjecture that finite fields are quasi-algebraically closed fields.
title: Chevalley–Warning theorem

body: [Lemma superposition_intensity of arXiv:2412.00279, 'Optimal local storage policy based on stochastic intensities and its large scale behavior'] If $\Phi = \sum_i \Phi_i$ is the superposition process, then $\mathcal{F}_t$ is a history of $\Phi$. Furthermore, the total stochastic intensity of $\Phi$ is simply $\lambda(t) = \sum_{i=1}^N \lambda_i(t)$. Moreover, $\lambda_i(t)$ is a stochastic intensity for process $i$ with respect to the enlarged history $\mathcal{F}_t$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lem 1 of arXiv:2604.12853, 'Coupling Markov Chains \\with a Common Image Chain'] Let $k \ge 0$ and $(a_0,b_0), \dots, (a_k,b_k) \in \Delta$ with $c_i = f(a_i) = g(b_i)$ for $0 \le i \le k$. Suppose $\upalpha_Z(c_0) > 0$. Then for each $m \ge k$, 
    \begin{align}
    \begin{split}
    
    \mathbb{P}&(W^m_0 = (a_0,b_0), \dots, W^m_k = (a_k,b_k)) \\  
        &   
         = \mathbb{E}\bigl[
        \mathbb{P}(X^m_{\le k} = (a_0, \dots, a_k) \mid Z)\, \mathbb{P}(Y^m_{\le k} = (b_0, \dots, b_k) \mid Z)
        \bigr] 
        \\
        & = 
        \mathbb{E}\bigl[
        \mathbb{P}(X^m_{\le k} = (a_0, \dots, a_k) \mid Z_{\le m})\, \mathbb{P}(Y^m_{\le k} = (b_0, \dots, b_k) \mid Z_{\le m})
        \bigr]
        \\
        & = 
        \frac{\upalpha_X(a_0)\upalpha_Y(b_0)}{\upalpha_Z(c_0)}\biggl(\prod_{i= 1}^{k}R((a_{i-1},b_{i-1}),(a_i,b_i))\bigg)\,\varphi_{m-k}(a_k,b_k)\,.
    \end{split}
    \end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem 1 of arXiv:2604.12853

body: Let gamma be the standard Gaussian measure on R^n. The ORNSTEIN-UHLENBECK SEMIGROUP is defined by MEHLER'S FORMULA P_t f(x) = integral f( e^{-t} x + sqrt(1 - e^{-2t}) y ) gamma(dy) for t >= 0. It is a Markov semigroup: P_0 = identity, P_{s+t} = P_s P_t, P_t 1 = 1, P_t preserves nonnegativity, gamma is INVARIANT (integral P_t f dgamma = integral f dgamma), and P_t is SELF-ADJOINT on L^2(gamma). Its generator is L f = Laplacian f - x . grad f, which satisfies the integration-by-parts identity integral (L u) v dgamma = - integral grad u . grad v dgamma. The Hermite polynomials diagonalise it: L He_alpha = - |alpha| He_alpha and P_t He_alpha = e^{-|alpha| t} He_alpha, so the n-th Wiener chaos is the eigenspace of eigenvalue -n. The COMMUTATION RELATION grad P_t f = e^{-t} P_t grad f follows by differentiating Mehler's formula under the integral. Two facts to keep straight: this is the semigroup for the standard Gaussian, and other normalisations of the generator (for example Laplacian/2 minus x . grad/2) rescale time and change the constants in the associated Poincare and logarithmic Sobolev inequalities. As t -> infinity, P_t f -> integral f dgamma, and the exponential rate of that convergence in L^2 is exactly 1, the spectral gap, which is the Gaussian Poincare inequality. [standard; e.g. Bakry, Gentil and Ledoux, Analysis and Geometry of Markov Diffusion Operators, Section 2.7]

[Prop prop-coexeq of arXiv:2504.04943, 'Emergence of \bl microbial \bl host dormancy \\ \bl during \bl a persistent virus epidemic'] Assume that $r\kappa\mu_1 \neq v \sigma$ and that both~(equation viruscoexcondq=0 of the paper) and~(equation viruscoexcond2 of the paper) hold (so that $(n_{1a}^*,n_{1i}^*,n_{3}^*)$ and $(\widetilde n_{2a},\widetilde n_{2d},\widetilde n_{2i},\widetilde n_3)$ are coordinatewise positive equilibria of the corresponding sub-systems, which in particular implies $mv>r+v$). Then the system~(equation 6dimvirus of the paper) has a unique coordinatewise nonzero equilibrium which we denote by 
$$
\mathbf x=(x_{1a},x_{1i},x_{2a},x_{2d},x_{2i},x_3).
$$ 
It satisfies
\[ x_3 = \frac{\lambda_2-\lambda_1}{qD}
\frac{(\kappa\mu_1+\sigma)(r+v)}{r\kappa\mu_1-v\sigma}, \addtocounter{equation}{1}\tag{\thesection.\arabic{equation}} \]
\[ x_{1a} + (1-q)  x_{2a} = \frac{\mu_3(r+v)}{D(mv-(r+v))} = n_{1a}^* = (1-q) \widetilde n_{2a}, \addtocounter{equation}{1}\tag{\thesection.\arabic{equation}} \]
and
\[ x_{1i}+x_{2i} = \frac{\mu_3 x_3}{mv-(r+v)}. \addtocounter{equation}{1}\tag{\thesection.\arabic{equation}} \]

Moreover,
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\mathbf x$ is coordinatewise positive if and only if  the invasion conditions\color{black}~(equation 1invades2 of the paper) and~(equation 2invades1 of the paper) both hold,  or, \color{black} equivalently
\[
\widetilde n_3 < x_3 < n_3^*.
\addtocounter{equation}{1}\tag{\thesection.\arabic{equation}} \]
\item It is never true that $n_3^* < x_3 < \widetilde n_3$. 
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Proposition 61 of arXiv:2608.12947, 'Branch-stationary max-stable fields on rooted trees'] The field
\begin{equation}
  U_v^\psi
  =
  \psi\left(
    \frac{\eta_v^{-\alpha}}{S_\psi}
  \right),
  \qquad v\in\mathcal T,
  
\end{equation}
has standard uniform margins and finite-dimensional copulas
\((C_K^\psi)\). In particular, these copulas extend continuously to
\([0,1]^K\) and form a projectively consistent family of Archimax
copulas.
 
The following statements are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item \(\eta\) is branch-stationary;
\item for every non-empty finite \(K\subset\mathcal T\),
\begin{equation}
  \ell_{aK}(x^a)=\ell_K(x),
  \qquad
  a\in\mathcal T,\quad x\in[0,\infty)^K;
  
\end{equation}
\item for every non-empty finite \(K\subset\mathcal T\),
\[
  C_{aK}(u^a)=C_K(u),
  \qquad
  a\in\mathcal T,\quad u\in(0,1]^K;
\]
\item for every non-empty finite \(K\subset\mathcal T\),
\[
  C_{aK}^\psi(u^a)=C_K^\psi(u),
  \qquad
  a\in\mathcal T,\quad u\in(0,1]^K;
\]
\item \(U^\psi\) is branch-stationary.
\end{enumerate}
 
If \(Z\) satisfies (equation 17 of the paper) and
\(\Theta=\Theta^{[\varnothing]}\), then
\begin{equation}
  \ell_K(x)
  =
  \E*{
    \max_{v\in K}x_v\Theta_v^\alpha
  },
  \qquad x\in[0,\infty)^K.
  
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition 61 of arXiv:2608.12947

DRAFT proof-audit material, independent referee check pending. For every integer d>=1 and epsilon>0 there exists a stationary finite-dependent {0,1} field on Z^d with probability of good at each vertex at least 1-epsilon and all nearest-neighbour good components finite. Construct it from iid Bernoulli(q) seeds. L(v) is a nearest seed in the l-infinity ball B_R(v), with lexicographic tie-breaking, or bottom if the ball is empty. A vertex is good exactly when its non-bottom label agrees with every nearest neighbour's label. Its indicator uses seeds in B_(R+1)(v), so index sets at l-infinity distance greater than 2(R+1) are independent. Each good component has one seed label s and lies in B_R(s). For a finite dimension-dependent constant K_d, P(v bad)<=exp(-q(2R-1)^d) +K_d q^(1/d); choosing q small then R large gives the claimed density. The dependence range varies with epsilon. This is correlated site percolation and does not refute iid critical bond percolation or a fixed-range domination theorem.
d is an integer>=1
iid seeds with 0<q<1
R is an integer>=1
Good connectivity is nearest-neighbour
title: High density with a growing dependence range need not percolate

[Defn 13 of arXiv:2506.19123, 'The longest increasing subsequence of Brownian separable permutons'] Let $n \geq 0, k \geq 1$ be integers, let $\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_k>0$ and $\alpha_0=\sum_{i=1}^k \alpha_i$. 
    \begin{itemize}
    \item 
    The Dirichlet distribution $\Dir \left( \alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_k \right)$ is the law on $k$-tuples of non-negative real numbers $(x_1, \dots, x_k)$ which sum up to $1$ given by the probability density function
     \[\frac{\Gamma(\alpha_0)}{\Gamma(\alpha_1)\cdots \Gamma(\alpha_k)} \prod_{i=1}^k x_i^{\alpha_i - 1}.\]

    
    \item The Dirichlet-multinomial distribution $\DirM \left( n; \alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_k \right)$ is the law on $k$-tuples of non-negative integers $(n_1, \dots, n_k)$ which sum up to $n$ given by the probability mass function
        \[ \frac{\Gamma(\alpha_0) \Gamma(n+1)}{\Gamma(n+\alpha_0)} \prod_{i=1}^k \frac{\Gamma(n_i+\alpha_i)}{\Gamma(\alpha_i) \Gamma(n_i+1)}. \]
    In other words, a $\DirM \left( n; \alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_k \right)$-distributed random variable $\mathbf{N}=\left( N_1, \dots, N_k \right)$ can be obtained as follows: let $\mathbf{D}=(D_1, \dots, D_k)$ follow the Dirichlet distribution $\Dir \left( \alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_k \right)$; then, conditionally on $\mathbf{D}$, sample the vector $\mathbf{N}$ as a multinomial vector with parameters $(n;\mathbf{D})$.
    \end{itemize}

[Lem 4 of arXiv:2511.22156, ''] Let $f\in C_c^\infty(\partial_o S_1-\{y=0\})$. 
	
(1). Let $h_1\in \tmcF_0|_{S_1\cup S_4}$ such that 
\begin{align*}
		&h_1=f\quad \hbox{on}\ \partial_o S_1-\{y=0\},\\
		
		&h_1\hbox{ is }\tmcE_0|_{S_1}\hbox{-harmonic in }(S_1\setminus\partial_o S_1)\cup\{y=0\},
\end{align*} 
and 
\[
h_1(x)=h_1(\psi(x))\quad\hbox{ for }x\in S_4.
\]   
Then, $h_1$ is $\tmcE_0|_{S_1\cup S_4} $-harmonic in $(S_1\cup S_4)\setminus\partial_o(S_1\cup S_4)$. 

(2). Let $h_2\in \tmcF_0|_{S_1\cup S_4}$ such that 
	\begin{align*}
		&h_2=f\quad \hbox{on}\ \partial_o S_1-\{y=0\},\\
		&h_2=0\qquad \hbox{on}\ \{y=0\},\\
		&h_2\ \hbox{is $\tmcE_0|_{S_1}$- harmonic in } S_1\setminus \partial_o S_1,
	\end{align*}    
and 
\[
h_2(x)=-\frac{\mu_0(S_1)}{\mu_0(S_4)}h_2(\psi(x))\quad\hbox{ for }x\in S_4.
\]
Then, $h_2$ is $\tmcE_0|_{S_1\cup S_4} $-harmonic in $(S_1\cup S_4)\setminus\partial_o(S_1\cup S_4)$.

[Df equiv_collar of arXiv:2605.14910, 'Sharp Phase Transition for the Formation of Infinite Tubes'] We say that two $k$-collars
  \[
  \delta\colon\mathbb{S}^{k-1}\times I_\varepsilon\to|\mathcal{K}_k^d|
  \quad\text{and}\quad
  \delta'\colon\mathbb{S}^{k-1}\times I_\varepsilon\to|\mathcal{K}_k^d|
  \]
  based at the same discrete $(k-1)$-sphere $S$ are \emph{equivalent} if there exists a continuous map
  \[
  H\colon\bigl(\mathbb{S}^{k-1}\times I_\varepsilon\bigr)\times[0,1]\to|\mathcal{K}_k^d|
  \]
  such that
  \begin{itemize}
    \item $H(\cdot,0)=\delta$ and $H(\cdot,1)=\delta'$, that is, $H$ is a homotopy between $\delta$ and $\delta'$;
    \item the map $H(\cdot,t)\colon\mathbb{S}^{k-1}\times I_\varepsilon\to|\mathcal{K}_k^d|$ is a $k$-collar based at $S$ for every $t\in[0,1]$~(in particular, each $H(\cdot,t)$ is injective).
  \end{itemize}

  We denote by $[\delta]$ the equivalence class of a $k$-collar $\delta$.
  For an equivalence class $\Delta=[\delta]$, we set $S_\Delta:=S_\delta$ and refer to it as the \emph{base sphere} of $\Delta$.
  (See Figure~(fig:collars of the paper).)
title: Equivalence class of $k$-collars

[Proposition 19 of arXiv:2511.09930, 'Martingale dimensions for a class of metric measure spaces'] Let $m\le n$. For each $f\in l(V_m)$ there exists a unique $h\in l(V_n)$ such that $h|_{V_m}=f$ and
\[
\cE^{(n)}(h,h)=\inf\{\cE^{(n)}(g,g)\mid g\in l(V_n)\text{ and }g|_{V_m}=f\}.
\]
Moreover, for any $w\in\tilde W_m$ and $x\in V_n\cap \tilde K_w$,
\[
\min_{\psi_w(V_0)}f\le h(x)\le \max_{\psi_w(V_0)}f.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition 19 of arXiv:2511.09930

The maximum is attained at S = span(v_1, ..., v_k) and the minimum at T = span(v_k, ..., v_n), where v_1, ..., v_n is an orthonormal eigenbasis of A*A with eigenvalues in decreasing order.

body:
[Corollary 27 of arXiv:2609.03403, 'Hyperpositive functions, sector bounded functions and a trace formula'] Let $F\in \mathcal{ HP}_{T,t}$. Then for every $z\in\mathbb C_r$, the matrix-valued function $F(z)$
      belongs to the closed matrix ball with center $T^{-1}$, left radius $(T^{-1}+tT)^{1/2}$ and right
      radius $T^{-1/2}$. When $m=1$ and using the notation $T=\beta$ in that case (to be consistent with our
      previous works \cite{MR4255499,MR4756530}), $F(z)$ belongs to the closed disk with center
      \[
        C(\beta)=\frac{1}{\beta}
      \]
      and radius
      \[
R(\beta)=\sqrt{t+\frac{1}{\beta^2}}.
\]
In that case it holds that
\[
(C(\beta))^2-(R(\beta))^2=-t.
  \]

[Proposition prop:geodesics of arXiv:2512.13200, 'Martingales on a Euclidean manifold with a boundary and reflected BSDEs in non-convex doma'] {Let Assumption (ass:3 of the paper) hold and let $\gamma$ be a geodesic in $\bar\mathcal{D}$.} Then, there exists a finite $N$ and a partition $0=t_1 <\cdots<t_{2N}=1$ such that one of the following two statements holds:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item For all integers $k$ equal to $1$ modulo $4$, the curve $\gamma$ does not turn to the left on $[t_k,t_{k+1}]$.
        \item For all even integers $k$, the curve $\gamma$ is a straight line on $[t_k,t_{k+1}]$.
        \item For all integers $k$ equal to $3$ modulo $4$, the curve $\gamma$ does not turn to the right on $[t_k,t_{k+1}]$.
    \end{itemize}
    or
    \begin{itemize}
        \item For all integers $k$ equal to $1$ modulo $4$, the curve $\gamma$ does not turn to the right on $[t_k,t_{k+1}]$.
        \item For all even integers $k$, the curve $\gamma$ is a straight line on $[t_k,t_{k+1}]$.
        \item For all integers $k$ equal to $3$ modulo $4$, the curve $\gamma$ does not turn to the left on $[t_k,t_{k+1}]$.
    \end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Prop of arXiv:2412.05999, 'Non-Archimedean GUE corners and Hecke modules'] The Hall-Littlewood polynomials $P_\lambda(x_1,\ldots,x_n;t)$ satisfy the following properties:

\begin{enumerate}[left=0pt]
\item They are monic and have the form
$$P_\lambda(x_1,\ldots,x_n;t) = x_1^{\lambda_1}x_2^{\lambda_2}\cdots x_n^{\lambda_n} + \text{(lower-order monomials in the lexicographic order)};$$

\item When $\lambda\in\Sig_n^+$ ranges over all nonnegative integer signatures of length $n$, the Hall-Littlewood polynomials $P_\lambda(x_1,\cdots,x_n;t)$ form a $\mathbb{Z}[t]$-basis of $\Lambda_n[t]$, where $\Lambda_n[t]:=\mathbb{Z}[t][x_1,\ldots,x_n]^{S_n}$ is the ring of symmetric polynomials in $n$ variables $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ with coefficients in $\mathbb{Z}[t]$;

\item When $\lambda\in\Sig_n$ ranges over all integer signatures of length $n$, the Hall-Littlewood polynomials $P_\lambda(x_1,\cdots,x_n;t)$ form a $\mathbb{Z}[t]$ basis of $\mathbb{Z}[t][x_1^{\pm 1},\ldots,x_n^{\pm 1}]^{S_n}$, the ring of symmetric Laurent polynomials in $n$ variables $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ with coefficients in $\mathbb{Z}[t]$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Unnumbered prop of arXiv:2412.05999, 'Non-Archimedean GUE corners and Hecke modules'

[Lemma 4 (Chain rule for relative entropy) of arXiv:2608.20337, 'Information on trajectories:\\ martingales and random times'] For path measures $Q \ll P$ on $(\Omega, \cF_T)$,
\[
  \KL(Q\|P)
  = \sum_{t=1}^T \E_Q\!\left[
      \KL\!\bigl(Q_t(\cdot | X_{1:t-1}) \,\|\, P_t(\cdot | X_{1:t-1})\bigr)
    \right]
  = \sum_{t=1}^T \E_Q[\log R_t].
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Chain rule for relative entropy

[Definition 26 (Admissible $d_L$-separated contour system) of arXiv:2608.20552, 'One-point fluctuations for exponential last passage percolation under upper-tail condition'] For a Gaussian or modified Gaussian family, we call
\beqq
    \cont_-^L(\cp^-+bL^{-1/2})
    \qquad\text{and}\qquad
    \cont_+^L(\cp^++bL^{-1/2}),
    \qquad b\in\R,
\eeqq
the left and right asymptotic contours, respectively, whenever the corresponding critical point exists.
For an Airy family with double critical point $\cp$, we call
\beqq
    \cont_-^L(\cp+bL^{-1/3})
    \qquad\text{and}\qquad
    \cont_+^L(\cp+bL^{-1/3}),
    \qquad b\in\R,
\eeqq
the left and right asymptotic contours, respectively. 
A contour system for $\J^{\bsigma}_{\btau}(L)$ is called \emph{admissible} if every $\xi_i^*$ is integrated over a left asymptotic contour for $\ff_{L,*}$, every $\eta_i^*$ is integrated over a right asymptotic contour for $\ff_{L,*}$, and the nesting prescribed by $\bsigma$ and $\btau$ is preserved.
For $d_L>0$, an admissible contour system is called \emph{$d_L$-separated} if any two contours carrying variables that appear on opposite sides of the same Cauchy determinant in \eqref{eq:Caucdt} are separated by a distance of at least $d_L$.
title: Admissible $d_L$-separated contour system

body:
[Proposition 5 (Generalized predictable Euler-Maruyama ``SDEs'' universally approximate SDEs in $\mathcal{H}_T^2(\mathbb{R}^{d_X})$) of arXiv:2607.14361, 'NeuralChaos: Optimal Adapted Approximation of Square Integrable Predictable Processes'] For measurable functions
\[
b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^{d_X}\to \mathbb R^{d_X},
\qquad
\Sigma:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^{d_X}\to \mathbb R^{d_X\times D},
\]
that are Lipschitz and of linear growth, and $\xi\in L^2(\mathcal{F}_0;\mathbb{R}^{d_X})$, we consider the process\footnote{Since the solution process has $\mathbb{P}$-a.s.\ continuous paths and is adapted, it is predictable.} $X_{\cdot} \in \mathcal{H}_T^2(\mathbb R^{d_X})$
solving the induced (Markovian) SDE
$$
X_t = \xi +\int_0^t\, b(s,X_s)\,ds + \int_0^t\, \Sigma(s,X_s)\,\ud W_s, \qquad \mbox{ for } t \in [0,T].
$$
For every approximation error $\varepsilon>0$, there exists some $\hat{X}_{\cdot}\in \mathfrak{B}$ satisfying
$
    \big\|
        \hat{X}-X
    \big\|_{\mathcal{H}_T^2(\mathbb R^{d_X})}
    <
    \varepsilon
$.
title: Generalized predictable Euler-Maruyama ``SDEs'' universally approximate SDEs in $\mathcal{H}_T^2(\mathbb{R}^{d_X})$

body: [Lemma lem:reduction_overall of arXiv:2609.01745, 'The Directional Localization Game on Graphs'] Let $G$ be the incidence graph of a finite projective plane of order $q$, and consider the partial-feedback game on $G$.  Suppose that at the end of a probing phase, all contaminated vertices are contained within $N(x) \cup N(y)$ for some non-adjacent $x \in \mathcal{P}$ and $y \in \mathcal{L}$, and let $i$ denote the number of contaminated line vertices.  If $i > 2$, then the cops can either win or ensure that at the end of some subsequent probing phase, the contamination will be contained in $N(u) \cup N(v)$ for some non-adjacent point vertex $u$ and line vertex $v$, and one partite set will contain at most $i-1$ contaminated vertices.

body: [Definition defrobustimage of arXiv:2607.06952, 'Universality for cokernels of partially random integral matrices'] Let $X$ be $(\varepsilon,\tau,A)$-balanced, and let $F$ in ${\mathrm{Hom}}(V,G)$ have depth $D$ for $X$. We say that $F$ has \emph{proper robust image} $H$ if, in addition, $H < FA^{-1}(V_{\setminus \tau})$.

[Proposition prop:app_wellposedness of arXiv:2507.22577, 'A Mean-Field Theory of $\Theta$-Expectations'] Let the system be defined as in Definition (def:ambiguous_dynamical_system of the paper). Assume:
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
    \item The functions $\Phi: \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}$ and $f_0: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ are Lipschitz continuous.
    \item The map $g: \mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R}) \to \Theta$ is Lipschitz continuous.
    \item The map $\theta \mapsto \mathcal{U}_\theta$ is Lipschitz continuous with respect to the Hausdorff distance, and each $\mathcal{U}_\theta$ is a non-empty, compact set given by a finite union of disjoint closed intervals. We also assume the global uncertainty set $\mathcal{K} := \bigcup_{\theta \in \Theta} \mathcal{U}_\theta$ is compact.
    \item The projection of the reference control $w_0$ onto each set $\mathcal{U}_\theta$ is unique.
\end{enumerate}
Then:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
    \item The system admits a unique local-in-time solution.
    \item Furthermore, if the matrix $C_1$ is symmetric positive definite and $1+3w \ge \delta > 0$ for all $w \in \mathcal{K}$ and for some constant $\delta$, then the solution is unique and global in time for any horizon $T>0$.
\end{enumerate}
title: Well-Posedness of the System

[Definition of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] A map $f\colon X\to Y$ is called a \emph{$G$-equivariant fibration} if it is a $G$-equivariant level fibration and for all closed subgroups $H\subset G$ and $H$-representations $V,W$, the naturality square
    \[
        \begin{tikzcd}
            X(V)\arrow[r,"\tilde\sigma"]\arrow[d,"f(V)"'] & \Omega^WX(V\oplus W)\arrow[d,"\Omega^Wf(V\oplus W)"]\\
            Y(V)\arrow[r,"\tilde\sigma"'] & \Omega^WY(V\oplus W)
        \end{tikzcd}
    \]
    for the adjunct structure maps is a homotopy pullback in $\textbf{\textup{$\bm H$-Top}}_*$.

    An orthogonal $G$-spectrum $X$ is called a \emph{$G$-$\Omega$-spectrum} if the unique map $X\to 0$ is a $G$-equivariant fibration, i.e.\ the adjunct structure map $X(V)\to \Omega^WX(V\oplus W)$ is an $H$-equivariant weak equivalence for each closed subgroup $H\subset G$ and all $H$-representations $V,W$.
title: Unnumbered definition of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'

body:
[Corollary cor:universal-principal-skeleton of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Fix $h\geq2$ and $k\geq3$.  Then
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal R^{[0]}(h,k)=\{M_{h,k}\},
 \qquad
 \mathcal R^{[1]}(h,k)
 =\{M_{h,k}-M_{h-r,k}:2\leq r\leq h\}.
\end{equation}
In particular, exactly $h$ attainable cardinalities have minimum active
rank at most one.  They are exactly the values whose realization-frequency
quasipolynomial has degree greater than $k-2$: the maximum has degree $k$,
the other $h-1$ values have degree $k-1$, and every remaining attainable
cardinality has degree at most $k-2$.

[Theorem Sklar's Theorem of arXiv:2609.02832, 'Copula Transformations for Data-Consistent Inversion'] Suppose the CDFs $F_1,\ldots,F_d$
are continuous.
Then there exists a unique copula
$C:[0,1]^d\to[0,1]$ such that the corresponding joint distribution function satisfies
\[
F(y_1,\ldots,y_d)
=
C(F_1(y_1),\ldots,F_d(y_d)).
\]
Moreover, if the joint distribution is absolutely continuous, then the copula admits a density $c$ satisfying
\[
\pi(y)
=
c(F_1(y_1),\ldots,F_d(y_d))
\prod_{i=1}^d
\pi_i(y_i).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Sklar's Theorem

Let $\mathcal{T}$ be a stably triangulated category with coproducts and $E \in \mathcal{T}$. An object $X$ is $E$-acyclic if $E \otimes X = 0$. An object $Y$ is $E$-local if $\operatorname{Hom}(X, Y) = 0$ for all $E$-acyclic $X$. A Bousfield localization with respect to $E$ is an exact functor $L_E: \mathcal{T} \to \mathcal{T}$ equipped with a natural transformation $\eta: \operatorname{id} \to L_E$ such that for every $X$, $L_E X$ is $E$-local and the fiber of $\eta_X$ is $E$-acyclic.
\mathcal{T} is a tensor-triangulated category with coproducts
E \in \mathcal{T} is a fixed object
title: Bousfield Localization Functor in Triangulated Categories

[Thm 16 (General case) of arXiv:2605.05986, '\bf Convergence rate of the occupation measure of { classes of ergodic processes toward th'] Let the assumptions of~\cref{thm:fractrao} be in force with $\zeta>{3/2}$. Then, 
\begin{itemize}
\item Very short Memory: If $\zeta>{5/2}$, $\ATROIS$ holds true for any $q\ge 1$ with $\gamma=1/2$. Thus,

body: In mathematics, the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma is a result named after William B. Johnson and Joram Lindenstrauss concerning low-distortion embeddings of points from high-dimensional into low-dimensional Euclidean space. The lemma states that a set of points in a high-dimensional space can be embedded into a space of much lower dimension in such a way that distances between the points are nearly preserved. In the classical proof of the lemma, the embedding is a random orthogonal projection.
title: Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma

[Proposition prop:root-sweep-dictionary of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Let $h\geq1$ and $k\geq2$.  One has the exact difference identity
\begin{equation}
 E_{h,k}-E_{h,k}=h\mathsf R_{k-1}\cap\mathsf A_{k-1}.
\end{equation}
For an ordered real tuple $a=(a_1<\cdots<a_k)$, write
\({\bf1}=(1,\ldots,1)\in\mathbb R^k\) and let
$a^\circ=a-k^{-1}(\sum_i a_i){\bf1}$ be its centered representative.  Let
$F_h(a)$ be the face of $\mathfrak Z_{h,k}$ exposed by $a^\circ$.  The
following data determine one another:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item the total preorder on $E_{h,k}$ induced by $u\mapsto u\cdot a$
      (equivalently, its ordered weak partition into level sets);
\item the complete ordered $h$-addition table of $a$, including ties;
\item the face $F_h(a)$.
\end{enumerate}
The dimension of $F_h(a)$ is the active relation rank $r_h(a)$.  In the
ambient space ${\bf1}^{\perp}$, its normal cone has dimension
$k-1-r_h(a)$, and the relative interior of that cone consists precisely of
the centered weights inducing the same complete table.  Moreover, the same
face determines every ordered addition table in degrees $1\leq j\leq h$.

Fix any field $K$.  If $a\in\mathbb Z^k$, put
$A=\{a_1,\ldots,a_k\}$ and define
\[
 \varphi_a:K[x_1,\ldots,x_k]\longrightarrow K[u,t,t^{-1}],
 \qquad x_i\longmapsto u t^{a_i},
 \qquad I_a=\ker\varphi_a,
\]
where $\deg u=1$ and $\deg t=0$.  Then the number of blocks in the face
label is the Hilbert value
\begin{equation}
 |hA|=\dim_K\bigl(K[x_1,\ldots,x_k]/I_a\bigr)_h.
\end{equation}
Thus the face records the equality rank and Hilbert/block label, while its
normal cone encodes the normalized shape, realization frequency, and integer
compression developed below.

[Definition 2 of arXiv:2607.06428, 'Impact of spinning on the early-warning signs in non-Markovian stochastic systems'] A stochastic process $(\mathbf{x}_t)_{t\geq 0}$ is called strictly stationary or strongly stationary if for all $k\ge0$ and all sequences $(t_1,\dots, t_m)\in\R^m_+$ we have
    $$(\mathbf{x}_{t_1},\dots,\mathbf{x}_{t_m})\overset{d}{=}(\mathbf{x}_{t_1+k},\dots,\mathbf{x}_{t_m+k}).$$
   The process $(\mathbf{x}_t)_{t\geq 0}$ is called second order stationary or weakly stationary, if we have for all $t\in\R$ $\E[|\mathbf{x}_t|]<\infty,~\E[|\mathbf{x}_t|^2]<\infty$ and for all $s,t,\tau\ge0$
    $$V_t(\tau)=V_s(\tau).$$
    As the autocovariance only depends on $\tau$, we drop the subscript and write $V(\tau)$ whenever we consider a stationary process.
title: Definition 2 of arXiv:2607.06428

Pourkamali-Macris Proposition3, independent-spectra version of the source coupling. Fix positive integers N<=M and lambda>0. Let sigma,sigma_tilde in[0,infinity)^N be independent random singular-value vectors, each with finite second moment. Let U in O(N),V in O(M) be independent normalized Haar matrices, independent of both vectors. Define S=U*diag_{N by M}(sigma)*V^T and S_tilde=U*diag_{N by M}(sigma_tilde)*V^T, so the pair shares its singular vectors. Let P_1,P_2 be the respective marginal signal priors. For j=1,2, take Y_j=sqrt(lambda)*S_j+G_j with iid N(0,1/N) Gaussian entries independent of the signal. Define Z_j(y)=E_{X~P_j} exp(N*sqrt(lambda)*Tr(X^T*y)-(N*lambda/2)*||X||_F^2), where the inner X is an independent prior draw, and F_j(lambda)=-(N*M)^(-1)*E log Z_j(Y_j) with expectation under the matching planted model. Then |F_1(lambda)-F_2(lambda)| <= (lambda/(2*N))*(sqrt(E||sigma||_2^2)+sqrt(E||sigma_tilde||_2^2))*sqrt(E||sigma-sigma_tilde||_2^2). The last expectation is over the independent spectral pair specified above, with its chosen coordinate ordering. The result is finite-dimensional; it does not by itself justify a limiting spectral-atom extension or convergence in expectation from mere weak convergence.
Finite N<=M and lambda>0.
Independent nonnegative spectral vectors with finite second moments; common independent Haar singular vectors.
Variance1/N iid Gaussian observation noise independent of each signal.

body:
Consider testing a simple null hypothesis H0: X has density f0 against a simple alternative H1: X has density f1 (with respect to a common dominating measure), at a fixed significance level alpha in (0,1). Define a test with rejection rule: reject H0 when f1(x) > k f0(x); accept H0 when f1(x) < k f0(x); and reject with some probability gamma in [0,1] when f1(x) = k f0(x); where the constant k >= 0 and the randomization probability gamma are chosen so that the test has size exactly alpha, i.e. Pr(reject H0 | H0) = alpha. Then this likelihood-ratio test is most powerful at level alpha: for every other test phi with size at most alpha, the power of phi under H1 is no greater than the power of the likelihood-ratio test.

[Proposition 16 of arXiv:2608.30875, 'A Decomposition Theorem for Topological Semi-small Maps'] Let $f:X \longrightarrow Y$ be an almost covering map, where $X$ is a closed topological manifold and $Y$ is a closed topological pseudomanifold. Suppose the fibered set $R = \bigsqcup_{\beta} T_{\beta} \subset Y$ is equipped with a suitable decomposition. Assume that $R$ is a closed topologically stratified space of codimension greater than or equal to $2$. Let $R = \bigsqcup_{\alpha} S_{\alpha}$, $T_{\beta} = \bigsqcup_{\gamma} V^{\beta}_{\gamma}\ \text{for each } \beta$, and 
	$Y = \bigsqcup_{\eta} W_{\eta}$
	be intrinsic stratifications. Furthermore, assume that the inclusion $R \xhookrightarrow[]{\phantom{.} i \phantom{.} } Y$ is locally flat. Then the decomposition
	\begin{align}
	Y = \bigl( W_{\eta_{\text{top}}} \setminus (R \cap W_{\eta_{\text{top}}}) \bigr) \;\bigsqcup_{\alpha,\eta,\beta,\gamma}\; \bigl( W_{\eta} \cap V^{\beta}_{\gamma} \cap S_{\alpha}\bigr)
	\end{align}
	is a refined stratification on $Y$, where $W_{\eta_{\text{top}}}$ denotes the top stratum of $Y$.
title: Proposition 16 of arXiv:2608.30875

[Lemma lemlocalex of arXiv:2606.29036, 'The limit law of the largest interpoint distance in a $d$-dimensional ellipsoid'] Let $x=x(e,\delta,w)$ and $y=x(-g,\delta',w')$, where
$e,g\in \mathbb{S}^{k-1}$ and $\langle e,g\rangle=\cos\theta$.
Then, as $\delta,\delta',\theta,\|w\|,\|w'\|\to 0$, we have
\[
 2-\|x-y\| = \frac{\delta+\delta'}{2} + \frac{\theta^2}{4}
- \frac{1}{4} \|A(w-w')\|^2 + r(\delta,\delta',\theta,w,w'),
\]
where
\[
r(\delta,\delta',\theta,w,w') = o\!\left(\delta+\delta'+\theta^2+\|w\|^2+\|w'\|^2
\right).
\]
The remainder is uniform in $e,g\in \mathbb{S}^{k-1}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
Let H and K be Hilbert spaces. A bounded operator T: H -> K is Hilbert-Schmidt if sum_{i in I} ||T e_i||^2 < infinity for some orthonormal basis (e_i)_{i in I} of H. The sum is then the same for every orthonormal basis of H, and ||T||_2 = (sum_i ||T e_i||^2)^{1/2} is the Hilbert-Schmidt norm. Equivalently, T is compact and sum_n s_n(T)^2 < infinity, with ||T||_2^2 = sum_n s_n(T)^2. Properties: ||T|| <= ||T||_2; ||T*||_2 = ||T||_2; every Hilbert-Schmidt operator is compact (it is the ||.||_2-limit, hence operator-norm limit, of finite-rank operators); the Hilbert-Schmidt operators S_2(H,K) form a Hilbert space under <A,B>_2 = sum_i <A e_i, B e_i> = tr(B*A), independent of the basis; and they form an ideal: ||A T B||_2 <= ||A|| ||T||_2 ||B|| for bounded A, B. Basis independence follows from sum_i ||T e_i||^2 = sum_i sum_j |<T e_i, f_j>|^2 = sum_j ||T* f_j||^2 for any orthonormal basis (f_j) of K.
H and K are Hilbert spaces
T: H -> K is a bounded linear operator

[Proposition classification_halfplane of arXiv:2603.05491, '\textbf{Local limits of uniform triangulations with boundaries in high genus}'] \begin{enumerate}
\item  For any $0 \le \lambda \le \lambda_c$, there exists a unique random triangulation of the half-plane\footnote{Here $\widetilde{\mathbb{H}}_{\lambda}$ is the analogue of $H_{\alpha}$ for $\alpha \le \frac{2}{3}$, and $\mathbb{H}_{\lambda}$ is the analogue of $H_{\alpha}$ for $\alpha \ge \frac{2}{3}$.} $\widetilde{\mathbb{H}}_{\lambda}$ characterized by the probabilities
\[
\mathbb{P}(t \subset \widetilde{\mathbb{H}}_{\lambda}) = \big(32h+4\big)^{|\partial^{*}t| - |\partial t|}\lambda^{v_{\mathrm{in}}}.
\]
In particular, we have $\widetilde{\mathbb{H}}_{\lambda_c} = \mathbb{H}_{\lambda_c}$.
\item  Let $H$ be a strongly Markovian random triangulation of the half-plane. Then $H$ is either of the form $\mathbb{H}_{\lambda}$ for some $0 < \lambda \le \lambda_c$ or $\widetilde{\mathbb{H}}_{\lambda}$ for some $0 \le \lambda \le \lambda_c$.

\item  Let $H$ be a weakly Markovian random triangulation of the half-plane. Then $H$ is a mixture of $\{\mathbb{H}_{\lambda}\}_{0 < \lambda \le \lambda_c} \cup \{\widetilde{\mathbb{H}}_{\lambda}\}_{0 \le \lambda \le \lambda_c}$.

\end{enumerate}

body: [Defi Closed walk of arXiv:2607.28817, 'Limiting spectral distribution for the adjacency matrix of the Watts--Strogatz random grap'] For any rooted graph $(G,o)$ and any $k\ge1$, a closed walk of length $k$ is a sequence of vertices $v_1,\dots,v_{k+1}$ such that $v_1=v_{k+1}$ and, for every $i\in\{1,\dots,k\}$, the edge $\{v_i,v_{i+1}\}$ is an edge of $G$. If, moreover, $v_1=o$, then the walk is called a closed rooted walk. The number of closed rooted walks of length $k$ in $(G,o)$ is denoted by $c_k(G,o)$.

[Theorem 13 of arXiv:2607.28578, 'On two differing geometric descriptions of the passage from microscopy to macroscopy in Ma'] Let $[f]$ be a regular covector. Then the following statements hold.
	\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
		\item The Otto and Stein density tangents agree if and only if
		\[
			\Mop_{\rho}\grad f=\grad f.
		\]
		\item The selected particle fields agree in $L^2(\rho;TM)$ if and only if
		\[
			\mathsf{S}_{\rho}\grad f=\grad f.
		\]
		\item Equality of the density tangents implies that the difference $\mathsf{S}_{\rho}\grad f-\grad f$ is vertical, namely it belongs to $\Ker\Aop_{\rho}$. Thus equal laws may retain different particle motions.
		\item The tangent defect satisfies the exact identity
		\begin{equation}
			\|\Kop^{\Stein}_{\rho}f-\Kop^{\Wass}_{\rho}f\|_{\dot H^{-1}_{\rho}}=\|(\Mop_{\rho}-\id)\grad f\|_{L^2(\rho)}.
		\end{equation}
	\end{enumerate}

body:
[Lem 25 of arXiv:2511.20322, 'Dissertation'] Let $A : \N_0 \to \R^{d\times d}$ and $x,B : \N_0 \to \R^d$ be sequences. Then the linear recurrence
	\[x_{n+1} = A_n x_n + B_n\]
	has the solution 
	\[x_n = x_0 \prod_{k=0}^{n-1}A_k + \sum_{l=0}^{n-1}\left(\prod_{k=l+1}^{n-1}A_k\right) B_l.\]
	\begin{proof}
		The statement holds for $n = 0$. Suppose it holds for $n\in \N$. Then,
		\begin{align*}
			x_{n+1} = & A_n x_n + B_n\\
			= & x_0 \prod_{k=0}^n A_k + \sum_{l=0}^{n-1}\left(\prod_{k=l+1}^n A_k\right) B_l + B_n \\
			= & x_0 \prod_{k=0}^nA_k + \sum_{l=0}^n \left(\prod_{k=l+1}^n A_k\right) B_l.
		\end{align*}
	\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: Publication record. Y. Shmalo, The discrepancy of Sylvester-Hadamard matrices in odd dimension (October 2026), proves that for the 2^k x 2^k Sylvester-Hadamard matrix H_k, disc(H_k) = 2^k - 2 rho(1,k), where rho(1,k) is the covering radius of the first-order Reed-Muller code RM(1,k). With the known values and bounds for that covering radius this settles Conjecture 13 of Randomstrasse101, Open problems of 2024 (arXiv:2504.20539): disc(H_k) = 2^((k+1)/2) holds for k = 1, 3, 5, 7 and fails for every odd k >= 9, where disc(H_k) <= (7/8) 2^((k+1)/2); in particular disc(H_9) <= 28 < 32. An exhaustive check for k <= 4 accompanies the paper. Paper and code: https://github.com/yspennstate/hadamard-discrepancy-odd (commit 0ec54610b38a). Not refereed.
title: Discrepancy of Sylvester-Hadamard matrices: disc(H_k) = 2^k - 2 rho(1,k), settling Conjecture 13 of Open problems of 2024 in odd dimension (Shmalo 2026, repository yspennstate/hadamard-discrepancy-odd)

[Definition 2 of arXiv:2512.05466, 'Stochastic Flows and Marked Stable Processes'] \cite[Definition 2.15]{AWYskew}
   Let $\cW$ be a white noise with respect to some filtration $\cF$.  Let $\overline{\delta}$ be a drift function with respect to ${\mathcal F}$.  
   We call a collection of non-negative processes $\cS=(\cS_{r,x}(a),\, x\ge r)_{r\in \bR,a\ge 0}$ a ${\rm BESQ}(\overline{\delta})$ flow driven by $\cW$ if 
   
    (1) The restriction of $\cS$ to each $A_i$ is a ${\rm BESQ}^{\delta_i}$ flow driven by $\cW$.

    (2) The regularity conditions of Definition \ref{def:BESQflow} hold.

If $E$ is a (possibly random) Borel set, we call $\rm BESQ(\overline{\delta})$ flow killed on $E$ the flow obtained from the $\rm BESQ(\overline{\delta})$ flow by absorbing the flow line $\cS_{r,\cdot}(a)$ at $0$ at time $\inf\{x \in E\cap (r,\infty) \,:\, \cS_{r,x}(a)=0\}$.

 If $E=\bR$, we will simply call it killed  $\rm BESQ(\overline{\delta})$ flow. We call general  $\rm BESQ(\overline{\delta})$ flow a $\rm BESQ(\overline{\delta})$ flow or a  killed $\rm BESQ(\overline{\delta})$ flow.

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For Bernoulli percolation, and more generally for FKG-satisfying, translation-invariant models with finite energy (including the random-cluster model for cluster weight q>=1), the sharpness-of-phase-transition theorem shows that below the critical point p_c, the probability of connection to distance n decays exponentially in n, proved without duality via a finite-size criterion: a box functional phi_p(S), built from crossing probabilities and a weighted sum over pivotal edges, is shown to satisfy a differential inequality in p that forces it to either stay bounded (subcritical, exponential decay) or blow up past a threshold (supercritical), with the threshold identified as p_c. This unifies and reproves the classical results of Menshikov and of Aizenman-Barsky with a single argument that is robust enough to extend to Z^d for every d, to general transitive graphs, and to the random-cluster model. The theorem does not give the exact value of p_c, does not determine critical behavior exactly at p_c (critical exponents are a separate, generally much harder, question), and the exponential-decay rate produced is not claimed to be sharp or explicit. Typical failure: Assuming the Duminil-Copin-Tassion argument extends automatically to a non-FKG regime, such as random-cluster parameters q<1 or certain long-range or antiferromagnetic models, where positive association fails; the driving differential inequality depends essentially on FKG-type monotonicity and on finite energy, and dropping either hypothesis breaks the exponential-decay conclusion outright rather than merely weakening it. Canonical reference: Duminil-Copin and Tassion, 2016, Communications in Mathematical Physics; Duminil-Copin, Raoufi and Tassion, 2019, Annals of Mathematics.
translation-invariant (or vertex-transitive) graph structure
the FKG inequality for the measure, which for the random-cluster model restricts to cluster weight q>=1
finite energy, or an analogous positive-conditional-probability condition, for the percolation-type model
existence of the box functional phi_p(S) and the differential inequality relating its p-derivative to itself

body:
If X is Bernoulli(p), 0 <= p <= 1, then for every n >= 1, kappa_n(X) = sum_{k=1}^{n} (-1)^{k-1} (k-1)! S(n,k) p^k, where S(n,k) is the Stirling number of the second kind. For example kappa_2 = p(1-p) and kappa_3 = p(1-p)(1-2p).
n is a positive integer
0 <= p <= 1
X takes values 0 and 1 with P(X = 1) = p
S(n,k) counts set partitions of [n] into k nonempty blocks

[Proposition 55 of arXiv:2605.02430, '\textbf{Scaling limit of the range of tree-valued branching random walks in random environ'] We fix $\alpha \ino (1, 2]$. Let $\mu$ satisfy (\ref{hypostaintro}). Let $\nu$ be a supercritical offspring distribution whose mean is denoted by $\ttm_\nu$. We assume that there exists $\ttb \ino (2, \infty)$ such that 
$\sum_{k\in \bbN} k^\ttb \nu(k)\leko \infty$. Let $(\bT, \boo)$ be an invariant GW($\nu$)-tree. 
Let $\tau_{n,\infty}$, $n\ino \bbN$, be GW($\mu$)-forests that are independent from $(\bT, \boo)$ and 
such that (\ref{skoroderie}) holds true. Let $( \widehat{\cW}^*_s (\tau_{n, \infty}))_{s\in \bbR_+}$ be as in (\ref{skoroderie2}). We denote by $(W'_s)_{s\in \bbR_+}$ a one-dimensional Brownian snake starting at $0$ and whose lifetime process is $H'$.  
We recall from (\ref{vutchi}) the definition of $\sigma_\nu$. Then for all $p\ino \bbN^*$ and for all real numbers $0\leqo s_1\leko \ldots \leko s_p$ and $\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_p$, $\bP$-almost surely
\begin{equation}

\lim_{n\to \infty}\bE \Big[\prod_{1\leq j\leq p} \exp \Big( i \tfrac{1}{\sigma_\nu \sqrt{a_n}} \lambda_j  \widehat{\cW}^*_{\! \lfloor ns_j\rfloor} (\tau_{n, \infty}) \Big)  
\, \Big| \, (\bT, \boo) , \tau_{n,\infty} \Big] = \bE \Big[\prod_{1\leq j\leq p} e^{i  \lambda_j  \widehat{W}'_{s_j}  }  
\, \Big| H' \Big] .
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition prop:covbounds of arXiv:2608.16915, 'Exact mean--covariance dynamics of the Weber field in the stochastic Lagrangian representa'] Let $\sigma_J:=\sup_x(\tr Q(x))^{1/2}$ and
$L_J:=\sup_x(\mathbb{E}\left\lvert J(x)\right\rvert_{\mathrm F}^2)^{1/2}\le\sigma_J+\sqrt3\,\left\lVert M\right\rVert_{L^\infty}$, and
for $0<\beta\le1$ set
\[
  \mathsf H_{J,\beta}:=\sup_{x\ne y}
  \frac{\bigl(\mathbb{E}\left\lvert \widetilde J(x)-\widetilde J(y)\right\rvert_{\mathrm F}^2\bigr)^{1/2}}{d(x,y)^\beta},
\]
where $d$ is the geodesic distance on $\mathbb{T}^3$. Then
$\left\lVert \mathcal R\right\rVert_{L^\infty}\le\left\lVert u_0\right\rVert_{L^\infty}\sigma_J$, and there is a dimensional
constant $C$ such that
\begin{equation}
  \left\lVert \mathcal R\right\rVert_{C^\beta}\le C\Big[
  \left\lVert u_0\right\rVert_{L^\infty}(\sigma_J+\mathsf H_{J,\beta})
  +\left\lVert \nabla u_0\right\rVert_{L^\infty}\,\sigma_J\bigl(\sigma_J+\sqrt3\,\left\lVert M\right\rVert_{L^\infty}\bigr)\Big].
\end{equation}

[Definition of arXiv:2507.08757, 'Strong existence and uniqueness of the tilt-indexed Busemann process in the planar corner '] A \emph{shift-covariant recovering $L^1(\widehat\Omega,\widehat{\mathfrak{S}},\widehat\mathbb{P})$ cocycle} is a shift-covariant $L^1$ measurable function 
${\widehat B}:\widehat\Omega\times\mathbb{Z}^2\times\mathbb{Z}^2\to\mathbb{R}$
such that ${\widehat B}$ is $\widehat\mathbb{P}$-almost surely a recovering cocycle.  
The collection of all such cocycles is denoted by $\widehat{\mathcal{K}}$, and its elements are called \emph{generalized Busemann functions}.

body: [Theorem 78 of arXiv:2609.03875, 'Measure theory without infinities'] Let $\mathcal Q$ be a $\sigma$-ring and $\fm{f}{\ms M_\sigma(\mathcal Q,\mf R)}$ be such that $f(\eta) = \mf F\eta$ for every $\eta\in \ms M_\sigma(\mathcal Q,\mf R)$. body: In mathematics, the Weierstrass M-test is a test for determining whether an infinite series of functions converges uniformly and absolutely. It applies to series whose terms are bounded functions with real or complex values, and is analogous to the comparison test for determining the convergence of series of real or complex numbers. It is named after the German mathematician Karl Weierstrass (1815–1897).

[Proposition prop:zero-info-sharpness of arXiv:2609.02155, 'Exact Limits of Random Projections for Preserving Geometry:\\ Distance Recovery, Nearest-N'] In the setting of (prop:zeroinfo of the paper), let
$r=\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ and $0<\varepsilon\le1$. There are universal
constants $c,C>0$ such that
\[
\Pr(\mathcal E_\varepsilon^{\mathrm{rep}})
\le \exp\!\left(-cr e^{-Cm\varepsilon^2}\right).
\]
Consequently, if
$\Pr(\mathcal E_\varepsilon^{\mathrm{rep}})\ge1-\delta$, then
\[
m\ge\frac1{C\varepsilon^2}
\log\!\left(\frac{cr}{-\log(1-\delta)}\right)
\]
whenever the logarithm is positive. In particular, for $\delta\le1/2$ and
$n/\delta$ sufficiently large,
$m=\Omega(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(n/\delta))$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Sharp dimension order for independent Gaussian replacement maps

body:
[Lemma 31 (Entropy transfer through the random large-gap side) of arXiv:2607.04138, 'Hives from deformed GUE minor processes'] \lab{lem:random-side-entropy}
For \(n\geq2\), let \(\Gamma_n^X\) and \(\Gamma_n^Y\) be the complete eigenvalue minor
processes of \(X_n\) and \(Y_n\), respectively, and let
\(R_n=\check\lambda_n\).  With the coordinate Lebesgue measures in which
Proposition~\ref{gt-rem}(iv) is volume-preserving, the following assertions
hold.
\begin{enumerate}
\item The auxiliary spectrum satisfies
\[
\bigl|\ent(R_n)\bigr|=O(n\log n).
\]
\item For the one-hive construction,
\[
\bigl|\ent(L_n\mid\Gamma_n^X)\bigr|=O(n\log n).
\]
For the double-hive construction one has the exact identity
\[
\ent(L_n\mid\Gamma_n^X,\Gamma_n^Y)
=
\ent(R_n)
+n\log\left(n^{10}\left(1-\frac1n\right)\right).
\]
In particular, this conditional entropy is also \(O(n\log n)\) in
absolute value.
\item The large-gap bijections of Proposition~\ref{gt-rem}(iv), which apply
on every outcome by \eqref{eq:large-gap-every-outcome}, have extensions which
retain the random side \(L_n\) and have block-triangular Jacobian of absolute
determinant one.
Consequently,
\[
\ent(h_n)=\ent(\Gamma_n^X,L_n)
=\ent(\Gamma_n^X)+\ent(L_n\mid\Gamma_n^X)
\]
and
\begin{align*}
&\ent\!\left(h_n^{(1)},h_n^{(2)}
       \hbox{ pasted along }L_n\right)\\
&\qquad=
\ent(\Gamma_n^X,\Gamma_n^Y,L_n)\\
&\qquad=
\ent(\Gamma_n^X)+\ent(\Gamma_n^Y)
+\ent(L_n\mid\Gamma_n^X,\Gamma_n^Y).
\end{align*}
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Entropy transfer through the random large-gap side

[Lem 5 ({\cite[Lemma 1.4) of arXiv:2608.13727, 'Hitting-time mixing for the star transposition shuffle'] {comparison-nestoridi}}]  Let \(P\) and \(Q\) be the transition matrices of two reversible Markov chains \(X_t\) and \(Y_s\) on a finite state space \(\cS\) that share the same eigenbasis and stationary measure \(\pi\). Let \(\varphi_i: \cS \to \bbC\) be a common orthonormal eigenbasis of \(\ell^2(\pi)\), with inner product
$\langle f,g\rangle_\pi:=\sum_{x\in\cS}f(x)\overline{g(x)}\pi(x),$
satisfying \[P \varphi_i = \alpha_i \varphi_i, \quad \text{and} \quad Q \varphi_i = \beta_i \varphi_i.\]
For every \(x \in \cS\), and \(t, s \geq 0\), we have \[4\|P^t(x,\cdot)-Q^{s}(x,\cdot)\|_{TV}^2
\;\le\;
\sum_{i\ge2}^{|\cS|} |\varphi_i(x)|^2\bigl(\alpha_i^{t}-\beta_i^{s}\bigr)^2.
\]
If $P$ and $Q$ are random walks on a group $S$, then
\[4\|P^t(x,\cdot)-Q^{s}(x,\cdot)\|_{TV}^2
\;\le\;
\sum_{i\ge2}^{|\cS|} \bigl(\alpha_i^{t}-\beta_i^{s}\bigr)^2. 
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Definition 4 of arXiv:2608.25772, 'Propagation of Chaos and Gaussian Fluctuations for Mean-field Coupled Maps'] Let $E$ be a Polish space and $\rho$ be a probability measure on $E$. A sequence $P_N$ of symmetric $N$-particle probability measures on $E^N$ for all $N\geq 1$ is said to be \textit{$\rho$-chaotic} if for all $k\geq 1$, $P_{N:k}$ converges weakly to $\rho^{\otimes k}$ as $N\to\infty$, where $P_{N:k}$ is the $k$-marginal of $P_N$.

body:
[Prop 4 of arXiv:2607.24170, '\large\bf ON NON-MONOTONICITY OF LOGARITHMIC ENERGY\\ FOR RANDOM MATRICES'] Let $\mu$ be a compactly supported probability measure on $\R$ with
a bounded density.  Then
\begin{equation}
 \cF_{\R}(\mu)-\frac34
 =
 \int\mathfrak{v}_{\mathrm{sc}}(x)\,\mu(\mathrm{d}x)
 +\int_0^\infty
 \frac{|\widehat\mu(t)-\widehat\sigma(t)|^2}{t}\mathrm{d}t,
\end{equation}
where
\[
 \widehat\mu(t)\overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}
 \int \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}tx}\mu(\mathrm{d}x).
\]
In particular,
\[
 \cF_{\R}(\mu)\geq\frac34,
\]
and the inequality is strict whenever $\mu((-\infty,-2)\cup
(2,\infty))>0$.

$(B_1,\ldots,B_N)$ we define $U=(U_1,\ldots,U_N)$ as a solution to the system
\begin{equation}
    
    dU_k
    =
    \sum_{i=1}^N a_{i,k}^{R}(t, \tilde f(U))\,dB_i
    + \sum_{i=1}^N h_{i,k}^{R}(t, \tilde f(U))\,dt
    + \sum_{\alpha\in R_+}
        H_{\alpha,k}^R(\tilde f(U))\,k_\alpha(t,\tilde f(U))\,dt,
\end{equation}
for every $k=1,\ldots,N$, with initial condition $U(0)=u_0\in\R^N$.

DRAFT independently checked special-case formula: w355's full-packet audit checked Section 5; w356 kept its d=2,k=2 specialization. No novelty or full KLS claim. Let d>=2, K=(d+1)(d+2), X be uniform on Delta_d={x_i>=0,sum_i x_i<=1}, m=(1,...,1)/(d+1), Sigma=(I-J/(d+1))/K with J the all-ones matrix, A=Sigma^(-1/2), Y=A(X-m), a=sqrt(2K), and v=Ae_1/a. Put Z=Proj_(v-perp)Y, T=<v,Y> and S=sum_(j=2)^d X_j. For every integer k>=1 put t=1-S, f(Y)=T t^k and M_p=(p+1)! d!/(d+p)!. Then E[f|Z]=0, E Var(f|Z)=(K/6) M_(2k+2), E|partial_v f|^2=M_(2k), and E|grad f|^2=[1+k^2(d-1)/(3(d+1))] M_(2k). Thus the exact directional quotient is R_(d,k)=(K/6)(2k+2)(2k+3)/[(d+2k+1)(d+2k+2)], while the full-gradient quotient is R_(d,k)/[1+k^2(d-1)/(3(d+1))]. The extra factor is the transverse gradient cost: grad_Y S is perpendicular to v and has squared norm 2(d-1)/((d+1)K). For d=2,k=2 these give variance 1/2, directional energy 1/3 and full energy 13/27. The family generalizes the separately submitted triangle witness and explicitly preserves all gradient terms.

[Lemma 14 (Refined ring lemma for RCP) of arXiv:2608.03575, '2608.03575'] Let $(G,\Theta)$ be a tame ADT satisfying (Z1)--(Z4), and assume that (Z2) is strengthened to (Z2'). Let $r:V\to(0,\infty)$ denote the radius function of an embedding in the plane. Then there exists a constant $C=C(\varepsilon_0,\varepsilon_1)$, where $\varepsilon_0$ is the constant in (Z2') and $\varepsilon_1$ is the tameness constant in the angle upper bound $\Theta(e)\leq \pi-\varepsilon_1$, such that for every edge $u\sim v$,
\[
\frac{r(v)}{r(u)} > e^{-C\cdot S(u)},
\]
where $S(u)=\sum_{v'\sim u}\deg(v')$ is the \emph{flower degree} of $u$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Definition SDS of arXiv:2603.12774, 'Synchronization by noise for stochastic differential equations driven by fractional Browni'] Let $\mathcal{B}$ be a Polish space equipped with the Borel $\sigma$-algebra $\sigma(\mathcal{B})$. 
	A quadruple $\left(\mathcal{B}, \{P_t\}_{t \geq 0}, \mathbf{P}, \{\vartheta_t\}_{t \geq 0}\right)$ is called a {stationary noise process} if the following properties hold.
	\begin{itemize}
		\item [(i)] The measure $\mathbf{P}$ is a probability measure on $(\mathcal{B}, \sigma(\mathcal{B}))$. Also, for each $t \geq 0$, the maps 
		$P_t: \mathcal{B} \times \mathcal{B} \to \mathcal{B}$ and 
		$\vartheta_t: \mathcal{B} \to \mathcal{B}$ 
		are measurable, and for every $\omega^- \in \mathcal{B}$, the random variables 
		$P_t(\omega^-, \cdot)$ and $\vartheta_t$ are independent.
		\item [(ii)] The family $\{\vartheta_t\}_{t \geq 0}$ forms a semiflow on $\mathcal{B}$, i.e. 
		$\vartheta_{t+s} = \vartheta_t \circ \vartheta_s$, and preserves $\mathbf{P}$, that is $(\vartheta_t)_{\star}\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{P}$.
		\item [(iii)] For $\omega^- \in \mathcal{B}$ and $t \geq 0$, define
		\[
		\mathcal{P}_t(\omega^-; \cdot) := (P_t(\omega^-, \cdot))_{\star}(\mathbf{P}).
		\]
		The family $\{\mathcal{P}_t\}_{t \geq 0}$ forms a Feller transition semigroup on $\mathcal{B}$.
		Moreover, $\mathbf{P}$ is the unique invariant measure of $\{\mathcal{P}_t\}_{t \geq 0}$.
		\item [(iv)] For all $\omega^-, \omega^+ \in \mathcal{B}$ and $t,s \geq 0$,
		\begin{align*}
			&\vartheta_t \circ P_t(\omega^-, \omega^+) 
			= P_t(\vartheta_t \omega^-, P_t(\omega^+, \omega^-)) = \omega^-,\\
			&P_{t+s}(\omega^-, \omega^+) 
			= P_t(P_s(\omega^-, \omega^+), \vartheta_s \omega^+).
		\end{align*}
	\end{itemize}
title: Definition SDS of arXiv:2603.12774

body: [Lemma 17 of arXiv:2609.03951, 'Generalized Semi-Riemannian Submersions and Foliations'] Let $(M,g)$ be a semi-Riemannian manifold, and let $\pi:(M,g) \to B$ be a submersion such that the horizontal distribution is locally generated by basic vector fields. If $U$ is vertical and $\tilde{X}$ is the horizontal lift of a vector field $X \in \mathfrak{X}(\mathcal{D})$, then $[U, \tilde{X}]$ is also vertical. If $\mathcal{D} = d\pi(\mathcal{H})$ is involutive, then $[\tilde{X}, \tilde{Y}] - \widetilde{[X,Y]}$ is vertical for any $X, Y \in \mathfrak{X}(\mathcal{D})$, where $\tilde{X}, \tilde{Y}$, and $\widetilde{[X,Y]}$ are the horizontal lifts of $X$, $Y$, and $[X,Y]$, respectively.

\begin{equation}

        d_{\rm TV}\bigl(\mathcal L(\mathcal E_\vartheta),
        \mathcal L_\Gamma(\Gamma_\vartheta)\bigr)\longrightarrow0,
        \qquad n\to\infty .
\end{equation}

probability space so that
\[
        \mathbb P(\mathcal E_\vartheta\ne\Gamma_\vartheta)\longrightarrow0. 
\]

body:
[Corollary 8 of arXiv:2506.12632, 'Point process convergence of extremes in $K$-symmetric exclusion'] Suppose $p$ satisfies Condition \ref{lighttail}, $\nu$ satisfies Condition \ref{initialprofilecond}, and $\eta_0 \sim \nu_L$, where $L \uparrow \infty$ as $t \to \infty$. If $\lim_{t\to\infty} L\big(\frac{\log t}{t}\big)^{1/2} > 0$, then for any $m \ge 1$, 
\begin{equation}
	\bigg( \frac{X^{(0)}_{t/K} - X^{(1)}_{t/K}}{\sigma b_t}, 
	\ldots, \frac{X^{(m-1)}_{t/K} - X^{(m)}_{t/K}}{\sigma b_t} \bigg) \underset{t\to\infty}{\Longrightarrow} \bigg( \log \frac{T_1}{T_0}, 
	\ldots, \log \frac{T_m}{T_{m-1}} \bigg), 
\end{equation}
where $\{\log\big(\frac{T_k}{T_{k-1}}\big) : k \ge 1\}$ are independent and $\log\big(\frac{T_k}{T_{k-1}}\big) \sim \text{Exponential}\,(k)$. If $L\big(\frac{\log t}{t}\big)^{1/2} \to 0$, then \eqref{eq:spacingdist} holds with $b_{t,L}$ in place of $b_t$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Corollary 8 of arXiv:2506.12632

body:
[Theorem thm:main of arXiv:2605.11108, 'Empirical Convergence of Even-Order Gromov--Wasserstein Functionals'] Let $\mu\in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)$ and $\nu\in \mathcal P(\mathcal Y)$, where
\[
    \mathcal X\subset \mathbb R^{d_x},
    \qquad
    \mathcal Y\subset \mathbb R^{d_y}
\]
are compact. Set
\[
    R:=\operatorname{diam}(\mathcal X)\vee \operatorname{diam}(\mathcal Y),
    \qquad
    d_\ast:=d_x\wedge d_y.
\]
By translation invariance, we may assume
\[
    \mathcal X\subset B_{d_x}(0,R),
    \qquad
    \mathcal Y\subset B_{d_y}(0,R).
\]
Let
\[
    \widehat\mu_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{X_i},
    \qquad
    \widehat\nu_n=\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n\delta_{Y_j},
\]
where $(X_i)_{i\ge1}$ are i.i.d.\ with law $\mu$, $(Y_j)_{j\ge1}$ are i.i.d.\ with law $\nu$, and the two
samples are independent. Then, for every pair of integers $r,k\ge1$,
\[
\mathbb E\Bigl|
\mathcal D_{r,k}(\mu,\nu)
-
\mathcal D_{r,k}(\widehat\mu_n,\widehat\nu_n)
\Bigr|
\lesssim_{r,k,d_x,d_y}
R^{4kr}
\begin{cases}
n^{-1/2}, & d_\ast<4,\\[2mm]
n^{-1/2}\log(en), & d_\ast=4,\\[2mm]
n^{-2/d_\ast}, & d_\ast>4.
\end{cases}
\]
Equivalently, if
\[
    \rho_n(d):=
    n^{-2/(d\vee 4)}\log(en)^{\mathbf 1_{\{d=4\}}},
\]
then
\[
\mathbb E\Bigl|
\mathcal D_{r,k}(\mu,\nu)
-
\mathcal D_{r,k}(\widehat\mu_n,\widehat\nu_n)
\Bigr|
\lesssim_{r,k,d_x,d_y}
R^{4kr}\rho_n(d_\ast).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm:main of arXiv:2605.11108

[Lemma lem:partial-line of arXiv:2608.20480, 'When Clean Data Hurts: Learning with Monotone \\ Corruptions Beyond Binary Classification'] Fix $B\in\mathcal{B}_r$, a $B$-line $L$, and $u,v\in L$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2em]
    \item If $t\notin B$, every target indexed by a state in $L$ is defined on every point $x(u,t,b)$ and gives the label $\lambda_{\{c_t(u),b\}}(c_t(u))$.
    \item If $t\in B$, all states in $L$ have the same $t$-cell, while their colors at $z_t$ enumerate $\mathbb{F}_q$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma liplemma of arXiv:2606.15203, 'The existence of invariant sublinear expectations for $G\text{-}$SDEs'] The function $\Lambda_{t,T}[\cdot]: L^2(\Omega,\mathcal{F}_t,P;\mathbb{R}^d) \to L^2(\Omega,\mathcal{F}_t,P;\mathbb{R})$ has the following properties, for each $\xi$, $\xi^{\prime}\in L^2(\mathcal{F}_t)$,\\
\rm{(1)} $\Lambda_{t,T}[\xi]\leq C_{\varphi}$;\\
\rm{(2)} $\vert \Lambda_{t,T}[\xi]-\Lambda_{t,T}[\xi^{\prime}]\vert\leq K_{\varphi}\vert \xi-\xi^{\prime} \vert$,\\
where $C_{\varphi} = \underset{x}{{\rm sup}} \ \varphi(x)$ and $K_\varphi$ is the Lipschitz constant of $\varphi$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma liplemma of arXiv:2606.15203

[Proposition prop:precision of arXiv:2608.04162, 'Correlation Matrices in High Dimensions:\\ The Elliptope as a Sample-Correlation Ensemble'] (i) Let $C_n$ be uniformly distributed on $\mathcal{E}_n$. Then
$$
\tfrac{1}{n}\operatorname{tr}(C_n^{-1})\rightarrow\infty,\qquad\text{in probability}.
$$
(ii) Let $\hat{C}_n$ be the sample correlation matrix of $n$ independent Gaussian variables based on $T$ observations, where $n/T\rightarrow c\in(0,1)$. Then
$$
\tfrac{1}{n}\operatorname{tr}(\hat{C}_n^{-1})\rightarrow\frac{1}{1-c},\qquad\text{almost surely}.
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition prop:precision of arXiv:2608.04162
