[Definition Convolutors \(\mathcal O'_C(\R^d)\) of arXiv:2512.04371, 'Constructive Approximation under Carleman's Condition, \\ with Applications to Smoothed An'] We denote by \(\mathcal O'_C(\mathbb{R}^d)\) the space of distributions \(T\in\mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R}^d)\) with the following property:
for every integer \(h\ge 0\) there exist an integer \(m(h)\ge 0\) and a finite family
\(\{f_p\}_{p\in\mathbb{N}^n,\ |p|\le m(h)}\subset C^0(\mathbb{R}^d)\) such that
\[
  T=\sum_{|p|\le m(h)} \partial_x^p f_p,
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
  \lim_{|x|\to\infty} (1+\left|x\right|)^{\,h}\, \left|f_p(x)\right|=0
  \ \ \text{for all } p\in\mathbb{N}^n,\ |p|\le m(h).
\]
Equivalently, \(\mathcal O'_C(\mathbb{R}^d)\) is the space of those distributions for which the convolution
operator \(\varphi\mapsto T*\varphi\) maps \(\mathcal S(\mathbb{R}^d)\) continuously into itself (“convolution
operators on \(\mathcal S\)”).
title: Convolutors \(\mathcal O'_C(\R^d)\)

body:
[Definition def:erase_two_sided of arXiv:2605.16086, 'Loop pruning and downward deviations for maximum local time of discrete-time simple random'] Let \(E\) be a finite set of loops and let \(\mathbf{s}=\mathbf{s}(-\infty,\infty)\) be a two-sided path. 
Suppose that the set of indices \(i\in\mathbb Z\) for which \((\mathbf{s}_{i-1},\mathbf{s}_i)\) is an \(E\)-cut step is unbounded both above and below.

We say that a step \((\mathbf{s}_{i-1},\mathbf{s}_i)\) is retained in the pruning of \(\mathbf{s}\) by \(E\) if there exist indices \(m_1< i\le m_2\) such that both boundary steps \((\mathbf{s}_{m_1-1},\mathbf{s}_{m_1})\) and \((\mathbf{s}_{m_2-1},\mathbf{s}_{m_2})\) are \(E\)-cut steps, and \((\mathbf{s}_{i-1},\mathbf{s}_i)\) is retained in the finite-window pruning
\[
\mathsf{Prune}\big(\mathbf{s}[m_1,m_2],E\big).
\]
(It is straightforward to check that this notion does not depend on the particular choice of \(m_1,m_2\).)

Collecting all retained steps in chronological order yields a two-sided path (defined up to translation), which we denote by \(\mathsf{Prune}(\mathbf{s},E)\).
title: Definition def:erase_two_sided of arXiv:2605.16086

body:
[Proposition thm.mtg of arXiv:2605.17725, 'Limit theorems for random walks with spatio-temporal drift'] Let $(X_{n,i}, \mathcal{F}_{n,i})_{1\le i\le k_n, n\ge 1}$ be a martingale difference array in $\mathbb{R}^d$ satisfying the following condition:
\begin{itemize}
    \item For every $\varepsilon > 0$,
$$
\sum_{i=1}^{k_n} \mathbb{E}\left[ X_{n,i} X_{n,i}^\top \mathbf{1}_{\{\norm{X_{n,i}} > \varepsilon\}} \mid \mathcal{F}_{n,i-1} \right] \xrightarrow{p} 0.
$$
\item There exists a non-random positive semi-definite matrix $\Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$ such that:
$$
\sum_{i=1}^{k_n} \mathbb{E}[X_{n,i}X_{n,i}^\top \mid \mathcal{F}_{n,i-1}] \xrightarrow{p} \Sigma.
$$
\end{itemize} 
Then $$\sum_{i=1}^{k_n} X_{n,i} \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}_d(0, \Sigma).$$

body: Over the abelian group G = Z2 x Z6 (element k written as (k div 6, k mod 6)), the squares L_i(x, y) = x + theta_i(y) are Latin whenever theta_i permutes G, and L_i is orthogonal to L_j exactly when theta_i - theta_j is a bijection. With theta_1 the identity, theta_2 = [0, 2, 1, 6, 8, 7, 5, 10, 3, 11, 4, 9] and theta_3 = [0, 3, 7, 9, 6, 4, 1, 5, 11, 10, 8, 2] give three pairwise orthogonal Latin squares of order 12, and the resulting orthogonal array OA(12, 5) with 144 rows covers every ordered pair exactly once in each of its ten coordinate pairs (strength 2, index 1). The cyclic group Z12 admits no such linear construction, since differences of units mod 12 are even; Z2 x Z6 satisfies the Hall-Paige condition for complete mappings. All three squares have 108 intercalates.

body:
[Theorem RDS_SDS_MEAU of arXiv:2603.12774, 'Synchronization by noise for stochastic differential equations driven by fractional Browni'] Under the assumptions of Lemma~(RR_TT of the paper), for every $\omega = (\omega^-, \omega^+) \in \mathcal{B}_H \times \mathcal{B}_H$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$, 
	let us denote the solution of the SDE~(equation MAIN of the paper) by $(\Phi^{t}_{(\omega^-, \omega^+)}(x))_{t \ge 0}$, i.e.,
	\begin{align*}
		\Phi^{t}_{(\omega^-, \omega^+)}(x) = x + \int_{0}^{t} F\big(\Phi^{s}_{(\omega^-, \omega^+)}(x)\big)\, \mathrm{d}s + \sigma B_{t}^{H}(\omega).
	\end{align*}
	Then the following assertions hold for $t \geq 0$, $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and $\omega = (\omega^-, \omega^+) \in \mathcal{B}_H \times \mathcal{B}_H$.
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item  
		The value $\Phi^{t}_{\theta_{-t}(\omega^-, \omega^+)}(x)$ is independent of $\omega^+$ and depends only on $\omega^-$. In particular, setting
		\[
		\varphi^{t}_{\omega^-}(x) := \Phi^{t}_{\theta_{-t}(\omega^-, \omega^+)}(x),
		\]
		where the shift map $(\theta_t)_{t \geq 0}$ is defined in~(equation semigr of the paper), entails a \( C^1 \)-SDS on \( \mathcal{X} = \mathbb{R}^d \) with the stationary noise process introduced in Lemma~(AJSJAsd of the paper). 
		
		\item It holds that $\Phi^{t}_{(\omega^-, \omega^+)}(x) = \varphi^{t}_{P_{t}(\omega^-, \omega^+)}(x)$. 
		Moreover, $\Phi$ is a $C^1$-RDS by Theorem~(RDS_SDS of the paper).  
		\item The SDS~$\varphi$ admits a unique invariant (and hence ergodic) measure~$\mu$ in the sense of Definition~(DEAFRS of the paper).  
		In addition, for the law of the solution $(\Phi^{t}_{(\omega^-, \omega^+)}(x))_{t \geq 0}$, we have the convergence
		\begin{align}
			\mathcal{L}\left(\Phi^{t}_{(\omega^-, \omega^+)}(x)\right) \xrightarrow{t \to \infty} (\Pi_{\mathbb{R}^d})_{\star} \mu,
		\end{align}
		in total variation.
		
		
			
			
	\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Defn Affine standard module and Gram product of arXiv:2506.01306, 'Asymptotic of Coulomb gas integral, Temperley-Lieb type algebras and pure partition functi'] Let $\widetilde{V}_{n,m}$ be the standard module, define the Gram inner product $\langle \cdot \mid \cdot \rangle_G$ on $\widetilde{V}_{n,m}$ by:
\[
\left\langle \alpha \mid \beta \right\rangle_G := 
\begin{cases}
0 & \text{if any two defects from } \alpha \text{ or } \beta \text{ are connected}, \\
a^{n_a} b^{n_b} & \text{otherwise},
\end{cases}
\]
where $n_a$ and $n_b$ denote the numbers of contractible and non-contractible loops formed in the concatenated diagram $\mathcal{G}(\alpha, \beta)$, and $a, b$ are loop weights.

[Prop global-lvl-GSp of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] Let $G$ be a compact Lie group. There exists a (unique) model structure on $\cat{$\bm{G}$-OrthSp}$ in which a map $f\colon X\to Y$ is a weak equivalence or fibration if and only if for every finite-dimensional inner product space $V$, $f(V)\colon X(V)\to Y(V)$ is a weak equivalence or fibration, respectively, in the $\mathcal G_{{\textup{O}}(V),G}$-equivariant model structure\footnote{We emphasize that this is different from the $\mathcal G_{G,{\textup{O}}(V)}$-model structure used to the define the \emph{$G$-equivariant} level weak equivalences.} on $\cat{$\bm{({\textup{O}}(V)\times G)}$-Top}$. We call this the \emph{$\bm G$-global level model structure} and its weak equivalences the \emph{$\bm G$-global level weak equivalences}. If $f\colon X\to Y$ is any cofibration in the model structure, then $f(V)$ is in particular a $\mathcal G_{{\textup{O}}(V),G}$-cofibration for every inner product space $V$, and likewise for the acyclic cofibrations.
    
    Moroever, the $G$-global level model structure is proper, topological, and cofibrantly generated with generating cofibrations
    \[
        I=\{\textbf{\textup{O}}(V,-)\smashp_\varphi G_+\smashp(\partial D^n\hookrightarrow D^n)_+ : \text{$V\in\textbf{\textup{O}}$, $H\subset {\textup{O}}(V)$, $\varphi\colon H\to G$, $n\ge0$}\}
    \]
    and generating acyclic cofibrations
    \[
        J=\{\textbf{\textup{O}}(V,-)\smashp_\varphi G_+\smashp(D^n\hookrightarrow D^n\times I)_+ : \text{$V\in\textbf{\textup{O}}$, $H\subset {\textup{O}}(V)$, $\varphi\colon H\to G$, $n\ge0$}\}.
    \] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Theorem thm:lehner-random of arXiv:2606.14687, 'Lehner's operator norm formulas, semidefinite programming, and spiked matrix models'] Let $\bm A_0, \bm A_1, \dots, \bm A_n \in \mathbb{C}^{d \times d}_{\mathsf{herm}}$.
    Then, the following hold, with convergences in probability as $m \to \infty$:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item Let $\bm W_1^{(m)}, \dots, \bm W^{(m)}_n \sim \GOE(m)$ independently. Then,
            \[ \lambda_{\max}\left(\bm A_0 \otimes \bm I_m + \sum_{i = 1}^n \bm A_i \otimes \bm W_i^{(m)}\right) \to \Lambda_{\mathsf{sc}}(\bm A_0, \bm A_1, \dots, \bm A_n). \]
        \item Let $\bm P_1^{(m)}, \dots, \bm P_n^{(m)}$ be projection matrices to independent Haar-distributed subspaces of $\mathbb{C}^m$ of dimension $m/2$ for each even $m$.
            Write $\bm R_i^{(m)} \colonequals \bm I_m - 2\bm P_i^{(m)}$ for each $m \geq 1$ and $i \in [n]$ (forming orthogonal reflection matrices).
            Then, taking the limit only over even $m$,
            \[ \lambda_{\max}\left(\bm A_0 \otimes \bm I_m + \sum_{i = 1}^n \bm A_i \otimes \bm R_i^{(m)}\right) \to \Lambda_{\mathsf{rad}}(\bm A_0, \bm A_1, \dots, \bm A_n). \]
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

On P_2(R^d), let F=G+tau H be convex under linear mixing, where tau>0 and H(mu)=integral log(dmu/dx) dmu for absolutely continuous mu, and +infinity otherwise. For every mu, G admits a first variation G_prime[mu] in C^1(R^d) of the form G_prime[mu](x)=a|x|^2/2+V[mu](x), with a,L>0 independent of mu and |grad V[mu](x)|<=L for every mu,x. A Wasserstein gradient flow here means a P_2-continuous distributional solution partial_t mu_t=div(mu_t grad G_prime[mu_t])+tau Delta mu_t, positive for t>0, which satisfies F(mu_t2)-F(mu_t1)=-integral_t1^t2 integral |grad G_prime[mu_s]+tau grad log(mu_s)|^2 dmu_s ds. Suppose there exist sigma_1,sigma_2,m,M>0 such that m gamma_1(x)<=mu_t(x)<=M gamma_2(x) for every t>=0 and almost every x, where gamma_i is the density of N(0,sigma_i^2 I_d). Assume 0<sigma_1<=sigma_2<sqrt(2) sigma_1 and finite initial gap h_0=F(mu_0)-inf F. Set r=sigma_2^2/sigma_1^2 and C=(2r-r^2)^(-d/2). Then for every t>=0, F(mu_t)-inf F <= [h_0^(-1)+m^2 t/(4 C M^2 sigma_1^2)]^(-1). If h_0=0 the right side means zero. In particular the result requires linear convexity of F, without requiring a log-Sobolev inequality for mu_t. The Gaussian-comparison factor C can grow exponentially with d when r>1 is fixed.

STATEMENT
Fix b=9/10,d=999/1000,nu=1-d,c=1/19,gamma=9/19 and constant
0<=e<1/2. Let (y_t,z_t,V_t,q_t), t in all integers, satisfy

 V'=d*V+nu*y^2, z'=y, q'*s'=y,

Assume sup_t V_t<infinity. Retain both branch labels at s=1:
L is permitted when s>=1; H when s<=1.
Let Gamma(V)=8*gamma*min(sqrt(V),1-e)^3/3, and define
 phi_L=-c*(y-z)^2/2-Gamma(V),
 phi_H=(y^2-b*z^2)/(1+b)-(y+q-z)^2/2-Gamma(V).
On every edge put Psi=phi'-phi-[(q')^2-2*y*q'].
Assume Psi=0 on EVERY edge. Finally assume F3 explicitly:
on every regular edge with source H label, w=1/s'>c.
Regular here means s>0 and s'>0; on regular edges p=1/s.

Then the entire PHYSICAL STATE history is either the origin
(y,z,V,q)=(0,0,0,0), or the exact alternating two-cycle
 (y_t,z_t,V_t,q_t)=(sigma_t*a,-sigma_t*a,a^2,-2*sigma_t*a),
 a=1/2-e>0, sigma_(t+1)=-sigma_t in {+1,-1}.
At e=0 the origin may have arbitrary permitted edge decorations u_t;
this statement does not assert uniqueness of those decorations.
Conversely both listed physical histories admit zero-dissipation
labeled full histories satisfying these hypotheses.

1. ANY ZERO VARIANCE FORCES THE ENTIRE ORIGIN HISTORY
Apply the explicit argument079, whose hypotheses are precisely the
nonnegative variance recursion, full negative history, the displayed
edge equations, and zero Psi. For completeness, the only singular
calculation it uses can be reconstructed directly from our definitions.
When e=0 and y=z=V=0, V'=z'=0, y'=-(1+b)*q'. Both labels are H.
The source potential is -q^2/2; substitution in the target potential
and subtracting (q')^2 gives
 Psi=b*(2-b)*(q')^2/2+q^2/2=99*(q')^2/200+q^2/2.
Thus zero Psi forces q=q'=0 and y'=0. Backwards variance induction
first gives y_j=V_j=z_j=0 for j<0; this identity gives q_j=0 and
propagates the origin forward. At e>0 the constraints instead give
q=0 when z=V=0, and the position equation propagates the origin.
This is proof079's full-history argument; a one-sided V0=0 start is
insufficient. No independent audit of079 is being asserted.

It remains to consider histories with V_t>0 for all t. Then all edges
are regular, including at e=0, so p,w are well-defined and positive.

2. POSITIVE PURE VARIANCE IS EXCLUDED
If at any time y=z=q=0,V>0, the predecessor has y=0,V_old=V/d>0.
Since u=s/s'>0, its position equation forces z_old=0 and then q_old=0.
Inductively V_(-k)=V*d^(-k), contradicting bounded variance.
This is the argument069; it uses b>0,d in(0,1), not a potential.
It excludes isolated equality alternatives only because a full bounded
negative-time history is assumed.

3. THRESHOLD LABELS ARE COVERED BEFORE THE OPEN BRANCHES
If s=1 or s'=1, equivalently p=1 or w=1, apply the labeled table074.
It covers both source labels at p=1 and both target labels at w=1.
All margins are positive, except for the low-source target-threshold
pure-variance edge y=z=q=0,V=(1-e)^2/d, excluded by Section2.
Its F3 requirement w>=c is implied by our strict F3 assumption for
source H labels. Its e_max can be taken equal to our fixed e<1/2.
Thus no threshold state or threshold edge can occur on this history.
The double-threshold cases also lie in that table (and were checked070).

4. OPEN BRANCHES FORCE THE CYCLE
Away from thresholds, use086's reconstructed equality table:
LL forces y=z=0, hence q=0 because s>0, excluded by Section2;
LH and HL are strictly positive, the latter using F3;
HH has equality only at the origin or exact two-cycle by084-085.
The origin has V=0, ruled out in the present case. Hence every state
is a cycle phase with a=1/2-e. On these phases s=s'=1/2,
u=1,q'=2*y, and the position equation gives y'=-y.
So the signs alternate for all integers; no switching phase or physical
jump is available. This proves the stated classification.

5. CONVERSE AND DEPENDENCY BOUNDARY
The origin satisfies every physical equation with u=1 (for e>0);
for e=0 any allowed u works, with q=q'=0. It has H labels since e<1/2.
At a cycle, s=1/2, u=1, both labels are H, Gamma(V')=Gamma(V),
and direct substitution gives Psi=0. F3 holds since w=2>c.
The variance bound holds for both histories.

This theorem assumes a full zero-Psi history and F3. It does NOT show
that an arbitrary corrected Adam path generates such a history, that
its omega-limit set is confined to these histories, or that nearby paths
enter cycle tubes. Compact limiting relations, bias-error control, and
transversality/null basins are still separate global021 obligations.

# Direct rational replacement for084's Bernstein step
Kind: special; target:1; status: proof (unaudited).
This replaces one certificate inside084. It is not a new claim, larger
parameter range, independent audit, or numerical bound.

HYPOTHESES AND DIRECTION.
b=9/10, d=999/1000, nu=1/1000, gamma=9/19,
chi=99/200, k=81/3800. Assume b<=u<1/sqrt(d), p>1,
w=up>1, U=1/p in(0,1). The denominator 3u(1-du^2) is
strictly positive. We prove a LOWER bound on the available Schur
coefficient, to compare with an UPPER bound on the square-completion cost.
There is no probability, independence hypothesis, variance proxy,
concentration inequality or asymptotic rate in this calculation.

1. Direct interval certificate.
Since d*(1001/1000)^2>1, we have u<1001/1000. Put
 N(u)=3du^2(u+1)-nu(2u+1)-(9/2)u^2
     =u^2*[3d(u+1)-9/2]-nu(2u+1).
On this interval the bracket is at least
 3d*(19/10)-9/2=11943/10000>0.
Therefore multiplying lower bounds for the two positive factors, and
using an upper bound in the term with a negative sign, gives
 N(u)>= (81/100)*(11943/10000)-(1/1000)*(1501/500)
      =964381/1000000>0.
This is an interval inequality; equality at every factor bound is not
asserted. In fact the upper endpoint for u is strict.

Consequently for the exact function in084,
 T(u)=[3du^2(u+1)-nu(2u+1)]/[3u(1-du^2)],
 T(u)-(3/2)*u/(1-du^2)=N(u)/[3u(1-du^2)]>0.
This proves the lower bound for T on the whole required interval
without a polynomial-basis conversion or sampled substitutions.

2. Carrying constants to the Schur remainder.
We have 0<1-du^2<=1-d*b^2=19081/100000<1/5 and gamma>=9/20.
Thus the available coefficient satisfies
 8gamma U T(u)>=12gamma U u/(1-du^2)
                  >=60gamma U u >=(243/10)U.
All denominators are positive; their reciprocals reverse their order.
The weak inequalities displayed are sufficient although some are strict.

For completeness the cost upper bound from084 uses A/p^2<=1/2,
|F1|/p<=1/2, F2<1 and det>=6w^2/25>0. These follow from
 A=p^2/2-p+(1/2+gamma+ku^2),
 F1/p=1/2-(1/2+chi*u^2)/p, F2=chi*u^2+1/2,
 1/2+gamma+k/d<1, chi/d<1/2,
and det=chi*w^2/2+gamma*F2*(1-u^2).
For u<=1 the determinant bound follows from chi/2>6/25.
For u>1 use w>1,F2<1,u^2<1/d and
 chi/2-6/25-gamma*(1/d-1)>0.
The cost is then bounded by
 gamma^2*(10u^2+6u+1)/[(6/25)w^2]
 <=75/(4w^2)=75U^2/(4u^2)<=625U^2/27.
Here 10u^2+6u+1<18 because u<1001/1000, and gamma<1/2.
Hence the remaining coefficient is at least
 (243/10)U-(625/27)U^2
 >=[(243/10)-(625/27)]U=(311/270)U>0.
The last step uses U^2<=U; no lower bound away from zero for U is needed.

CHECK AND LIMITS.
CLEAN for this replacement calculation: the interval bounds and constant
arithmetic re-derive with their stated directions. A small Fraction-only
script records the exact rational endpoints and margins. It checks only
these algebraic inequalities, not the whole084 proof. The raw Psi
quadratic identity, epsilon-comparison derivative, centering identity and
Schur formula remain084's separate proof obligations. No independent
reviewer PASS is created here. Numerical reviewer support recorded in
RESULTS.jsonl is separate and is not used in this argument.

Fan and Wang (arXiv:2005.11879, Assumption 3.2(b), PDF p.5) assume a twice differentiable activation with globally bounded first and second derivatives, E sigma(Z)=0 and E[(sigma(Z))^2]=1 for standard Gaussian Z. Theorem 3.7 retains Assumption 3.2: fixed depth; independent standard Gaussian weights; approximately pairwise orthogonal input columns with deviations epsilon_n n^(1/4) tending to zero, bounded input norm and total squared norm deviations; a limiting input Gram empirical distribution; and positive finite limiting sample-to-hidden-width ratios. Together with Lemma 3.5 it describes the limiting empirical NTK eigenvalue distribution through conjugate-kernel matrices. Section 2.2 footnote 2 (p.4) explicitly distinguishes this weak empirical convergence from convergence of extreme eigenvalues. Raw ReLU has Gaussian mean 1/sqrt(2pi), second moment 1/2 and a corner at zero. Centering and dividing by sqrt(1/2-1/(2pi)) repairs its moments but not differentiability. Thus neither raw nor centered normalized ReLU is directly covered by the stated theorem. A separate nonsmooth approximation argument, and a separate outlier argument, are needed. This is a source-coverage note, not a claimed extension.
Use of the theorem as stated; no unproved extension by approximation

[Theorem 30 (Bauer--Fike, \cite{BF}) of arXiv:2607.08696, 'Spectrum of Directed Inhomogeneous Random Graphs'] Let $\deterministic$ be a $n \times n$ matrix such that $\deterministic=P_nDP_n^{-1}$ for an invertible matrix $P_n$ and a diagonal matrix $D$. Let $H_n$ be a $n \times n$ arbitrary matrix and $\eps_n = \|P_n\|\|P_n^{-1}\|\|H_n\|$. 
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[(i)] Then the spectrum of $\deterministic+H_n$ is contained in the union $\bigcup_{i= 1}^n \mathcal{B}(\lambda_i(\deterministic),\eps_n)$.
        \item[(ii)] Moreover, if for $I \subseteq [n]$ it holds
        $$\bigcup_{i \in I} \mathcal{B}(\lambda_i(\deterministic),\eps_n) \cap \bigcup_{i \in I^\complement} \mathcal{B}(\lambda_i(\deterministic),\eps_n)=\emptyset,$$
        then $\deterministic+H_n$ has exactly $|I|$ eigenvalues inside $\bigcup_{i \in I} \mathcal{B}(\lambda_i(\deterministic),\eps_n)$.
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 76 (Identification of an evaluated block reconstruction) of arXiv:2606.29292, 'Intrinsic Gaussian Tensor Geometry and Random Operator Spectra'] Let $1\le p,r<\infty$ and let
$U_j,U\in L^p(\Omega;\Sch_r(\cC,\cE))$ satisfy $U_j\to U$ in that
space.  Suppose that a random bounded operator $T:\cC\to\cE$ satisfies
the following on an event $\Omega_0$ of probability one:
\[
 U_j(\omega)x\longrightarrow T(\omega)x
 \qquad(x\in\cC,\ \omega\in\Omega_0).
\]
Then $U=T$ almost surely.

[Prop radial-incidence of arXiv:2606.26049, '\textsc{Face volume densities of positive-intensity and ideal Poisson--Voronoi tessellatio'] Let \(d\geq2\), let \(k\in\{0,1,\ldots,d-1\}\), and put \(q= d-k\).
For \(\mathbf x=(x_0,\ldots,x_q)\in(\mathbb H^d)^{q+1}\), let
$$
L(\mathbf x)=\{y\in\mathbb H^d:\operatorname{dist}(y,x_0)=\operatorname{dist}(y,x_1)=\ldots=\operatorname{dist}(y,x_q)\}.
$$
For \(y\in L(\mathbf x)\), write
\(\rho(y,\mathbf x)=\operatorname{dist}(y,x_0)=\operatorname{dist}(y,x_1)=\ldots=\operatorname{dist}(y,x_q)\)
for the common distance.  Then, for every non-negative measurable function
\(h:\mathbb H^d\times[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty]\),
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
&\int_{(\mathbb H^d)^{q+1}}
\int_{L(\mathbf x)}
h\bigl(y,\rho(y,\mathbf x)\bigr)\,
\mathcal H^k(\mathrm d y)\,
\mathcal H^{d(q+1)}(\mathrm d\mathbf x)
\\
& =
A_{d,q}
\int_{\mathbb H^d}
\int_0^\infty
h(y,r)\,
\sinh^{(d-1)(q+1)}(r)\,\mathrm d r\,
\mathcal H^d(\mathrm d y),
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
where $A_{d,q}$ is given by (equation eq:Adq of the paper). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma lem:cond-uniqueness of arXiv:2605.03703, 'Scaling Limits of Bivariate Nearly-Unstable Hawkes Processes and Applications to Rough Vol'] Let $(V^1,V^2,\beta^1,\beta^2)$ be a triangular weak solution in the sense
of Definition~(def:triangular-solution of the paper), define the inherited-noise
process
\begin{equation}
Z_t^1:=\gamma_{12}\nu_1\int_0^tL_{12}(t-s)\sqrt{V_s^1}\,d\beta_s^1,
\end{equation}
and let $\mathcal G:=\sigma(V_s^1,Z_s^1:0\le s\le1)$.  Then $V^2$
satisfies
\begin{equation}
V_t^2=b_2(t)+Z_t^1+\nu_2\int_0^tK_2(t-s)\sqrt{V_s^2}\,d\beta_s^2,
\end{equation}
and
\[
\mathcal L\bigl(V^2\mid\mathcal G\bigr)=Q\bigl(b_2+Z^1\bigr)
\qquad\text{a.s.},
\]
where $Q$ is the kernel of Theorem~(thm:ALP-extension of the paper) for
$(K,\nu)=(K_2,\nu_2)$.

Let R be a commutative ring with 1, let I be an ideal contained in the Jacobson radical J(R) (the intersection of all maximal ideals), and let M be a finitely generated R-module. If I M = M then M = 0. Consequences: if N is a submodule with M = N + I M then M = N; and if elements m_1, ..., m_k of M have images generating M / I M, then they generate M. For a local ring (R, m) and finitely generated M this reads: M = m M implies M = 0, and a subset of M generates M if and only if its image spans the k-vector space M / m M, k = R / m.
M finitely generated (the lemma fails for infinitely generated modules, e.g. M = Q over the localisation of Z at a prime)

on \((0,\infty)\), satisfies \(\lim_{\xi\to\infty}k(\xi,\eta)=0\), and
\[
        A:=
        \int_0^\infty
        \sqrt u
        \left(
        \int_0^\infty |\partial_1 k(u,\eta)|^2\,\mathrm d\eta
        \right)^{1/2}
        \,\mathrm du
        <\infty .
\]
Then the integral operator \(K\) on \(L^2(0,\infty)\) with kernel \(k\) is trace

\[J(y)=\inf_{x\in {\mathcal X }: y=f(x)}\{I(x)\}.\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition def solution for NBC of arXiv:2504.06238, 'Infinite Boundary Friction Limit for Weak Solutions of the Stochastic Navier-Stokes Equati'] Let  $u_0: \Omega \rightarrow L^2_{\sigma}$ be $\mathcal{F}_0-$measurable and $\alpha_n \in C^2(\partial \mathscr{O}; \mathbb{R})$. A process $u^n$ which is progressively measurable in $\bar{W}^{1,2}_{\sigma}$ such that for $\mathbbm{P}-a.e.$ $\omega$, $u^n_{\cdot}(\omega) \in C\left([0,T];L^2_{\sigma}\right) \cap L^2\left([0,T];\bar{W}^{1,2}_{\sigma}\right)$, is said to be a weak solution of the equation ((NSalphan of the paper)) if it satisfies the identity
\begin{align} \nonumber
     \inner{u^n_t}{\psi} = \inner{u_0}{\psi} - \int_0^{t}\inner{\mathcal{L}_{u^n_s}u^n_s}{\psi}ds &- \nu\int_0^{t} \inner{u^n_s}{\psi}_1 ds + \nu\int_0^t \inner{(\kappa - \alpha_n)u^n_s}{\psi}_{L^2(\partial \mathscr{O}; \mathbb{R}^2)}ds\\ &+ \frac{1}{2}\int_0^{t}\sum_{i=1}^\infty \inner{B_iu^n_s}{B_i^*\psi} ds - \int_0^{t} \inner{Bu^n_s}{\psi} d\mathcal{W}_s
\end{align}
for every $\psi \in \bar{W}^{1,2}_{\sigma}$, $\mathbbm{P}-a.s.$ in $\mathbb{R}$ for all $t\in[0,T]$. Moreover $u^n$ is said to be unique if for any other such process $v^n$, $u^n$ and $v^n$ are indistinguishable.

Let X_n converge in distribution to a real random variable X and let Y_n converge in probability to a real constant c. Then (X_n,Y_n) converges jointly in distribution to (X,c). Consequently X_n+Y_n converges in distribution to X+c, X_n Y_n converges in distribution to cX, and, if c!=0, X_n/Y_n converges in distribution to X/c. For the quotient, define its value arbitrarily on {Y_n=0} when necessary; that event has probability tending to zero. Convergence Y_n=>c in distribution is equivalent to convergence Y_n->c in probability, so either hypothesis gives the same conclusion for a constant target. With a nonconstant target, separate marginal convergence alone does not identify the joint limit: if X is a nondegenerate symmetric random variable, X_n=X and Y_n=-X, then both marginal laws converge to the law of X, but X_n+Y_n=0 does not converge to the law of 2X. A random second limit is allowed when joint convergence (X_n,Y_n)=>(X,Y) is supplied; the continuous mapping theorem then gives the corresponding sum and product limits, and the quotient limit if P(Y=0)=0. [Re-derived local source, M9; textbook cross-reference: van der Vaart, Asymptotic Statistics, Theorem 2.8.]
X_n => X in distribution
Y_n -> c in probability with c a CONSTANT (not a random variable)

[Definition Discrete connection on a graph of arXiv:2602.08591, 'The Yang--Mills measure on compact surfaces as a \\ universal scaling limit of lattice gau'] A \emph{discrete connection} on $\mathbb{G}$ is a map
\[
g : \mathbb{E}_+ \cup \mathbb{E}_- \longrightarrow G
\]
such that for every $e \in \mathbb{E}_+$ we have
\[
g(e_+) = g(e_-)^{-1}.
\]
For an edge $e\in \mathbb{E}_+\cup \mathbb{E}_-$, we denote by $i(e)$ and $f(e)$ the vertices such that $e=(i(e),f(e))$. A path in $\mathbb{G}$ is a sequence of edges  $a_1,\dots,a_n$ such that $f(a_k)=i(a_{k+1})$ for all $k=1,\dots,n-1$. If $c = a_1 \cdots a_n$ is a path in $\mathbb{G}$, given as a concatenation of oriented edges $a_i \in \mathbb{E}_+ \cup \mathbb{E}_-$, we define the \emph{holonomy} of $g$ along $c$ by
\[
\mathrm{Hol}(g,c) \coloneqq g(a_1)\cdots g(a_n) \in G.
\]
title: Discrete connection on a graph

[Proposition 5 of arXiv:2609.03634, 'Joint Laws of Maximum Drawdown and Maximum Drawup for Spectrally Negative L\'{e}vy Process'] Consider a spectrally negative L\'{e}vy process $X$ with $q$-scale functions $W^{(q)}$ and $Z^{(q)}$. Let $a<0$, $b>0$, $x\in[0,b]$, and $q\geq0$. Then, for $v>0$,
\[
\mathbb E_x\left[e^{-q\tau_a^-};\,M_{\tau_a^-}^{+}\leq v,\ S_{\tau_a^-}\leq b\right]
=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle
e^{-\left((x-a)\frac{W_+^{(q)\prime}(v)}{W^{(q)}(v)}\right)},
& 0<v\leq b-x,\\[1.3em]
\displaystyle
e^{-\left((b-a-v)\frac{W_+^{(q)\prime}(v)}{W^{(q)}(v)}\right)}
\left[
Z^{(q)}(x-b+v)-Z^{(q)}(v)\frac{W^{(q)}(x-b+v)}{W^{(q)}(v)}
\right],
& b-x<v\leq b-a,\\[1.3em]
\displaystyle
Z^{(q)}(x-a)-Z^{(q)}(b-a)\frac{W^{(q)}(x-a)}{W^{(q)}(b-a)},
& b-a\leq v.
\end{cases}
\]
In particular,
\[
\mathbb E_x\left[e^{-q\tau_a^-};\,M_{\tau_a^-}^{+}\leq v\right]
=
\exp\!\left(-(x-a)\frac{W_+^{(q)\prime}(v)}{W^{(q)}(v)}\right).
\]

[Theorem thm: connected cutsets of arXiv:2503.21737, 'High-intensity Voronoi percolation on manifolds'] Let $M$ be simply connected. Let $G=(V,E)$ be a graph such that $V\subset M$. Assume that to each $x\in V$ we can associate an open connected set $O(x)\subset M$ containing $x$ such that
\begin{enumerate}[i)]
\item $\bigcup_{x\in V}O(x)=M$,
\item $O(x)\cap O(y)\ne \emptyset $ if and only if $\{x,y\}\in E$ (for $x\neq y$).
\end{enumerate}
    Then for all $x,y\in V$, any minimal cutset separating $x$ from $y$ is connected in $G$.
    
    If we further assume that $G$ is one-ended and locally finite\footnote{We call a graph $G=(V,E)$ \emph{one-ended} if for any finite set $\Gamma\subset V$ the induced subgraph on $V\setminus \Gamma$ has a unique infinite connected component.
    We call \(G\) \emph{locally finite} when each of its vertices has finite degree.}
    (which holds, for instance, if $M$ itself is one-ended, the sets $O(x)$ are all bounded and any bounded set \(B \subset M\) intersects at most finitely many of the sets \(O(x)\)), then any minimal cutset separating $x$ from infinity is connected in $G$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm: connected cutsets of arXiv:2503.21737

  it holds for $x,y\in \RR$ with $|x-y|\le 1$ and all $k>k_0$
  \begin{align}
    
    |f_{\infty}'(x)|
    \ + \
    |f_k'(x)|
    &
    \ \lesssim \
    g_\gamma(x)
    \,,
    \\
    
    |
    f_{\infty}'(x)
    -
    f_{\infty}'(y)
    |
    \ + \
    |
    f_k'(x)
    -

[Definition def:online of arXiv:2509.02432, 'A threshold for online balancing of sparse i.i.d. vectors'] Let $\mu$ be a probability distribution in $\RR^n$,
and $T$ a time horizon.
Define the {\it optimal expected online discrepancy} as
$$
\mathrm{ondisc}(\mu,T):=\inf\limits_{\sigma=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_T)}{\mathbb E}\Big[\,\max\limits_{t\leq T}
\Big\|\sum_{s\in [t]} \sigma_s X_s\Big\|_\infty \Big],
$$
where $(X_1,\dots,X_T)\sim \mu^{\otimes T}$, and the infimum is taken over all online algorithms $\sigma=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_T)$ (as in (def:online of the paper)).
title: Optimal expected online discrepancy

        The unsigned Stirling numbers of the first kind $\sfir{n}{k}$ are given by the coefficients of the rising factorial:

[Theorem thm:smallsubmatricesimplymixing of arXiv:2607.06813, 'Mixing of Glauber Dynamics on High Overlap Gibbs Measures'] Let $\delta\in(0,1)$ and let $J\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ symmetric such that
    \[
    \max_{\substack{\mathcal{S}\subset [n] \\ |\mathcal{S}|\leq \delta n}}\left\|J_{\mathcal{S},\mathcal{S}}\right\|\leq \frac15,
    \]
    then, there exists $\theta\geq 0$, which may depend on $\|J\|$ and $\delta$ but not on $n$, 
    such that lazy Glauber Dynamics for the quadratic Gibbs distribution on $\{\pm 1\}^n$ given by
    \[
    \nu(x) \propto \exp\left(\frac12x^\top J x + \theta \mathbf{1}^\top x\right),
    \]
    mixes, in total variation distance, in time polynomial on $n$. Moreover $\theta$ can be taken to be a universal constant times $\|J\|/{\delta}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 10 of arXiv:2608.24356, 'Another solvable population dynamic\\ with uniform ancestral memory'] The following assertions hold:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)]
The function $\Lambda$ is $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ and convex on $\R^S$. Its gradient  $\nabla \Lambda$, viewed as a row vector,  takes values in the subspace  of probability measures on $S$ with full support.
\item[(ii)] The Fenchel--Legendre transform $\Lambda^* $ is a strictly convex function. 

\item[(iii)] For any $\boldsymbol{\rho}\in \mathcal{P}_S$ with full support, there exists $\blambda_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}\in \R^S$ such that
\[\nabla \Lambda(\blambda_{\boldsymbol{\rho}})=\boldsymbol{\rho} \quad \text{and} \quad \Lambda^*(\boldsymbol{\rho} )=\boldsymbol{\rho}  \blambda_{\boldsymbol{\rho}} - \Lambda(\blambda_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}). \]
Moreover, for any $\boldsymbol{\rho}'\in \mathcal{P}_S$ different from $\boldsymbol{\rho}$, there is the strict inequality
\[ \Lambda^*(\boldsymbol{\rho}' )- \boldsymbol{\rho}'  \blambda_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}  > \Lambda^*(\boldsymbol{\rho} )-  \boldsymbol{\rho} \blambda_{\boldsymbol{\rho}} . \]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition Support of a measure of arXiv:2605.10491, 'Zero-couplings of infinite measures with cyclically monotone support and multivariate regu'] Let $(X,\mathcal{T})$ be a topological space and let $\mathcal{B}(X)$ denote the Borel $\sigma$-algebra on $X$. 
The support of a measure $\mu$ on $(X,\mathcal{B}(X))$ is the closed set consisting of all points $x$ in $X$ such that every open neighborhood of $x$ receives a positive mass
\[
	\operatorname{spt}\mu = \left\{ 
				x\in X \mid 
				\forall \mathrm{N}\in\mathcal{N}_x(\mathcal{T}) : \mu(\mathrm{N})>0
				\right\}
\]
Equivalently, we have 
$$
\operatorname{spt}\mu = \bigcap\left\{F: F^c\in\mathcal{T}, \text{ and } \mu(X\setminus F) = 0 \right\}. 
.$$

[Theo 3 of arXiv:2608.30578, 'Compactly Supported Solutions near a Nehari Critical Value'] Assume that $0<\alpha<1$, $|\Omega^+|>0$, $|\Omega^-|>0$, and
$m\in L^\infty(\Omega)$. Suppose that there exist $\rho_0>0$ and $m_{\rho_0}^-$ such that
\begin{equation}
	\mathcal C_{\rho_0}\subset\Omega^-
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
	-m(x)\geq m_{\rho_0}^-
	\qquad\text{for a.e. }x\in\mathcal C_{\rho_0}.
\end{equation}
Let $u_\lambda^+$ be the non-negative weak solution of \eqref{Eq1} given by
Theorem~\ref{thm1}. Then there exists $\sigma<0$ such that, for every
$\lambda<\sigma$, the solution $u_\lambda^+$ has compact support in
$\Omega$.

More precisely, there exists $\rho\in(0,\rho_0)$, independent of all
sufficiently negative $\lambda$, such that
$u_\lambda^+=0$ in $\mathcal C_\rho$. Consequently,
\[
\operatorname{supp}u_\lambda^+
\subset
\{x\in\Omega:\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)\geq\rho\}
\Subset\Omega.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Lemma lem_sing_connection of arXiv:2607.24640, 'The Yang-Mills measure on surfaces via Morse theory'] There is a 1-1 correspondence between gauge equivalence classes of pairs
$(L,\nabla)$, where $L\to\Sigma$ is a nontrivial complex line bundle of
degree $k$ equipped with a smooth connection $\nabla$, and gauge
equivalence classes of pairs $(\Sigma\times\mathbb C,\nabla^s)$, where
$\nabla^s$ is a singular connection whose connection $1$--form is a
current of degree $1$ on $\Sigma$ satisfying
\[
\alpha = k\,\frac{dz}{z}+\beta,
\]
in a holomorphic coordinate system $z$ centered at $ \mathrm{argmax} (f)$, with
$\beta$ smooth. Moreover, every such singular connection is smooth on
$\Sigma\setminus\{ \mathrm{argmax} (f)\}$ and its connection $1$--form belongs
globally to $H^{-\varepsilon}(\Sigma)$ for every $\varepsilon>0$.

In
particular, we have the fundamental residue equation: 
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{ c_1(L,\nabla)= \frac{i}{2\pi}  F_\nabla = -\frac{i}{2\pi}  d\alpha + k[ \mathrm{argmax}  (f)] }
\end{equation}  
on $\Sigma$, where the singular contributions cancel. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma lem_sing_connection of arXiv:2607.24640

body:
[Theorem 6 (Borovoi's image theorem in terms of the Brauer group) of arXiv:2609.02819, 'Adelic Points and Unramified Brauer Approximation for Classifying Stacks'] Let $S\subset\Omega_k$ be finite.  Define
\[
 \Lambda_{G,S}:BG(\bA_k^S)\longrightarrow P_G^\vee
\]
by
\begin{equation}
 \Lambda_{G,S}\bigl((\xi_v)_{v\notin S}\bigr)
 :=\sum_{v\notin S}\ev_v(\xi_v),
\end{equation}
and let
\[
 \lambda_{G,S}:BG(\bA_k^S)\longrightarrow P_G^\vee/E_S
\]
be the composite with the quotient map.  Then
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{im}\bigl(BG(k)\longrightarrow BG(\bA_k^S)\bigr)
 =\ker(\lambda_{G,S}).
\end{equation}
Equivalently, an away-from-$S$ family $\xi^S$ is global if and only if
\begin{equation}
 \Lambda_{G,S}(\xi^S)\in E_S.
\end{equation}
Moreover, the plain localization map is surjective if and only if
\begin{equation}
 E_{\Omega_k\setminus S}\subseteq E_S.
\end{equation}
For connected reductive $G$, these are precisely Main Theorem~3.7 and
Corollary~3.9 of \cite{BorovoiLocalization}, with Borovoi's localization set
equal to $\Omega_k\setminus S$.

[Thm thm-boltzmann-ldp of arXiv:2510.26123, 'Directed distances in bipolar-oriented triangulations:\\ exact exponents and scaling limit'] For $r\in\mathbbm N$, let $(M(r) ,z(r))$ be sampled from the Boltzmann distribution on bipolar-oriented triangulations with right boundary length $r$ and a marked left boundary vertex (Definition~(def-boltzmann-right of the paper)). 
Let $\operatorname{Source}(r)$ and $\operatorname{Sink}(r)$ denote the source and sink vertices of $M(r)$. 
For each $\delta \in (0,1)$, there exists $A = A(\delta)  > 1$ such that for each $r\in \mathbbm N$, it holds with probability at least $1-\delta$ that the following is true.  
\begin{itemize}
\item $A^{-1} r^{3/2} \leq  \operatorname{LDP}_{M(r)} \mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft(  \operatorname{Source}(r)  , \operatorname{Sink}(r)  \aftergroup\egroup\originalright) \leq A r^{3/2}$. 
\item $ \operatorname{SDP}_{M(r)} \mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft(  \operatorname{Source}(r)  , \operatorname{Sink}(r)  \aftergroup\egroup\originalright) \leq A r^{3/4}$.
\item There exists a vertex $y$ on the right boundary of $M(r)$ such that 
\begin{equation*}
\operatorname{SDP}_{M(r)} \mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft(  \operatorname{Source}(r)  , y \aftergroup\egroup\originalright) \geq A^{-1} r^{3/4} .
\end{equation*}
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: In probability theory, a Lévy process, named after the French mathematician Paul Lévy, is a stochastic process with independent, stationary increments: it represents the motion of a point whose successive displacements are random, in which displacements in pairwise disjoint time intervals are independent, and displacements in different time intervals of the same length have identical probability distributions. A Lévy process may thus be viewed as the continuous-time analog of a random walk.

[Theorem thm:introduction-continuous-spectrum of arXiv:2607.25616, 'Stealthy point processes and lattice induction'] Let $\Gamma\leq\mathbb R^d$ be a full-rank lattice and let
$(Z,\nu)$ be a nontrivial weakly mixing
probability-preserving Borel $\Gamma$-space. Then $\smash{\operatorname{Ind}_{\Gamma}^{\mathbb R^d}(Z)}$
admits a generating stealthy Delone cross-section $Y$. Writing
\[
    \sigma_Y
    :=
    \sigma_{Y,\mu_{\Gamma,Z}}
    =
    \sigma_{(\kappa_Y)_*\mu_{\Gamma,Z}},
\]
one has a decomposition
\[
    \sigma_Y
    =
    \sigma_Y^{\mathrm{tor}}
    +
    \sigma_Y^Z,
\]
where
\[
    \operatorname{supp}\sigma_Y^{\mathrm{tor}}
    \subset
    \Gamma^*\setminus\{0\},
    \qquad
    0\neq\sigma_Y^Z
    \ll
    \widetilde{\mathfrak m}_{Z,\nu}^0.
\]
In particular, $\sigma_Y$ has a nonzero continuous component. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition prop:entropy-decomposition of arXiv:2605.17082, 'Spectral Purification in Reversible Markov Chains: Hidden Parameters, Observable Equivalen'] The spectral entropy satisfies
\[
S_{\rm spec}(k)
=
H(\alpha_2(k))
+
(1-\alpha_2(k))H(q(k)),
\]
where
\[
H(\alpha)
=
-\alpha\log\alpha-(1-\alpha)\log(1-\alpha),
\]
and
\[
H(q)
=
-\sum_{i\ge3}q_i\log q_i.

[Lemm l:BM-maximum-drift of arXiv:2607.18194, 'Temperature chaos in directed polymers'] Let $W$ be a Brownian motion of variance $4$ started from $W(0)=0$.
    Then for all $T>0$, all $\kappa>0$, and all $\mu\in\mathbb{R}$,
    \begin{align*}
        \mathbb{P}\left(
            \max_{z\in[0,T]}\left(W(z) + \mu z\right) \leqslant \kappa
        \right)
        \leqslant C\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}} + |\mu|\right)\kappa,
    \end{align*}    
    where $C>0$ is a universal constant.

Fix a non-negative integer~$\tau$. 
Let $\overline{z}\in (\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0})^j$ be a $j$-tuple such that, for all $x\in [j]$, $z_x \geq \lambda W_x/4$. 
Let $Y$ be a \emph{$j$-jammed} process with send sequence~$\overline{p}$, start time~$\tau$, birth rate~$\lambda$, and initial population size distribution~$\mathsf{Po}(\overline{z})$.
Then for all integers~$t>\tau$,
\begin{itemize}

\mathcal{E}^{Y,\mathcal{N}}_{\leq t} \cap \mathcal{E}^{Y,\mathbf{s}}_{\leq t-1} ) \geq 1- 1/i^{\alpha_{\mathrm{b}}}  $, and

\item 
$\mathbb{P}(   {\mathcal{E}^{Y,\mathcal{N}}_t} \mid
\mathcal{E}^{Y,\mathcal{N}}_{\leq t-1} \cap \mathcal{E}^{Y,\mathbf{s}}_{\leq t-1} ) \geq 1-
1/i^{\alpha_{\mathrm{b}}}$. 
 

\end{itemize}

body: In topology, a covering or covering projection is a map between topological spaces that, intuitively, locally acts like a projection of multiple copies of a space onto itself. In particular, coverings are special types of local homeomorphisms. If $p:{\tilde {X}}\to X$ is a covering, $({\tilde {X}},p)$ is said to be a covering space or cover of $X$, and $X$ is said to be the base of the covering, or simply the base. By abuse of terminology, ${\tilde {X}}$ and $p$ may sometimes be called covering spaces as well. Since coverings are local homeomorphisms, a covering space is a special kind of étalé space.

body:
[Proposition 13 (Boundary variance trend for a powered Choquet integral) of arXiv:2607.16502, 'Asymptotic Behavior of Path Functionals for Vector-Valued Gaussian Processes at High Level'] For the process \eqref{eq:nonstationary-model-example} and the functional
\eqref{eq:choquet-excess-example}, the following asymptotics hold as
\(u\to\infty\).  The constants in
\eqref{def:H-choquet-nonstationary-example} and
\eqref{def:P-choquet-nonstationary-example} exist, are finite and positive in
the regimes in which they are used.
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
  \item If \(\alpha<\beta\), then
  \begin{equation}
    
    \pk{ C_T^{(\theta)}(u)>L u^{-2\theta/\alpha} }
    \sim
    \mathcal H_{\alpha,c,b}^{\mathrm{Ch},\theta}(L)\,
    \Gamma(1/\beta+1)\,(ab^2)^{-1/\beta}\,
    u^{2/\alpha-2/\beta-1}\,
    \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-b^2u^2/2}.
  \end{equation}
  \item If \(\alpha=\beta\), then
  \begin{equation}
    
    \pk{ C_T^{(\theta)}(u)>L u^{-2\theta/\beta} }
    \sim
    \mathcal P_{\alpha,a,c,b}^{\mathrm{Ch},\theta}(L)\,
    u^{-1}\,
    \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-b^2u^2/2}.
  \end{equation}
  \item If \(\alpha>\beta\), then the Gaussian local fluctuation no longer
  appears in the leading constant and
  \begin{equation}
    
    \pk{ C_T^{(\theta)}(u)>L u^{-2\theta/\beta} }
    \sim
    \frac{1}{b}e^{-b\ell_{L,\theta}}\,
    u^{-1}\,
    \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-b^2u^2/2}.
  \end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
Let
\[
  \mathfrak t_{\theta}(u,L)
  =
  \inf\left\{0<t\le T:
  \Gamma_{[0,t]}^{\mathrm{Ch},\theta}\bigl(u(X-u b)\bigr)>L_u
  \right\},
\]
where \(L_u=L u^{-2\theta/\alpha}\) in the case \(\alpha<\beta\) and
\(L_u=L u^{-2\theta/\beta}\) in the cases \(\alpha\ge\beta\).  If
\(\alpha<\beta\), then for every \(S\ge0\),
\begin{equation}
  
  \pk{
    u^{2/\beta}\mathfrak t_{\theta}(u,L)\le S
    \,\middle|\,
    \mathfrak t_{\theta}(u,L)\le T
  }
  \to
  \frac{\Gamma(1/\beta)-\Gamma(1/\beta,ab^2S^\beta)}{\Gamma(1/\beta)}.
\end{equation}
If \(\alpha>\beta\), define, for \(S>0\), the unique number
\(y_{S,\theta}>0\) by
\begin{equation}
  
  \int_0^\infty
  \mes\{t\in[0,S]:y_{S,\theta}-ab t^\beta>r\}^\theta\,dr=L .
\end{equation}
Then, for every \(S>0\),
\begin{equation}
  
  \pk{
    u^{2/\beta}\mathfrak t_{\theta}(u,L)\le S
    \,\middle|\,
    \mathfrak t_{\theta}(u,L)\le T
  }
  \to
  \exp\{-b(y_{S,\theta}-\ell_{L,\theta})\}.
\end{equation}

[Definition def:chemical of arXiv:2607.02367, 'Flux solutions for stochastic chemical systems with sources and sinks'] Assume that $\mathcal R$ is a set of bidirectional chemical reactions between elements of $\Omega $, i.e. 
 $\mathcal R := \{ S_\rho \}_{\rho=1}^r \cup  \{ S_{- \rho }\}_{\rho=1}^r $ where $S_{\rho_1} \neq - S_{\rho_2 } $ for every $\rho_1 \neq \rho_2 $. Assume that $ \mathcal R_s $ is a set of sources and sinks, i.e.  $\mathcal R_s := \{e_k \}_{k \in \Omega_c}  \cup  \{ - e_{ k  }\}_{\Omega_c }  $ with $ \Omega_c \subset \Omega$.  
 Assume that $\mathcal K := \{ R_\rho  \}_{ \rho =1 }^r \cup \{ R_{-\rho}\}_{\rho=1}^r  $ is the set of kinetics associated with the chemical reactions $S_\rho, S_{- \rho } \in \mathcal R $ and $\mathcal K_s := \{ \alpha_k  \}_{ k \in \Omega_c }  \cup \{ \beta_k  \}_{ k \in \Omega_c } $ is the set of the chemical rates associated with the sources and sinks. 
 We say that  $(\Omega, \mathcal R,  \mathcal R_s , \mathcal K, \mathcal K_s )$ is a chemical system. Moreover 
 \begin{itemize}
\item if $ \Omega_c \neq \emptyset $, then we say that $(\Omega, \mathcal R,  \mathcal R_s , \mathcal K, \mathcal K_s )$ is a chemical system with sources and sinks. 
\item If $ \Omega_c = \emptyset $, then we say that $(\Omega, \mathcal R,  \mathcal R_s , \mathcal K, \mathcal K_s )$ is a chemical system without sources and sinks. We denote it with $(\Omega, \mathcal R,  \mathcal K)$. 
\end{itemize}
title: Chemical system

[Proposition p:preserve of arXiv:2605.03718, 'Potential Hessian Ascent III:\\ Sampling the Sherrington--Kirkpatrick Model at $\beta < 1/'] The following operations preserve real stability and (strong/complete) log-concavity.\footnote{(s/c) log-concave is to be read as strongly log-concave or completely log-concave or log-concave, respectively.}
    \begin{enumerate}[itemsep=0.1em]
        \item Product: If $p,q$ are real stable (respectively, log-concave) then $p\cdot q$ is real stable (log-concave).
        \item Symmetrization: If $p(z_1,\ldots, z_n)$ is real stable ((s/c) log-concave), then $p(z_1,z_1,z_3,\ldots, z_n)$ is real-stable ((s/c) log-concave).
        \item 
        Specialization: If $p(z_1,\ldots, z_n)$ is real stable ((s/c) log-concave), then $p(a,z_1,\ldots, z_n)$ is real-stable ((s/c) log-concave) for $a\in \mathbb R$ ($a\geqslant 0$).
        \item External field: If $p(z_1,\ldots, z_n)$ is real stable ((s/c) log-concave), then so is $q(z_1,\ldots, z_n) = p(w_1 z_1,\ldots, w_n z_n)$ for any $w_1,\ldots, w_n\geqslant 0$.
        \item Differentiation: If $p$ is real stable or strongly or completely log-concave, then so is $\partial_{i} p$. 
        \item Homogenization: If $p$ is real stable, then $p^{\mathrm{hom}}(z_1,\ldots, z_{n+1}) = z_{n+1}^{\deg p}p\pa{\fc{z_1}{z_{n+1}},\cdots, \fc{z_n}{z_{n+1}}}$ is real stable. 
        
        \item Polarization ([anari2024trickle], [branden2020lorentzian]): Suppose $p(z_1,\ldots, z_n) = \sum_{\alpha \in \mathbb N_0^n} c_\alpha z^\alpha$ is homogeneous and strongly log-concave with degree at most $\kappa_i$ in $z_i$. Then so is its polarization with degree $\kappa$, $\operatorname{polar}_\kappa(p)$, defined by 
        \[
        \operatorname{polar}_\kappa(p) = \sum_{\alpha \in \mathbb N_0^n} c_\alpha \prodo in \rc{\binom{\kappa_i}{\alpha_i}} e_{\alpha_i}(z_{i1},\ldots, z_{i\kappa_i})
        \]
        as a polynomial in $z_{ij}$, $i\in [n]$, $j\in [\kappa_i]$, where $e_k(y_1,\ldots, y_n) = \sum_{S\in \slice{n}{k}} y^S$ is the $k$th elementary symmetric polynomial.

[Lemma 17 of arXiv:2608.28528, 'Strong solutions of SDEs with critical discontinuities in diffusion coefficients'] Assuming that the form-bound $\nu$ is sufficiently small, the sequence $\sigma^\varepsilon(t,\cdot):=\eta_\varepsilon \ast \sigma(t,\cdot)$, satisfies, for all $\varepsilon$ sufficiently small, uniformly in a.e.\,$t \in \mathbb R$, 

$1'$) $\|\sigma^\varepsilon(t,\cdot)\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb R^{d})} \leq \|\sigma(t,\cdot)\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb R^{d})} $ 

$2'$) $
\sigma^\varepsilon(t,\cdot) (\sigma^\varepsilon(t,\cdot))^{\top} \geq \frac{\kappa}{4}I;
$

$3'$) \eqref{nabla_sigma} holds for $\sigma^\varepsilon$ with the same form-bound $\nu$ and constant $c_\nu$, i.e.\,independent of $\varepsilon$;

$4'$)  ($\mathbf{H}$) holds for $\sigma^\varepsilon$ with the same H\"{o}lder continuity exponent and constant.

$5')$ $$\|\sigma(t,\cdot)-\sigma^\varepsilon(t,\cdot)\|_{L_\rho^2(\mathbb R^d)} \leq C_1\varepsilon, \quad t \in \mathbb R.$$

$6'$) Set $a=\sigma\sigma^{\top}$, $a^\varepsilon=\sigma^\varepsilon(\sigma^\varepsilon)^{\top}$. Then 
$$
\nabla_k a^\varepsilon \rightarrow \nabla_k a \quad \text{ in } [L_{\loc}^2(\mathbb R,L^2_\rho(\mathbb R^d))]^{d \times d} \text{ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$}
$$
for all $1 \leq k \leq d$. That is, we have componentwise convergence of the derivatives of $a^\varepsilon$, which in particular implies the convergence of the row-divergence operators $\nabla a^\varepsilon \rightarrow \nabla a$ in $[L_{\loc}^2(\mathbb R,L^2_\rho(\mathbb R^d))]^{d}$.

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Location of Brownian modes at large time structural calculation Result: For the classical mode, let m be the initial mean and mu_k=E[(X-m)^k]. The source exponential-moment assumption yields the asymptotic expansion mode(t)=m-mu_3/(2*t)+(mu_5-6*mu_2*mu_3)/(8*t^2)+O(t^-3). In particular the mode tends to the initial mean, and the leading displacement has sign opposite the third central moment. Check: Set s=1/t and H(h,s)=E[(X-m-h)*exp(-s*(X-m-h)^2/2)]. The exponential quadratic moment makes H analytic near(0,0), with H_h=-1 there. The implicit function theorem gives h=a*s+b*s^2+O(s^3). Expanding H gives a=-mu_3/2 and b=mu_5/8-3*mu_2*mu_3/4. The associated density stationary point is a strict local maximum since H_h remains negative; the source large-time unimodality identifies it with the unique global mode. Obstruction: This is an author-checked asymptotic partial answer, with no novelty claim. It does not provide a uniform explicit finite-time error constant or solve the free-Brownian half.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-p0177-location-of-brownian-modes-at-large-time
No independent review

[Definition def.balanced of arXiv:2603.11043, 'An asymptotically optimal bound for the concentration function of a sum of independent int'] Let $(\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_n) \in (0,1]^n$. A standard extremal sequence $(X_i)$ for $(\alpha_i)$ will be
    called 
    
    \emph{balanced}
    
    if each index $i \in \{1,\dots,n\}$ 
    can be mapped 
    
    bijectively to
    $j_i \in \{1, \dots, n\}$ 
    so that $X_{j_i} \sim - X_i$.

    We call $(\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_n) \in (0,1]^n$ \emph{balanced} if
    a balanced standard extremal sequence exists for $(\alpha_i)$, equivalently, if for each $\alpha \in (0,1]$ either $\alpha^{-1}$ is an odd integer or $|\{i: \alpha_i=\alpha\}|$ is even. We call $(\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_n)$ \emph{strongly balanced} if $|\{i: \alpha_i=\alpha\}|$ is even for each $\alpha \in (0,1]$.

    $\mathbb P(\sum X_i = 0)$ equals $\mathcal{Q}(\sum X_i)$ and is the same for each standard extremal balanced sequence $(X_i)$ for $(\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_n)$.
    We denote this probability by ${t_{SE}^{bal}}(\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_n)$.
title: Definition def.balanced of arXiv:2603.11043

\[

\]

body: [Lemma 17 of arXiv:2603.02806, 'The Price of Robustness: Stable Classifiers Need Overparameterization'] Let X ⊂Rd be bounded and path-connected, and let f : X →{−1, 1}. Then the signed distance function df is 1-Lipschitz. This is a classical fact, a special case of the Eikonal equation. For completeness, we include a direct proof inspired by Liu & Hansen (2024, Prop. 7.5).
title: Lemma 17 of arXiv:2603.02806: The Price of Robustness: Stable Classifiers Need Overparameterization

[Lemma 2DHD-lemma6.4 of arXiv:2604.21591, '\bf Long-time dynamics of stochastic 2D hydrodynamic-type evolution equations driven by mu'] Under the hypotheses of Lemma (2DHD-lemma6.3 of the paper). There exists a $$
	\varepsilon_0=\min\left\{\sqrt{\frac{\mu\lambda_1}{2\widehat{L}_{gv}}},\sqrt{\frac{\mu\lambda_1}{12L_g+2\mathbf{c}_4L_g+8\mathbf{c}_4\widetilde{L}_g}}\right\}>0
	$$
	 such that for all $\tau \in \mathbb{R}$, $t>1$ and $\varepsilon_1, \varepsilon_2 \in (0,\varepsilon_0]$, the solution $ u$ of system ((2DHD-1.1 of the paper)) satisfies
	\begin{align*}
			&~\mathbb{E}\left[\mathfrak{P}(\tau,\tau-t,u_{\tau-t})\| u(\tau,\tau-t,u_{\tau-t})\|_V^2\right]\\
			&\leq \rho_4 e^{-\widetilde{\kappa} t}\mathbb{ E}\left[\|u_{\tau-t}\|_{H}^2\right]+\rho_4\left(\int_{-\infty}^{\tau} e^{-\widetilde{\kappa} (\tau-s)}\|f(s)\|_{H}^{4}ds\right)^{1/2}+\rho_4
		\end{align*}
		with
		\begin{align}}
			\mathfrak{P}(\tau,\tau-t,u_{\tau-t})=e^{-\frac{27
					\mathbf{c}_0^2}{2\mu^3}\int_{\tau-t}^{\tau} \|u(s,\tau-t,u_{\tau-t})\|_H^2 \|u(s,\tau-t,u_{\tau-t})\|_V^2ds},
		\end{align}
	where $u_{\tau-t}\in L^{4}(\Omega,\mathscr{F}_{\tau-t};H)$, $\rho_4>0$ is a positive numbers independent of $\varepsilon_1, \varepsilon_2$, $\tau$, $t$ and $u_{\tau-t}$, and $\widetilde{\kappa}$ is the same number as in (equation LSWs6.3 of the paper).

body: [Definition def:characteristic_pt of arXiv:2609.04045, 'Heat content and spectrum for subordinated sub-Laplacians'] For an open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb{G}$ with $C^1$-boundary, a point $p\in\partial \Omega$ is said to be a \emph{characteristic point} if $\mathcal{H}_p\subseteq T_p(\partial\Omega)$, that is, the horizontal  normal ( i.e. the horizontal projection of the Euclidean normal) at $p$ to the boundary of $\Omega$ is zero. We say that $\partial \Omega$ is completely non-characteristic if it does not have any characteristic points.
title: Characteristic points

[Definition 1 (Hermite rank) of arXiv:2606.04179, 'Functional Scaling Limits of Interpolated Correlated Random Walks in Hölder Topology'] Let \(\gamma(dx) = \frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp(-\frac{x^2}{2}) dx\) be the standard Gaussian measure.
    The Hermite rank \(\hermRank = \hermRank(\feature)\) of a function \(\feature \in L^2(\gamma)\) is defined as
    the smallest integer \(\hermRank \in \nat_0\) such that \(c_\hermRank \neq 0\)
    in the expansion of \(\feature\) in terms of the Hermite polynomials \(H_k\):
    \begin{equation}
            
        \feature(x) = \sum_{k=0}^\infty c_k H_k(x).
    \end{equation}
    Equivalently, the Hermite rank is given by \(\hermRank = \hermRank(\feature) \coloneq \min\set{k\in \nat_0: \scp{\feature, H_k}_{L^2(\gamma)} \neq 0}\).
title: Hermite rank

 g'(1)\leq g(2)-g(1).
\]

[Lemma 3 (Normal-family compactness and the Abelian boundary estimate) of arXiv:2608.24616, '2608.24616'] The functions $J_{t,\varepsilon}$ are holomorphic on
\[
        \mathcal S_r:=\{s\in\mathbb C:r<\Re s<2\},
\]
and, for either sign, $(J_{t,\varepsilon})_{t>0}$ is a normal family on
$\mathcal S_r$.  In addition,
\begin{equation}
 \lim_{s\uparrow2}(2-s)\sup_{t>0}|J_{t,\varepsilon}(s)|=0,
        \qquad s\in(r,2).
\end{equation}
Consequently, every locally uniform subsequential limit $J_\varepsilon$
satisfies
\begin{equation}
        (2-s)J_\varepsilon(s)\longrightarrow0
        \qquad(s\uparrow2).
\end{equation}

[Proposition prop:canonical-chart-uniformization of arXiv:2605.02104, '\textbf{Chart-Generated Probability Geometry\\and Kolmogorov Expectations}'] Let $X$ be a real-valued random variable with continuous strictly increasing distribution function
\[
F_X\colon I\to (0,1)
\]
on an interval $I\subseteq \mathbb{R}$. Then:

\begin{enumerate}
\item $F_X$ is a probability coordinate chart on $I$ in the sense of Definition~(def:prob-chart of the paper);

\item the transformed variable
\[
U:=F_X(X)
\]
is uniformly distributed on $(0,1)$;

\item the associated barycenter satisfies
\[
b_{F_X}(X)=F_X^{-1}\!\bigl(\mathbb{E}(U)\bigr)
      =F_X^{-1}\!\left(\frac12\right).
\]
\end{enumerate}

Let f: {0, 1}^n -> {0, 1}, n >= 2, under the uniform measure, q_j(f) = P(f(X) != f(X with bit j flipped)) and I_flip(f) = sum_j q_j(f). Fix a coordinate i and let f_0, f_1 be the restrictions x_i = 0, 1 on the remaining (n - 1)-cube. Then q_j(f) = (q_j(f_0) + q_j(f_1))/2 for j != i, q_i(f) = E[(f_1 - f_0)^2], and so I_flip(f) = q_i(f) + (I_flip(f_0) + I_flip(f_1))/2. Also Var(f) = (Var f_0 + Var f_1)/2 + (a_1 - a_0)^2/4 with a_b = E f_b, and the Poincare defect D(f) = I_flip(f) - 4 Var(f) satisfies D(f) = (D(f_0) + D(f_1))/2 + Var(f_1 - f_0).

[Proposition prop:extrinsic-persistency of arXiv:2608.29708, 'Intuitionistic and Constructive Modal Logics for Classical Modal Logicians'] {bozic_models_1984}}] 
  Let $\mathfrak{F} = (W, \leq, \sqsubset)$ be an f-frame. Then:
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*)]
    \item $\mathfrak{F} \in \FrameClass{\Box\text{-p}}$ iff $\Vdash^e_\mathfrak{M}$ is $\Box$-persistent for every $\mathfrak{M}$ based on $\mathfrak{F}$.
    \item $\mathfrak{F} \in \FrameClass{\Diamond\text{-p}}$ iff $\Vdash^e_\mathfrak{M}$ is $\Diamond$-persistent for every $\mathfrak{M}$ based on $\mathfrak{F}$.
  \end{enumerate}
  \begin{proof}
    (1 $\Rightarrow$) Take any $\mathfrak{M} = (\mathfrak{F}, V)$ and $\varphi \in \mathscr{L}_\Box$, then use an induction on the construction of $\varphi$.
    Consider the case when $\varphi = \Box \psi$. Take any $x, x'$ such that $x \leq x'$ and $x \Vdash^e_\mathfrak{M} \Box \psi$.
    Take any $y'$ such that $x' \sqsubset y'$, then by the $\Box$-p condition, there is $y$ such that $x \sqsubset y \leq y'$.
    Here, $x \Vdash^e_\mathfrak{M} \Box \psi$ implies $y \Vdash^e_\mathfrak{M} \psi$,
    and the induction hypothesis implies $y' \Vdash^e_\mathfrak{M} \psi$.
    Therefore, $x' \Vdash^e_\mathfrak{M} \Box \psi$.

    (1 $\Leftarrow$)  Suppose that $\mathfrak{F} \notin \FrameClass{\Box\text{-p}}$, then there are $x, x', y'$ such that $x \leq x' \sqsubset y'$ but no $y$ such that $x \sqsubset y \leq y'$.
    Take a fresh variable $p^\ast \in \mathord{\mathrm{PropVar}}$, then we construct a countermodel $\mathfrak{M} = (\mathfrak{F}, V)$ by letting $w \in V(p) \mathrel{\ratio\Leftrightarrow} (p \ne p^\ast \mathrel{\text{or}} \exists v\,(x \sqsubset v \leq w))$.
    Here, each $V(p)$ is upward closed with respect to $\leq$.
    Then, $x \Vdash^e_\mathfrak{M} \Box p^\ast$ by $\forall z \sqsupset x\,(z \Vdash^e_\mathfrak{M} p^\ast)$, and $x' \nVdash^e_\mathfrak{M} \Box p^\ast$ by $y' \nVdash^e_\mathfrak{M} p^\ast$.

    (2 $\Rightarrow$) Take any $\mathfrak{M} = (\mathfrak{F}, V)$ and $\varphi \in \mathscr{L}_\Diamond$, then use an induction on the construction of $\varphi$.
    Consider the case when $\varphi = \Diamond \psi$. Take any $x, x'$ such that $x \leq x'$ and $x \Vdash^e_\mathfrak{M} \Diamond \psi$,
    then there is $y$ such that $x \sqsubset y \Vdash^e_\mathfrak{M} \psi$.
    Now that $x' \geq x \sqsubset y$, then by the $\Diamond$-p condition, there is $y'$ such that $x' \sqsubset y' \geq y$.
    Here, $y \leq y'$ implies $y' \Vdash^e_\mathfrak{M} \psi$ by the induction hypothesis.
    This and $x' \sqsubset y'$ imply $x' \Vdash^e_\mathfrak{M} \Diamond \psi$.

    (2 $\Leftarrow$)  Suppose that $\mathfrak{F} \notin \FrameClass{\Diamond\text{-p}}$, then there are $x, x', y$ such that $x' \geq x \sqsubset y$ but no $y'$ such that $x' \sqsubset y' \geq y$.
    Take a fresh variable $p^\ast \in \mathord{\mathrm{PropVar}}$, then we construct a countermodel $\mathfrak{M} = (\mathfrak{F}, V)$ by letting $w \in V(p) \mathrel{\ratio\Leftrightarrow} (p \ne p^\ast \mathrel{\text{or}} w \geq y)$.
    Here, each $V(p)$ is upward closed with respect to $\leq$.
    Then, $x \Vdash^e_\mathfrak{M} \Diamond p^\ast$ by $y \Vdash^e_\mathfrak{M} p^\ast$, and $x' \nVdash^e_\mathfrak{M} \Diamond p^\ast$ by $\forall z' \sqsupset x'\,(z' \nVdash^e_\mathfrak{M} p^\ast)$.
  \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem thm:quantum_natural_time_cutting of arXiv:2412.04005, '$\SLE_{\kappa}(\rho)$ processes in the light cone regime on\\ Liouville quantum gravity'] Fix $\kappa \in (0,4) , \rho \in (\kappa/2 - 4, -2) \cap (-2 -\kappa/2 , -2)$, and suppose that $\mathcal {W} = (\mathbf{H},h,0,\infty)$ is a quantum wedge of weight $\rho + 4$. Let $\eta$ be an ${\rm SLE}_{\kappa}(\rho)$ process in $\mathbf{H}$ from $0$ to $\infty$ with a single force point of weight $\rho$ located at $0_+$ and assume that $\eta$ is independent of $h$.  Then the following hold:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item The law of the beaded surface consisting of the components of $\mathbf{H} \setminus \eta$ which are to the right of $\eta$ is that of a quantum wedge of weight $\rho + 2$.
\item Let ${\mathfrak q}_{u}$ be the first capacity time $t$ for $\eta$ that the local time at $0$ of the Bessel process $Y$ which encodes the weight $\rho + 2$ wedge is equal to $u$. For each $u > 0$, we have (as path-decorated quantum surfaces) that $(h,\eta)$ and $(h \circ f_{{\mathfrak q}_{u}}^{-1} + Q\log|(f_{{\mathfrak q}_{u}}^{-1})'|,f_{{\mathfrak q}_{u}}(\eta))$ have the same law,  where $(f_t)$ is the forward centered Loewner flow corresponding to $\eta$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

For a finite graph G with inherited positive edge weights, C_m(G;v) is the sum of product weights over simple paths of exactly m edges starting at v, with a free terminal vertex; C_0(G;v)=1 for a retained v. In a uniform n-step origin-started SAW law, a realized k-edge prefix eta has a suffix law on G_eta with exact remaining length n-k, where G_eta deletes earlier prefix vertices and retains its tip. Obstacle avoidance therefore uses C_(n-k)(G_eta minus A;tip)/C_(n-k)(G_eta;tip), multiplied by the prefix-avoidance indicator. An all-length partition sum defines a different conditional law.

body: [Abstract of arXiv:2609.03793, 'Typical martingale diverges on a co-$\sigma$-porous set'] We consider the space of $L^p$-bounded martingales on the Cantor space for $p\in[1,\infty]$. Equipping the Cantor space with two standard metrics, we show that under both, a typical martingale diverges at a typical point. By a ``typical martingale'', we mean an element of a co-$\sigma$-porous set when $p\in[1,\infty)$ and of a co-porous set when $p=\infty$. Specifically, we show that while a typical martingale diverges on a co-$\sigma$-porous set with respect to the first metric, no martingale diverges on a co-$\sigma$-porous set with respect to the second metric. Finally, we investigate the key factors determining whether the divergence set can be co-$\sigma$-porous.
title: Abstract of arXiv:2609.03793: Typical martingale diverges on a co-$\sigma$-porous set

[Corollary 6 of arXiv:2511.06414, 'Non-uniform Edgeworth expansions for weakly dependent random variables and their applicati'] Let $h:\bbR\to\bbR$ be  an a.e. differentiable function so that $H_m=\int\frac{|h'(x)|}{(1+|x|)^m}dx<\infty$.  
\vskip0.1cm
 Under Assumption \ref{GrowAssum} and \ref{DerAss}, for all  $1\leq r\leq m-2$ we have
$$
\left|\bbE[h(W_n)]-\int h(x)d\Psi_{r,n}(x)\right|\leq C_nH _mB_n^{-r},\,\, C_n\to 0.
$$
In particular, for every $q<m$ we have 
$$
\left|\bbE[W_n^q]-\int x^qd\Psi_{r,n}(x)\right|\leq R_m C_nB_n^{-r},\,  C_n\to 0.
$$
and 
$$
\left|\bbE[|W_n|^q]-\int |x|^q d\Psi_{r,n}(x)\right|\leq R_m C_nB_n^{-r},\,  C_n\to 0
$$ 
where $R_m$ depends only on $m$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Corollary 6 of arXiv:2511.06414

[Definition def:moment-problems of arXiv:2606.21391, 'Extreme points and faces in the moment problem'] Building on Definition~(def:moment-constraints of the paper), we assume that $\mathbf{p}\colon X\to\mathbb{R}^d$ 
and $f\colon X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ are measurable with respect to the $\sigma$-algebra 
$\mathcal{F}$. We define the linear optimization problems
\begin{align}

g_\mathrm{fin}(C) & \textstyle
:= \inf\{ \int f\mathrm{d}\mu : \mu\in G_\mathrm{fin}(C) \},\\

g_\mathrm{a.i.}(C) & \textstyle
:= \inf\{ \int f\mathrm{d}\mu : \mu\in G_\mathrm{a.i.}(C) \}
\end{align}
on the spaces $G_\mathrm{a.i.}(C)\subset G_\mathrm{fin}(C)$ of finitely atomic measures. If $f$ is 
bounded below by a real constant, then we also define
\begin{align}

g(C) & \textstyle
:= \inf\{ \int f\mathrm{d}\mu : \mu\in G(C) \},\\

g_\mathrm{ext}(C) & \textstyle
:= \inf\{ \int f\mathrm{d}\mu : \mu\in \ext G(C) \}.
\end{align}
The optimization problem $g(\mathbf{q})$ in (equation eq:PM of the paper) at a specific point $\mathbf{q}\in\mathbb{R}^d$ 
is an example of the problem of moments [shapiro01]. This problem is also known 
as the generalized moment problem if $\mathcal{F}=\mathcal{B}(X)$ is the Borel $\sigma$-algebra on a Borel 
[lasserre10], closed [henrion-etal20], or compact [klerk-laurent19] set 
$X$ in $\mathbb{R}^k$. Loosely speaking, we refer to each of 
(equation eq:PM-atomic of the paper)--(equation eq:PM-ext of the paper) as a \emph{generalized moment problem}.
title: Generalized moment problems

[Prop 20 of arXiv:2605.23659, '2605.23659'] Let \(g\) be the right-continuous inverse of the function
\[
h(x) := \frac{x^\alpha}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)K(x)},
\]
and, for each \(i\in I_{0,\mathrm{sub}}\), let \(g_i\) be the right-continuous inverse of the function
\[
x\longmapsto \frac{x^{\tilde{\alpha}_i}}{\Gamma(1-\tilde{\alpha}_i)K_i(x)}.
\]
For \(i\in I_0\), define
\begin{align}
X^{(i)}_\lambda(t):=
\begin{cases}
\frac{\Gamma^{(i)}_{\lambda t}}{g(\lambda)} & (i\in I_{0,\mathrm{dom}}\cup I_{0,\mathrm{res}}),\\
\frac{\Gamma^{(i)}_{\lambda t}}{g_i(\lambda)} & (i\in I_{0,\mathrm{sub}}),
\end{cases}
\quad (t\ge0),
\end{align}
and
\begin{align}  
X^{(i)}(t):=
\begin{cases}
\xi^{(i)}(t) & (i\in I_{0,\mathrm{dom}}),\\
\tilde{\xi}^{(i)}(t) & (i\in I_{0,\mathrm{sub}}),\\
0 & (i\in I_{0,\mathrm{res}}),
\end{cases}
\quad (t\ge0),
\end{align}
where the family
\[
\bigl((\xi^{(i)})_{i\in I_{0,\mathrm{dom}}},(\tilde{\xi}^{(i)})_{i\in I_{0,\mathrm{sub}}}\bigr)
\]
consists of independent stable subordinators characterized by
\[
E[e^{-q\xi^{(i)}(t)}]=\exp(-t\beta_i q^\alpha)
\quad (i\in I_{0,\mathrm{dom}}),
\]
and
\[
E[e^{-q\tilde{\xi}^{(i)}(t)}]=\exp(-t\tilde{\beta}_i q^{\tilde{\alpha}_i})
\quad (i\in I_{0,\mathrm{sub}}),
\]
for \(q,t\ge0\).
Then
\[
\bigl(X^{(i)}_\lambda\bigr)_{i\in I_0}
\xrightarrow[\lambda\to\infty]{d}
\bigl(X^{(i)}\bigr)_{i\in I_0}
\]
on \(D([0,\infty),\bR^{I_0})\).
title: Prop 20 of arXiv:2605.23659

body:
[Theorem 10 of arXiv:2605.25715, '2605.25715'] Let $\Phi$ be a non-constant polynomial on $\R^d$ of even degree $m\ge 2$ and homogeneous decomposition $\Phi(x)=\sum_{k=0}^m \Phi_k(x)$. Let $\mu=e^{2 \Phi}\,dx$. Suppose that there exist constants $c\in\mathbb{R}$ and $\alpha>d/2$ such that the estimate
\begin{eqnarray}
 \Phi(x)\le c-\alpha\log\|x\|
\end{eqnarray}
holds outside some arbitrarily large compact set. Choose a constant $C>0$, such that $V:=-\Phi+C\ge 1$. Let $A=(a_{ij})_{1\le i,j\le d}$ be a symmetric and positive definite matrix of real numbers, and $\mathbf{P}$ a polynomial vector field in $\R^d$ of degree $n\ge 0$, such that 
\begin{eqnarray}
\langle \nabla\Phi, \mathbf{P}-A\nabla\Phi \rangle+\frac12\mathrm{div}(\mathbf{P}-A\nabla\Phi)=0.
\end{eqnarray}
Let $(P_t)_{t>0}$ be the regularized semigroup associated with the $L^1$-closed extension of $(L^{A,\mathbf{P}}, C_0^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^d))$ (see \cite{LST22}), and suppose that there exist constants $N_0\in \N$ and $M>0$ such that
\begin{eqnarray}
L^{A,\mathbf{P}}V \leq M V \quad \text{on } \mathbb{R}^d \setminus \overline{B}_{N_0}.
\end{eqnarray}
Then $(P_t)_{t>0}$ is conservative (cf. \cite[Lemma 3.26]{LST22}) and $\mu$ is the unique finite invariant measure for $(P_t)_{t>0}$\ and the unique finite infinitesimally invariant measure for $(L^{A,\mathbf{P}}, C_0^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^d))$ as well as a finite infinitesimally invariant measure for $(L^{\widetilde{\mathbf{P}}}, C_0^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^d))$. If, in addition, the regularized semigroup associated with the
$L^1$-closed extension of $(L^{\widetilde{\mathbf P}},C^\infty_0(\mathbb R^d))$
is conservative, then $\mu$ is also the unique finite invariant
measure for this semigroup.
Moreover, if $\mathrm{div}(\mathbf{P}-A\nabla\Phi)=0$, then 
\[
\widetilde{\mathbf{P}}:=\nabla \Phi +\mathbf{B}, \qquad \mathbf{B}:=\mathbf{P}-A\nabla\Phi
\]
is the unique SOHHD for $\widetilde{\mathbf{P}}$.

      T &\leq C \left( \|\psi_{0}\|_{\widehat{L}^{p_{0}}} \right)^{-\frac{\alpha-1}{1-\frac{\alpha-1}{2p_{0}}-\frac{1}{\nu}}}.

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Examine whether the moment condition controls the back-and-forth trap time and hence the regeneration-time tail. Result: The quantity 1/(1 - omega(0,e) omega(0,-e)) is the expected number of returns of the two-site back-and-forth excursion between 0 and e, so the moment condition bounds the expected holding time in two-site traps but not in larger traps (a trap of k sites in a line has holding time controlled by products of k such ratios, whose expectation is not bounded by the first-moment condition). Proposition 2.21 of the source shows the condition is necessary; sufficiency would need a bound on the expected time spent in traps of every size, i.e. on E[tau_1 | D = infinity]. A natural sufficient strengthening is a moment condition on the exit time from every finite box, which is implied by the two-site condition only under an additional assumption on the transition probabilities to move away. I therefore see the question as open in the sense that the two-site condition is strictly weaker than what the regeneration argument needs, and the Dirichlet case works because of the specific reversal identity of Dirichlet environments (Sabot's exit-time integrability). No new result. Obstruction: Two-site moment condition does not control larger traps; the Dirichlet argument uses a special reversal identity.

body:
Let $E = \frac{1}{n} X^T X$ be the sample covariance of $n$ i.i.d. rows in $\mathbb{R}^p$ with population covariance $C$ (rows $C^{1/2} z_i$ with $z_i$ having i.i.d. entries of mean zero, variance one and finite twelfth moment), in the regime $p, n \to \infty$ with $q = p/n \to q_0 \in (0, \infty)$, and assume the spectral distribution of $C$ converges to a limit with bounded support. Let $\lambda_k, u_k$ be the sample eigenvalues and eigenvectors and let $g_E(z) = \frac{1}{p}\operatorname{tr}(z I - E)^{-1}$ be the Stieltjes transform of the sample spectrum, and $g(z) = \int (z - x)^{-1} F(dx)$ that of its almost-sure limit $F$, the limiting sample spectral distribution, with $g(\lambda - i0) := \lim_{\eta \downarrow 0} g(\lambda - i\eta)$ inside the bulk (the finite-sample $g_E(\lambda - i\eta)$ has no useful limit as $\eta \downarrow 0$: it diverges at each sample eigenvalue and is real between them). THEOREM (Ledoit and Peche, 2011, Theorem 4; in the form of Bun, Bouchaud and Potters 2017). The oracle eigenvalues $\xi_k^{\mathrm{or}} = u_k^T C u_k$, as the weighted measure $\frac{1}{p}\sum_k \xi_k^{\mathrm{or}} \delta_{\lambda_k}$, converge almost surely to $\xi(\lambda) F(d\lambda)$ on $(0, \infty)$, where $$\xi(\lambda) = \frac{\lambda}{\big|\, 1 - q_0 + q_0\, \lambda\, g(\lambda - i0) \,\big|^2};$$ informally $\xi_k^{\mathrm{or}} \approx \xi(\lambda_k)$ for sample eigenvalues inside the bulk (the theorem is about the weighted measure, not a limit for each $k$). This limit depends on the population covariance $C$ only through the observable sample spectrum, so it is a consistent, computable estimator (the rotationally invariant estimator, RIE, or nonlinear shrinkage): replace each sample eigenvalue by $\xi(\lambda_k)$, keep the sample eigenvectors. In practice $g_E$ is evaluated at $\lambda_k - i\eta$ with a small $\eta$ of order $n^{-1/2}$ times the eigenvalue scale, and the result is floored at a small positive fraction of the bulk level. When $C = \sigma^2 I$ the formula returns $\sigma^2$ for every eigenvalue (the Marchenko-Pastur spread is entirely removed); for a spike above the bulk it returns approximately the debiased population spike. Applying the formula to a matrix whose largest eigenvalue is a signal one is trying to keep, and flooring relative to that top eigenvalue, destroys the small eigenvalues that the inverse depends on.
i.i.d. rows C^{1/2} z with z having i.i.d. mean-zero unit-variance entries and finite twelfth moment
p/n -> q_0 in (0, infinity)
the population spectral distribution converges to a limit with bounded support
the formula is used inside the bulk; isolated spikes are handled by the BBP correction

Then there are implications:
\[
E\text{ polystable}\implies E\text{ admits a harmonic norm} \implies E\text{ semistable}.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm:nonarch_harm of arXiv:2609.00978

body:
[Theorem 9 (Asymptotics for $\alpha \to \alpha_b, \tilde{\alpha}_b$) of arXiv:2512.09136, 'On the Green's functions and Martin boundary structure of a planar diffusion in a disconti'] Let $z_0 \in \R^2$ and let $\alpha_0 = \alpha_b$. Assume $x_{max}^+ > x_{max}^-$, i.e., $\alpha_b \in (0,\pi)$ (cases A and D of Figure~\ref{anglesalphab}). Define
\begin{equation}
    K_+^2 = \frac{\Sigma_{22}^+\big(y(\alpha_b) - Y^-(x(\alpha_b))\big)}{4|\sin(\alpha_b)| \left( \Sigma^+_{11}\sin^2(\alpha_b) - 2\Sigma^+_{12} \sin (\alpha_b) \cos (\alpha_b) + \Sigma^+_{22} \cos^2(\alpha_b) \right)}.
\end{equation}
Then:
\begin{itemize}
    \item[$(i)$] If $\alpha > \alpha_b$, then \eqref{cas_1} holds.
    \item[$(ii)$] If $\alpha < \alpha_b$ and $r(\alpha_b - \alpha)^2$ is bounded, then \eqref{cas_1} holds.
    \item[$(iii)$] If $\alpha < \alpha_b$, $r(\alpha - \alpha_b)^2 \to +\infty$, and $\frac{e^{K_+^2 r (\alpha_b - \alpha)^2}}{r(\alpha_b - \alpha)^{3/2}} \to 0$,
    then \eqref{cas_1} holds.
    \item[$(iv)$] If $\alpha < \alpha_b$, $r(\alpha - \alpha_b)^2 \to +\infty$, and
    $\frac{e^{K_+^2 r (\alpha_b - \alpha)^2}}{r(\alpha_b - \alpha)^{3/2}} \to +\infty,$
    then
    \begin{equation}
    g^{z_0}(r\cos(\alpha), r\sin(\alpha))
    \underset{r\to\infty \atop \alpha\to\alpha_b}{\sim}  C_{br} f_0(z_0) \frac{e^{-r(\cos(\alpha)x(\alpha_b) + \sin(\alpha)y(\alpha_b))}}{r^{3/2} (\alpha_b - \alpha)^{3/2}},
    \end{equation}
    where $f_0(z_0) > 0$ is given by \eqref{f(z_0)branch} and $C_{br} = |\sin(\alpha_b)|^{3/2} C_0$ (see \eqref{eq:C_0}).
    \item[$(v)$] If $\alpha < \alpha_b$ (resp. $\alpha > \alpha_b$), $r(\alpha - \alpha_b)^2 \to +\infty$, and
    \[
    \frac{e^{K_+^2 r (\alpha_b - \alpha)^2}}{r(\alpha_b - \alpha)^{3/2}} \to c > 0,
    \]
    then
    \begin{equation}
    g^{z_0}(r\cos(\alpha), r\sin(\alpha))
    \underset{r\to\infty \atop \alpha\to\alpha_b}{\sim} \left( C(\alpha_b) h_{\alpha_b}(z_0) + c\, C_{br} f_0(z_0) \right) \frac{e^{-r(\cos(\alpha)x(\alpha) + \sin(\alpha)y(\alpha))}}{\sqrt{r}},
    \end{equation}
    where $h_{\alpha_b}(z_0)$ is given by \eqref{Harm1}.
\end{itemize}

Now assume that $x_{max}^+ < x_{max}^-$ (cases B and C of Figure~\ref{anglesalphab}). Then, the analogous cases $(i)$ to $(v)$ hold. More precisely, let
\[
K_-^2 = \frac{\Sigma_{22}^- \big(z(\alpha_b) - Z^+(x(\alpha_b))\big)}{4|\sin(\alpha_b)| \left( \Sigma^-_{11} \sin^2(\alpha_b) - 2 \Sigma^-_{12} \sin(\alpha_b) \cos(\alpha_b) + \Sigma^-_{22} \cos^2(\alpha_b) \right)}.
\]
\begin{itemize}
    \item[$(i)$-$(iii)$] In cases $(i)$ to $(iii)$, replace $K_+^2$ by $K_-^2$ and the conditions $\alpha < \alpha_b$ (resp. $\alpha > \alpha_b$) by $\alpha > \alpha_b$ (resp. $\alpha < \alpha_b$). Then, \eqref{cas_1'} holds in these cases.
    \item[$(iv)$-$(v)$] In cases $(iv)$ to $(v)$, replace $K_+^2$ by $K_-^2$ and the condition $\alpha < \alpha_b$ by $\alpha > \alpha_b$. Then, the corresponding asymptotics hold replacing $y(\alpha)$ by $z(\alpha)$. Namely, in case $(iv)$,
    \begin{equation}
    g^{z_0}(r\cos(\alpha), r\sin(\alpha))
    \underset{r\to\infty \atop \alpha\to\alpha_b}{\sim} C_{br} f_0(z_0) \frac{e^{-r(\cos(\alpha) x(\alpha_b) + \sin(\alpha) z(\alpha_b))}}{r^{3/2} |\alpha_b - \alpha|^{3/2}},
    \end{equation}
    where $f_0(z_0) > 0$ is given by \eqref{f(z_0)col}. In case $(v)$,
    \begin{equation}
    g^{z_0}(r\cos(\alpha), r\sin(\alpha))
    \underset{r\to\infty \atop \alpha\to\alpha_b}{\sim} \left( C(\alpha_b) h_{\alpha_b}(z_0) + c\, C_{br} f_0(z_0) \right) \frac{e^{-r(\cos(\alpha) x(\alpha) + \sin(\alpha) z(\alpha))}}{\sqrt{r}},
    \end{equation}
    where $h_{\alpha_b}(z_0)$ is given by \eqref{Harm1'}.
\end{itemize}

The symmetric result holds for $\alpha_0 = \tilde{\alpha}_b$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Asymptotics for $\alpha \to \alpha_b, \tilde{\alpha}_b$

Own work draft; status: proof (unaudited), w714-T272-C002 version 2; independent review and priority determination pending. Let d>=1 and f_theta(x)=m^-1 sum_j a_j sigma(m^-1 sum_i B_ji sigma(w_i dot x)), with |sigma|, |sigma prime|, |sigma double prime|<=1 and sigma in C2. Assume ||x||<=1, |y|<=1; independently initialize both networks with identical iid laws for w_i in [-1,1]^d, a_j in [-1,1], and B_ji in [-1,1], with the three arrays independent. Train every array on half squared loss by fresh conditionally unbiased SGD, with deterministic nonnegative base steps eta_k, multipliers m on a,w and m^2 on B, and sum eta_k<=T<infinity. The two runs may use independent minibatch sequences. There exist consistent permutations of both hidden layers, chosen from the initial boundary weights, for which the expected supremum positive excess of population half-squared loss along parameter interpolation over the endpoint loss chord is <=C(d,T)[m^(-1/(d+2))+sqrt(sum eta_k^2)]. Therefore eta_max<=m^(-2/(d+2)) gives expected barrier O_{d,T}(m^(-1/(d+2))). The method uses the established cut-norm/operator inequality for correlated middle edges, deterministic all-layer SGD stability in boundary-L1 plus middle-cut norm, and a normalized-Hilbert martingale comparison to population-gradient Euler dynamics. This does not cover ReLU, unbounded Gaussian initialization, fixed nonzero SGD step in the width limit, or training horizon tending to infinity. Finite exact sublemma checks pass; the full proof has no independent PASS and the Lean sublemma attempt returned runtime unverified.

body:
[Definition Bessel potential spaces of arXiv:2609.01984, 'Instantaneous shrinking of supports for stochastic PDEs\footnote{JY was supported by a KIA'] Let $1<p<\infty$ and $\eta\in\mathbb{R}$. The space $H_p^\eta=H_p^\eta(\mathbb{R})$ is the set of all tempered distributions $u$ on $\mathbb{R}$ satisfying
\[
\|u\|_{H_p^\eta}
:=
\|(1-\Delta)^{\eta/2}u\|_{L_p}
=
\left\|
\mathcal F^{-1}\left[
(1+|\xi|^2)^{\eta/2}\mathcal F(u)(\xi)
\right]
\right\|_{L_p}
<\infty .
\]
Similarly, $H_p^\eta(\ell_2)=H_p^\eta(\mathbb{R};\ell_2)$ is the space of
$\ell_2$-valued functions $g=(g^1,g^2,\ldots)$ satisfying
\[
\|g\|_{H_p^\eta(\ell_2)}
:=
\left\|
\left|(1-\Delta)^{\eta/2}g\right|_{\ell_2}
\right\|_{L_p}
<\infty .
\]
For $\eta=0$, we set $H_p^0:=L_p$ and $H_p^0(\ell_2):=L_p(\ell_2)$.
title: Bessel potential spaces

Let V be an affine algebraic set and p in V. If H_1, ..., H_d are general hyperplanes through p such that p is an isolated point of V intersect H_1 intersect ... intersect H_d, then dim_p(V) <= d. Furthermore, if d is minimal, then dim_p(V) = d.
