body:
[Lemma lem:Fs of arXiv:2607.08551, 'Weighted-threshold Coupon Collection'] Fix $s\in[0,1)$ and define
\[
F_s(\alpha):=
(1-s)\int_0^1 x^{-s}\Bigl(1-e^{-(1-s)\alpha x^{-s}}\Bigr)\,dx,
\qquad
\alpha\ge 0.
\]
Then $F_s$ is continuous, strictly increasing, satisfies $F_s(0)=0$, and
\[
\lim_{\alpha\to\infty}F_s(\alpha)=1.
\]
Hence, for every $\theta\in(0,1)$ there exists a unique $\alpha_{s,\theta}>0$ such that
\[
F_s(\alpha_{s,\theta})=\theta.
\]

body: [Theorem 2.3 (de Finetti’s Theorem) of arXiv:2603.10190, 'Hoeffding-Type Concentration Bounds for Exchangeable Random Variables'] Let $X$ be a standard Borel space. A probability measure $p$ on $X^{\mathbb{N}}$ is exchangeable if and only if there exists a unique probability measure $\rho$ on $PX$ such that, for every $A\in\mathcal{B}(X^{\mathbb{N}})$, $p(A)=\int_{PX}q^{\otimes\mathbb{N}}(A)\rho(\mathrm{d}q).$ In particular, for every $M\in\mathbb{N}$ and every $A\in\mathcal{B}(X^{M})$, $p_{M}(A)=\int_{PX}q^{\otimes M}(A)\rho(\mathrm{d}q),$ where $p_{M}$ denotes the $M$ -dimensional marginal of $p$.

body:
[Defi 4 of arXiv:2511.10535, 'Eigenvalues of Brownian Motions on $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$'] Let $(\A,\tau)$ be a $W^\ast$-probability space, and let $a\in\A$ (just $L^2(\A,\tau)$ suffices).  Then $a^\ast a = |a|^2$ is selfadjoint, and so has a spectral measure $\mu_{|a|^2}$: the unique compactly-supported probability distribution on $\R_+$ whose moments are given by $\int x^k \mu_{|a|^2}(dx) = \tau[(a^\ast a)^k]$ (see \eqref{eq.spectral.meas}).  Denote by $\nu_a$ the push-forward of $\mu_{|a|^2}$ under $x\mapsto\sqrt{x}$; in other words, $\nu_a$ is the spectral measure of $|a|:=\sqrt{a^\ast a}$.

For $z\in\C$, define the {\bf log potential} $U_a\colon\C\to\R\cup\{-\infty\}$ by
\[ U_a(z):= \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^\infty \log(x)\,\nu_{a-z}(dx). \]
It is a subharmonic function, and so its (weak) Laplacian is a positive Radon measure.  In this case it is a probability measure: the {\bf Brown measure of $a$}
\[ \mu_a:= \Delta U_a \quad \text{i.e.} \quad
\int_{\C} \psi\,d\mu_a = \int_{\C} \Delta\psi(z)\, U_a(z)\,dz \qquad \forall\,\psi\in C^\infty(\C). \]
The Brown measure is then also uniquely defined by 
\[ \int_{\C} \log |\lambda-z|\,\mu_a(d\lambda) = U_a(z). \]

[Theorem 12 of arXiv:2605.28377, 'Geometric functionals of Brownian motion on Hermitian symmetric spaces of non-compact type'] Let $(X(t))_{t \ge 0}$ be a Brownian motion on $\Omega$ and let $(S(t))_{ t \ge 0}$ be the associated stochastic area process. Then, as $t \to +\infty$, one has the convergence in distribution
\[
\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}\, S(t)
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\mathcal{N}(0,\gamma  r),
\]

body: The Weierstrass convergence theorem (a locally uniform limit of holomorphic functions is holomorphic and derivatives converge locally uniformly) has no real-variable analogue and does not upgrade to uniform convergence on the whole domain. (1) Real failure: f_n(x) = sin(n^2 x)/n converges to 0 uniformly on R, but the derivatives f_n'(x) = n cos(n^2 x) do not converge to the derivative of the limit — at x = 0, f_n'(0) = n → ∞ — so uniform convergence of real functions carries no information about derivatives. More dramatically, by the Weierstrass approximation theorem every continuous nowhere differentiable function on [0,1] is a uniform limit of polynomials, so uniform limits of real-analytic functions need not be differentiable anywhere. The complex proof uses the Cauchy estimates, which need holomorphy on a two-dimensional neighborhood: a bound on |g| on a disk controls all derivatives at the center. (2) Only locally uniform: f_n(z) = z^n/n converges to 0 uniformly on all of D, yet f_n'(z) = z^{n-1} has supremum 1 on D for every n and does not converge uniformly on D. So the derivative statement must be quoted with 'uniformly on compact subsets'; deducing a uniform derivative bound up to the boundary from a uniform bound on the functions is a genuine error, and controlling it requires extra input (a larger domain of holomorphy, or boundary regularity). (3) The hypothesis is convergence on compact subsets of the open set, not convergence on the closed set: a sequence converging uniformly on the closed unit disk still gives derivative convergence only on |z| ≤ r < 1 unless the functions are holomorphic on a larger disk.
title: Pitfall: differentiating a uniform limit is a complex-analytic phenomenon, and only locally uniform

[Theorem thm:joint of arXiv:2602.14617, 'Stochastic Burgers equation driven by multiplicative Rosenblatt noise: local existence, un'] Let $u \in \mathcal{Y}_{T_0}$ be the unique local mild solution. For any $\varepsilon > 0$, $p \ge 2$, $\alpha < H-1/2$, and $\gamma < 1/2$, there exists $C_{p,\varepsilon,\alpha,\gamma} > 0$ such that for all $t,s \in [\varepsilon, T_0]$ and $x,y \in \mathbb{R}$,
\[
\mathbb{E}[|u(t,x)-u(s,y)|^p] \le C_{p,\varepsilon,\alpha,\gamma} \bigl( |t-s|^{p\alpha} + |x-y|^{p\gamma} \bigr).
\]
Consequently, $u$ admits a modification locally Hölder continuous in time of order $\alpha$ and in space of order $\gamma$.

[Definition def:level of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] A map $f\colon X\to Y$ in $\cat{$\bm{G}$-OrthSp}$ is called an \emph{$G$-equivariant level fibration} if for every finite-dimensional inner product space $V$, $f(V)\colon X(V)\to Y(V)$ is a fibration in the $\mathcal G_{G,{\textup{O}}(V)}$-equivariant model structure, i.e.~if $f(V)^H$ is a Serre fibration for every closed subgroup $H\subset G$ and every continuous group homomorphism $H\to O(V)$. Analogously, we define the \emph{$G$-equivariant level weak equivalences} as those $f$ such that $f(V)$ is a $\mathcal G_{G,{\textup{O}}(V)}$-weak equivalence for all finite-dimensional inner product spaces $V$. 

    A map is called a \emph{$G$-equivariant cofibration} if it has the left lifting property against all maps that are simultaneously $G$-equivariant level fibrations and $G$-equivariant level weak equivalences.
title: Definition def:level of arXiv:2608.28504

[Definition def: partition procedure in sle of arXiv:2606.13147, 'Scaling limits of the single-curve interface and outermost loops in the planar random fiel'] Fix a sufficiently small constant $\iota>0$, and set
$M=\iota r^{3\kappa}N.$
For a box $\mathsf{B}$, write
$S_\gamma(\mathsf{B}):=\sum_{x\in\mathsf{B}}{\operatorname{dist}}(x,\gamma)^{-1/4}.$
We define the following recursive partition procedure. We first partition $\Lambda_N$ into boxes of side length $M$. Given a current box $\mathsf{B}$, we proceed as follows.

If
$
S_\gamma(\mathsf{B})<M^{7/4},
$
we leave $\mathsf{B}$ unchanged.
If
$
S_\gamma(\mathsf{B})\ge M^{7/4},
$
we divide $\mathsf{B}$ into two sub-boxes according to the following rule. Suppose, after translation and rotation if necessary, that
$
\mathsf{B}=[1,a]\times[1,b],
1\le a\le b.
$
For \(0\le c\le b\), let
$
\mathsf{C}_1(c)=[1,a]\times[1,c],
\mathsf{C}_2(c)=[1,a]\times[c+1,b],
$
with the convention that empty boxes are omitted. We choose \(c\) so that
$
\big|S_\gamma(\mathsf{C}_1(c))-S_\gamma(\mathsf{C}_2(c))\big|
$
is minimized, and replace \(\mathsf{B}\) by the two boxes \(\mathsf{C}_1(c)\) and \(\mathsf{C}_2(c)\).

We repeat this procedure until every current box \(\mathsf{B}\) satisfies
$
S_\gamma(\mathsf{B})<M^{7/4}.
$
The resulting collection of boxes is denoted by
$
\mathsf{B}_1,\ldots,\mathsf{B}_n.
$
Finally, we set
$
\mathsf{B}_i^+=\mathsf{B}_i\cap\Lambda^+,
\mathsf{B}_i^-=\mathsf{B}_i\cap\Lambda^-.
$
title: Definition def: partition procedure in sle of arXiv:2606.13147

body: Publication record. For a conditioned Galton-Watson tree, or more generally a simply generated tree, T_n with n vertices and l_k(T_n) its number of vertices at distance k from the root, Conjecture 21.1 of S. Janson, Simply generated trees, conditioned Galton-Watson trees, random allocations and condensation (Probab. Surveys 9, 2012) states that E l_k(T_n)^r -> E l_k(T^)^r for every integer r >= 1 and every k >= 1, T^ the local limit, and the same for real r > 0. Y. Shmalo, Moments of level widths in conditioned Galton-Watson trees (October 2026) shows that if the offspring law xi is critical and E xi^(r+1) < infinity for a real r >= 1, then l_k(T_n)^r, n >= 1, is uniformly integrable for every k, so E l_k(T_n)^r -> E Z_k^(r+1) with Z_k the size of generation k of the unconditioned process; with the cases that follow from Fatou's lemma this proves the conjecture for every integer r >= 1, and for every real r > 0 except when 0 < r < 1 and xi is critical with infinite variance and E xi^(r+1) < infinity. Paper: https://github.com/yspennstate/level-width-moments (commit dd48a4b11b9d). Not refereed.
title: Janson Conjecture 21.1 (arXiv 20.1) proved: moments of level widths in conditioned Galton-Watson trees converge to those of the local limit (Shmalo 2026, repository yspennstate/level-width-moments)

[Defn def:D of arXiv:2609.01458, 'Confluence relations for $q$-analogues of multiple zeta values'] For adjacent $u,v\in\hat{\mathcal{F}}$, define
\[
D(u,v)\in\mathbb{Q}\hat{\mathcal{F}}\otimes\Omega
\]
as follows. When
\[
u=\mathbb{L}_{k_{1},\dots,k_{d}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{d}),v=\mathbb{L}_{k_{1},\dots,k_{d}}(x_{1},\dots,qx_{j},\dots,x_{d}),
\]
we put
\[
D(u,v)\coloneqq\mathbb{L}_{k_{1},\dots,k_{j}-1,\dots,k_{d}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{d})\otimes e_{0}
\]
for $k_{j}>1$, and
\begin{align*}
D(u,v) & \coloneqq-\mathbb{L}_{k_{1},\dots,\widehat{k_{j}},\dots,k_{d}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{j-1}x_{j},\dots,x_{d})\otimes e_{q^{-m}}\\
 & \qquad+\mathbb{L}_{k_{1},\dots,\widehat{k_{j}},\dots,k_{d}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{j}x_{j+1},\dots,x_{d})\otimes(e_{q^{-m}}-e_{0})
\end{align*}
for $k_{j}=1$ and $x_{j}=q^{m}z$, and
\begin{align*}
D(u,v) & \coloneqq\mathbb{L}_{k_{1},\dots,\widehat{k_{j}},\dots,k_{d}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{j-1}x_{j},\dots,x_{d})\otimes(e_{q^{-m}}-e_{0})\\
 & \qquad-\mathbb{L}_{k_{1},\dots,\widehat{k_{j}},\dots,k_{d}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{j}x_{j+1},\dots,x_{d})\otimes e_{q^{-m}}
\end{align*}
for $k_{j}=1$ and $x_{j}=q^{-m}z^{-1}$. Here, we understand that
\[
\mathbb{L}_{k_{1},\dots,\widehat{k_{j}},\dots,k_{d}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{j-1}x_{j},\dots,x_{d})=\mathbb{L}_{k_{2},\dots,k_{d}}(x_{2},\dots,x_{d})
\]
when $j=1$, and
\[
\mathbb{L}_{k_{1},\dots,\widehat{k_{j}},\dots,k_{d}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{j}x_{j+1},\dots,x_{d})=0
\]
when $j=d$. When
\[
u=\mathbb{L}_{k_{1},\dots,k_{d}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{d}),v=\mathbb{L}_{k_{1},\dots,k_{d}}(x_{1},\dots,q^{-1}x_{j},\dots,x_{d}),
\]
we define $D(u,v)$ by
\[
D(u,v)\coloneqq-D(v,u).
\]

    \big( \sqrt{n}(X_{0,n} - x_0), \sqrt{n}(G_n - g) \big)
    \xrightarrow{d} (\mathscr{X}_0, \mathscr{G})
    \qquad \text{in } \mathcal{E} \times C^0_b(E, \mathcal{E}),
    \]
    where the limit $(\mathscr{X}_0, \mathscr{G})$ is Gaussian. Then $X_n$ exhibits Gaussian fluctuations:
    \[
    \mathscr{X}_n := \sqrt{n}(X_n - x)
    \xrightarrow{d} \mathscr{X} 
    \qquad \text{in } C^1([0,+\infty), \mathcal{E}),
    \]
    where the limit $\mathscr{X}$ is Gaussian and characterized as the unique solution of
    \begin{equation} 
      \dot{\mathscr{X}}(t) = (\mathrm{d}_{x(t)} g)(\mathscr{X}(t)) + \mathscr{G}(x(t)), 
    \qquad t \ge 0, \qquad \mathscr{X}(0) = \mathscr{X}_0.
    \end{equation}
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Corollary 3 of arXiv:2606.25494

[Definition newCminus of arXiv:2607.19651, 'Metastability and phase transition in a social network model with multiple opinions'] For any opinion $o\in\mathcal{O}$, a consensus set for $o$ is defined in the following way
\begin{equation}
    \mathcal{C}^o = \{u \in \mathcal{S}:u\neq 0, u(a,o)\geq 0 ,u(a,p)\leq 0, \forall a\in\mathcal{A}, \forall p\in\mathcal{O}\setminus\{o\}\}.
\end{equation}
Note that for any $u\in \mathcal{C}^o$, there exists at least one actor $a\in \mathcal{A}$ such that $u(a,o)>0$.
    A consensus set for another opinion than $o\in\mathcal{O}$ is defined as follows:
    \[
    \mathcal{C}^{-o}=\bigcup_{p\in\mathcal{O}\setminus\{o\}}\mathcal{C}^p .
    \]
title: Consensus sets

[Theorem 3 (Optimal $L^r-$moment bound) of arXiv:2506.20789, 'Central limit theory for Peaks-over-Threshold partial sums of long memory linear time seri'] Let Assumptions~\ref{asu:coef},~\ref{asu:G_n} and~\ref{asu:f} hold. If $\gamma_G<\gamma_0$, then, for any $\delta>0$,
  \[
         \norm{
         \sum_{t=1}^n
         (G_n(X_t)
         \ - \
         \EE[G_n(X_0)])
         \ - \
         G_{\infty,n}'(0)
         \sum_{t=1}^n X_t
         }_{L^{r_0}(\PP)}
         \ \lesssim\
         n^{\kappa_0+\delta}
         \,,
  \]
  where $\lesssim$ denotes inequality up to a multiplicative constant $C>0$ independent of $n$.
  Consequently, if one has $G_{\infty,n}'(0) \neq 0$ for sufficiently large $n$, and if for some $\delta>0$ one has $n^{\kappa_0+\delta - d - 1/\alpha}/G_{\infty,n}'(0) \to 0$ as $n\to\infty$, then
  \[
  \frac{n^{-d-1/\alpha}}{G_{\infty,n}'(0)} \sum_{t=1}^n
         (G_n(X_t)
         \ - \
         \EE[G_n(X_0)])
         \ - \
         n^{-d-1/\alpha}
         \sum_{t=1}^n X_t \stackrel{L^r(\PP)}{\longrightarrow} 0.
   \] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Optimal $L^r-$moment bound

[Corollary 15 of arXiv:2605.14206, 'The clumsy coupon collector's problem'] As a formal power series, the generating function of
the distribution is
\[
  \sum_{n=0}^\infty \PP\left(T_{m,p} \leq n\right) z^n =
    \left[(1-z)
      \sum_{\ell=0}^m
      \binom{m-m/z}{\ell}
      (-1)^\ell
      \left(\frac{1}{1-p}\right)^\ell
    \right]^{-1}
\]
while the generating function of the tails is
\[
  \sum_{n=0}^\infty \PP\left(T_{m,p} > n\right) z^n = 
  \frac{1}{1-z} - \left[(1-z)
      \sum_{\ell=0}^m
      \binom{m-m/z}{\ell}
      (-1)^\ell
      \left(\frac{1}{1-p}\right)^\ell
    \right]^{-1}.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Corollary 15 of arXiv:2605.14206

Let \(D\subset H\) be a measurable bounded set, and $0<|D|<\infty$. Then there exists a constant \(C=C(n,s,p)>0\) such that, for every \(x\in H\),
\[
\int_{H\setminus D} \frac{dy}{|x-y|^{n+sp}} \ge C|D|^{-sp/n}.
\]

body: [Definition of arXiv:2605.02226, 'Finitely Dependent Processes on Subshifts'] A subshift $X $ is \textbf{strongly irreducible} (SI) if there exists $k \in \mathbb{N}$ such that for any two subsets $F$ and $F'$ in $G$ with $d(F, F') > k$ and any pair of globally allowed patterns $ a \in A^F$ and $ b \in A^{F'}$, we have $[a] \cap [b] \neq \emptyset$, that is, there exists $ x \in X$ such that $ x|_{F} = a$ and $ x|_{F'} =b$. The smallest such $k$ is called the SI distance for $X$.

[Lemma lem:sec5-mellin of arXiv:2607.18070, 'The Brownian loop-catcher'] Let \(\mathsf P,\mathsf Q\) be laws on one-sided filling hulls such that
\(\mathsf P[\xi\in H]=\mathsf Q[\xi\in H]=0\).  Suppose
\[
 \int\mathbf 1_{\{H\cap C=\varnothing\}}e^{-\lambda m_\mathbb{D}(H,C)}
 \,\mathsf P(\,\mathrm d H)
 =\int\mathbf 1_{\{H\cap C=\varnothing\}}e^{-\lambda m_\mathbb{D}(H,C)}
 \,\mathsf Q(\,\mathrm d H)
\]
for every radial filling hull \(C\) from \(\xi\) to an interior point.
Then, for every \(z\in\mathbb{D}\),
\[
 \mathsf P[z\in\mathbb{D}\setminus H]
 =\mathsf Q[z\in\mathbb{D}\setminus H].
\]
title: Lemma lem:sec5-mellin of arXiv:2607.18070

Internal demographic noise model where diffusion vanishes at zero with square-root rate

[Definition def:tridiag of arXiv:2412.04579, 'Solvable Families of Random Block Tridiagonal Matrices'] Let $r, n\ge 1$. An $(rn)\times(rn)$ matrix $\mathbf{T}$ is called an ${\mathbb{F}}$-valued $r$-block Jacobi matrix if it is a ${\mathbb{F}}$-Hermitian block tridiagonal matrix built from $r\times r$ blocks satisfying the following conditions. The diagonal blocks $\mathbf{A}_1, \dots, \mathbf{A}_n$ are $r\times r$ ${\mathbb{F}}$-Hermitian matrices. The off-diagonal blocks $\mathbf{B}_1, \dots, \mathbf{B}_{n-1}$ above the diagonal are lower triangular with positive diagonal entries, see (equation eq:T of the paper).
 We denote the set of such matrices by $\mathfrak{M}_{n,\beta, r}$,
 \begin{align}
 \mathbf{T}=
 \left[\begin{array}{ccccc}
 \mathbf{A}_1& \mathbf{B}_1 & 0 &\dots & \\
 \mathbf{B}_1^{\dag} & \mathbf{A}_2 &\mathbf{B}_2 &\dots \\
 0&\ddots & \ddots & \ddots &0 \\
 & 0 & \mathbf{B}_{n-2}^\dag &\mathbf{A}_{n-1} &\mathbf{B}_{n-1} \\
 & & 0 & \mathbf{B}_{n-1}^\dag & \mathbf{A}_n\\
 \end{array} \right].
 \end{align}
title: Definition def:tridiag of arXiv:2412.04579

[Defn 18 (Exact $C^*$-algebra) of arXiv:2507.00346, 'The strong convergence phenomenon'] A $C^*$-algebra $\mathcal{B}$ is called \emph{exact} if for every
finite-dimensional subspace $\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathcal{B}$ and
$\varepsilon>0$, there exists $D\in\mathbb{N}$ and a linear embedding
$u:\mathcal{S}\to \M_D(\mathbb{C})$ such that 
$$
	\|(u\otimes\mathrm{id})(x)\| \le \|x\| \le
	(1+\varepsilon)\|(u\otimes\mathrm{id})(x)\|
$$
for every $C^*$-algebra $\mathcal{A}$ and
$x\in\mathcal{S}\otimes\mathcal{A}$.

body: Publication record. Y. Shmalo, Heat across an edge of an arc-transitive graph (October 2026), addresses Aldous and Fill, Reversible Markov Chains and Random Walks on Graphs, Open Problem 7.30, which asks for a monotonicity property of random walk on arc-transitive graphs stronger than P_i(X_{2t} = j) <= P_i(X_{2t} = i). It proves that on every finite connected 1-walk-regular graph, in particular every finite connected arc-transitive graph and every distance-regular graph, the heat-kernel ratio H_t(x,y)/H_t(x,x) is strictly increasing in t for every edge xy, where H_t = exp(-t(I - A/d)); the derivative is the variance of the Laplacian eigenvalue under the exponentially tilted spectral measure of x. The same holds for the lazy walk in discrete time. On a regular graph that is not 1-walk-regular the ratio across an edge can exceed 1 and decrease (an exact rational certificate on a 4-regular graph of Regev and Shinkar), while its average over the neighbours of x is always increasing. A Lean 4 file checks the finite inequality behind the variance bound. Paper and code: https://github.com/yspennstate/arc-transitive-edge-heat (commit 258ba70a8fd2). Not refereed.
title: Heat across an edge of a 1-walk-regular graph: H_t(x,y)/H_t(x,x) is strictly increasing in t, on Aldous-Fill Open Problem 7.30 (Shmalo 2026, repository yspennstate/arc-transitive-edge-heat)

The bound also holds if the integral is infinite; normalizability is a separate condition. This is a fixed-radius integral estimate, not a uniform directional fourth-moment upper bound.

body: Let alpha, beta, gamma, delta be nonnegative functions on the subsets of a finite set such that for all A, B: alpha(A) beta(B) <= gamma(A union B) delta(A intersect B). Then for all families X, Y: alpha(X) beta(Y) <= gamma(X join Y) delta(X meet Y), where f(X) = sum of f over X, X join Y = {A union B}, X meet Y = {A intersect B}. This single inequality implies FKG, Kleitman, and much of correlation theory on distributive lattices.

[Lemma 4 (Partition estimate for exponentially-weighted sums) of arXiv:2512.04646, '\textbf{Canonical Rough Path over Tempered Fractional Brownian Motion: Existence, Construc'] Let $\alpha > 1$, $\beta > 0$, and let
$\mathcal{P} = \{0=t_0 < t_1 < \cdots < t_N=T\}$ be a partition of
$[0,T]$ with mesh $\delta := \max_{0\le i\le N-1}(t_{i+1}-t_i)$.
Write $\Delta_i := t_{i+1}-t_i$. Then
\begin{equation}

\Sigma(\mathcal{P}) :=
\sum_{i,j=0}^{N-1} \Delta_i^{\alpha}\,\Delta_j^{\alpha}\,
e^{-\beta|t_i-t_j|}
\le C(\alpha,\beta,T)\,\delta^{2\alpha-2},
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}

C(\alpha,\beta,T)
= T + \frac{2T}{\beta}(1+c_0)
\end{equation}
for some absolute constant $c_0>0$, and $C(\alpha,\beta,T)$ is
bounded uniformly in $\delta\in(0,1]$.
title: Partition estimate for exponentially-weighted sums

[Lemma 14 of arXiv:2605.25715, '2605.25715'] Let $\mathbf{G} \in L^p_{loc}(\mathbb{R}^d, \mathbb{R}^d)$ for some $p\in(d,\infty)$, $A=(a_{ij})_{1\le i,j\le d}$ be a symmetric and positive definite matrix of real numbers,  and let $(P_t)_{t>0}$ be the regularized semigroup associated with the $L^1$-closed extension of $(L^{A,\mathbf{G}}, C_0^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^d))$, defined by
$$
L^{A,\mathbf{G}}f = \frac12 \mathrm{trace}(A\nabla^2 f) + \langle \mathbf{G}, \nabla f \rangle, \quad f \in C_0^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^d)
$$
(see \cite{LST22}). Let $T$ be a $d \times d$ strictly positive definite symmetric matrix. If there exist constants $N_0\in \N$ and $M>0$ such that
$$
\langle \mathbf{G}(x), Tx \rangle \leq M \|x\|^2, \quad \text{for a.e. } x \in \mathbb{R}^d \setminus \overline{B}_{N_0},
$$
then $(P_t)_{t>0}$ is conservative.

Let n>=2 be finite and V be a real symmetric 3 by 3 matrix with eigenvalues lambda1>lambda2>0>lambda3. Consider self-inclusive normalized attention dot x_i=(I-x_i*x_i^T) sum_j exp(beta*x_i^T*V*x_j)*V*x_j / sum_j exp(beta*x_i^T*V*x_j) on (S^2)^n, so Q^T K=V. Fix a unit top eigenvector e1. There exists B(V,n)>0 such that for every beta>B(V,n), all 2^n configurations x_i=s_i*e1, s_i in {+1,-1}, are locally asymptotically stable and have open positive-volume basins. For a nonconstant sign pattern with r=n_plus/n_minus, a sufficient criterion from Remark 5.3 is lambda1>|log r|/(2 beta) and lambda_k<lambda1*((c-r)*(c*r-1))/(r*(c^2-1)) for k=2,3, where c=exp(2 beta lambda1). This is a known local stability result; it neither classifies all attracting equilibria nor proves an almost-everywhere limit theorem.

body:
Let f be a nonconstant entire function and M(r) = max_{|z| = r} |f(z)|. The order of f is ρ = limsup_{r→∞} (log log M(r))/(log r) in [0, ∞]; equivalently ρ = inf{λ ≥ 0 : M(r) ≤ exp(r^λ) for all sufficiently large r}, with the infimum of the empty set taken to be ∞. Constant functions are assigned order 0. If 0 < ρ < ∞ one further distinguishes the type σ = limsup_{r→∞} log M(r)/r^ρ. Examples: every nonconstant polynomial has order 0; exp(z), sin z, cos z and 1/Γ have order 1; exp(z^n) has order n; cos(sqrt z) has order 1/2; exp(exp(z)) has infinite order. If f has finite order ρ and nonzero zeros (a_n) listed with multiplicity, then Σ_n |a_n|^{-s} < ∞ for every s > ρ; the exponent of convergence of the zeros, λ = inf{s > 0 : Σ_n |a_n|^{-s} < ∞}, satisfies λ ≤ ρ, and the inequality can be strict (exp(z) has order 1 and no zeros at all).
f is entire
M(r) denotes the maximum modulus on the circle of radius r
title: Order of an Entire Function

[Thm main of arXiv:2507.09120, 'Chemical distance in graphs of polynomial growth'] Let $G = (V,E)$ be a transitive graph of polynomial growth.
   Then, for every $p_0 > p_c$, there exist $c(p_0) >0$ and $K(p_0) < \infty$

[Lemma 5 (Mixed edge) of arXiv:2607.23887, '2607.23887'] Let $S\subset\N^2$ be finite and $\Delta=\mathrm{conv}(S)\subset\mathbb
R_{\ge0}^2$. Suppose the weight $w(a,b)=a-b$ takes both a positive and a
negative value on $S$. Then there is an integral linear form
$\ell(a,b)=ca+db$ with $c+d>0$ such that, writing
$\lambda=\min_{\alpha\in S}\ell(\alpha)$ and $F=\{\alpha\in S:\ell(\alpha)=\lambda\}$,
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $\lambda/(c+d)\ge0$, and
\item[(ii)] $w$ does not have one strict sign on $F$: either $w$ vanishes
somewhere on $F$, or $w$ takes both signs on $F$.
\end{enumerate}

[Lemma 29 of arXiv:2606.17501, 'Critical spectral behavior and large deviations for geometric $\alpha$-stable processes'] Let $\psi \in C_0^\infty(\mathbb{R}^d)$ be a non-negative function,
  and define $K_\psi(y) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} (\psi(x)-\psi(y))^2 J(x,y)dx$.
  Then the Green potential of $K_\psi(y)dy$ is uniformly bounded
  on $\mathbb{R}^d$, i.e.,
\begin{equation*}
    \sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}^d} \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} G(x, y)K_\psi(y)dy < \infty.
\end{equation*}

[Definition def-sect of arXiv:2609.02769, 'Divergence-Free Approximation in Sobolev and Lebesgue Spaces on general unbounded domains '] Let $\omega\in[0,\pi)$. We define the closed sector of angle $\omega$ in the complex plane by
	$$
	\Sigma_\omega
	:=
	\{0\neq z\in\mathbb{C}:|\arg z|\leq\omega\}\cup\{0\}=
	\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft\{
	re^{i\varphi}: r\geq0,\ |\varphi|\leq\omega
	\aftergroup\egroup\originalright\}.
	$$
	A linear operator $\mathcal{T}$ on a
	Banach space $\mathbb{X}$, with dense domain and range, is said to be \emph{sectorial
		of type $\omega$} if its spectrum contained in $\Sigma_{\omega}$, that is, 
	$$
	\sigma(\mathcal{T})\subseteq\Sigma_\omega,
	$$ where 
$\sigma(\mathcal{T}):=\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft\{\lambda\in\mathbb{C}:\lambda\mathrm{I}-\mathcal{T}\ \text{ is not invertible on }\ \mathbb{X}\aftergroup\egroup\originalright\}.$	
Moreover, for every $\theta\in(\omega,\pi)$, the resolvent operators satisfy the uniform bound
\begin{align*}
	\sup\limits_{\lambda\notin\Sigma_{\theta}}\|\lambda(\lambda\mathrm{I}-\mathcal{T})^{-1}\|_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{X})}<\infty.
\end{align*}
title: Definition def-sect of arXiv:2609.02769

Taking $r= (1-\sum_{i=k+1}^d x^0_i)/{(2d)}$,  there exist two positive constants $c_1(x^0)$, $c_2(x^0)$ such that for any $x_1,\dotso, x_k \in (0,r)$,
    \begin{align*}

  &\leq \nabla^2 g(x_1,\dotso, x_k, x^0_{k+1},\dotso,x^0_d) \\
  &\leq  c_2(x^0)Diag(1/x^2_1,\dotso,1/x^2_k, 1,\dotso ,1),

[Theorem 4 (Bayes contraction, with a schedule-only constant) of arXiv:2608.23094, 'One Inverse Step is a Convex Program:\\ Bayes-Limit Calibration of Diffusion Inversion'] For the inversion map \eqref{eq:fixedpoint}, under Assumptions~\ref{ass:tube} and \ref{ass:unimodal} with $d<D$,
\[
\rhog\ \le\ \rhog^{\star}=\frac{|B_t|}{\sigma_{t+1}}=1-e^{-h_t}\ <\ 1
\]
for every schedule with $\abar_T>0$, every stride and every parametrisation, the bound being approached only as $h_t\to\infty$. Hence $\rhog=\rhog^{\star}\Sc_{t+1}$ identically, so the bound is attained exactly when $\Sc_{t+1}=1$, i.e.\ when $\M$ is flat in some normal direction. A measured $\rhog\ge1$ is an over-stiffness of the trained score rather than a property of one-step inversion, and it is a property of \emph{Picard} alone: damping with $\eta<2/\Lambda_t$ converges at every $\rhog$, at rate $\tanh(h_t/2)$ when optimal inside the tube, and Newton and Anderson are insensitive to $\Lambda_t$. \emph{(Proof: App.~\ref{app:proofs}.)} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Bayes contraction, with a schedule-only constant

[Definition D_TWGroot of arXiv:2510.26724, 'Sharp Fuss-Catalan thresholds in graph bootstrap percolation'] A graph $T$ is called a 
{\em tree witness graph (TWG)} for  the 
edge $e$ if either 
\begin{enumerate}
\item $T=e$; or else 
\item for some copy 
$H^{(e)}$ of $K_r$ 
with $e\in E(H^{(e)})$ there are TWGs 
$T_f$ for each edge $f\in E(H^{(e)}\setminus e)$
such that $T_f$ and $T_{f'}$ are vertex disjoint
outside of $H^{(e)}$ 
for all $f\neq f'\in E(H^{(e)}\setminus e)$, 
and $T=\bigcup_{f\in E(H^{(e)}\setminus e)}T_f$.
\end{enumerate}
In case (2) we call $H^{(e)}$ the {\it root} of $T$
and the $T_f$ its {\it primal branches}.

body:
[Theorem 2 of arXiv:2608.23960, 'Learning from Uncertainty-dependent Missing Labels for Semi-supervised Classification'] Let \(\theta_0\) denote the true parameter of the augmented complete-data model
\(p_{\theta_0}(Y,Z,M)\), where \(M\) is the mechanism-generated missingness
indicator. Let
\[
  S_{\rm aug}(Y,Z,M;\theta_0)
  =
  \nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(Y,Z,M)\big|_{\theta=\theta_0}
\]
be the corresponding augmented complete-data score, and define
\[
  \mathcal I_{\rm aug}(\theta_0)
  =
  \operatorname{Var}\{S_{\rm aug}(Y,Z,M;\theta_0)\}.
\]
Let \(\mathcal G\) be any observed sigma-field obtained by coarsening the
augmented data, for example
\[
  \mathcal G=\sigma(Y,M,Z^{\rm obs},R),
\]
where \(R\) denotes any design randomization. Define the design information
\[
  \mathcal I_{\rm des}(\theta_0)
  =
  \operatorname{Var}\!\left[
    E\{S_{\rm aug}(Y,Z,M;\theta_0)\mid \mathcal G\}
  \right].
\]
Then
\[
  \mathcal I_{\rm des}(\theta_0)
  \preceq
  \mathcal I_{\rm aug}(\theta_0).
\]
Consequently, no regular estimator based on the coarsened observed experiment
can have asymptotic variance below the information bound for the augmented full
experiment, whenever the relevant information matrices are nonsingular. Equality
can occur only when the augmented complete-data score is
\(\mathcal G\)-measurable almost surely. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 2 of arXiv:2608.23960

\sqrt{\pi_t(k)}=\langle k\rvert\,e^{-i\theta(t)J_y}\,\lvert n\rangle,\qquad
\theta(t)=\arccos\bigl(e^{-2t}\bigr),

\end{equation}

and the right side is real and nonnegative. Consequently
$\sigma^{\mathrm{FR}}_t=e^{-i\theta(t)J_y}\,\ketbra{n}{n}\,e^{i\theta(t)J_y}$, so the
Fisher--Rao lift of the relaxing law is itself a rigid rotation of a spin
coherent state, about the $y$ axis, run on exactly the Ehrenfest quantum
clock.

W_\omega^2(\mu,\nu)

\lVert \bar{\mu}-\bar{\nu}\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}
+
C_\mu

\bigl(\bar{\nu}(i)\wedge\bar{\mu}(i)\bigr)
H\bigl(\hat{\nu}_i\mid\hat{\mu}_i\bigr)
\\
&\leq
\lVert \bar{\mu}-\bar{\nu}\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}
+
C_\mu H(\nu\mid\mu).
\end{aligned}
\]

[Defn Chordal link pattern of arXiv:2505.16093, 'Multiple chordal SLE($\kappa$) and quantum Calogero-Moser system'] Given $\boldsymbol{x}=\{x_1,x_2,...,x_n\}$ on the real line, a link pattern is a homotopically equivalent class of non-intersecting curves connecting pair of boundary points (links) or connecting boundary points and the infinity (rays). The link patterns with $n$ boundary points and $m$ links are called $(n,m)$-links, denoted by ${\rm LP}(n,m)$.

The number of chordal $(n,m)$-links is given by $|{\rm LP}(n,m)|=C_{n}^{m+1}-C_{n}^{m}$.
title: Chordal link pattern

Multiplication form: there exist a finite measure space (M, μ), a unitary U: H → L²(M, μ) and a real-valued μ-measurable function f on M, finite μ-a.e., such that x ∈ D(A) iff f·(Ux) ∈ L²(M, μ), and U A U^{-1} g = f g for all g ∈ U D(A). Projection-valued measure form: there is a unique projection-valued measure E on the Borel sets of ℝ with A = ∫_ℝ λ dE(λ), meaning D(A) = {x ∈ H : ∫ λ² d⟨E(λ)x, x⟩ < ∞} and ⟨Ax, y⟩ = ∫ λ d⟨E(λ)x, y⟩ for x ∈ D(A), y ∈ H; E is supported on σ(A) ⊂ ℝ. Borel functional calculus: for Borel φ: ℝ → ℂ, φ(A) = ∫ φ(λ) dE(λ) is defined on D(φ(A)) = {x : ∫ |φ|² d⟨E x, x⟩ < ∞}; the map φ ↦ φ(A) is a *-homomorphism, φ(A) is bounded with ‖φ(A)‖ = sup of |φ| on σ(A) when φ is bounded and continuous, φ(A) is self-adjoint iff φ is real-valued a.e., and φ(A) is unitary if |φ| = 1. In particular e^{itA} (t ∈ ℝ) is unitary and, when A ≥ 0, e^{-tA} (t ≥ 0) is a self-adjoint contraction.
H is a complex Hilbert space, separable for the finite-measure multiplication form

body:
[Proposition 7 of arXiv:2608.26038, 'Rotated semicircle laws for permanental roots of Gaussian random matrices'] For every \(x\in\R\),
\begin{align}
  H_N\sim\Pp_{2,N}:\qquad
  &\E[P_N(\ii x)P_N(-\ii x)]
  =
  \int_{\R^2}
  \prod_{\ell=1}^2(x-\ii y_\ell)^N
  \,\dd\Gamma_{2,N}(y_1,y_2),
  \\
  H_N\sim\Pp_{1,N}:\qquad
  &\E[P_N(\ii x)P_N(-\ii x)]
  =
  \int_{\R^2}
  \prod_{\ell=1}^2(x-\ii y_\ell)^N
  \,\dd\Gamma_{4,N}(y_1,y_2).
  
\end{align}
The integrals are absolutely convergent.

body:
[Lemma lem:parity of arXiv:2608.01253, 'The pseudo-quantum representation of \\finite reversible Markov chains'] Run the uniformised chain of (sec:setup of the paper), a Poisson$(\Lambda)$ clock with
$P$-moves at the ticks, and start the doubled chain at $(i,+)$. At time $t$ the
doubled chain is at $(j,+)$ if the original chain is at $j$ after an even number of
ticks, and at $(j,-)$ if after an odd number. Consequently, for the embedding
$\widehat\pi_0=\binom{\pi_0}{0}$,

\begin{equation}
\widehat T_t\binom{\pi_0}{0}
=\binom{\,e^{-s}\cosh(sP^{T})\,\pi_0\,}{\,e^{-s}\sinh(sP^{T})\,\pi_0\,},
\qquad s=\Lambda t,

\end{equation}

so the two sheets carry the even and odd halves of the Poisson representation
(equation eq:poisson-rep of the paper), and their sum returns $T_t\pi_0$.

body:
[Theorem 4 of arXiv:2605.25715, '2605.25715'] Let $\widetilde{\mathbf{G}}\in L^p_{loc}(\mathbb{R}^d, \mathbb{R}^d)$ for some $p\in(d,\infty)$. Suppose that $(L^{\widetilde{\mathbf{G}}}, C_0^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^d))$ admits a unique infinitesimally invariant measure $\mu$. (Here unique is meant up to a multiplicative constant.) Write $\mu=\exp(2 \Phi)\,dx$, with $\Phi \in H^{1,p}_{loc}(\R^d)$ (cf. Remark \ref{definvaranrem}), and set $\mathbf{B}:=\widetilde{\mathbf{G}}-\nabla \Phi$. Then it holds:
\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)] $\widetilde{\mathbf{G}}=\nabla \Phi+\mathbf{B}$ is the unique WHHD for $\widetilde{\mathbf{G}}$.
  \item[(ii)] If there exists an OHHD for $\widetilde{\mathbf{G}}$, then it is unique and 
 \[
 \widetilde{\mathbf{G}}=\nabla \Phi+\mathbf{B}
 \]
is the unique OHHD for $\widetilde{\mathbf{G}}$.
\item[(iii)] An OHHD for $\widetilde{\mathbf{G}}$ exists, if and only if $\mathrm{div}_{dx}(\mathbf{B})=0$ or $\langle \nabla \Phi, \mathbf{B} \rangle = 0$.\\
(In particular, if $\langle \nabla \Phi, \mathbf{B} \rangle \not =0$ on $V$ for some measurable set $V$ with $dx(V)>0$ or if $\mathrm{div}_{dx }(\mathbf{B})\not =0$, then there is no OHHD for $\widetilde{\mathbf{G}}$.)
\end{itemize}

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Exact integral manipulation, Palm calculus, mass transport, limiting obstruction or conditional construction Result: For a finite weighted edge set, choosing an edge proportionally to its weight and then a uniform endpoint samples vertices with probability proportional to weighted degree. Thus a uniform-vertex limit need not equal the endpoint limit when degrees or weights vary. Even knowledge of both endpoint marginals does not identify their joint boundary law: an equal mixture of pairs (0,0),(1,1) and an equal mixture of (0,1),(1,0) have the same marginals but disjoint supports. Product-edge convergence must retain the endpoint-pair measure and horizontal/vertical edge weights. Check: Each incident edge contributes half its sampling weight to a vertex, proving the degree bias. The two binary pair laws both have Bernoulli(1/2) marginals, checking the independent loss of correlation information. Obstruction: No convergence estimate for the actual product-graph endpoint measure is proved. The pair-law example is an information diagnostic, not a constructed graph counterexample.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-p0421-convergence-of-edge-measured-product-graph-voronoi-diagrams
No independent review

[Lemma lemma_simm of arXiv:2606.27549, 'On Analytically Tractable Multidimensional Diffusions via Doob $h$-Transforms, with Resett'] Under the assumptions of Theorem (teo_1 of the paper), let ${\bf X}_t$ be the diffusion process having infinitesimal moments ((2.5bc of the paper)). 
Let the underlying diffusion process $\widehat{\bf X}_t$ have symmetric transition p.d.f.\ satisfying Eq.\ (equation cond_simm of the paper), and let the transformation ${\bf\Psi}({\bf x},t)$ and the function $\varphi({\bf x},t)$ fulfill the conditions stated above. 
Then, the transition p.d.f.\ of ${\bf X}_t$ satisfies the following symmetry relation:

\begin{equation}
 f({\bf x},t\,|\,{\bf y},\tau)
 =\frac{h({\bf x})}{h({\bf y})}\,
 \frac{h({\bf \Psi}({\bf y},\tau))}{h({\bf \Psi} ({\bf x},t))}
 \,
 \frac{\varphi({\bf x},t)}{\varphi({\bf y},\tau)}\,|J({\bf x},t)|\,
    {f}({\bf \Psi} ({\bf x},t),t\,|\,{\bf \Psi} ({\bf y},\tau),\tau),
    \qquad \forall \;{\bf x},{\bf y}\in{\cal D}, \quad t>\tau\geq 0.
 
\end{equation}

        the test which rejects the null hypothesis if $\sqrt n\mathsf{GW}_p(\mu_{0,n},\mu_{1,n})^p$ exceeds the $(1-\alpha)$-quantile of $\hat L_n$ is of asymptotic level $\alpha$. Otherwise, if $\mathsf{GW}_p(\mu_0,\mu_1)>0$, the asymptotic power of the test is $1$ given almost every realization of the samples. [Lemma 29 (Positive feedback projection) of arXiv:2608.12492, 'Weak Limits of Wiener Chaos: Primitive--Fock Classification and Hilbert--Stein Extraction'] Let $K\ge0$ be a nonzero bounded operator on a Hilbert space and let
$z$ be a vector.  With the convention $P_{\{0\}}=0$, one has
\begin{equation}
 \norm{P_{\R Kz}z}^2
 \ge\frac{\ip z{Kz}}{\norm K_{\op}}.
 
\end{equation}
If $K=0$, its contribution is declared to be zero and no quotient is
formed.

[Lemma lem:uniform-approximate-Goh of arXiv:2609.02710, 'Asymptotic Mean Value Laplacian\\ on equiregular sub-Riemannian manifolds'] Let $X^\lambda=(X_1^\lambda,\ldots,X_k^\lambda)$ be a jointly smooth
family of vector fields on $\mathbb R^n$, all supported in one fixed compact set,
with $\lambda\in\Theta$.  Let $\mathcal A\subset\Theta\times
L^2([0,1];\mathbb R^k)$ be compact for the strong $L^2$ topology, and assume
that every $(\lambda,u)\in\mathcal A$ is energy minimizing between its
endpoints and that
\[
 \sup\{\|u\|_{L^\infty}:(\lambda,u)\in\mathcal A\}<\infty.
\]
Write $E_\lambda$ for the endpoint map from $0$, set
\[
 J(u):=\frac12\|u\|_{L^2}^2,\qquad F_\lambda:=(E_\lambda,J),
\]
and let $\operatorname{ind}_{-}(Q)$ denote the maximal dimension of a
subspace on which a quadratic form $Q$ is negative definite.  For every
$\kappa>0$ and integer $N\ge1$, there is $\Lambda>0$ with the following
property.  If $(\lambda,u)\in\mathcal A$ and
$(\bar p,\bar p_0)\in(\mathbb R^n)^*\times\mathbb R$ is nonzero and satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \bar pD_uE_\lambda=\bar p_0D_uJ,\qquad
 |\bar p|\ge\Lambda|\bar p_0|,
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{ind}_{-}\!\left(
  \left.(\bar p,-\bar p_0)\cdot D_u^2F_\lambda
  \right|_{\ker D_uF_\lambda}\right)<N,
\end{equation}
then the adjoint covector $p(t)$ with terminal value $p(1)=\bar p$
satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \left|p(t)[X_i^\lambda,X_j^\lambda](\gamma_{0,u}^\lambda(t))\right|
 \le\kappa|\bar p|
 \qquad(0\le t\le1, 1\le i,j\le k).
\end{equation}

[Theorem thm:spec-ind of arXiv:2411.09075, 'Weak Poincar{\'e} Inequalities, Simulated Annealing, and Sampling from Spherical Spin Glas'] The following \emph{local-to-global principle} reduces proving a \Poincare inequality to establishing bounds on the spectrum of \emph{influence matrices}.
    Suppose for {\bf every} $S\subseteq [N]$, and {\bf every} pinning $x_S$ of coordinates in $S$, the spectral norm of its \emph{influence matrix} $\Psi_{S,x_S}$ is at most $\alpha$, then the Glauber dynamics chain satisfies a $n^{-O(\alpha)}$-\Poincare inequality.
    Here, the influence matrix $\Psi_{S,x_S}$ is an $(n-|S|)\times(n-|S|)$ matrix indexed by vertices $v\notin S$, where
    \[
        \Psi_{S,x_S}[a,b] \coloneqq \Pr[x_a = +1 | x_b = +1] - \Pr[x_a = -1 | x_b = +1]\mper
    \] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

\[
\bm{\mu}_F := (1-\gamma, \ldots, 1-\gamma) \in \mathbb{R}^k.
\]
For $\bm{v} \in \mathbb{R}^{k}$, define $\bm{v}^t$ recursively by
\begin{equation}
\bm{v}^0 = \bm{v}, \qquad \text{ and } \qquad \forall t \geq 1,\,\, \bm{v}^{t} =  A_{0} \bm{v}^{t-1} + \frac{1-\gamma}{\beta}\bm{e}_1.

If $\beta^{-1} \not\in \mathbb{N}$, then there exists constants $C>0$ and $0 < r < 1$ such that for all $\bm{v} \in \mathbb{R}^{k}$,

body: Given measurable spaces (X, F) and (Y, G), a function f : X -> Y is measurable if the preimage of every set in G lies in F. For real-valued f it suffices that {x : f(x) > a} in F for every real a (the sets (a, infinity) generate the Borel sigma-algebra). Measurability is preserved under sums, products, sups/infs of countable families, and pointwise limits - which is why it is the right regularity class for integration.

# Unrestricted random-mean DDPM learning for equilateral three-Gaussian teachers

This is a restricted-case candidate theorem, dependent on unaudited C06--C10. It removes the zero-centroid optimization constraint from C08/C09. It does not claim the general well-separated K=3 target, established novelty, or finite-precision complexity.

## 1. Statement

Let d>=2, R>=1 be known, E have two orthonormal columns, and u_1,u_2,u_3 be the unit equilateral vertices in R^2. The original law is the equal-weight mixture of N(R E u_j,I_d). The plane E is unknown to the algorithm. Choose the small noisy radius a according to C10: for a sufficiently small fixed absolute rho,

    sigma_0=1/(80 sqrt(d)),
    S=10 log(100/(sigma_0 rho)),
    a^2<=c rho exp(-76(S+1)).                         (1)

For a polynomial upper runtime bound, choose equality in (1) with sufficiently small absolute c, rather than allowing arbitrarily smaller a. Put tau=a/R and sigma=sqrt(1-tau^2)>=1/2. For independent original samples X_i and Gaussian noises Y_i, set W_i=tau X_i+sigma Y_i. Optimize the ordinary empirical DDPM loss

    Lhat(M)=n^(-1)sum_i ||s_M(W_i)+Y_i/sigma||^2,
    s_M(x)=-x+sum_j softmax_j(m_j.x-||m_j||^2/2)m_j.

All d-by-3 means are free parameters. Initialize their entries iid N(0,3a^2/(2d)), independently of data/noise. Use physical Euclidean GD with step one.

For 0<epsilon<1, 0<eta<=1/100, sufficiently many polynomially many samples yield

    min_pi ||M_T-a E U_pi||_F<=a epsilon             (2)

with probability at least 553/1600-eta>1/3, at

    T=O(a^(-2)log d+a^(-4)log(C/epsilon)).            (3)

The population version succeeds with probability at least 553/1600. These are real-arithmetic statements, counting exponentials as score evaluations. Sampling and arithmetic costs are polynomial in d,1/epsilon,1/eta, with an enormous fixed dimension exponent from (1). To estimate the original law, rescale means by R/a, and choose epsilon=2 epsilon_TV/R (or smaller than one); matching implies TV error at most R epsilon/2 by Gaussian KL, Pinsker and mixture convexity. Consequently costs are also polynomial in R and the inverse prescribed original-law error. Unknown radius and finite-precision implementation remain outside the statement.

## 2. Population trajectory

Use C10's exact decomposition M=a b 1^T+a c Z V^T, c=sqrt(3/2), V=sqrt(2/3)U^T. C10 proves entry, except on a set of initialization probability at most 1-79/200. Conditional on that good event, the covariance surrogate's entry angle is uniform in either determinant branch. Removing the three unstable sectors of total angular measure 1/8 leaves probability 553/1600.

At entry, the actual mean configuration is in the full tube around the equilateral subspace, projected radius in [0.9,1.1], angular margin from each unstable boundary bounded below by a fixed delta, and normal error at most C rho. Reduce the fixed rho and the constant c in (1) as needed to preserve the margins of C08. C10's full normal contraction and quadratic tangent forcing give, in normalized Euclidean mean coordinates J=M/a,

    ||w_k||<=C rho exp(-c_1 a^2 k),
    tangent error per step <=C a^2 ||w_k||^2.         (4)

Its accumulated size is at most C rho^2. The same sector-barrier and radial-inward arguments in C08 therefore apply. The restricted dynamics in the equilateral subspace are unchanged by allowing additional coordinates: invariance makes them exactly the C02/C03 radius-angle dynamics, up to fixed coordinate normalization constants. In particular normal and radial rates are order a^2, angular rate order a^4, and the angular maximum stays outside the chosen sector. Thus

    |r_k-1|+alpha_k+||w_k||<=C exp(-c_2 a^4 k).       (5)

Here alpha is distance to the nearest matching angular minimum; the radial estimate tracks that minimum exactly, as established in C08, rather than claiming an O(a^2) radius floor. Equation (5) yields (2),(3) for the population loss. The fastest centroid direction causes no loss: its order-one contraction was included in C10's normal Hessian argument, and its divergent rescaled linear field has zero tangent projection.

## 3. Uniform empirical approximation with a free centroid

The finite-sample argument needs no symmetry of the empirical objective. Work on ||b||<=11, ||Z||_F<=5 and define the two rescaled fields

    h_b=-a^(-4) partial_b F_a,
    h_Z=-a^(-4) grad_Z F_a,

and their empirical analogues. For any 0<zeta<1, with probability at least 1-eta,

    sup ||(hhat_b-h_b,hhat_Z-h_Z)||<=zeta            (6)

when n is a sufficiently large polynomial in d,1/a,1/zeta,1/eta. Although h_b itself contains -2a^(-2)b, this is polynomially bounded on the parameter box; no uniform-in-a boundedness of the population field is asserted.

Here is a direct extension of C09's concentration proof. Let

    B=C_0(d+1/a+1/zeta+1/eta+1)^2,
    n=ceil(B^100),                                  (7)

with sufficiently large absolute C_0. Both ||W|| and ||Y|| exceed B only with probability at most C exp(-c B^2), uniformly in the teacher plane. This follows by their Gaussian norm moment generating functions and the bounded mean shifts ||a E u_j||=a. The mean parameter norm is at most C a on the fixed b,Z box. Softmax derivatives of fixed order are bounded combinations of probabilities; logit derivatives are polynomials in W and bounded means. Differentiating the per-pair loss once or twice in the normalized b,Z coordinates therefore gives a polynomial envelope. More explicitly, a first score derivative is bounded by C a(1+||W||), its second derivative by C a^2(1+||W||)^2, and the score norm by ||W||+C a. Hence rescaled loss gradient is bounded by C a^(-3)(1+||W||)(1+||W||+||Y||), and its derivative by a fixed polynomial bounded by C B^12 on ||W||,||Y||<=B. Fixed-coordinate factors c, sqrt(3) and the three means change only C. The same bounds hold for a slightly enlarged fixed parameter box, allowing Lipschitz extension along segments.

Truncate the per-pair fields to zero outside this safe event for the proof only. Their expectation differs from the untruncated population field by at most polynomial(d,1/a) exp(-c B^2), using the polynomial envelope, Gaussian moments and Cauchy--Schwarz. This is smaller than zeta/10 for sufficiently large C_0. All n actual sample pairs are safe with probability at least 1-eta/4; the algorithm uses the original untruncated objective.

Parameter nets now have dimension 3d instead of 2d. A mesh zeta/(100 C B^12) in the fixed parameter box and a 1/2 direction net have combined log cardinality at most C d log B. The elementary bounded-scalar MGF inequality proved in C09 gives per-net tail at most 2 exp[-c n zeta^2/B^24]. Since zeta>=1/B and n>=B^100, this exponent is at least c B^74 and dominates both net entropy and log(1/eta). The direction net converts scalar bounds to Euclidean field bounds, and the parameter Lipschitz bound extends to all points. Allocating failures and adding expectation bias proves (6). This event is simultaneous over parameters and therefore covers all iterates without a data/iterate independence assumption. Choosing B^100 instead of B^80 only loosens the polynomial sample bound.

## 4. Entry with persistent empirical perturbations

Take zeta=c_* a^2 epsilon with sufficiently small absolute c_*. The exact coordinate metric gives

    b_+=b-(partial_b F_a)/(3a^2)+(a^2/3)e_b,
    Z_+=Z-(2 grad_Z F_a)/(3a^2)+(2a^2/3)e_Z,
    ||(e_b,e_Z)||<=zeta.                            (8)

In particular

    ||b_k||<=2^(-k)||b_0||+C(a^4+a^2 zeta).

Since zeta<=a^2, its floor remains O(a^4). The transient centroid impulse into Z is still O(a^2||b_0||^2). The additional direct shape error contributes C zeta exp(76(S+1)) to the entry comparison. Thus, reducing c in (1), the total comparison error C(a^2+zeta)exp(76(S+1)) stays below the entry tolerance. The full parameter box is retained by the same stopped induction as C10. The good initialization-and-surrogate-angle event remains of probability 553/1600; actual empirical rotational invariance is neither assumed nor needed.

## 5. Full tube with persistent empirical perturbations

In normalized Euclidean J coordinates, (8) adds an error of size at most C a^2 zeta per physical step. C10's integrated physical normal Hessian therefore implies

    ||w_{k+1}||<=(1-c a^2)||w_k||+C a^2 zeta,
    ||w_k||<=C rho exp(-c a^2 k)+C zeta.             (9)

The population tangent forcing remains quadratic. Together with the direct empirical error, it has a decaying contribution C a^2 rho^2 exp(-c a^2 k) and a persistent contribution C a^2 zeta. The first has summable total C rho^2. The second must not be summed over all time: near the sector boundary, the restricted angular drift is inward by c a^4 delta, whereas the persistent perturbation is at most C a^2 zeta. Our choice zeta=c_* a^2 epsilon makes the former dominate. Exactly the moving barrier in C09, decreased only by partial sums of the transient errors, keeps a fixed angular margin. The radial annulus has an order-a^2 inward margin, also dominating these perturbations. This closes the normal/radial/angular tube induction together.

Inside the retained sector, the resulting recurrences are

    alpha_{k+1}<=(1-c a^4)alpha_k
                 +C a^2 rho^2 exp(-c' a^2 k)+C a^2 zeta,
    |r_{k+1}-1|<=(1-c a^2)|r_k-1|
                 +C a^4 alpha_k^2+C a^2||w_k||^2+C a^2 zeta.

Geometric convolution gives

    alpha_k+|r_k-1|+||w_k||
       <=C exp(-c'' a^4 k)+C' zeta/a^2.             (10)

The normal floor is O(zeta), the radial floor O(zeta+zeta^2/a^2), and the angular floor O(zeta/a^2); thus (10) uses the largest. Choose c_* to make the final term a sufficiently small multiple of epsilon, and take the time in (3). The Euclidean coordinate metric yields (2).

## 6. Probability and limitations

The initialization-and-angle event has probability at least 553/1600. Uniform empirical control fails with probability at most eta. A union bound, without multiplying dependent probabilities, yields success at least 553/1600-eta. At eta=1/100 this is 537/1600>1/3. Population control sets empirical error to zero and uses the larger probability. A repeated-run selection guarantee is not claimed.

The teacher is still centered, equilateral, equally weighted and spherical, with known radius and covariance. There is no imposed centering on learned parameters or initialization and no known plane or orbit augmentation. General triangles, unknown radius/covariance, unequal weights, finite precision and the full T309 target remain open. C06's anisotropic population local minimum prevents treating equilateral geometry as innocuous. The result is an unaudited candidate restricted theorem, not a finding of novelty.

Least trusted steps: C10's free-centroid analytic estimates, the uniform gradient/Lipschitz envelope over all free means, and the persistent-error tube barrier. Exact symbolic probability and metric checks support only their finite algebra. body: In abstract algebra, a composition series provides a way to break up an algebraic structure, such as a group or a module, into simple pieces. The need for considering composition series in the context of modules arises from the fact that many naturally occurring modules are not semisimple, hence cannot be decomposed into a direct sum of simple modules. A composition series of a module M is a finite increasing filtration of M by submodules such that the successive quotients are simple and serves as a replacement of the direct sum decomposition of M into its simple constituents.
title: Composition series

body: [Definition 8 (Shared-scale uniform vs.\ allocation-flexible) of arXiv:2608.25188, 'Transforms for LLM Quantization:\\ The Great Inversion and Format Co-Design'] We contrast two settings by two freedoms they grant: to allocate bits across coordinates, and to give each coordinate its own scale. A quantizer is \emph{shared-scale uniform} if every coefficient of a group is stored at the same bit-width on a uniform grid with a single shared scale, so no bits can be re-allocated between coordinates: the per-group \texttt{INT4} grid of a deployed low-bit kernel (\texttt{MXFP4} and \texttt{NVFP4} are shared-scale on a \emph{non-uniform} element grid, a second axis taken up in \Cref{sec:format}). It is \emph{allocation-flexible} if the coder may spend a different number of bits on different coordinates under a fixed \emph{total}-rate budget: realized by unequal (but deterministic) bit assignment, by entropy coding of the indices, or both, as in a classical transform coder. \textbf{Every deployed LLM GEMM kernel is shared-scale, fixed-allocation}, for the datapath reasons developed in \Cref{sec:inversion}; the classical transform-coding theory of \Cref{sec:classical} is allocation-flexible.
title: Shared-scale uniform vs.\ allocation-flexible

[Lemma 24 of arXiv:2608.03497, 'Connective Constants on Nested Fractal Graphs'] Let \(w\) be a self-avoiding walk, and let \(\Delta\) be an \(r\)-cell
which contains neither endpoint of \(w\).  If
\(\Gamma_\Delta(w)\ne\varnothing\), then
\(S_\Delta^{-1}\Gamma_\Delta(w)\) is a boundary forest in \(F_r\).
Moreover, it may be replaced by any other boundary forest with the same
boundary state.  The replacement yields a self-avoiding walk with the same
endpoints as \(w\).  Such replacements may be performed
simultaneously in any finite collection of distinct \(r\)-cells.

body: The Boolean satisfiability problem SAT - given a propositional formula (equivalently, a formula in conjunctive normal form), decide whether some assignment of truth values to its variables makes it true - is NP-complete: SAT belongs to NP, and every language in NP admits a polynomial-time many-one reduction to SAT. The restriction 3-SAT (CNF with exactly three literals per clause) is also NP-complete. Hence SAT is in P if and only if P = NP.

Introduce Boolean variables y(t, j, s) asserting 'at time t, cell j holds symbol s'. Clauses of bounded size enforce: (1) consistency - each cell holds exactly one symbol; (2) initialization - row 0 encodes the start configuration of N on x; (3) locality of transition - the content of any cell at time t + 1 is determined by the three cells above it at time t (the head moves one cell per step), so for every position a constant-size set of clauses allows exactly the 2 by 3 windows consistent with some nondeterministic transition of N; (4) acceptance - some row contains the accept state. The total number of variables and clauses is polynomial in n (about p(n)^2 cells times constants), and the formula is constructible from x in polynomial time. [Proposition pro:heredity-covering-numbers of arXiv:2606.21556, 'Mean field limit of non-exchangeable interacting diffusions on co-evolutionary networks'] Consider a metric space $(\mathcal{X},d_\mathcal{X})$, any $\alpha\in(0,1]$ and any $R>0$, and define the subset $\mathcal{K}_R\subset C(K,\mathbb{R}^d)$ given by
$$\mathcal{K}_R:=\left\{\Phi\in C(K,\mathbb{R}^d):\,\max\{\Vert \Phi\Vert_\infty,[\Phi]_\alpha\}\leq R\right\},$$
where, as usual, we define the uniform norm, and the $\alpha$-H{\"o}lder seminorm by
$$\Vert \Phi\Vert_\infty:=\max_{x\in K}|\Phi(x)|,\quad [\Phi]_\alpha:=\sup_{\substack{x,y\in K\\x\neq y}}\frac{|\Phi(x)-\Phi(y)|}{(d_\mathcal{X}(x,y))^\alpha},\quad \Phi\in C(\mathcal{K},\mathbb{R}^d).$$
Then, $\mathcal{K}_R$ is a compact subset of $C(K,\mathbb{R}^d)$ and we have
$$\mathcal{N}_\varepsilon(\mathcal{K}_R)\leq \left(4+\frac{72R^2}{\varepsilon^2}\right)^{d\,\mathcal{N}_{\frac{\varepsilon^{1/\alpha}}{2(3R)^{1/\alpha}}}(K)},$$
for every $\varepsilon>0$.

[Definition of arXiv:2608.30973, 'Pseudo-Anosov flow and dynamics on guts'] Let \((N,\gamma)\) be a sutured manifold. A properly embedded essential annulus A in \(M\) is called a \emph{product annulus} if it does not cobound a solid cylinder and its two boundary components \(\partial _{+}A\) and \(\partial _{-}A\) of \(A\) lies in \(R_{+}\) and \(R_{-}\), respectively.
A properly embedded disk \(D\) in \(M\) is called a \emph{product disk} if its boundary intersects \(s(\gamma)\) at exactly two points.
We call both product annuli and product disks \emph{product decomposition surfaces}.

In the contrast, we say \(A\) is a \emph{non-product annulus} if it is neither a product annulus nor boundary-parallel to \(R_{+}\cup R_{-}\).

[Lemma 76 of arXiv:2608.07239, 'Unified framework for asymptotically uniform iterative construction of generalised random '] For $r=0,\ldots,\alpha-1$ and distinct vertices $s_1,\ldots,s_d\in S$ for some constant $d\geq1$, we have

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Optimal stationary stopping under Markov-chain lumping structural calculation Result: For a genuinely lumpable partition, the K=1 inequality follows directly. Start the fine chain in any state of a chosen coarse block and use a fine-chain stopping time attaining stationarity. Its projection has the coarse-chain path law. Any extra fine information can be represented by auxiliary conditional randomness in the coarse filtration, so this yields a randomized coarse stopping rule with stationary terminal law and the same expected duration. Taking maxima proves the claim in this special case. Check: Equivalently disintegrate the stopped fine path given each successively observed coarse path; the conditional continuation probabilities give an adapted randomized coarse stopping rule. The conclusion requires strong lumpability, because otherwise the projected fine path is not the Markov chain defined by stationary-flow matching. Obstruction: For arbitrary partitions, equality of one-step stationary flows does not identify multi-step path laws. The stopping-time projection argument therefore fails at its first premise. A full comparison needs a different potential-theoretic argument and the later lifting result must be reconciled.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-p0242-optimal-stationary-stopping-under-markov-chain-lumping
No independent review

body:
[Definition 7 of arXiv:2607.26894, 'Stability in stochastic hypergraph matching II: weights, batch arrivals, and continuous ti'] \hfill
	\begin{itemize}
		\item A matching policy $\Phi$ is said to be size-based if we relax the condition $S^c(t), S^b(t) \in \mathcal{H}_t$ to $S(t) = S^c(t) + S^b(t) \in \mathcal{H}_t$. In particular, it ignores the individual batches, which is specified by the batch arrival process $S^b(t)$, and only takes into account the total size $S(t)$.
		\item A matching policy $\Phi$ is said to be Markovian if for all $0 \leq s \leq t$, its behaviour in the future $Q(t)$ depends only on the current buffer state $X(s)$ and the arrivals in-between $(S(t'))_{s \leq t' \leq t}$, with possibly some randomisation. Specifically, for all $B \in \mathcal{B}(K_V)$, we have
		\[
		\P\left[Q(t) \in B \mid \mathcal{H}_s, (S(t'))_{s < t' \leq t}\right] = \P\left[Q(t) \in B \mid s, X(s), (S(t'))_{s \leq t' \leq t}\right].
		\]
		If the kernel does not depend on $s$, then we say that the matching policy is stationary.
	\end{itemize}
title: Definition 7 of arXiv:2607.26894

[Thm q-difference_of_qMPL of arXiv:2609.01458, 'Confluence relations for $q$-analogues of multiple zeta values'] Let $j\in\{1,\dots,d\}$. If $k_{j}>1$,
then we have
\begin{align*}
 & \mathrm{Li}_{q;k_{1},\dots,k_{d}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{d})-\mathrm{Li}_{q;k_{1},\dots,k_{d}}(x_{1},\dots,qx_{j},\dots,x_{d})\\
 & =\mathrm{Li}_{q;k_{1},\dots,k_{j}-1,\dots,k_{d}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{d}).
\end{align*}
If $k_{j}=1$, then, assuming that $x_{j}\neq1$, we have
\begin{align*}
 & \mathrm{Li}_{q;k_{1},\dots,k_{d}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{d})-\mathrm{Li}_{q;k_{1},\dots,k_{d}}(x_{1},\dots,qx_{j},\dots,x_{d})\\
 & =\frac{x_{j}}{1-x_{j}}\mathrm{Li}_{q;k_{1},\dots,\widehat{k_{j}},\dots,k_{d}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{j-1}x_{j},\dots,x_{d})\\
 & \quad-\frac{1}{1-x_{j}}\mathrm{Li}_{q;k_{1},\dots,\widehat{k_{j}},\dots,k_{d}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{j}x_{j+1},\dots,x_{d}).
\end{align*}
Here, we regard the first term as $\frac{x_{1}}{1-x_{1}}\mathrm{Li}_{q;k_{2},\dots,k_{d}}(x_{2},\dots,x_{d})$
when $j=1$, and the second term as $0$ when $j=d$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Dfn 15 ({\cite[p.\ 110) of arXiv:2605.27974, 'Discrete approximation of semi-Dirichlet forms with non-symmetric perturbations of resista'] {FOT}}]
    Let $(\mathcal{E},\mathcal{F})$ be a Dirichlet form on $L^2(X, \mu)$ and assume that 
    $\mathcal{F} \subset C(X)$ and that $\mathcal{F}$ is dense in 
    $(C(X),\norm{\cdot}_{\infty})$. Then, for any $f \in \mathcal{F}$, 
    there exists a unique finite Borel measure $\nu_{f}$ on $X$ which satisfies 
    \begin{align}
        \int_{X}g\,d\nu_{f}=2\mathcal{E}(fg,f)-\mathcal{E}(g,f^{2}), 
        \quad g \in \mathcal{F}.
    \end{align}
     The measure $\nu_{f}$ is called the energy measure of $f$. Also, for any 
     $f,g \in \mathcal{F}$, we define a signed measure $\nu_{f,g}$ by 
    \begin{equation}
        \nu_{f,g} \coloneqq \frac{1}{2}(\nu_{f+g}-\nu_{f}-\nu_{g}).
    \end{equation}
    $\nu_{f,g}$ is called the mutual energy measure of $f$ and $g$. Then, we have 
    $\abs{\nu_{f,g}(B)} \leq \nu_{f}(B)^{1/2}\nu_{g}(B)^{1/2}$
    for any Borel set $B$ of $X$.

body:
Let f ∈ C^1(R) and let u ∈ L^∞(R × (0,∞)) be a weak solution of u_t + f(u)_x = 0 that is piecewise C^1: away from finitely many disjoint C^1 curves x = s_i(t) it is C^1, and it has C^1 one-sided traces u_-(t) (from x < s_i(t)) and u_+(t) (from x > s_i(t)) on each curve. Each curve then satisfies Rankine-Hugoniot, σ := s_i'(t) = ( f(u_-) - f(u_+) ) / ( u_- - u_+ ) when u_- ≠ u_+. Such a u is a Kruzhkov entropy solution if and only if at every point of every discontinuity curve the chord condition holds: for every k strictly between u_- and u_+, ( f(k) - f(u_-) ) / ( k - u_- ) ≥ σ ≥ ( f(k) - f(u_+) ) / ( k - u_+ ). Equivalently: if u_+ < u_-, the graph of f on [u_+,u_-] lies on or below the chord joining (u_+,f(u_+)) to (u_-,f(u_-)); if u_- < u_+, the graph of f on [u_-,u_+] lies on or above that chord. If f is strictly convex, this is equivalent to the Lax shock inequalities f'(u_-) ≥ σ ≥ f'(u_+), i.e. to u_- > u_+: a strictly convex flux admits only downward jumps.
f ∈ C^1
u is a weak solution which is piecewise C^1 with C^1 shock curves and one-sided traces (the equivalence as stated is for this piecewise-smooth class; Kruzhkov's definition is what governs general L^∞ solutions)
the chord condition must hold at EVERY point of EVERY discontinuity curve
Rankine-Hugoniot alone is not sufficient: it fixes σ but permits inadmissible jumps

body:
[Theorem 13 (CRT scaling limit of the critical cluster; conditional on Hypothesis~\ref{hyp:red}) of arXiv:2608.15987, 'Threshold cascades of interacting diffusions on unimodular random trees: a conditional bra'] Assume Hypothesis~\ref{hyp:red}, criticality $\rho(M)=1$, irreducibility and aperiodicity as in Theorem~\ref{thm:32}, and in addition that the offspring distributions admit finite exponential moments: $\E[e^{t\deg}]<\infty$ for some $t>0$ (e.g.\ bounded degrees, or Poissonian $g$). Then there is an explicit constant $\Sigma\in(0,\infty)$, computable from the second-moment matrices of the offspring law and the Perron eigenvectors of $M$ (Appendix~\ref{app:miermont}), such that, conditionally on $\{|S|=n\}$,
\[
\Big(S,\ \frac{\Sigma}{\sqrt n}\,d_{\mathrm{gr}},\ \mathrm{unif}_S\Big)\ \xrightarrow{(d)}\ \big(\mathcal T_e,d_e,\mu_e\big)\qquad(n\to\infty)
\]
in the GHP topology, where $d_{\mathrm{gr}}$ is the graph distance on the cluster and $\mathrm{unif}_S$ the uniform probability measure on its vertices. In particular the height of the conditioned cluster is of exact order $\sqrt n$, with the Brownian-excursion law of the CRT height, and the shape of the critical cascade cluster is universal: independent of the drifts, thresholds, hazard-domain structure, and boundary geometry, all of which enter only through the single scale factor $\Sigma$.

body:
[Lemma 30 (Coordinate representation) of arXiv:2603.28734, 'Free energy analyticity of the disordered XY model and Debye screening in the 2D Coulomb g'] Let $G$ be a finite graph and $\beta\in[0,\infty)$.
    Define $\mu_{G,\beta}'$ as the probability measure on
    \[
        \tau:=(\alpha,\omega,\eta)\in [0,\tfrac\pi2]^V\times\{0,1\}^E\times\{0,1\}^E:=\Pi_G
    \]
    with density
    \begin{align}
        &
        \diff\mu_{G,\beta}'(\tau)
        \propto
        \textstyle
        \left(\prod_{u\in V}\diff\alpha_u\right)
        \\
        &
        \qquad\qquad
        \textstyle
        \cdot
        2^{k(\omega)}
        \left(
            \prod_{uv\in \omega}
                (1-\e^{-2\beta(\cos\alpha_u)(\cos\alpha_v)})
            \middle)\middle(
            \prod_{uv\not\in\omega}
                e^{-2\beta(\cos\alpha_u)(\cos\alpha_v)}
            \right)
            \\&
            \qquad\qquad
            \textstyle
            \cdot
            2^{k(\eta)}
            \left(
                \prod_{uv\in \eta}
                     (1-\e^{-2\beta(\sin\alpha_u)(\sin\alpha_v)})
                \middle)\middle(
                \prod_{uv\not\in\eta}
                    e^{-2\beta(\sin\alpha_u)(\sin\alpha_v)}
                \right).
    \end{align}
    Here $k(\rho)$ denotes the number of connected components of $(V,\rho)$.

    Now obtain a sample $\sigma\in(\S^1)^V$ as follows:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item Sample $\tau\sim\mu_{G,\beta}'$,
        \item Sample $\xi\in\{-1,+1\}^V$ by flipping a fair coin for each connected component of $\omega$,
        \item Sample $\zeta\in\{-1,+1\}^V$ by flipping a fair coin for each connected component of $\eta$,
        \item Set $\sigma_u:=\xi_u\cos\alpha_u + i\cdot \zeta_u\sin\alpha_u$ for each $u\in V$.

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Strict interface speedup in half-plane inhomogeneous FPP structural argument Result: For constant times a on one half-plane and b on the other, let c=min(a,b)>0. Every path with vertical displacement n costs at least cn. A path taking a bounded horizontal detour into the cheaper half-plane, moving n steps vertically, then returning costs cn+O(1). Thus the interface time constant is exactly c, so there is no strict speedup beyond both homogeneous models. Check: The lower bound uses path length at least n; the explicit path gives a matching upper bound after division by n. Obstruction: Random switching between regions may exploit complementary favorable segments. The deterministic comparison cannot characterize when that advantage is strictly positive.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-p0120-strict-interface-speedup-in-half-plane-inhomogeneous-fpp

[Defn 11 of arXiv:2607.04730, 'Variance gamma approximation to sums of triplewise independent random variables'] Let $W$ be a mean-zero rv with finite, non-zero variance $\sigma^2$. We say that $W^{*(n)}$ has the $W$-zero biased distribution of order $n$ if for all $n$ times
differentiable functions $f$ for which $\mathbb{E}[Wf(W)]$ exists,
\[
\mathbb{E}[Wf(W)]
= \sigma^2 \mathbb{E}\!\left[A_n f\left(W^{*(n)}\right)\right],
\]   
where $A_n f(x)=x^{-1}T^{n} f(x)$
and
$Tf(x)=x f^\prime (x)$. Here $T^{n}$ denotes $n$-times compositions of $T$, that is, $T^n = T \circ T \circ \cdots \circ T $ $(n \text{ times}).$

[Lemma lem:ank-unified of arXiv:2607.00731, 'Sharp Asymptotics for the Largest Component in the Subcritical Regime of Preferential Atta'] Let
\[
\Psi_n=\log\frac{1}{1-\varepsilon}+(\alpha+2)\log\!\left(1-\frac{\varepsilon}{\alpha+2}\right).
\]
Then
\[
\Psi_n=\frac{\alpha+1}{2(\alpha+2)}\varepsilon^2+O(\varepsilon^3),
\]
where the \(O(\varepsilon^3)\) remainder is uniform in \(n\). Moreover, for every fixed \(B<\infty\) there exist constants
\(0<c_1<c_2<\infty\), depending only on \(B\) and \(\alpha_*\), such that, for all sufficiently large \(n\),
uniformly for $2\le k\le B\varepsilon^{-2}\log x_n,$ we have
\[
c_1 k^{-3/2}e^{-\Psi_n k}\le a_{n,k}\le c_2 k^{-3/2}e^{-\Psi_n k}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\mathbb E C_k^{(n,m)}=\Theta\!\bigl(nk^{-5/2}e^{-\Psi_n k}\bigr).
\]

For bond percolation on the square lattice Z^2, p_c = 1/2, and moreover theta(1/2) = 0: there is no infinite open cluster AT the critical point. The two halves have separate histories and separate proofs. HARRIS (1960) proved theta(1/2) = 0, which gives p_c >= 1/2. KESTEN (1980) proved that theta(p) > 0 for every p > 1/2, giving p_c <= 1/2. The self-duality of Z^2 bond percolation at p = 1/2 - the dual of the open configuration at parameter p is a configuration at parameter 1 - p on an isomorphic lattice - makes 1/2 the ONLY candidate but does not by itself decide the critical behaviour, which is why the theorem is hard. The corresponding value for SITE percolation on Z^2 is not known; for site percolation on the triangular lattice the answer is 1/2 by the same duality mechanism, and that is the case where conformal invariance at criticality is proved. [Harris (1960); Kesten (1980), Comm. Math. Phys. 74; see Grimmett, Percolation, 2nd ed., Chapter 11, or Bollobas-Riordan, Percolation]
bond percolation on the square lattice Z^2
the Harris half as sketched uses Burton-Keane uniqueness, self-duality, the square-root trick and a planar topological argument
the Kesten half is stated but not proved in this node

By the Burton-Keane theorem the infinite open cluster is almost surely unique, and by self-duality the dual configuration at 1/2 has the same law, so the dual also has a unique infinite closed cluster almost surely. Fix eps > 0 and choose a box [-n, n]^2 large enough that with probability at least 1 - eps the infinite open cluster meets the box. Let A_left, A_right, A_top, A_bottom be the four increasing events that the corresponding side of the box is joined to infinity by an open path off the box. By symmetry of the square lattice these four have the same probability, and their union has probability at least 1 - eps. The SQUARE-ROOT TRICK gives P(A_side) >= 1 - eps^{1/4}, so with probability close to 1 all four occur simultaneously. The same argument in the dual gives four closed dual arms from the four sides with probability close to 1. But an open path leaving the box to the left and one leaving to the right, joined through the unique infinite open cluster, separate the plane in a way that is incompatible with a closed dual path leaving the top and one leaving the bottom joined through the unique infinite closed dual cluster - two disjoint infinite crossings of the plane in perpendicular directions cannot coexist by a planar topological argument. [Corollary 7 (Growth of the eigenfunctions, $\varepsilon>0$ and $\frac{1}{3}<\gamma<1$) of arXiv:2603.29473, '$\chi^2$--cut-off phenomenon for Galerkin projections of Fokker--Planck equations with mon'] \hfill

	\noindent
	Let $V$ be the potential defined in \cref{def:V} for some $\gamma>0$ and let $\varrho_{\varepsilon,\infty}$ be the density function given in \cref{ec:invm}.
	Assume that $\frac{1}3 < \gamma < 1$ and let $v \in L^2_{\varrho_{\varepsilon,\infty}}$ be a solution to the eigenvalue problem
	\begin{equation*}
		-\varepsilon v'' + V' v' = \lambda_{\varepsilon} v \quad \text{on } \R,
	\end{equation*}
	for $\lambda_\varepsilon = \lambda \varepsilon^{\frac{\gamma-1}{\gamma+1}} > 0$ with $\lambda$ being an eigenvalue of $\mathcal{L}_1$.
	Then it follows that
	\begin{equation*}
		v(x)
		\approx e^{\lambda \frac{|x \varepsilon^{-\frac{1}{1+\gamma}}|^{1-\gamma}}{1-\gamma}}\quad \textrm{ in }\quad
		[x^* \varepsilon^{\frac{1}{1+\gamma}},\infty),
	\end{equation*}
	where $x^*$ is the turning point defined in \cref{thm:main:3prime}. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] A function $f:\mathbb R^N\to\mathbb R^M$ is continuously differentiable,
$$f(x+t)\simeq f(x)+f'(x)t$$
with $f'(x)$ linear, and $x\to f'(x)$ continuous, precisely when it has partial derivatives,
$$\frac{df_i}{dx_j}(x)=\lim_{t\to 0}\frac{f_i(x+te_j)-f_i(x)}{t}$$
which depend continuously on $x$. In this case the derivative is
$$f'(x)=\left(\frac{df_i}{dx_j}(x)\right)_{ij}\in M_{M\times N}(\mathbb R)$$ 
acting on the vectors $t\in\mathbb R^N$ by usual multiplication.

body:
[Theorem thm:conv-immig of arXiv:2412.03325, 'Functional limit theorem for branching processes \\ in nearly degenerate varying environme'] Assume that the BPVEI $(Y_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ defined in (equation eq:Y of the paper) satisfies the conditions (C1)--(C3) and (C4) or (C4') holds. Then, for any $0<\varepsilon \leq 1$,
\[
\mathcal{L} ((Y_{A(nt)})_{t \geq  \varepsilon}) 
\stackrel{\mathcal{D}}{\longrightarrow} \mathcal{L} ((W(\log t))_{t \geq \varepsilon}),
\]
as $n\to \infty$, 
where $(W(u))_{u\geq \log \varepsilon}$ is a continuous time branching 
process with immigration with initial distribution having g.f.,
\[
\log f_Y(s) 
= 
\begin{cases}
-\sum_{k=1}^{\kappa} 
\frac{2^k\lambda_k}{\nu^k} \left( \log\left( 
1+\frac{\nu}{2}(1-s)\right) +
\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}\frac{\nu^i}{i2^i}
(s-1)^i\right), & \nu > 0, \\
\sum_{k=1}^{\kappa} \frac{\lambda_k}{k} (s-1)^k, & \nu = 0,
\end{cases}
\]
with parameters $\alpha = 1+\nu$, $\beta = \sum_{k=1}^{\kappa}(-1)^{k+1}\lambda_k$,
and
\[
\begin{split}
f(s) & = (1+\nu)^{-1} \left(1+\frac{\nu}{2} + \frac{\nu}{2}s^2\right), \\
h(s) & = 1 + \beta^{-1} \sum_{k=1}^{\kappa} \lambda_k (s-1)^k,
\end{split}
\]
offspring and immigration g.f.'s, where $\kappa=K-1$ or $\kappa=\infty$ depending on whether condition (C4) or (C4') holds. The transition generating function of $W$ is given by
\begin{equation*} 
G_y(s, t) = \mathbf{E} \left[ s^{W(t + u)} | W(u) = y \right] = 
\frac{f_Y(s)}{f_Y(h_{e^{-t}}(s))} \left( h_{e^{-t}}(s) \right)^y.
\end{equation*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

In undirected nearest-neighbor FPP on Z^d, d>=2, with iid nonnegative edge weights, suppose disjoint positive-mass low and high sets satisfy low weights in [ell,a] and high weights at least b>a. If an integer k>=1 satisfies k(b+ell-2a)>2a, then with probability p_high^(2k^2+k)*p_low^(2k+2)>0 the unrestricted time from (0,0) to (k,k) is strictly below the minimum over all coordinate-monotone paths. This is a finite event and gives no exponent bound.

body:
[Thm of arXiv:2506.01306, 'Asymptotic of Coulomb gas integral, Temperley-Lieb type algebras and pure partition functi'] Let $j \in \{1,\ldots,n\}$ and suppose $\mathcal{Z}$ is a positive solution to the system of PDEs, such that the limit
\[
\lim_{x_j,x_{j\pm1} \to \xi} \left|x_j - x_{j\pm1}\right|^{-\Delta} \cdot \mathcal{Z}(x_1,\ldots,x_n)
\]
exists and is nonzero for all fixed $\{x_k\}_{k \neq j, j\pm1}$ and $\xi$ in a suitable interval. Let $(X_t^{(1)},\ldots,X_t^{(n)})$ solve the SDE with drift $b^{(j)} = \kappa \, \partial_j \log \mathcal{Z}$. Let $\tau$ be any stopping time such that $|X_t^{(k)} - X_t^{(l)}| \geq \varepsilon$ and $|X_t^{(k)} - X_t^{(l)}| \leq 2\pi - \varepsilon$ for all $k \neq l$ and $t \leq \tau$. Then the process $Y_t = |X_t - X_t^{(j\pm1)}|$ is absolutely continuous with respect to a linear time change of a Bessel process of dimension
\[
\delta = 1 + 2\Delta + \frac{4}{\kappa}.
\]

Depending on the value of the fusion limit:
\begin{itemize}
    \item If the limit (equation fusion1 of the paper) is nonzero, then $\Delta = \frac{\kappa - 6}{\kappa}$ and $\delta = 3 - \frac{8}{\kappa} < 2$, implying that $Y_t$ may hit zero with positive probability.
    \item If the limit (equation fusion1 of the paper) vanishes but the limit (equation fusion2 of the paper) is nonzero, then $\Delta = \frac{2}{\kappa}$ and $\delta = 1 + \frac{8}{\kappa} > 2$, so $Y_t$ remains strictly positive almost surely.
\end{itemize}

with respect to \(U_{\mathfrak{S}_n}\), and let \(\sigma\in \mathfrak{S}_n\) be distributed with respect to \(\mu_n^t\).
Then, we have
\[
\mathbf P\left(\sum_{i=1}^m X_{ii}(\tau)^2>l^2\sqrt{\frac 1m+\frac 1l}\right)=O\left(
\sqrt{\frac1m+\frac1l}\right),
\]
and
\[
\mathbf P\left(\sum_{i=1}^m X_{ii}(\sigma)^2>l^2\sqrt{\frac 1m+\frac 1l}\right)=O\left(
\sqrt{\frac1m+\frac1l}\right).
\]

[Defn 6 (Partition function and free energy) of arXiv:2605.07050, 'Universality of the fluctuations of the free energy in generalized Sherrington--Kirkpatric'] For an $N \times N$ Wigner matrix $W = (W_{ij})$ and a prior $\caX$, we define the partition function $Z_N(\beta)$ and the free energy $F_N(\beta)$ at inverse temperature $\beta > 0$ by
\[
	Z_N \equiv Z_N(\beta) = \E_{\caX} \left[ \exp \left( \beta N \sum_{i<j} W_{ij} \frac{x_i x_j}{\| \bsx \|^2} \right) \right], \qquad F_N \equiv F_N(\beta) = \frac{1}{N} \log Z_N.
\]
Here, when $\| \bsx \| = 0$, we define $x_i x_j / \| \bsx \|^2 = 0$ for all $i, j$.
title: Partition function and free energy

\begin{align*}
&d\widetilde\theta=-\widetilde p\,dt,
\\

\\
&d\widetilde r=(\gamma\widetilde p+\gamma\widetilde r)\,dt+\sqrt{2\gamma\eps/L}\,dB_{t},
\end{align*}
which we denote by
$\widetilde Z_t=(\widetilde\theta_t,\widetilde p_t,\widetilde r_t)$,
has a unique non-explosive strong solution.  Its drift term $\widetilde b$
given by
\[

=\left(-p,\ L^{-1}\nabla U(\theta)-\gamma r,\ \gamma p+\gamma r\right),
\]
and $\operatorname{div}\widetilde b=\gamma d$.

[Definition 2 of arXiv:2609.01362, '{Double cluster swapping for spin models: \\Pfaffian relations and sharpness}'] Let $W =\{ v_1,v_2,\ldots, v_{n} \} \subseteq V$.
	We say that $\left<\cdot \right>_G$ satisfies \emph{Pfaffian relations} on the set $W$ if for any subset $I\subseteq [n]$,
	\begin{equation}
        \Big \langle  \prod_{i\in I}\vp_{v_i} \Big \rangle_G = \Pf(M_I),
    \end{equation}
    where $M$ is the $n\times n$ skew-symmetric matrix with 
    $M_{i, j} = \langle \vp_{v_i} \vp_{v_j} \rangle$ for $i<j$, 
    and $M_I$ is its restriction to $I \times I$. 
    The Pfaffian of $M_I$, denoted $\Pf(M_I)$ here, is the positive square root of the determinant of $M_I$.

body:
[Definition 2 of arXiv:2608.05185, '\large\bf ON THE HEAT FLOW CONJECTURE FOR RANDOM MATRICES'] A tracial \(*\)-probability space is a unital \(*\)-algebra
\(\mathscr{A}\) over \(\C\), together with a linear functional
\(\varphi:\mathscr{A}\to\C\) satisfying
\[
 \varphi(\mathbf{1})=1,\qquad
 \varphi(a^*a)\geq0,\qquad
 \varphi(ab)=\varphi(ba)
 \quad (a,b\in\mathscr{A}).
\]
If \(\mathscr{A}\) is a unital \(C^*\)-algebra, we call
\((\mathscr{A},\varphi)\) a tracial \(C^*\)-probability space.
The elements of \(\mathscr{A}\) are noncommutative random variables, and
their joint \(*\)-distribution is the collection of all mixed moments
\(\varphi(R(a_1,\ldots,a_k,a_1^*,\ldots,a_k^*))\).
A sequence \((\mathbf{M}_N)\) converges almost surely in
\(*\)-distribution to an element \(\mathsf{m}\in\mathscr{A}\) if, for
every noncommutative polynomial \(R\) in two indeterminates,
\begin{equation}
 \tr_N R(\mathbf{M}_N,\mathbf{M}_N^*)
 \longrightarrow \varphi(R(\mathsf{m},\mathsf{m}^*))
 \qquad\text{almost surely}.
\end{equation}
title: Definition 2 of arXiv:2608.05185
