body:
[Lemma 7 of arXiv:2604.20617, 'Structured random perturbations of \\ tridiagonal twisted Toeplitz matrices'] Consider two matrices $M$ and $N$ of size $r \times r$ and $s \times s$ respectively, and call $M'$ the matrix obtained by removing the last row and column from $M$ and $N'$ the one obtained by removing the first row and column from $N$. Define also two rectangular matrices $X$ and $Y$ of rank 1 and size $s \times r$ and $r \times s$ respectively, whose entries are all $0$ except for $(X)_{1,r}=:x$ and $(Y)_{r,1}=:y$. Then if we define the $2 \times 2$ block matrix
\[ A = \begin{pmatrix}
M & Y \\
X & N
\end{pmatrix} \]
we have
\[ \det A  = \det M \det N - x y \det M' \det N' . \]
\begin{proof}
We prove the formula through the Laplace expansion of the determinant. For a matrix $T$, we denote by $\mu_{i,j}(T)$ the minor obtained by removing the $i$-th row and $j$-th column from $T$. Using Laplace expansion on the $r$-th row of $A$ we get
\[ \det A = \sum_{i=1}^{r+1} (-1)^{i+r} A_{r,i}~\mu_{r,i}(A)  . \]
Now we notice that $\mu_{r,i}(A) = \mu_{r,i}(M) \det N $ for $i \leq r$. Then we have
\[ \det A = \left( \sum_{i=1}^r (-1)^{i+r} M_{r,i}~\mu_{r,i}(M) \right) \det N + (-1)^{2r+1} y~\mu_{r,r+1}(A) = \det M \det N - y~\mu_{r,r+1}(A). \]
Then we observe that if we remove the $r$-th row and $r+1$-th column from $A$ we get the following block matrix:
\[ \begin{pmatrix}
M' & M^r & 0 \\
0 & x & N_1 \\
0 & 0 & N'
\end{pmatrix}, \]
where $M^r$ denotes the $r$-th column of $M$ without $M_{r,r}$ and $N_1$ denotes the first row of $N$ without $N_{1,1}$. It is then obvious to see that
\[ \mu_{r,r+1}(A) = x \det M' \det N', \]
and that concludes the proof.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 7 of arXiv:2604.20617

Literature update: the general dimension-free O(1/k) rate was already proved by Derezinski-Dong, arXiv:2606.29593v1 Theorem 3.1, and explicit affine historical forgetting by Schliserman-Koren, arXiv:2610.25469v1 Corollary 3. This draft is not a new frontier-rate advance. Owner campaign claim w708-T366-spectrum-006 v1, proof (unaudited); independent correctness and novelty review pending. For iid unit normals n in finite dimension, set Q=E[nn^T], Phi(Y)=E[(I-nn^T)Y(I-nn^T)], and let L be the number of distinct positive eigenvalues of Q. Then Phi^k(Q)<=2^(L-1)Q for every k>=0. Consequently the expected full-task residual after k projections from deterministic e_0 is <=2^(L-1)||e_0||^2/(k+1). Arbitrary eigenvalue multiplicities and noncommutative covariance orbits are allowed. For T uniformly sampled task labels, the separately proved historical bridge gives occurrence mean <=2(2^(L-1)+1)||e_0||^2/k and distinct-observed-label mean <=[8(2^(L-1)+1)+1]||e_0||^2/k for k>=1, without the conventional factor 1/2. The constant depends on L; this method alone does not give the known dimension-free result.
finite-dimensional real space
iid unit-normal rank-one projections
L counts distinct positive eigenvalues, not multiplicities
historical conclusions use uniform finite task labels and claim history-003 v1

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:52384ec146a97c637effa6866063d05add6aa32e421aac730f674daf3b8d50c5","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/52/52384ec146a97c637effa6866063d05add6aa32e421aac730f674daf3b8d50c5.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:cd2f3f83d887be6ab0beedc74485d64894519f3e5b7c2092d50cb6f156aaca2d","bundle_entry_key":"kaczmarz-finite-distinct-covariance-spectrum-inverse-time","bundle_id":"population.t366-finite-spectrum-and-twirl-obstruction-002","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"randomized numerical linear algebra and continual learning","draft":"w708/bundle_002.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:optimization.randomized.projections:kaczmarz-finite-distinct-covariance-spectrum-inverse-time","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Finite covariance spectrum: candidate beyond commutative covariance orbits

Rung: proof (unaudited). Claim w708-T366-spectrum-006 v1, kind narrowed, Target 2.
Independent correctness and novelty assessment remain pending. The argument is not attributed to the source paper.
Hardest remaining piece: make the constant independent of the number of distinct eigenvalues.

Let Q be a rank-one task covariance, so tr Q=1. Let L be the number of distinct positive eigenvalues
rho_1>...>rho_L>0. No assumption that the exact covariance map preserves a commutative algebra.
The Dereziński-Dong Lemma 10 majorant, N_0=Q, N_(t+1)=N_t(I-2Q)+||N_t|| Q, dominates Phi^t(Q).
Its eigenvalues x_i(t), with multiplicities merged, satisfy

    x_i(0)=rho_i,
    x_i(t+1)=(1-2rho_i)x_i(t)+rho_i m(t), m(t)=max_j x_j(t).

Proved below, subject to independent audit: N_t<=2^(L-1)Q for all t>=0.
Consequently the population residual is <=2^(L-1)||e_0||^2/(k+1), uniformly in d,T and geometry
at fixed L. Historical occurrence and distinct-label bounds follow from the bridge with C=2^(L-1).

## Basic side conditions

All x_i are nonnegative: x_i'=(1-rho_i)x_i+rho_i(m-x_i)>=0.
The maximum is nonincreasing: if rho_i<=1/2 then x_i'<=(1-rho_i)m<=m;
if rho_i>1/2 then x_i'<=rho_i m<=m.
Zero spectral values have zero coordinate forever and are omitted. If m=0, all future iterates vanish.
For two different positive spectral values, rho_i+rho_j<=tr Q=1.

## The maximizing spectral value never increases

Choose the smallest rho among all current maximizing coordinates. If j maximizes and rho_i>rho_j:
for rho_i<=1/2, x_i'<=(1-rho_i)m<(1-rho_j)m=x_j';
for rho_i>1/2, x_i'<=rho_i m<=(1-rho_j)m=x_j'.
Thus a coordinate with a larger rho cannot overtake the chosen maximizer at the next step.
On equality choose the smaller rho again. The distinct maximizing phases are therefore at most L,
and their rho values strictly decrease.

## Geometric phase-area argument

If a phase begins at t_j with maximum H_j and maximizing value rho_j, while this phase lasts
m(t)=(1-rho_j)^(t-t_j) H_j. Its total area over any finite prefix is <=H_j/rho_j.
For every coordinate, x_i(t+1)<=x_i(t)+rho_i m(t), hence
x_i(t)<=rho_i[1+sum_(s<t)m(s)].
If A is the area before a phase, its starting height satisfies H_j<=rho_j(1+A), so the
area after completing that phase is <=2A+1. After j completed phases it is <=2^j-1.

Fix a time in phase j (phases numbered from 1). If rho_i>=rho_j, then
x_i(t)<=m(t)<=H_j<=2^(j-1)rho_j<=2^(L-1)rho_i.
If rho_i<rho_j, at least one spectral value remains below the current winner, so j<=L-1.
The area including the current phase prefix is <=2^j-1, giving
x_i(t)<=2^j rho_i<=2^(L-1)rho_i.
These two cases cover all coordinates. All denominators are positive phase eigenvalues.

## Two positive eigenvalues

This gives C=2 for arbitrary task geometry whenever Q has at most two distinct positive eigenvalues.
The special case has a direct proof: the high-rho coordinate decays geometrically until the low-rho
coordinate wins; it never wins again. Before the switch, summing the high coordinate bounds the
low coordinate by twice its initial eigenvalue. After the switch, the low coordinate decays geometrically.

## Potential failure checks

The exact trace-one hypothesis is used to prevent an eigenvalue above 1/2 retaking the maximum.
The tie convention must rule out winner cycling; the set of winning rho values, not only one coordinate,
is used. Repeated eigenvalues merge because their recurrences and starts agree exactly.
This is a majorant bound; no independence of scalar coordinates is asserted or needed.
No claim of novelty until the finite-spectrum literature comparison is complete.

## Conversion to the named forgetting target

Set C=2^(L-1). Positivity of Phi and Phi^ell(Q)<=C Q imply
Phi^k(Q)<=C Phi^j(Q) for every 0<=j<=k. The projection energy identity gives
sum_(j=0)^k E[e_j'Q e_j]<=||e_0||^2, including the last summand by taking one further update.
Therefore E[e_k'Q e_k]<=C||e_0||^2/(k+1).
For T uniformly sampled task labels, the proved historical bridge in
simplex_quasidomination.md gives occurrence mean <=2(C+1)||e_0||^2/k and distinct-seen-label
mean <=[8(C+1)+1]||e_0||^2/k, for k>=1. Losses omit a conventional factor 1/2.
The bridge is a separate unaudited claim, w708-T366-history-003 v1.

## Verification and limits

The source is arXiv:2604.09909v1, Lemma 10, Section 3, PDF p7; its scalar recurrence is on p8.
The source provides domination, not the finite-spectrum phase argument stated here.
Exact Fraction checks: scripts/check_finite_spectrum.py; logs/verify_finite_spectrum.txt.
They check 27880 states with L=1..7, arbitrary sampled eigenvalue multiplicities, hierarchical
spectra and endpoints including rho=1. These checks supplement the proof and are not a proof
over all spectra. No floating-point bound or Lean certificate is claimed.
Focused searches of the two retrieved frontier papers and the brain returned no finite-L theorem;
this is not an exhaustive novelty search. Existing dimension-dependent rates may overlap at fixed
rank. The specific scope here is a constant depending only on distinct spectral values, with
arbitrarily large multiplicities and arbitrary rank-one task geometry.

[Proposition 31 (Beta-Wishart particles in type $B_N$) of arXiv:2605.23529, 'Generalized Bessel-Dunkl diffusions'] Let $\beta>0$, $\gamma\in\R$, and assume
\begin{equation*}
    \delta>\beta(N-1).
\end{equation*}
Then, for every initial condition $\lambda(0)\in\Cc_B$, the system \eqref{eq:example:MSB-system} has a global strong solution.  The solution is non-sticky, namely
\begin{equation*}
    \int_0^t
    \mathbf 1_{\{\lambda_i(s)=\lambda_j(s)\}}\,ds
    =0,
    \qquad
    1\le i<j\le N,
    \qquad
    t<\life{\lambda},
    \qquad
    \text{a.s.},
\end{equation*}
and
\begin{equation*}
    \int_0^t
    \mathbf 1_{\{\lambda_i(s)=0\}}\,ds
    =0,
    \qquad
    1\le i\le N,
    \qquad
    t<\life{\lambda},
    \qquad
    \text{a.s.}
\end{equation*}
Moreover, pathwise uniqueness and uniqueness in law hold in the class of non-sticky solutions.

body:
[Proposition 9 (Hilbert-tensor embedding and finite-dimensional approximation) of arXiv:2606.29292, 'Intrinsic Gaussian Tensor Geometry and Random Operator Spectra'] Let
\[
  \mathscr H
  :=\cH_1\otimes\cdots\otimes\cH_m\otimes\conj{\cC}\otimes\cE.
\]
For $K\in\mathscr H$ and $S\subset[m]$, the flattening $\Flat_S(K)$ is Hilbert--Schmidt and
\begin{equation}

  \|\Flat_S(K)\|_{\Sch_2}=\|K\|_{\mathscr H}.
\end{equation}
Consequently, the natural identification on algebraic tensors extends to a
canonical linear isometric isomorphism between $\mathfrak T_{m,2}$ and
$\mathscr H$.  For every $2\le r<\infty$, the identity
on algebraic tensors extends to a continuous injection
\begin{equation}

  \mathscr H\hookrightarrow\mathfrak T_{m,r},
  \qquad
  \|K\|_{\mathfrak T_{m,r}}\le\|K\|_{\mathscr H}.
\end{equation}

Let $P_\nu^N$, $P_\cC^N$, and $P_\cE^N$ be finite-rank orthogonal
projections increasing strongly to the identity, and put
\begin{equation*}
  Q_N:=P_1^N\otimes\cdots\otimes P_m^N
  \otimes\conj{P_\cC^N}\otimes P_\cE^N.
\end{equation*}
Then $Q_N$ extends contractively to every $\mathfrak T_{m,r}$ and
\begin{equation}

  \|Q_N\mathbf K-\mathbf K\|_{\mathfrak T_{m,r}}\longrightarrow0
  \qquad(\mathbf K\in\mathfrak T_{m,r}).
\end{equation}

[Lemma lem:gaussian_law of arXiv:2602.19773, 'Regularization of a stationary point process by a stationary increments perturbation'] Let $f$ and $g$ defined as in (equation eq:exp_function of the paper). Then,
		\begin{align*}
			&\@ifnextchar[{\@withe}{\@withoute}{f(B)} =\exp{-\frac{\Sigma_{f}^{2}}{2}},\\
			&\@ifnextchar[{\@withe}{\@withoute}{\overline{g(B)}} =\exp{-\frac{\Sigma_{g}^{2}}{2}},\\
			&\@ifnextchar[{\@withe}{\@withoute}{f(B)\overline{g(\theta_{t}B)}}=\exp{-\frac{\Sigma_{f}^{2}+\Sigma_{g}^{2}-2\Sigma_{f,g}(t)}{2}},\\
			\intertext{with}
			&\Sigma_{f}^{2}=\sum_{1 \leq j,k \leq n}a_{j}a_{k}\Sigma_{t_{j}, t_{k}},\\
			&\Sigma_{g}^{2}=\sum_{1 \leq j,k \leq n}b_{j}b_{k}\Sigma_{t_{j}, t_{k}},\\
			&\Sigma_{f,g}(t)=\sum_{1 \leq j,k \leq n}a_{j}b_{k}(\Sigma_{t_{j},t+t_{k}}-\Sigma_{t_{j},t})=\sum_{1 \leq j,k \leq n}a_{j}b_{k}V_{-t_{j},t_{k}}(t).
		\end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 54 of arXiv:2609.02267, 'Locally Conformally Flat Manifolds with Positive Scalar Curvature: Kleinian Groups, Moduli'] Let $d\ge1$, $\alpha>0$, and $2\le q<\infty$, with $\alpha q\le d$.
Set $p:=q/(q-1)$, $\theta:=p-1=1/(q-1)\in(0,1]$, and
$s:=d-\alpha q\ge0$.  For a finite positive Radon measure $\nu$ on
$\mathbb{R}^d$ write
\[
 \mathcal{W}^\nu(x)
 :=
 \int_0^1\left(\frac{\nu(B(x,r))}{r^s}\right)^{\theta}\frac{dr}{r}.
\]
If $E\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ is nonempty and compact with
$\mathcal{C}_{\alpha,q}^{\mathbb R^d}(E)=0$, then there is a Radon
probability measure $\mu$ with
\[
 \operatorname{supp}\mu=E,
 \qquad
 \mathcal{W}^\mu(x)=+\infty\quad\text{for every }x\in E.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

given by (lem:2.1 of the paper) is finite and smooth on $\mathbb{R}^n$,
and its Hessian $\nabla^2\varphi$ is positive definite at every point.
Moreover, the map
\[
    \nabla\varphi:\mathbb{R}^n\longrightarrow K
\]
is a diffeomorphism. For all $y\in\mathbb{R}^n$, the Monge--Amp\`ere equation
\[
    \rho(\nabla\varphi(y))\det\nabla^2\varphi(y)
    =e^{-\varphi(y)}
\]
holds pointwise. Equivalently, since $\nabla^2\varphi$ is positive
definite, for all $y\in\mathbb{R}^n$,
\[
    \log\det\nabla^2\varphi(y)
    =-\varphi(y)+V(\nabla\varphi(y)).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lem 2 of arXiv:2607.24166, 'Strong rate of convergence for the Euler--Maruyama scheme of additive fractional SDEs with'] Let $q \ge 1, H \in (0, 1)$.
    For $0\le s\le t\le1$, set
    \[
    c(s,t):=\sqrt{(2H)^{-1}}\,|t-s|^H .
    \]
    Then the following assertions hold.
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item There exists a constant $C = C(q, d, H) > 0$ such that for all $0 \le s \le t \le 1$
              \begin{equation*}
                \|B^H_t - B^H_s\|_{L^q} = C|t - s|^H.
              \end{equation*}
        \item $\bE^s[f(B^H_t)] = P_{c^2(s, t)} f(\bE^s[B^H_t])$, for any measurable function $f: \bR^d \to \bR$ and $0 \le s \le t \le 1$.
        \item There exists a constant $C = C(q, d, H) > 0$ such that for all $0 \le s \le u \le t \le 1$ with $t - u \le u - s$ 
              \begin{equation}
                \|\bE^s[B^H_t] - \bE^s[B^H_u]\|_{L^q} \le C|t - u| |t - s|^{H - 1}.
              \end{equation}
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

\]

faces of $\mathcal A_{\eps,\vartheta}^\pm$, excluding its inner and outer
$q_1$-faces.  For every fixed $\vartheta>0$, there is $c_{\rm tan}>0$ such that,
for all sufficiently small $\eps$,
\[
H(z)-U(\sigma)\ge c_{\rm tan}\eps R_\eps^2,
\qquad z\in
\Gamma_{\eps,\vartheta}^{-,\rm tan}\cup
\Gamma_{\eps,\vartheta}^{+,\rm tan}.
\]
Let
\[
\bar f_{\eps,\vartheta}^-
:=j_\eps+\chi_{\eps,\vartheta}^-(1-j_\eps),
\qquad
\bar f_{\eps,\vartheta}^+
:=(1-\chi_{\eps,\vartheta}^+)j_\eps.
\]
Then, for some $N<\infty$,
\[
\frac{\eps}{Z_\eps}
\sum_{\varsigma\in\{-,+\}}
\int_{\Gamma_{\eps,\vartheta}^{\varsigma,\rm tan}}
e^{-H/\eps}
\left|\mathsf M\nabla\bar f_{\eps,\vartheta}^\varsigma\right|\,dS
\le C_\vartheta R_\eps^N e^{-c_{\rm tan}R_\eps^2}
\mathfrak K_{\sigma,\eps}
=o_\eps(\mathfrak K_{\sigma,\eps}).
\]

[Lemma 27 of arXiv:2608.17374, '\textbf{On the Pseudo-Mixing of Kac's Walk}'] Fix notation as in Definition~\ref{def:C4_epoch}, let $P$ be the one-step transition kernel of the $k$-column walk, and let $W_D$ denote Wasserstein distance with cost $D$. There is a universal constant $\rho_{\mathrm{loc}}>0$, independent of $n$ and $k$, such that $\rho_{\mathrm{loc}}\leq \min(1,\rho_D)$ and the following holds. If $X_0,Y_0\in \mathrm{St}(n,k)$ satisfy $D(X_0,Y_0)\leq \rho_{\mathrm{loc}}$, then
\be
W_D\left(P^{T_{\mathrm{epoch}}}(X_0,\cdot),P^{T_{\mathrm{epoch}}}(Y_0,\cdot)\right)
\le (1+C_D\rho_{\mathrm{loc}})\Big((1-\kappa)^{T_{\mathrm{contr}}}+\delta_{\mathrm{epoch}}\Big)D(X_0,Y_0),
\ee
where $\delta_{\mathrm{epoch}}=T_{\mathrm{contr}}\delta_{\mathrm{step}}$. In particular, for all $n > N_{0}$ sufficiently large,
\be 
W_D\left(P^{T_{\mathrm{epoch}}}(X_0,\cdot),P^{T_{\mathrm{epoch}}}(Y_0,\cdot)\right)
\le n^{-1}D(X_0,Y_0).
\ee

[Definition 4 of arXiv:2608.30089, 'On the Coefficients of Hurwitz-Type Matrix Polynomials'] Let $(s_{j})_{j=0}^{2n}$ (resp.\ $(s_{j})_{j=0}^{2n+1}$) be a Stieltjes positive sequence. Furthermore, let 
$v_j$, $u_{1,j}$, $u_{2,j}$ and $R_j$ be as in 
(\ref{60a}),  (\ref{66})  and (\ref{o1.6}), respectively. Let
\begin{equation}
 P_{1,0}(z):=I_q, \ \ Q_{1,0}(z):=0_q, \ \ P_{2,0}(z):=I_q, \ \
Q_{2,0}(z):=s_0. 
\end{equation}
For $j\geq 1$,  set
\begin{align}
P_{1,j}(z):=&(-Y_{1,j}^* H_{1,j-1}^{-1},\,I_q)R_j(z)v_j, \\
P_{2,j}(z):=&(-Y_{2,j}^*  H_{2,j-1}^{-1},\,I_q)R_j(z)v_j, \\
Q_{1,j}(z):=&-(-Y_{1,j}^*
H_{1,j-1}^{-1},\,I_q)R_j(z)u_{1,j},\\
Q_{2,j}(z):=&-(-Y_{2,j}^*  H_{2,j-1}^{-1},\,I_q)R_j(z)u_{2,j}. 
\end{align}
The matrix polynomials $Q_{1,j}$ and $Q_{2,j}$
 are called second-kind polynomials with respect to $P_{1,j}$ and  $P_{2,j}$,
respectively.

[Corollary 13 (Fixed-$\alpha$ expiring collector) of arXiv:2604.26298, 'The Expiring Coupon Collector\\ Sliding-Window Surjection Flux and Rare-Entry Laws'] Let \(0<\alpha<1\) be fixed and put \(M=\floor{\alpha n\log n}\).  For all sufficiently large \(n\),
\[
        \mu_{n,M}T_{n,M}\Rightarrow\Exp(1),
\]
where
\[
        \mu_{n,M}=\frac{(n-1)(n-1)!S(M-1,n-1)}{n^M}.
\]
Consequently, for every fixed \(r\ge1\),
\[
        \Ebb(\mu_{n,M}T_{n,M})^r\to r!,
\]
and
\[
        \log T_{n,M}=n^{1-\alpha}+o_{\mathbb P}(n^{1-\alpha}),
        \qquad
        \log \Ebb T_{n,M}=n^{1-\alpha}+o(n^{1-\alpha}).
\]
If \(\alpha>1/2\), then the sharper normalization is
\[
        n^{-\alpha}e^{-n^{1-\alpha}}T_{n,M}\Rightarrow\Exp(1),
\]
and in particular
\[
        \Ebb T_{n,M}\sim n^\alpha e^{n^{1-\alpha}},
        \qquad
        \Var(T_{n,M})\sim n^{2\alpha}e^{2n^{1-\alpha}}.
\]

[Theorem 60 (Critical typed target and causal quotient) of arXiv:2608.08756, 'Infinite-Dimensional L\'evy Area and Spectral Ancestry'] The product \eqref{cc:eq-ito-two-product} is associative and preserves
\(\mathscr I^{(2)}_{\mathrm{fin}}(H)\).  The map
\begin{equation}
 \Pi_2(x,\mathbb x,Q)
 :=\bigl(x,\operatorname{Alt}_2\mathbb x,Q\bigr),
 \qquad
 \operatorname{Alt}_2\mathbb x:=\tfrac12(\mathbb x-\mathbb x^*),
 
\end{equation}
is a group isomorphism from \(\mathscr I^{(2)}_{\mathrm{fin}}(H)\) onto
\(\mathscr G_{\mathrm{fin}}(H)\), where
\[
 (x,A,Q)\circ(y,B,R)
 =\left(x+y,A+B+\tfrac12x\wedge_{\mathrm{op}}y,Q+R\right).
\]
Its inverse is the exact reconstruction
\begin{equation}
 \mathbb x=\tfrac12x\otimes x+A-\tfrac12Q.
 
\end{equation}
Thus, after the typed quasi-shuffle relation has been imposed, passage to
the split state loses no degree-two information.

Let \(E\subset H\) be finite dimensional and let \(X\) be an
\(E\)-valued c\`adl\`ag semimartingale.  Put
\begin{align*}
 X_{s,t}&:=X_t-X_s,\\
 \mathbb X^I_{s,t}
 &:=\int_{(s,t]}(X_{r-}-X_s)\otimes\mathop{}\!\mathrm dX_r,\\
 A_{s,t}&:=\operatorname{Alt}_2\mathbb X^I_{s,t},
 \qquad
 Q_{s,t}:=[X]_t-[X]_s.
\end{align*}
There are versions for which, on one event and for every
\(0\leq s\leq u\leq t\),
\begin{equation}
 (X_{s,t},A_{s,t},Q_{s,t})
 =(X_{s,u},A_{s,u},Q_{s,u})
  \circ(X_{u,t},A_{u,t},Q_{u,t}).
 
\end{equation}
Moreover,
\begin{equation}
 \mathbb X^I_{s,t}
 =\tfrac12X_{s,t}^{\otimes 2}+A_{s,t}-\tfrac12[X]_{s,t}.
 
\end{equation}
At every jump time \(t\), with \(z=\Delta X_t\), the relative state is
\begin{equation}
 (X_{t-,t},A_{t-,t},Q_{t-,t})=(z,0,z\otimes z).
 
\end{equation}

For every bounded linear map \(L:H\to K\),
\[
 L_\#(x,A,Q):=(Lx,LAL^*,LQL^*)
\]
is a homomorphism on the finite-rank groups and extends continuously to the
critical completions of \Cref{cc:thm-critical-split-completion}.  On the
typed core set
\[
 L_\#(x,\mathbb x,Q):=(Lx,(L\otimes L)\mathbb x,LQL^*).
\]
Then
\(\Pi_2(L_\#(x,\mathbb x,Q))=L_\#\Pi_2(x,\mathbb x,Q)\).

AUTHOR PROOF DRAFT, unaudited; novelty is unestablished. Gaussian-product rectangular heat has bounded-density physical boundary values, almost-everywhere time continuity, and weak transport velocity H+(kappa-1)/(2x), conditional on the stated checked real population-Wishart equation. For S=UV^T/n, independent real Gaussian factors, M/n->beta>0, p/n->kappa>1, and noise sqrt(t/n)G, the symmetric positive-singular-law Cauchy transform g satisfies partial_t g=-partial_z(g^2+(kappa-1)g/z)/2 for t>0. A quartic with leading coefficient t and four distinct asymptotic roots controls density regularity; claim024 supplies the origin gap. Supporting proof draft, not a completed target.
Independent standard real Gaussian factors and noise.
Positive finite hidden-rank ratio and strictly rectangular aspect kappa>1.
Real population-Wishart equation stated in the proof and sourced in claim022.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:b64336b2038a578fb40553fcc57c6954c453dec462b4bb6cfe2d36e15f6f0505","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/b6/b64336b2038a578fb40553fcc57c6954c453dec462b4bb6cfe2d36e15f6f0505.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:9548f3adc68903b67cd441efcd18bebcb2f7ac02a496d314a765992a9a4498a7","bundle_entry_key":"gaussian-product-rectangular-heat-quartic-transport-w718","bundle_id":"population.t287-rectangular-reference-c1-and-noncentered-comparison-v1","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Gaussian channels and extensive-rank matrix inference","draft":"w718/bundle_009.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.gaussian_channels:gaussian-product-rectangular-heat-quartic-transport-w718","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Real Gaussian-product heat: algebraic density regularity and transport

Claim draft w718-T287-025, version 1. Kind: moved; target: 2. Status: proof (unaudited), conditional on the precisely stated population-Wishart equation below, already sourced for claim 022. This is a supporting lemma; novelty is unestablished. It does not assert completion of Target 2.

## Model and statement

Let M/n->beta>0 and p/n->kappa>1. Let U (n by M), V (p by M), and G (n by p) have independent standard real normal entries and be mutually independent. Put Y_t=UV^T/n+sqrt(t/n)G, t>0. Let rho_t be the deterministic limiting law of the n positive singular values, symmetrized with equal mass on both signs. Thus rho_t is a probability measure with no rectangular zero-padding. Write a=kappa-1 and

g(z,t)=integral (z-x)^(-1) rho_t(dx), Im z>0.

For every compact interval J contained in (0,infinity), rho_t has a density p_t supported in a common compact set disjoint from zero. Its Cauchy transform is uniformly bounded up to the real axis on bounded x, for t in J. For each fixed t0>0, p_t(x) and H_t(x)=Re g(x+i0,t) are continuous in t at t0 for almost every real x. In particular p_t is continuous in every finite L^r norm. Finally

partial_t g = -(1/2) partial_z (g^2+a g/z),                (1)

and, for every continuously differentiable real test function f on a neighborhood of the common support,

integral f d rho_v - integral f d rho_u
 = integral_u^v integral f'(x)[H_t(x)+a/(2x)]rho_t(dx)dt.  (2)

All transforms use the convention g~1/z and Im g<0 in the upper half-plane. H here has no 1/pi factor.

## Primary input and the equation

Conditional on U, the columns of Y_t are independent real normals with covariance (C_n+tI)/n, where C_n=UU^T/n. The population law of C_n tends to the free-Poisson law tau_beta with mean beta. The checked real population-Wishart theorem (Silverstein 1995, Theorem 1.1 and equation (1.4)) supplies the limiting equation

g(z,t)=integral [z-(c+t)(g(z,t)+a/z)]^(-1) tau_beta(dc).   (3)

For clarity the conversion is as follows. The standard squared-singular-value Stieltjes transform m(lambda)=integral (x-lambda)^(-1) nu_t(dx) satisfies

m(lambda)=integral [kappa(c+t)(1-1/kappa-(lambda/kappa)m(lambda))-lambda]^(-1) tau_beta(dc).

Set lambda=z^2 and g=-z m(z^2) to obtain (3), initially for large purely imaginary z and then by analytic continuation. This sign conversion and covariance scaling are essential. The free-Poisson transform q=G_tau(u), with q~1/u, satisfies u q^2-(u+1-beta)q+1=0; equivalently u=1/q+beta/(1-q) on that branch. It follows either by applying the same population-Wishart equation to identity covariance, or directly by clearing its scalar quadratic.

Set h=g+a/z, q=gh and u=z/h-t, initially at large z where all denominators are nonzero. Equation (3) says q=G_tau(u). With v=zg and w=z^2, clearing denominators gives

P(v,w,t)=(v w-t v(v+a))(w-v(v+a))-w^2-(beta-1)w v(v+a)=0. (4)

Analytic continuation makes (4) valid throughout the upper half-plane, including any point at which an intermediate division was unavailable. We use (3), not arbitrary roots of (4), to specify the physical branch.

## Common support, gap and time continuity

The Gaussian two-sphere net argument bounds the operator norms of U/sqrt(n), V/sqrt(n) and G/sqrt(n) by deterministic constants outside events tending to zero. Consequently rho_t is supported in [-R,R], uniformly for t in J. Supporting claim 024 gives epsilon>0, uniform for t in J, such that rho_t((-epsilon,epsilon))=0. These statements concern the deterministic limiting laws; they do not take an uncountable union of finite-dimensional exceptional events.

Couple Y_t and Y_u with the same U,V,G. The singular-value Hoffman-Wielandt inequality gives, for their empirical positive singular laws eta_n,t,

E W2(eta_n,t,eta_n,u)^2 <= (p/n)(sqrt(t)-sqrt(u))^2.

Both empirical laws converge weakly in probability to deterministic limits. Extracting an almost surely convergent subsequence and using lower semicontinuity of quadratic transport cost followed by Fatou proves

W2(rho_t,rho_u)^2 <= kappa(sqrt(t)-sqrt(u))^2.            (5)

Symmetrization cannot increase this coupling cost. Thus g(z,t) is continuous in t at every point strictly in the upper half-plane.

## Uniform Cauchy bound and bounded densities

As a polynomial in v, (4) has degree four and leading coefficient t. On compact sets of z and t in J its other coefficients are bounded. The elementary polynomial root bound |v|<=1+max_{j<4}|b_j/t| applies: for a monic polynomial, a root of larger modulus would have its highest term strictly dominate the sum of the lower terms by the geometric-series bound. Therefore g=v/z is bounded uniformly for epsilon/2<=|z|<=R+2, Im z>0. For |z|<epsilon/2 the spectral gap gives |g|<=2/epsilon. For large real part the support bound gives the usual inverse-distance bound. This proves a uniform bound B on |g(x+i eta,t)| for all x in a fixed bounded interval, 0<eta<=1, t in J.

For each real interval I, Stieltjes inversion and the bound -Im g<=B imply rho_t(I)<=B|I|/pi, with endpoints obtained by monotone approximation. Hence rho_t is absolutely continuous with density bounded by B/pi. In particular there is no residual singular mass at branch points. Boundary values exist almost everywhere; the algebraic analysis next gives a more explicit statement away from finitely many points.

## Finitely many exceptional points and continuity in time

Fix t0>0. The discriminant of P in v is a polynomial in w. It is not the zero polynomial. Here is a direct verification that avoids choosing numerical roots. For real w tending to positive infinity, the following four simple asymptotic branches exist by the analytic implicit-function theorem:

* For bounded v, divide P by w^2 and use 1/w as the small variable. The limiting equation is v-1=0, whose root is simple.
* Put w=R^2 and v=R y; divide P by R^5. As 1/R tends to zero the limiting equation is y-y^3=0. The roots y=1 and y=-1 are simple and give two distinct branches.
* Put v=w y; divide P by w^4. With 1/w as small variable the limiting equation is t0 y^4-y^3=0. Its root y=1/t0 is simple.

These give four distinct roots at scales 1, sqrt(w), -sqrt(w), w/t0 for sufficiently large w. Therefore the discriminant has only finitely many zeros in w. Apart from finitely many real x satisfying that discriminant at w=x^2, and x=0, all roots are simple.

At any such nonexceptional x, the complex analytic implicit-function theorem gives four locally distinct analytic branches in (z,t) near (x,t0). In a sufficiently small neighborhood, their disjoint root neighborhoods contain all roots. For Im z>0 and real t near t0, the physical g is continuous by (5), so its branch label cannot change on this connected domain. It therefore extends as one of these analytic branches to eta=0 and is jointly continuous there. At x=0 the uniform spectral gap gives analytic continuation directly. Thus H_t(x) and p_t(x)=-Im g(x+i0,t)/pi are continuous in t at t0 outside a finite set. Uniform bounds and common compact support give the asserted finite-L^r continuity of p_t by dominated convergence. The same argument gives local L^r continuity of H_t; outside a fixed compact set its tail is uniformly O(1/|x|).

## Exact transport algebra

Let R0=G_tau'(u). Differentiate q=gh=G_tau(z/h-t) at large z. Since h=g+a/z, this yields

D g_t=-R0,
D g_z=R0(1/h+a/(z h^2))+a g/z^2,
D=2g+a/z+R0 z/h^2.

Here D~kappa/z, so division is valid for sufficiently large z. Put r=a/z. Multiplying the desired identity g_t+(g+r/2)g_z-a g/(2z^2)=0 by D cancels its terms without R0. The remaining coefficient, multiplied by 2h^2, is exactly

-2(g+r)^2+(2g+r)(g+2r)-r g=0.

This proves (1) near infinity. It also gives derivatives of every moment: the physical root v~1 is analytic in 1/z near infinity and in t near any t0>0, by the simple bounded-root construction above. Comparing its Laurent coefficients is legitimate on a common circle outside the support. We now identify these derivatives with the right side of (2), avoiding any assumption that density time derivatives already exist.

Define H_e(x)=Re g(x+i e,t). It is uniformly bounded on the common support and tends to H_t almost everywhere. For nonreal z, symmetrization and Fubini give

integral H_e(x)/(z-x) rho_t(dx)
 = (1/2) double-integral [(x-y)^2/((x-y)^2+e^2)] /[(z-x)(z-y)] rho_t(dx)rho_t(dy).

The bounded density makes the diagonal null, so dominated convergence gives integral H_t(x)/(z-x)rho_t(dx)=g(z,t)^2/2. Evenness and the gap give integral x^-1 rho_t(dx)=0 and integral [x(z-x)]^-1 rho_t(dx)=g(z,t)/z. Thus for V_t=H_t+a/(2x),

integral V_t(x)/(z-x)rho_t(dx)=(g^2+a g/z)/2.

The velocity is uniformly bounded on the common support. Differentiating this last identity with respect to z identifies the Laurent coefficients of the right side of (1) with integral k x^(k-1)V_t rho_t. Coefficient comparison therefore proves (2) for polynomials. For a C1 test f on a fixed containing interval, approximate f' uniformly by polynomials, integrate those polynomials to approximate f and f' simultaneously, and pass in the integrated identity using the uniform velocity bound. This proves (2). No multiplication of dependent probabilities or differentiation of a merely convergent sequence of MI functions occurs.

## Remaining work

The entropy chain rule and real rectangular radial-density calibration are not proved in this file. They are required before concluding Gaussian-reference MI differentiability or general rectangular MMSE extremality. The least trusted step for external audit here is the boundary-branch continuation argument; its finite exceptional set, continuity on the upper domain, and uniform Cauchy bound must all be retained.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:965a7f6569046bdab574a5d8dade402280c470a6610623c9409c56ed763549bc","revision_digest":"sha256:50bf03e0ebe0e096e8ec202ae39b13a5d25fd4c237863e7af9c7e523a30ae60d","source_id":"owner:w718:T287:gaussian-product-rectangular-heat-quartic-transport-w718","source_revision":"2026-10-21 w718-T287-025 version1, proof unaudited","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

body:
[Lemma lem:stationarity_L1 of arXiv:2605.15401, 'Noise Tradeoffs, Stationary Information Flow, and Structural Balance in Unit-Birth Network'] Consider a CTMC on a countable state space $S$ with transition rates $q(x,y)$
and total exit rate $\Lambda(x)=\sum_{y\neq x}q(x,y)$. Suppose $\pi$ is a
stationary distribution with full support and
\[
\mathbb{E}_\pi[\Lambda(X)]<\infty.
\]
Let $\varphi:S\to\mathbb{R}$ satisfy
\begin{equation}
\sum_{x\in S}\pi(x)\sum_{y\neq x}q(x,y)|\varphi(y)-\varphi(x)|<\infty.
\end{equation}
Then, for every $x\in S$, the series
\[
\sum_{y\neq x} q(x,y)\,|\varphi(y)-\varphi(x)|
\]
is finite, and hence
\[
(L\varphi)(x):=\sum_{y\neq x} q(x,y)\big(\varphi(y)-\varphi(x)\big)
\]
is absolutely convergent and well defined. Moreover, $L\varphi\in L^1(\pi)$
and
\[
\mathbb{E}_\pi\!\big[(L\varphi)(X)\big]=0.
\]

\(C=C(H,a,R,r)<\infty\) such that, for all \(s,t\in[a,R]\) with

\begin{equation}
  |K_H(t,u)-K_H(s,u)|
  \leq C|t-s|^{2H}K_H(r,u).
  
\end{equation}
The reflected statement holds on \([-R,-a]\) with a fixed
\(r\in(-a,0)\).

Method: Diameter-squared upper bound for transitive mixing explicit structural calculation Result: The cycle illustrates the missing spectral information. On the N-cycle, lazy eigenvalues are1-sin^2(pi*k/N). Since sin(pi*k/N)>=2*k/N for k<=N/2, the chi-square bound from a point is at most2*sum_(k>=1) exp(-8*t*k^2/N^2). At t=C*N^2 this sum is as small as desired for a universal C, proving the proposed diameter-squared order in this case without a log N penalty. Check: Use symmetry k versus N-k and(1-x)^(2t)<=exp(-2tx). The Gaussian series converges and tends to0 as C increases. The cycle diameter is floor(N/2) and its degree is2. Obstruction: For a general transitive graph, the gap alone bounds all N-1 modes by the same exponential and introduces log N. A uniform bound on low-frequency multiplicities or spectral mass strong enough to remove that factor is missing.

[Definition def:discrete_continuous_coupling of arXiv:2411.13964, 'Long-time analysis of a pair of on-lattice and continuous run-and-tumble particles with ja'] Let $X(t) = (x(t), (\sigma^1(t), \sigma^2(t)))$ be a continuous
  process as defined in definition
  (def:continuous_process_min_max_construction of the paper), with fixed
  parameters $\omega$ (resp. $\alpha$ and $\beta$) and $\ell$, and
  $\sigma^1(t)$ and
  $\sigma^2(t)$ two independent Markov jump
  processes with the transition rates of figure
  (fig:single_speed_transition_rates_slowman_2016 of the paper)
  (resp. (fig:single_speed_transition_rates_slowman_2017 of the paper)). Denote
  by $0 = T_0 < T_1 < \cdots$ the jump times of the couple
  $(\sigma^1, \sigma^2)$. For $L \ge 2$, let $N_1^L$ and $N_2^L$ be
  two independent Poisson processes with parameter
  $\gamma_L = (L - 1)/\ell$ independent of the $\sigma^i$.

  Recursively define $y^L$ by setting
\[
y^L(0) = \left\lfloor (L-1)x(0)/\ell\right\rfloor+ 1 \ \text{and}\  	z^L(t) := y^L(T_k) + \sum_{i = 1, 2} (-1)^i \sigma^i(T_k)
  \left[ N^L_i(t) - N^L_i(T_k) \right],
\]
  \begin{itemize}    
  \item if $(\sigma^1(T_k), \sigma^2(T_k)) \neq \pm (1, 1)$
$$
y^L(t) = \max \left[1,  \min \left[ L, z^L(t)  \right] \right] \text{ for } t \in [T_k, T_{k+1}],
$$
\item if $(\sigma^1(T_k), \sigma^2(T_k)) = \pm (1, 1)$
$$
y^L(t) = p_L \left( z^L(t) \right) \text{ for } t \in
[T_k, T_{k+1}]
$$
where $p_L : \mathbb Z \rightarrow \{1, \ldots, L\}$ is given by
$$
p_L(k + 2 m L) =
\left\{
\begin{array}{cl}
k &\text{ for } m \in \mathbb Z \text{ and } 1 \le k \le L, \\
2L + 1 - k &\text{ for } m \in \mathbb Z \text{ and } L + 1 \le k \le 2L.
\end{array}
\right.
$$
\end{itemize}

Finally, set $Y^L(t) = (y^L(t), (\sigma^1(t), \sigma^2(t)))$.

[Theorem th:main of arXiv:2602.04673, 'Brownian paths as loop-decorated SLEs'] There exist couplings of $(\gamma^{nD},\mathbb{L}^{nD},S^{nD}\coloneqq {\Xi}(\gamma^{nD},\mathbb{L}^{nD},1,B^n ))$ over the positive integers $n$, with
$\gamma^{nD}$, $\mathbb{L}^{nD}$ and $B^n$ distributed as above, such that the following holds.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item For all $n\in \mathbb{N}$, $S^{nD}$ is a simple random walk started from $0$ and stopped when it first reaches $\partial D$.
  \item As $n\to \infty$
  $(\phi^*_n(\gamma^{nD}),\phi_n(\mathbb{L}^{nD}) )$ converges almost surely toward $(\gamma,\mathcal{L})\sim \mu^\gamma\otimes \mu^{\mathcal{L}}$ for the topology of $d_{{\mathscr{R}}_0}$. In particular,
  $\phi^*_n(\gamma^{nD})$ converges almost surely toward $\gamma$ and
  $\phi_n(\mathbb{L}^{nD})$ converges almost surely toward $\mathcal{L}$ (for the respective distances $\rho$ and $d$ defined in~(equation eq:def:dist of the paper))
  \item As $n\to \infty$, $\phi_n(S^{nD})$
  converges almost surely for the topology of $d_\infty$.  The limit $W$ is distributed as a Brownian motion started from $0$ and stopped when it first reaches $\partial D$, and $W$ is almost surely equal to ${\Xi}(\gamma, \mathcal{L})$.
  \end{itemize}
  In particular, if $(\gamma, \mathcal{L})\sim \mu^\gamma\otimes \mu^{\mathcal{L}}$, then
  ${\Xi}(\gamma, \mathcal{L})$ is distributed as a Brownian motion started from $0$ and stopped when it first reaches $\partial D$.

[Corollary 5 of arXiv:2609.03726, 'Inverse Scattering for Single Photons in Quantum Optics'] Let $n\geq 2$, let $\delta> 1/2$, and let $l\geq 0$ be an integer.
Then there exists $C=C_{\delta,l}>0$ such that, for all
$k\geq 1$, $\varepsilon\geq 0$, and
$f\in H^l_\delta(\mathbb R^n)$,
\begin{equation}
    \|R_k^\varepsilon f\|_{H^l_{-\delta}}
    \leq
    C_{\delta,l}\|f\|_{H^l_\delta}.
\end{equation}
For $\varepsilon=0$, the operator $R_k^\varepsilon$ in
\eqref{eq:frac_Hl_est} is understood as the outgoing boundary value $R_k^0$.
Moreover, for every fixed $k\geq 1$ and every
$f\in H^l_\delta(\mathbb R^n)$,
\begin{equation}
    R_k^\varepsilon f \to R_k^0 f
    \quad \text{in } H^l_{-\delta}(\mathbb R^n)
    \quad \text{as } \varepsilon\to0^+.
\end{equation}

[Theorem 5 (Exponential profile of intrinsic volumes) of arXiv:2605.11995, 'Intrinsic volumes of \(\ell_p\)-balls and a continuum of Maxwell--Poincar\'e--Borel laws f'] Let $1 < p < \infty$.  
Then, as $n\to\infty$,
$$
\sup_{j\in \{0,\dots, n\}} \left|\frac 1n \log V_{j}(n^{1/p}\mathbb B_p^n) - g_p\left(\frac jn\right)\right|  \to 0
$$
with the exponential profile
$$
g_p(\alpha) :=
\kappa_{p}(\alpha)
+
\sup_{\theta>0}\Psi_{p,\alpha}(\theta),
\qquad
\alpha \in [0,1],
$$
where $\Psi_{p,\alpha}(\theta)$ is the phase function from Proposition~\ref{prop:maximizer_Phi_p_beta},  and
\[
\kappa_{p}(\alpha):=
\frac{\alpha}{p}\Bigl(1-\log\frac{\alpha}{p}\Bigr)
+(1-\alpha)\log(p-1)
-\alpha\log\alpha-(1-\alpha)\log(1-\alpha)
-\frac{1-\alpha}{2}\log\pi.
\]
Here and in the following, we adopt  the convention \(0\log 0=0\). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Exponential profile of intrinsic volumes

[Thm 3 of arXiv:2506.21829, 'Some notes on Lamperti's recurrence of stochastic sequences'] Assume that \eqref{1}, integrability condition \eqref{2} and assumptions \eqref{4.3}, \eqref{4.4}, \eqref{4.5} and \eqref{4.6} are satisfied.
Then the stochastic sequence is recurrent if, as $x\to\infty$, we almost surely have
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\frac{p\mathsf{E}\{X_{n+1}-X_n~|~X_n=x, X_{n+1}>X_n, X_{n-1},\ldots, X_0\}}{q\mathsf{E}\{X_{n}-X_{n+1}~|~X_n=x, X_{n+1}<X_n, X_{n-1},\ldots, X_0\}}\\
&\leq1+\frac{R}{x}+O\left(\frac{1}{x^{1+\epsilon}}\right),
\end{aligned}
\]
where $R(x)=\mathsf{E}\{|X_{n+1}-X_n|~\big|~X_{n}=x, X_{n-1},\ldots, X_0\}$, and $R$ is the limit with probability $1$ of $R(x)$ as $x\to\infty$.
If instead
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\frac{p\mathsf{E}\{X_{n+1}-X_n~|~X_n=x, X_{n+1}>X_n, X_{n-1},\ldots, X_0\}}{q\mathsf{E}\{X_{n}-X_{n+1}~|~X_n=x, X_{n+1}<X_n, X_{n-1},\ldots, X_0\}}\\
&\geq1+\frac{R\theta}{x},
\end{aligned}
\]
for some $\theta>1$ and almost all large $x$, then the stochastic sequence is transient.
title: Thm 3 of arXiv:2506.21829

Let $\alpha\coloneqq(1-d_s/2)^+$ and fix $\delta\in(0,d_s/2\wedge 1)$. For $k\geq 0$, let

			\[
			\mathbb{P}_x(\mathcal{A}_k^c)\leq C_r\begin{cases}
				N^{d_s/2-r\delta} & \text{if } d_s<2,\\[3pt]
				N^{1-r\delta}(1{+}\log N)^{r-1} & \text{if } d_s=2,\\[3pt]
				N^{1-r\delta} & \text{if } d_s>2\,.
			\end{cases}\,
			\]
			\item $\mathbb{E}_x[Y_k^p]\leq C\,N^p$ uniformly in~$x$ and~$k$.
			\item For every $q\in[1,p)$ and $r$ large enough, $\mathbb{E}_x[Y_k^q\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{A}_k^c}]=O(2^{-3k})$ uniformly in~$x$.
		\end{enumerate}

[Lemma 20 of arXiv:2607.22470, 'A Logarithmic Fluctuation Hierarchy for Sequential Interacting Diffusions'] Fix \(n,k\ge0\) and let \(\varphi,\psi\in C_c^\infty(\R^d)\). Then
\begin{align}

\left\langle
M^{N,n}(\varphi),M^{N,k}(\psi)
\right\rangle_t
&=
\frac1N
\sum_{i=1}^N
h_n(i/N)h_k(i/N)
\int_0^t
\nabla\varphi(X_s^i)\cdot
\nabla\psi(X_s^i)\,\dd s.
\end{align}
Moreover, as \(N\to\infty\),
\begin{equation}
\left\langle
M^{N,n}(\varphi),M^{N,k}(\psi)
\right\rangle_t
\to
\frac{(n+k)!}{n!\,k!}
\int_0^t
\left\langle
\bar\rho_s,
\nabla\varphi\cdot
\nabla\psi
\right\rangle \dd s
\end{equation}
in \(L^1\), uniformly in \(t\in[0,T]\).

body: For an elliptic curve E over a number field K, the group E(K) of K-rational points is finitely generated: E(K) is isomorphic to a finite torsion group times Z^r, where r is the rank. The proof combines the weak Mordell-Weil theorem (E(K)/mE(K) finite, via Kummer theory and finiteness of class and unit groups) with a descent using height functions. Ranks are computable in practice but no general algorithm is proven; the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture ties r to the order of vanishing of the L-function at s = 1.

Define S_n(s)=(A_n+s^(-1)*Phi_n-zI)^(-1) and f_n(s)=alpha^(-1)+gamma*tr(S_n(s)Phi_n),tr=Tr/n. Suppose the empirical eigenvalue distributions of A_n and Phi_n converge weakly to deterministic probability measures,the limit for Phi_n is not delta_0,and f_n(s)->f(s) for every s in the open upper half-plane. Then s=f(s) has at most one solution with Im(s)>0. Existence is not part of this assertion. No uniform operator-norm bound on A_n or Phi_n is required by this source corollary. Draft,independent review pending.
The matrices,parameters and pointwise limits are as specified;gamma,alpha,z are fixed across n.
Weak spectral limits are probability measures and the covariance limit is not the point mass at0.
tr is normalized trace and compared roots lie strictly in the upper half-plane.

body:
[Lem 14 (Renewal--reward CLT) of arXiv:2607.28865, 'First-Passage Percolation on Spread-out line graphs: Microscopic Regime'] Let $\{(X_i,Y_i)\}_{i\ge1}$ be i.i.d.~with $X_i\in\dN$,
\begin{align*}
\E X_1=\mu\in(0,\infty),
\qquad
\E Y_1=\nu\in\dR,
\qquad
\E X_1^2+\E Y_1^2<\infty.
\end{align*}
Define
\begin{align*}
S_m:=\sum_{i=1}^m X_i,
\qquad
R_m:=\sum_{i=1}^m Y_i,
\qquad
N_t:=\max\{m\ge0:S_m\le t\},
\qquad
R(t):=R_{N_t}.
\end{align*}
Then, as $t\to\infty$,
\begin{align}
t^{-1/2}\cdot (R(t)-t\cdot {\nu}/{\mu})
\Longrightarrow
\N(0,\sigma^2),
\end{align}
where $\sigma^2 = \frac{1}{\mu} \var\left(Y_1-\nu/{\mu}\cdot X_1\right)$.
Equivalently,
\begin{align}
t^{-1/2}\cdot (R(t)-\E R(t))
\Longrightarrow
\N(0,\sigma^2).
\end{align}

body:
[Definition eq:IB of arXiv:2608.09368, 'A proof of Ross's conjecture for two-site moving-target search'] A $2\times2$ matrix is \emph{strictly totally positive} if all of its
minors are positive.  Writing
\[
 B=\begin{pmatrix}b_{11}&b_{12}\\ b_{21}&b_{22}\end{pmatrix},
\]
this means simply
\[
 b_{11},b_{12},b_{21},b_{22}>0,
 \qquad \det B>0.
\]
For a positive column vector $v=(v_1,v_2)^\top$, define its projective
slope by
\[
 \operatorname{sl}(v):=\frac{v_1}{v_2}.
\]
Multiplying $v$ by a positive scalar does not change this ratio, so the
slope records the ray spanned by $v$, rather than its magnitude.  This
is the only projective-geometric idea needed below.  If $b^{(1)},b^{(2)}$ are the two columns of a strictly totally positive
$B$, then
\[
 \operatorname{sl}(b^{(2)})=\frac{b_{12}}{b_{22}}
 <\frac{b_{11}}{b_{21}}=\operatorname{sl}(b^{(1)}).
\]
We call the interval between these two slopes the \emph{projective
interval} of $B$:
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal I(B):=
 \left[\frac{b_{12}}{b_{22}},\frac{b_{11}}{b_{21}}\right].
 
\end{equation}
For the identity matrix, which is not entrywise positive, we use the
convenient convention
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal I(I):=[0,\infty].
 
\end{equation}
title: Total positivity and projective slope

[Proposition prop:green-potential-L2-Cb of arXiv:2608.02459, 'Response Calculus for Spectral Simplicity\\ and Joint Eigenvalue Densities'] Fix $x\in\Omega_{\rm Fr}\cap\Omega_{\rm op}$.  For
$\theta\in L^2(M_x)$, define
\[
 u_\theta(z):=\int_DG_D(z,w)\theta(w)\,M_x(dw),
 \qquad z\in D.
\]
Then $u_\theta\in C_b(D)$ and
\begin{equation}
 [u_\theta]_{M_x}=G_x\theta,
 \qquad
 \|u_\theta\|_\infty
 \le K_G(x)^{1/2}\|\theta\|_{L^2(M_x)}.
\end{equation}
Moreover, the continuous representative is unique:
\[
 v\in C_b(D),\quad [v]_{M_x}=G_x\theta
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 v=u_\theta\quad\text{on }D.
\]

[Lemma lm:diffusedecompose of arXiv:2411.07125, 'Mixing on the cycle with constant size perturbation'] Assume $\mathcal{B}_1$.
There exists a constant probability $\mu_1>0$ with the following. For any fixed $X_0=\xi_0$ there is an event $\mathcal{B}_{X_0}$ with $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{B}_{X_0} \mid \mathcal{B}_2, y)\ge \mu_1$, and
for any $\hat y \in Y = [-\lambda_3\sqrt{\rho}n^{\frac{1}{2k+2}},\lambda_3\sqrt{\rho}n^{\frac{1}{2k+2}}]^k$ conditionally on $\mathcal{B}_2\cap \mathcal{B}_{X_0}\cap\{y=\hat y\}$ the overall hitting time $\omega_L(\hat y)$ is equidistributed with
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{L_h} \tau_1^i+ Z_{n,\hat y},
\]
which is a sum of independent variables: 
\begin{itemize}[itemsep=0pt, topsep=0pt]
    \item $\tau^i_1$ is an i.i.d.\ series, each is a hitting time of $+1$ from $0$ conditioned to not backtrack to $-\log^2n$ (on $\mathbb{Z}$), in the usual biased setup;
    \item $Z_{n,\hat y}$ is a non-negative variable with $\mathbb{E}(Z_{n,\hat y})=O(\rhon^{\frac{1}{k+1}} \log^2n)$.
\end{itemize}

Let us express the position given by $\hat y$ as $f(\hat y) = h_j+s\in V$, where $s$ stands for the location within the arc. Conditioned on the event $\mathcal{B}_2\cap\mathcal{B}_{X_0}\cap\{y=\hat y\}$ the overall hitting time $\omega_L^-$, for a bit ahead of the last hub visited on the track, is equidistributed with an expression similar as above:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{L_h-s+\log^2n} \tau_1^i+ Z_{n,\hat y}.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition 8 of arXiv:2608.31099, '\bf On (fake) Stationarity in Stochastic Volterra Equations with Affine Drift and Regular '] Let $\lambda>0$ and let $\alpha\!\in (1,+\infty) \setminus \mathbb{N}$.\\
		\smallskip
		\noindent $(a)$ The function \((-1)^{\lfloor \alpha \rfloor}F_{\alpha}\) is completely monotonic(thus convex), hence infinitely differentiable on $\mathbb{R}_+^*$.
		
		
		\smallskip
		\noindent $(b)$ 	The $\lambda$-resolvent $R_{\alpha, \lambda}$ satisfies $ R_{\alpha,1}= e_{\alpha}$ and $R_{\alpha, \lambda} = R_{\alpha,1}(\lambda^{1/\alpha}\cdot)$. The function $R_{\alpha, \lambda}$ is infinitely differentiable i.e. $\mathcal C^\infty$ on $(0, +\infty)$. Moreover $R_{\alpha, \lambda}(0)=1$, $R_{\alpha,\lambda}\!\in {\cal L}^{r}(\R_+)$ for every $r>\frac{1}{\alpha}$ and $\alpha<2$.
		
		$f_{\alpha, \lambda} (t):= -R'_{\alpha, \lambda} (t) $ is infinitely differentiable and satisfy : $\forall\, t>0, \quad f_{\alpha, \lambda} (t)=$
		{\small 
			\[
			\lambda^{\frac{1}{\alpha}}\left(\int_0^{+\infty} e^{-\lambda^{\frac{1}{\alpha}}tu}uH_{\alpha}(u)du - \frac{2}{\alpha} \sum_{n=0}^{\lfloor \frac{\alpha-1}{2} \rfloor} \exp\left[t \lambda^{\frac{1}{\alpha}} \cos\left(\frac{(2n+1)\pi}{\alpha}\right)\right] \cos\left[t \lambda^{\frac{1}{\alpha}} \sin\left(\frac{(2n+1)\pi}{\alpha}\right)- \frac{(2n+1)\pi}{\alpha}\right]\right)
			\]
		}
		so that, \( R_{\alpha,\lambda} \) converges to \( a \in [0,1) \) and $f_{\alpha,\lambda} \!\in {\cal L}^{2\beta}(\R_+)$ for every $\beta >0 $
		provided  $\alpha \in (1,2)$.
		
		
			
			
			
			
		
		\noindent $(c)$ 
		Furthermore, the function \( R_{\alpha,\lambda} \) satisfies assumption \(({\cal R}_\lambda)\) (i), namely \( R_{\alpha,\lambda} \) converges to \( 0 \), and the function \( f_{\alpha,\lambda} \) satisfies a $\vartheta$-H\"older regularity of the form~\eqref{eq:Regulf}
		
		 if and only if \( \alpha \in (1,2) \). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem thm:terraces of arXiv:2607.24705, 'Derangetropy Operators'] For the harmonic kernel $w_{k}$, whose reaction
		$\varphi_{k}(u) = -\sin(2\pi k u)/(2\pi k)$ has balanced wells at
		the
		lattice $\{j/k\}$, monotone data with exponentially localized
		tails develop a propagating terrace with all speeds
		zero~[ducrot2014]: the solution converges, locally uniformly
		along its interfaces, to a stack of $k$ standing kinks, each a
		$1/k$-scaled copy of the canonical kink by the cell conjugacy of
		Section~(sec:iteration of the paper), so the density resolves into $k$
		secant-like bumps of mass exactly $1/k$ located near the
		crystallization quantiles of the limit~(equation eq:crystallization of the paper).
		The terrace is not a steady state at finite separations: bump
		positions move by exponentially small interactions of Carr--Pego
		type~[carr1989]; the resulting slow motion, constructed by
		Carr and Pego on bounded intervals and adapted here at sketch
		level, spreads the terrace with separations growing
		logarithmically, and nothing coarsens, monotone kinks being unable
		to annihilate. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Terraces: crystallization made smooth

[Lem 28 (Aubin--Lions--Simon compactness criterion) of arXiv:2607.28238, 'Well-posedness and large deviations for the obstacle problem of first-order stochastic con'] Let
\[
B_0\subset B\hookrightarrow B_1
\]
be three Banach spaces, where the first embedding is compact and the second one is continuous.
For $1\leq p<\infty$, let $\mathcal{G}$ be a bounded subset of $L^p(0,T;B_0)$ such that
\[
\lim_{\tau\downarrow0}\sup_{u\in \mathcal{G}}\Vert u(\cdot+\tau)-u(\cdot)\Vert _{L^p(0,T-\tau;B_1)}=0.
\]
Then, $\mathcal{G}$ is relatively compact in $L^p(0,T;B)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition 19 of arXiv:2606.22611, 'Upper and Lower Bounds on Expected Soft Maxima\\of Gaussian Processes'] Let $X = (X_t)_{t \in T}$ be a centered  Gaussian process with a finite index set $T$. Let a subset $A \subset T$ with $\diam(A) \le a$ be given, and let $\cA = \set{ A_1,\ldots,A_n}$ be a partition of $A$. For any $\mu \in \eP(T)$ supported on $A$, let  $\mu^i \deq \mu(\cdot|A_i)$ be the 
conditional probability measure given $A_i$. Then, for any $\beta \ge 0$ we have
\begin{align*}
 \eF_\beta(X;\mu) \le \max_{i \le n} \eF_\beta(X; \mu^i)
  + C a \sqrt{\eta(n,a\beta)},
\end{align*}
where $C > 0$ is a universal constant.
title: Proposition 19 of arXiv:2606.22611

body:
[Cor of arXiv:2608.26876, 'Local Bousfield classes via homological support'] Let $Y \subseteq \Spc(\cat T^c)$ be a Thomason subset. Then:
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item $\cat T$ has the h-detection property if and only if $\cat T|_{Y^c}$ has the (relative) h-detection property
			and $\cat T_Y^{\wedge}$ has the relative h-detection property.
		\item $\cat T$ has the h-codetection property if and only if $\cat T|_{Y^c}$ has the (relative) \mbox{h-codetection} property
			and $\cat T_Y^{\wedge}$ has the relative h-codetection property.
		\item $\cat T$ is h-stratified if and only if $\cat T|_{Y^c}$ is (relatively) h-stratified
			and $\cat T_Y^{\wedge}$ is relatively h-stratified.
	\end{enumerate}

I_{K_*, M_*} ~:= \{(s, K) \,:\, s \in \mathcal{S}_o,\, K: \mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{Z}^d} \rightarrow \mathbb{N},\, K \leq K_*,\, |s| + 4\area(K) \leq M_*\},
\]
and define the space
\begin{equation*}
	\Theta_{K_*, M_*} := \mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft\{f = (f(s, K))_{(s, K) \in I_{K_*, M_*}} \,:\, f(\emptyset, K) = \mathds{1}_{\{K = 0\}}\aftergroup\egroup\originalright\}.
\end{equation*}

[Proposition prop:L2-thin of arXiv:2411.03609, 'Asymptotically optimal Wasserstein couplings for the small-time stable domain of attractio'] The coupling $(\bm{D}^{\bm{X},\kappa},\bm{D}^{\bm{Y},\kappa},\bm{J}^{\bm{X},\kappa},\bm{J}^{\bm{Y},\kappa})$ defined in~(equation eq:comp_Poisson_measures of the paper) and~(equation eq:thining_coupling_defn of the paper) satisfies
\begin{equation}

\mathds{E}\bigg[\sup_{t\in[0,1]}\big|\bm{D}^{\bm{X},\kappa}_t-\bm{D}^{\bm{Y},\kappa}_t\big|^2\bigg]
\leqslant 4\int_{\mathbb{R}^d_{\bm{0}}}\1_{B_{\bm{0}}(\kappa)}(\bm{w})|\bm{w}|^2|f_{\bm{X}}(\bm{w})-f_{\bm{Y}}(\bm{w})|
    \mu(\mathrm{d}\bm{w}).
\end{equation}
Moreover, if $\nu_{\bm{X}}(\mathrm{d}\bm{w})\1_{\mathbb{R}^d \setminus B_{\bm{0}}(\kappa)}(\bm{w})$ and $\nu_{\bm{Y}}(\mathrm{d}\bm{w})\1_{\mathbb{R}^d \setminus B_{\bm{0}}(\kappa)}(\bm{w})$ have a finite second moment, then 
\begin{gather*}
\mathds{E}\bigg[\sup_{t\in[0,1]}\big|\bm{D}^{\bm{X},\kappa}_t+\bm{J}^{\bm{X},\kappa}_t-(\bm{D}^{\bm{Y},\kappa}_t+\bm{J}^{\bm{Y},\kappa}_t)-\bm{m}_\kappa t\big|^2\bigg]
\leqslant 4\int_{\mathbb{R}^d_{\bm{0}}}|\bm{w}|^2|f_{\bm{X}}(\bm{w})-f_{\bm{Y}}(\bm{w})|
    \mu(\mathrm{d}\bm{w})\quad\text{and}\\
\mathcal{W}_2(\bm{X},\bm{Y})
\leqslant |\bm{\gamma}_{\bm{X},\kappa}-\bm{\gamma}_{\bm{Y},\kappa}+\bm{m}_\kappa|
    + 2 d^{1/2} |\bm{\Sigma_X}-\bm{\Sigma_Y}|
    + 2\bigg(\int_{\mathbb{R}^d_{\bm{0}}}|\bm{w}|^2|f_{\bm{X}}(\bm{w})-f_{\bm{Y}}(\bm{w})|
    \mu(\mathrm{d}\bm{w})\bigg)^{1/2},
\end{gather*}
where the mean $\bm{m}_\kappa:=\mathds{E}[\bm{J}^{\bm{X},\kappa}_1-\bm{J}^{\bm{Y},\kappa}_1]
=\int_{\mathbb{R}^d_{\bm{0}}}\bm{w}\1_{\mathbb{R}^d \setminus B_{\bm{0}}(\kappa)}(\bm{w})
(f_{\bm{X}}(\bm{w})-f_{\bm{Y}}(\bm{w}))\mu(\mathrm{d}\bm{w})$
is finite.

[Proposition prop:exact-variance of arXiv:2606.21006, 'Law of the Iterated Logarithm for Weighted Sums of Functionals of Long-Memory Gaussian Seq'] Assume \(((A1 of the paper))\), \(((A3 of the paper))\), and \(((A4 of the paper))\), \(\alpha m<1\), and \(2d+\alpha m<1\). Then
\[
    \operatorname{Var}(S_{n,m})\sim\sigma_m^2v_n^2.
\]
where
\[
\sigma_m^2
=
\frac{J_m^2c^m}{m!}
\int_0^1\int_0^1
x^{-d}y^{-d}|x-y|^{-\alpha m}\,dx\,dy.
\]
The integral is finite. Moreover,
\(
A_n^2=\operatorname{Var}(S_n)\sim \operatorname{Var}(S_{n,m}).
\)

Consequently, \(A_n\sim\sigma_m v_n\), and \(A_n\) is regularly varying with index \(H\). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Thm 3.1 of arXiv:2606.16237, 'The Backward Stochastic Partial Differential Integral Equations: Solvability and Compariso'] Assume that Assumptions (ass:b1 of the paper)--(mz4 of the paper) hold. If
$f_0 \in \mathbb{H}^{-1}$ and $\varphi \in L^2_{\mathscr{F}_T}(\Omega; L^2)$,
then BSPDIE (equation eq:2.1 of the paper) admits a unique weak solution $(u,q,r) \in \mathbb{S}^2(H^0) \cap \mathbb{H}^1 \times \mathbb{H}^0 \times \mathbb{H}^{\nu,0}$ satisfying
\[
\mathbb{E} \left[\sup_{0 \leq t \leq T} \|u(t)\|_0^2 \right] + |||u|||_1^2 + |||q|||_0^2 + |||r|||_{\nu,0}^2 \leq C \left( |||f_0|||_{-1}^2 + \mathbb{E}[\|\varphi\|_0^2] \right),
\]
where $C = C(L, \kappa, \alpha, \delta, T)$ is a positive constant.

body:
[Lemma 15 of arXiv:2609.00867, '2609.00867'] Suppose that \(\rho_t\) is a positive classical solution of
\eqref{eq:fluctuation-limit-equation} and that
\[
 \sup_{0\le t\le T}\left(
 \norm{\rho_t}_{L^\infty}+\norm{D^2\psi_t}_{L^\infty}
 \right)<\infty.
\]
When \(s=0\), suppose in addition that, for some \(a,q>0\),
\[
 \sup_{0\le t\le T}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{a|x|^q}\rho_t(x)\dd x<\infty.
\]
Suppose that \(F^N\) is an entropy solution in the sense of
Definition~\ref{def:coulomb-entropy-solution}, with \(\mathbb R^3\) and
\(g_{3,1}\) replaced by \(\mathbb R^d\) and \(g\), respectively.  Then the following
estimates hold.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] For every family of globally Lipschitz vector fields
\((u_t)_{0\le t\le T}\) with
\(\sup_t\norm{Du_t}_\infty<\infty\),
\begin{equation}
 \sup_{N\ge2}\sup_{0\le t\le T}
 \E_{F^N(t)}\abs{\cU_{N,\rho_t}(q_{u_t})}<\infty.
\end{equation}
\item[(ii)] The modulated free energy satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal E_N(t)
 \le \mathcal E_N(0)
 -\frac1N\int_0^t
   \E_{F^N(r)}\cU_{N,\rho_r}(q_{\nabla\psi_r})\dd r,
 \qquad 0\le t\le T.
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}

[Corollary cor:1-2moment of arXiv:2605.01444, 'From second moments to pairwise negative correlation: \\applications to minimal and unifor'] Let ${\ensuremath{\mathbb P}} $ be either ${\ensuremath{\mathbb P}} _\mathrm{MST}$ or ${\ensuremath{\mathbb P}} _\mathrm{UST}$ on $K_n$, and let ${\ensuremath{\mathbb E}} $ be the corresponding expectation. Let $e$ and $f$ be adjacent edges, and let $e$ and $e'$ be non-adjacent edges. Set
	\[
	p_0 = {\ensuremath{\mathbb P}} [\omega(e)=1],\quad
	p_1 = {\ensuremath{\mathbb P}} [\omega(e)=\omega(f)=1],\quad
	p_2 = {\ensuremath{\mathbb P}} [\omega(e)=\omega(e')=1].
	\]
	Then
	\[
	p_0 = \frac{2}{n},\qquad
	p_1 = \frac{{\ensuremath{\mathbb E}} \big[\sum_{x\in V(K_n)}\deg(x;\omega)^2\big]-2(n-1)}{n(n-1)(n-2)},
	\]
	and
	\[
	p_2 = \frac{4\big[n(n-1)-{\ensuremath{\mathbb E}} \big(\sum_{x\in V(K_n)}\deg(x;\omega)^2\big)\big]}{n(n-1)(n-2)(n-3)}.
	\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Proposition 8 of arXiv:2609.03070, 'Variants of order semicontinuity in Banach lattices'] Assume that $F$ is a vector lattice with PPP and let $Q\subset F_{+}$ and $e\in F$ be such that $e=\bigvee Q$. Then, for every $0\le r<1$ there is a disjoint $D\subset F_{+}$ such that $\bigvee D=re$ and for every $d\in D$ there is $q\in Q$ such that $d\le q$. Moreover, if $Q$ is countable then $D$ can also be chosen to be countable.

[Proposition prop:equality-reduction of arXiv:2609.03904, 'Extremal Families for Matchings in Permutations'] Let $n\geq2$, $s\geq2$, and $\mathcal F\subseteq S_n$ satisfy $\nu(\mathcal F)<s$.
Then
\[
   |\mathcal F|\leq(s-1)(n-1)!.
\]
If equality holds, then $s\leq n+1$ and
\begin{equation}
   |\mathcal F\cap L|=s-1
   \qquad\text{for every }L\in\mathcal L_n.
   
\end{equation}

\[

\]

[Lemma lem:RR of arXiv:2607.05671, 'Bi-infinite systems of singularly interacting Brownian particles and the KPZ equation'] Fix $\theta \in (0,1)$ and let $T, K_1$ be as above.
For $a_0\in \mathbb{R},  t_0 \ge 0$, $(x,t) \in B(a_0, t_0)$ and $\varepsilon, \delta \in (0,1)$, define $H(x,\varepsilon,\delta):= [x-\sigma\varepsilon^{-1/4}\delta-(\delta \log \delta^{-1})^{1/2}, x-\sigma\varepsilon^{-1/4}\delta+(\delta \log \delta^{-1})^{1/2}]^c$, and
$$
R(x,t, t_0, a_0, \varepsilon, \delta):= \int_{H(x,\varepsilon,\delta)} (\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(t,u)- \mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(t_0,a_0)) p_{\delta}(u-x) du.
$$
Then, for each $r\ge 1$, there exists $C \in (0,\infty)$ such that, for all  $\varepsilon, \delta \in (0,1)$ satisfying $\sigma \varepsilon^{-1/4}\delta + c^*\delta \le \frac{1}{4}(\delta \log \delta^{-1})^{1/2}$,
$$\sup_{(a_0, t_0) \in K_1\times [0,T]} \left\|\sup_{(x,t) \in B(a_0, t_0, \theta)} |R(x,t, t_0, a_0, \varepsilon, \delta)|\right\|_r \le C\delta^{1/8}.

body:
[Lemma 21 (One-hive marginal of the  quadruply augmented double hive law) of arXiv:2607.04138, 'Hives from deformed GUE minor processes'] \lab{lem:double-one-hive}
Assume \(\bar a,\bar b,\bar d>0\), and assume either \(\bar f>0\), or
\[
\bar f^2<0,
\qquad
\bar a^2+\bar b^2+\bar d^2+\bar f^2<0.
\]
Let \(p_{\mathrm{dbl}}\) be the density on \(\mathbb D^4\) from
Lemma~\ref{lem:double-maxent}.  Put
\[
T=\bar a^2+\bar b^2+\bar d^2+\bar f^2.
\]
Define the geometric side lengths
\[
a^2=\frac{\bar a^2(T-\bar a^2)}{T},\qquad
b^2=\frac{\bar b^2(T-\bar b^2)}{T},
\]
\[
d^2=\frac{\bar d^2(T-\bar d^2)}{T},\qquad
f^2=\frac{\bar f^2(T-\bar f^2)}{T},
\]
and
\[
c_*^2=
\frac{(\bar a^2+\bar b^2)(\bar d^2+\bar f^2)}{T}.
\]
In the second case these quantities are still positive, since
\(\bar d^2+\bar f^2<-(\bar a^2+\bar b^2)\).
Let \(h_1\) denote the first hive, so that
\[
h_1\in H_n(\alpha,\beta;\nu).
\]
Then the marginal law of \(h_1\) is
\[
\mathcal H_n(a,b,c_*).
\]
Similarly, the marginal law of the second hive is
\(\mathcal H_n(d,f,c_*)\); in the case \(\bar f^2<0\), this is understood
using the symmetry of the three boundary components to place the imaginary
raw parameter in the third slot of Theorem~\ref{thm:gaussian1}.  Moreover,
\(c_*\) is the value of the glued side selected by Lemma~\ref{lem:doublehive}:
it maximizes
\[
x\mapsto
\frac{\Delta_{abx}^2}{abx}\frac{\Delta_{xdf}^2}{xdf}.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: One-hive marginal of the  quadruply augmented double hive law

[Proposition p:VerificationPolarityManifolds of arXiv:2411.14936, 'Massive Particle Systems,\\Wasserstein Brownian Motions,\\ and the Dean--Kawasaki Equation'] Assume~$d\geq 2$.
Then, the canonical form satisfies~(equation eq:QPP of the paper).
\begin{proof}
It is clear from the definition of~(equation eq:QPP of the paper) that the assertion is local in nature.
Thus, it suffices to show the statement when~$M$ is compact, possibly with boundary.
In this case, the role of the weight~$\phi$ is irrelevant, since~$e^{\inf\phi}\mssE_{g,\car}\leq \mssE_{g,\phi}\leq e^{\sup\phi}\mssE_{g,\car}$ with~$0<\inf \phi\leq \sup \phi <\infty$.
The presence of a (smooth) boundary too does not play any role.
Thus, it suffices to show the assertion for the canonical form on closed manifolds.
This follows as in the proof of~[LzDS17+].
Alternatively, the assertion can be deduced from standard results about the relation between (Bessel) capacities and Hausdorff dimension.
Indeed, since~$d\geq 2$, the diagonal~$\Delta M$ has (Hausdorff) co-dimension greater than or equal to~$2$, and it is thus $\mssE$-polar, cf.\ e.g.~[Zie89] with~$\alpha= 1$,~$p= 2$ and~$n\eqdef d$.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition p:VerificationPolarityManifolds of arXiv:2411.14936

[Lemma lem_decode of arXiv:2608.15344, 'A Harris recurrent continuous-time Markov process without wide-sense regenerative structur'] There exists a Borel measurable function $c:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathcal{V}$ with the following property. Let
\[
p=(p_0,p_1,\dots,p_m),\;\;\;\;q=(q_0,q_1,\dots,q_n)
\]
be two finite simple directed paths (no vertex is visited more than once) with the same initial vertex ($p_0=q_0$) and the same terminal vertex ($p_m=q_n$). If
\[
d=\sum_{i=1}^ml(p_{i-1},p_i)-\sum_{i=1}^nl(q_{i-1},q_i)\neq0,
\]
then $c(d)$ is a non-initial vertex occurring in both $p$ and $q$, i.e., 
\[
c(d)\in\{p_1,\dots,p_m\}\cap\{q_1,\dots,q_n\}.
\]

[Definition 9 ($\kappa$-controlled second moment) of arXiv:2607.08696, 'Spectrum of Directed Inhomogeneous Random Graphs'] Let $\kappa \ge 1$. A complex random
variable $X$ is said to have $\kappa$-controlled second moment if it satisfies the following upper and lower bounds: $\E[|X|^2] \le \kappa$ and
\[
\E[{\rm Re}(zX - w)^2\one_{\{|X| \le \kappa\}}] \ge \tfrac{1}{\kappa} {\rm Re}(z)^2
\]
for all complex numbers $z, w$.
title: $\kappa$-controlled second moment

[Corollary 10 (sectional curvatures) of arXiv:2609.03332, 'Singularity Models of Finite-Time K\"ahler-Ricci Flows'] For the metric \eqref{eq:ansatz-metric}, let $X_i \in \mathcal{H}_i$ and $Y_j \in \mathcal{H}_j$ be $g$-unit horizontal vectors, orthogonal to one another when the blocks coincide, and set	
	\[
	\tau_i \;:=\; F_i^2\; \pi^*\omega_i(X_i, Y_i) \;=\; g(J X_i, Y_i) \;\in\; [-1, 1] \,.
	\]
	Thus, $\tau_i = \pm 1$ iff $Y_i = \pm J X_i$, and $\tau_i = 0$ iff the plane is totally real. Then the sectional curvatures of the frame planes are:
	
	\emph{(i) Radial planes.}
	\[
	K(\nu, \xi^*) \;=\; -\frac{H''}{H} \,, \qquad K(\nu, X_i) \;=\; -\frac{F_i''}{F_i} \,.
	\]
	
	\emph{(ii) Vertizontal planes.}
	\[
	K(X_i, \xi^*) \;=\; \frac{q_i^2 H^2}{4 F_i^4} \;-\; \frac{H'}{H}\,\frac{F_i'}{F_i} \,.
	\]
	
	\emph{(iii) Horizontal planes within a block.}
		\[
	K(X_i, Y_i) \;=\; \frac{K_{g_i}(\pi_* X_i, \pi_* Y_i)}{F_i^2} \;-\; \frac{3\, q_i^2 H^2}{4 F_i^4}\;\tau_i^2 \;-\; \frac{F_i'^2}{F_i^2} \,,
	\]
		where $K_{g_i}$ denotes the sectional curvature of $(N_i, g_i)$.
	
	\emph{(iv) Horizontal planes across blocks.} For $i \neq j$,
	\[
	K(X_i, Y_j) \;=\; -\,\frac{F_i'}{F_i}\;\frac{F_j'}{F_j} \,,
	\]
		the classical doubly-warped-product value: the connection form is invisible on cross-block planes. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: sectional curvatures

[Proposition 5 of arXiv:2608.29855, 'Growth of Simple Closed Geodesics in closed Hyperbolic $3$-Manifolds'] For every $0<\varepsilon<1$ there exist a finite set
$S\subset\Gamma^+$, an open spherical disk
$D\subset\partial\hts$, and constants $\alpha,R>0$ such that,
with
$$
U_S\coloneqq \max_{s\in S}d(o,so),
$$
the following hold:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item $s(\overline D)\subset D$ for every $s\in S$, and the sets
$s(\overline D)$ are pairwise disjoint;
\item the positive semigroup on $S$ is free;
\item for every bi-infinite sequence $(s_j)_{j\in\Z}$ with
$s_j\in S$, if $P_0=e$, $P_{j+1}=P_js_{j+1}$, and $x_j=P_jo$, then
\begin{equation}
    \alpha|p-q|
\le
d(x_p,x_q)
\le
U_S|p-q|
\qquad(p,q\in\Z);
\end{equation}
\item every periodic positive $S$-word corresponds to a loxodromic element of $\Gamma^+$ and has a periodic broken geodesic at Hausdorff distance at most $R$ from its axis;
\item
$$
\frac{\log|S|}{U_S}>2-\varepsilon.
$$
\end{enumerate}

 \quad{\rm and}\quad

[Definition of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] Let $\textbf{\textup{U}}\subset\ul\CAT_T$ be any full $T$-subcategory. We say that a $T$-$\infty$-category has \emph{$\textbf{\textup{U}}$-colimits} if the $T_{/A}$-$\infty$-category $\textup{fgt}_A^*{\mathcal{C}}$ has ${\mathcal{K}}$-shaped colimits for every $A\in T$ and ${\mathcal{K}}\in\textbf{\textup{U}}(A)\subset\CAT_{T_{/A}}$. If also ${\mathcal{D}}$ has $\textbf{\textup{U}}$-colimits, then we say that a $T$-functor $F\colon{\mathcal{C}}\to{\mathcal{D}}$ is $\textbf{\textup{U}}$-cocontinuous if $\textup{fgt}_A^*F$ preserves ${\mathcal{K}}$-shaped colimits for all $A\in T$ and ${\mathcal{K}}\in\textbf{\textup{U}}(A)$.

    Dually, we define what it means to have \emph{$\textbf{\textup{U}}$-limits} and to be \emph{$\textbf{\textup{U}}$-continuous}.

[Corollary of arXiv:2609.00105, 'Weighted composition operators and classification of weighted Hardy spaces'] Let $\mathcal{H}$ be a weighted Hardy space with the scalar Pick property and let $\rho$ be a bounded non-zero functional on $\mathcal{H}$. Then the following are equivalent:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $\rho(\phi g)=\rho(\phi)\rho(g)$ for all $\phi\in\operatorname{Mult}(\mathcal{H})$ and all $g\in\mathcal{H}$.
        \item $\rho(fg)=\rho(f)\rho(g)$ whenever $f,g\in\mathcal{H}$ such that $fg\in\mathcal{H}$.
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

\]

[Definition 12 (\cite{xia1996vector}) of arXiv:2608.30589, 'Vector-Valued Wavelet Bases as Hilbert $\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})$-Module Bases: A Construc'] We say that $\Phi$ is a scaling function for a vector-valued multiresolution analysis $\{V_j\}_{j\in \mathbb{Z}}$ of $L^2(\mathbb{R}^d,\mathbb{R}^m)$ if the sequence $\{V_j\}_{j\in \mathbb{Z}}$ satisfies:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(VMRA\arabic*)}]
\item $V_{j}\subset V_{j+1}$ for all $j\in \mathbb{Z}$.
\item $\bigcap_{j\in\mathbb{Z}} V_j=\{0\}$ and $\bigcup_{j\in \mathbb{Z}} V_j$ is dense in $L^2(\mathbb{R}^d,\mathbb{R}^m)$.
\item $h\in V_j$ if and only if $h(A\cdot)\in V_{j+1}$ for all $j\in\mathbb{Z}$.
\item $h\in V_j$ if and only if $h(\cdot-k)\in V_{j}$ for all $j\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $k\in\mathbb{Z}^d$.
\item The sequence $\{\Phi(\cdot-k)\}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}^d}$ is an orthonormal basis of $V_0$.
\end{enumerate}

Let A be a real n by n matrix with rows r_1,...,r_n. Put V_0={0} and V_{k-1}=span(r_1,...,r_{k-1}). Then |det A|=product_{k=1}^n dist(r_k,V_{k-1}), with Euclidean distance. The identity includes singular matrices: dependence makes at least one factor zero. It is deterministic and requires neither independent rows nor nonzero entries. For a random matrix with independent rows, each distance may subsequently be studied conditional on the earlier rows, but the distance factors need not be independent.
Real square matrix; Euclidean row norm

Let Delta be a real d-by-k matrix of rank r_star>=1, C a positive definite d-by-d matrix and G=C Delta. Let A be d-by-h, B h-by-k with h>=r_star. Consider simultaneous factor GD A_next=A-eta C(AB-Delta)B^T and B_next=B-eta A^T C(AB-Delta), at any finite steps eta, initialized at arbitrary A_0 and B_0=0. Then row(B_t) is contained in row(Delta)=row(G) at every integer t>=0, equivalently B_t(I-P)=0 for the orthogonal projector P onto row(Delta). This inclusion version of the known zero-factor alignment component is the content used from Zhang-Liu-Chen, LoRA-One, arXiv:2502.01235, Theorem 3.1 and Appendix C.1 Theorem C.10 (printed pp.26-27). It does not imply that A_t has aligned, that B_t has full rank, or that the product has fitted Delta. The induction applies to the noiseless quadratic C-metric loss; with additive noise the sample gradient generally has larger rank, so a rank-r_star invariant signal subspace no longer follows.
Real exact-rank-r_star target; positive definite input covariance; h>=r_star
Zero initial output-side factor, arbitrary input-side factor; simultaneous ordinary GD on the noiseless covariance quadratic
Conclusion is a row-space inclusion, not rank equality or residual convergence

body:
[Proposition 18 of arXiv:2608.30589, 'Vector-Valued Wavelet Bases as Hilbert $\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})$-Module Bases: A Construc'] The family $\{\mathbf{V}_j\}_{j\in\mathbb{Z}}$ is an MRA of $L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)$ with dyadic dilation $2$ and integer
translations. Moreover, for each $j\in\mathbb{Z}$ one has the orthogonal decomposition
\[
\mathbf{V}_{j+1}
=
\mathbf{V}_j\ \oplus\ \bigoplus_{\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^d\setminus\{0\}} \mathbf{W}_j^{(\epsilon)},
\]
where
\[
\mathbf{W}_j^{(\epsilon)}
=
\bigotimes_{\ell=1}^d X_{j}^{(\epsilon_\ell)},
\qquad
X_{j}^{(0)}=V_j,\ \ X_{j}^{(1)}=W_j.
\]
In particular,
\[
L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)
=
\mathbf{V}_0\ \oplus\ \bigoplus_{j\ge 0}\ \bigoplus_{\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^d\setminus\{0\}} \mathbf{W}_j^{(\epsilon)},
\]
and the associated orthonormal wavelet basis consists of the usual $2^d-1$ wavelet types (one for each
$\epsilon\neq 0$), obtained by tensoring the scalar scaling functions and mother wavelets componentwise.

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Conservation, explicit coupling reduction, exact law comparison or spectral calculation Result: Finite-volume stationarity gives pi_V*K_v,V=pi_V for addition at v. To pass this identity through a local limit, truncate the avalanche at a radius r. If its influence on an observed window leaves that ball with probability at most epsilon_r, uniformly in outer V, then for each bounded local test f the discrepancy between the full and truncated expectations is at most 2*||f||_infinity*epsilon_r. The truncated operator is local and continuous, so subsequential limits inherit addition invariance if epsilon_r tends to zero. Check: Use the same stacks up to the exit from the radius-r ball. On the no-exit event the two evaluations agree, giving the bound directly. This requires a uniform probability estimate; finite-volume almost-sure stabilization alone is not enough. Obstruction: Uniform localization is missing and may fail for critical avalanches. Even inherited addition invariance would still need a uniqueness theorem to identify all subsequential limits.

Version1, 20 October2026. Target3, kind moved. Proofs (unaudited).
These are direct finite-chain estimates and do not assume C026's functional
entrance limit. They use the independent positive-moment estimates of C027
and the exact inverse moments and drift calculations of C044/C045.
Literature novelty is not asserted.

Let K0>0 be fixed and

    K_(j+1)=n^(-1)sum_(i=1)^n tanh(sqrt(K_j)Z_(j,i))^2,

with independent standard Gaussian rows and layers. This is unshaped,
zero-bias tanh at weight variance1/n. Let V_j=1/(nK_j). These reciprocals
are finite almost surely; for sufficiently large n their required moments
are integrable by C044. No bounded replacement or extinction convention
is needed. Set Q=max(1,K0), so0<K_j<=Q at every layer.

## C046: quantitative mesoscopic variance law

For each finite T there are C_(K0,T),n0 such that for n>=n0,

    E|k K_k-1/2|<=C_(K0,T)[k^(-1/2)+sqrt(k/n)],
                                           1<=k<=floor(Tn).   (1)

Thus k_n K_(k_n)->1/2 in L1 when k_n->infinity and k_n/n->0.

Proof. C027's explicit positive moment bounds give, including k=0,1 by
increasing the constant,

    E K_j^p<=C_(K0,p,T)/(j+1)^p, p=1,2, j<=Tn.                (2)

The coarse reciprocal multiplier estimates C045(5) give

    E V_j<=C_(K0,T)(j+1)/n,
    E V_j^2<=C_(K0,T)(j+1)^2/n^2.                            (3)

Indeed, conditionally on K_j=q and V_j=v,
E V_(j+1)^p <=(1+C/n)v^p+(C/n)v^(p-1) for p=1,2.
Sum first for p=1, then for p=2, starting at V0=1/(nK0). All moments
are finite: conditional inverse sample moments are uniformly finite by
C044 on0<q<=Q, and iteration through finitely many layers preserves this.

Let M_k be the martingale of centered reciprocal increments. C045(5)
and (3) imply

    ||M_k||_2<=C[sqrt(k^3/n^3)+sqrt(k)/n].

The drift estimate C045(6), (2)-(3), and Minkowski give

    ||V_k-V0-2k/n-M_k||_2
        <=C[k(k+1)/n^2+log(k+1)/n+k/n^2
                                      +k(k+1)/n^(5/2)].

This is the C040 martingale argument with K replacing theta and a=2.
It uses no independence between the current state and its conditional
drift; only orthogonality of martingale differences across layers.
Consequently for Z_k=nV_k/k,

    ||Z_k-2||_2<=C[k^(-1/2)+sqrt(k/n)].

Since 1/Z_k=kK_k has a uniformly bounded second moment by (2), inversion
is controlled exactly as in C040: on Z_k>=1 the inverse map is Lipschitz;
on its complement Chebyshev and Cauchy-Schwarz bound the L1 contribution
by C||Z_k-2||_2. This proves(1).

In particular, for fixed t>0 and N=floor(nt),

    sum_(k=1)^(N-1) E K_k=(1/2)log(n)+O_(K0,t)(1),            (4)

because the absolute error term in E K_k is bounded by
C[k^(-3/2)+1/sqrt(nk)], whose sum is bounded through N<=tn.

## C047: a logarithmic bias for the exact reciprocal mean

For every fixed K0>0 and t>0,

    E[1/(nK_floor(nt))]
      = exp(2t)-1 -(5/6)exp(2t)log(n)/n+O_(K0,t)(1/n).        (5)

The limiting mean exp(2t)-1 is the mean of the reciprocal SDE
dV=(2V+2)dt+sqrt(2)VdW,V0=0. This numerical coefficient identifies the
leading logarithmic correction, not the coefficient of the remaining1/n
term. The statement concerns an exact integrable raw reciprocal mean,
unlike the ReLU angle reciprocal.

Proof. Write h=1/n. The exact conditional mean of the limiting linear
diffusion after time h from v is

    L_h(v)=(v+1)exp(2h)-1.

C045(4), subtracting the h^2 coefficient2v+2 of L_h(v)-v, gives on
K=q<=epsilon

    E[V_next | v]-L_h(v)
      =[2v-6-5/(3v)]/n^2+rho_n(v),
    |rho_n(v)|<=C[v/n^(5/2)
                   +(1+v+1/v+1/v^2)/n^3+v exp(-cn)].        (6)

On epsilon<q<=Q, v<=1/(n epsilon). The global inverse sample moment
bound gives E V_next<=C_Q v<=C/n. Both L_h(v)-v and the displayed main
correction in(6) are also O(1/n), since1/v=nq<=nQ. Hence the remaining
defect is bounded by C_Q/n on this large-variance range.

Along the exact chain, the expected number of large-variance visits is
bounded by epsilon^(-2)sum E K_k^2<=C_(K0,T), by (2). On the small range,
use (2)-(3) and1/V_k=nK_k in(6). Summation through N<=Tn yields

    sum_(k=0)^(N-1) E|rho_n(V_k)|<=C_(K0,T)/n.               (7)

For clarity, the inverse-square contribution is at most
n^(-1)sum E K_k^2=O(1/n); the inverse first-power contribution is
O(log(n+1)/n^2); the v/n^(5/2) term sums to O(n^(-3/2)); all remaining
terms are smaller or O(1/n). The large-variance bound was included
separately, so(7) does not apply the small-q Taylor series globally.

Let w_k=exp(2(t_n-(k+1)/n)), t_n=N/n. The affine nature of L_h makes
conditional-mean telescoping exact:

    E V_N - [(V0+1)exp(2t_n)-1]
      =sum_(k=0)^(N-1) w_k E[E(V_(k+1)|V_k)-L_h(V_k)].       (8)

All expectations are legitimate by (3). The weighted sum of the errors
in(7) remains O(1/n). The nonsingular correction2V_k-6 in(6) contributes
O(1/n), using (3). The singular correction contributes

    -(5/(3n)) sum_(k=0)^(N-1) w_k E K_k.

The k=0 term is O_(K0,t)(1/n). For k>=1,
|w_k-exp(2t)|<=C_t(k+1)/n, so (2) bounds the total weighted occupation
error by a constant. Equation(4) therefore gives

    sum_(k=1)^(N-1) w_k E K_k
                        =(exp(2t)/2)log(n)+O_(K0,t)(1).

Insert this into(8), and use V0=1/(nK0), |t_n-t|<=1/n. The initial-state
and fractional-layer effects are O(1/n). This proves(5).

## Scope

C047 is a first finite-width correction for an exactly critical unshaped
tanh scalar observable; it does not prove Target3's all-order uniform
finite-width cumulant expansion. Its proof does not require C026 and
never replaces the model by the shaped tanh model in Li-Nica-Roy.
Independent review is required for C044's inverse-tail deletion, the
coefficient -5/3 in C045, and the global summation of the small-q remainder.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:33310ec7d7ee9992c8f2862dbcd7608afde5016da91276ffa01336685b6b5ff6","revision_digest":"sha256:515fe058a5192e3ef08957c4adfba4362dd6ba75e9ef9800f5baddd34aefb3eb","source_id":"own-work:T244-w691-C047:v1","source_revision":"2026-10-20-v1","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Lemma 20 of arXiv:2606.11271, '\LARGE The $K$-th nearest neighbor random walk on a Poisson point process gets trapped'] On $\cE_n$, there exist $m \in \{1,\dots,n-1\}$, $T \in \cT_m$, an embedding $x$ of $T$

		\item For all edges $v \to w$ of $T$, $\|x(w)-x(v)\| \le r(v)+1$.
		\item $An \le M \sum_{v} (r(v)+1)$.
	\end{enumerate}

[Lemma lem:comXs of arXiv:2510.26724, 'Sharp Fuss-Catalan thresholds in graph bootstrap percolation'] Suppose that $S$ is a 
partial TWG for a given edge $e$, 
with 
\begin{itemize}
\item $\sigma=\sigma(S)$ many vertices not in $e$; and 
\item edge efficiency $\mathcal E=\mathcal E(S)$. 
\end{itemize}
Suppose also that $V$ 
is a vertex set of size $(r-2)k+2$
that contains 
\begin{itemize}
\item all vertices in $S$; 
\item the edge $e$; and 
\item an additional 
$\sigma'=(r-2)k-\sigma$
other vertices.
\end{itemize}
Then the number of $k$-TWGs $T$ for $e$ 
on $V$  
such that $S\subsetneq T$ is at most
\[
k^{c(\mathcal E+1)}\gamma^{\sigma'}\sigma'!,
\]
for some constants $c$ 
depending only on $r$.

[Theorem thm:ross of arXiv:2608.09368, 'A proof of Ross's conjecture for two-site moving-target search'] For every stochastic matrix (equation eq:M of the paper), every
$\alpha_1,\alpha_2\in[0,1]$, and every $C_1,C_2>0$, the two-site
moving-target search problem admits a deterministic stationary threshold
selector that is optimal for the extended expected-total-cost criterion.
Whenever the value is finite for every initial belief, this selector is an
ordinary finite-cost optimal policy.  The parameter vectors for which the
value is not finite for every belief are classified explicitly in
Section~(sec:boundary of the paper). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
