body:
Let f be twice continuously differentiable on [a,b]. For the composite trapezoidal rule with n equal subintervals of width h = (b-a)/n and nodes x_k = a + k*h, approximating the integral by T_n = h * ( f(x_0)/2 + f(x_1) + ... + f(x_{n-1}) + f(x_n)/2 ), the error satisfies integral_a^b f(x) dx - T_n = -( (b-a) * h^2 / 12 ) * f''(xi) for some xi in (a,b). In particular, | integral_a^b f(x) dx - T_n | <= ( (b-a) * h^2 / 12 ) * max_{x in [a,b]} |f''(x)|, so the error shrinks quadratically in h (equivalently as 1/n^2) as the number of subintervals grows.

[Corollary 14 (First and second variation equations) of arXiv:2606.15432, 'A Concavity Theorem for the Parisi PDE'] Let \(\gamma\in\Opendenseset_\alpha\) and
\(h,h_1,h_2\in\Hoelder{\alpha/2}([0,1])\). Then
\(V_h^\gamma\in\mathcal X_1\) is the unique solution of
\begin{equation}

\begin{cases}
-\partial_s V_h^\gamma
=
\gamma(s)L_s^\gamma V_h^\gamma
+
\dfrac12h(s)v^\gamma,
& (s,x)\in[0,1)\times\R,
\\[0.6ex]
V_h^\gamma(1,x)=0,
& x\in\R,
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
where \(v^\gamma\) is the quantity fixed in Section~\ref{sec:preliminaries}.
Moreover, \(W_{h_1,h_2}^\gamma\in\mathcal X_1\) is the unique solution of
\begin{equation}

\begin{cases}
\begin{aligned}
-\partial_s W_{h_1,h_2}^\gamma
={}&
\gamma(s)L_s^\gamma W_{h_1,h_2}^\gamma
+
h_1(s)L_s^\gamma V_{h_2}^\gamma
+
h_2(s)L_s^\gamma V_{h_1}^\gamma
\\
&+
\gamma(s)s\,\partial_xV_{h_1}^\gamma\,\partial_xV_{h_2}^\gamma,
\end{aligned}
& (s,x)\in[0,1)\times\R,
\\[0.6ex]
W_{h_1,h_2}^\gamma(1,x)=0,
& x\in\R.
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
The map \(h\mapsto V_h^\gamma\) is linear, and
\((h_1,h_2)\mapsto W_{h_1,h_2}^\gamma\) is symmetric bilinear.

[Theorem thm:deconv of arXiv:2411.16058, 'Gaussian deconvolution on $\mathbb R^d$ \\ with application to self-repellent Brownian mot'] Let $d > 2$, let $a_d = \frac{ \Gamma(\frac{ d-2 } 2 ) }{ 2\pi^{d/2}}$, 
and let $J,g$ obey Assumption~(ass:J of the paper). 
Then the Fourier integral solution $H(x)$ to (equation eq:JH of the paper), given in (equation eq:Hint of the paper), obeys
\begin{align} 
H(x) = 
\frac{ a_d \int_\Rd g(y) dy }{ \sqrt{\det \Sigma} } \frac 1 { ( x \cdot \Sigma^{-1} x )^{(d-2)/2} } 
	+ o\bigg( \frac 1 {\abs x^{d-2}} \bigg)
	\qquad \text{as $\abs x \to \infty$},
\end{align}
where $\Sigma$ is a diagonal matrix $\Sigma = \mathrm{diag} ( \int_\Rd x_i^2 J(x) dx : 1 \le i \le d )$. 

Additionally, if $g(x) = o(\abs x^{-(d-2)})$ as $\abs x\to \infty$, 
then the solution $G(x) = H(x) + g(x)$ to (equation eq:JG of the paper) obeys the same asymptotics (equation eq:H_asymp of the paper). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma fgt-simpl-structure of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] Let $\textbf{\textup{C}}$ be a simplicial model category, and let $\textbf{\textup{D}}\subset\textbf{\textup{C}}$ be a full simplicial subcategory closed under weak equivalences. Assume moreover that $\textbf{\textup{D}}$ is locally fibrant. Then the inclusion $N(\textbf{\textup{D}}_0)\hookrightarrow N_\Delta(\textbf{\textup{D}})$ of the nerve of the underlying unenriched category induces an equivalence after localizing at the weak equivalences.
    \begin{proof}
        By the previous corollary, $\textbf{\textup{D}}$ is closed under $\Delta^1\otimes-$, while Lemma~(lemma:hom-equiv-we of the paper) shows that any homotopy equivalence is a weak equivalence. The claim is now an instance of [HA]*{Proposition 1.3.4.7}.
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition type_stochastic of arXiv:2411.05235, 'A comparative study of three mathematical approaches applied to the reversal of AMR'] \textbf{Stability of an Equilibrium Point of a Stochastic Differential Equation.}\\
Let $\xi$ be an equilibrium point of ((SDE of the paper)). We say that:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $\xi$ is a stable equilibrium point in probability of ((SDE of the paper)) if and only if for every $\epsilon > 0$ and $r \in (0, 1)$ there exists a $\delta > 0$ such that for all $x_0 \in I$, $|x_0 - \xi| < \delta$, it holds that $$\mathbb{P}\Big(|X(\cdot, t; x_0) - \xi| < \epsilon, \text{ for all } t \in \mathbb{R}_{0}^{+}\Big) \geq 1 - r.$$ In the contrary case, we say that $\xi$ is an unstable equilibrium point of ((SDE of the paper)).
    \item $\xi$ is an asymptotically stable equilibrium point in probability of ((SDE of the paper)) if and only if $\xi$ is a stable equilibrium point in probability of ((SDE of the paper)) and for every $r \in (0, 1)$ there exists a $\delta > 0$ such that for all $x_0 \in I$, $|x_0 - \xi| < \delta$, it holds that $$\mathbb{P}\Big(\lim_{t \to \infty} X(\cdot, t; x_0) = \xi \Big) \geq 1 - r.$$   
    \item $\xi$ is a globally asymptotically stable equilibrium point in probability of ((SDE of the paper)) if and only if $\xi$ is a stable equilibrium point in probability of ((SDE of the paper)) and for all $x_0 \in I$, it holds that $$\mathbb{P}\Big(\lim_{t \to \infty} X(\cdot, t; x_0) = \xi \Big) = 1.$$
\end{enumerate}
Where $X(\cdot, t; x_0)$ represents the global solution $X$ of ((SDE of the paper)) that starts at $x_0$ at time $t.$

body: [Lemma 7 of arXiv:2609.02225, '\textbf{The direct moving plane method for weak solutions of the fractional $p$-Laplacian}'] Let \(1<p\le 2\) and $0<q<\frac{np}{n-sp}-1$. Suppose that $0\le u\in W_{\mathrm{loc}}^{s,p}(\mathbb R^n) \cap L_{sp}^{p-1}(\mathbb R^n)$ is a weak solution of \eqref{eq:whole-space-lane-emden}. Then there exists \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), depending only on \(n,s,p\), such that \(u\) admits a representative satisfying $u\in C^\alpha_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^n)$.

[Lem gen Kac of arXiv:2608.25471, 'Exact Hausdorff measures and fine geometry of collisions of independent Markov processes'] {Kajino_Noda_26_Kac}}]  
  Let $A=(A_{t})_{t \geq 0}$ be a PCAF and let $\nu$ be the associated smooth measure.
  Let $F \colon (0,\infty) \times \Omega \to [0,\infty]$ be 
  $\mathcal{B}((0,\infty)) \otimes \EuScript{F}_{\infty}$-measurable, set
  $F_{t}(\omega) \coloneqq F(t, \omega)$ for $(t, \omega) \in (0,\infty) \times \Omega$,
  and assume that the following conditions are satisfied:
  \begin{enumerate} [label = \textup{(\roman*)}]
    \item  
    there exists a set $\Lambda \in \EuScript{F}_{\infty}$ with $P_x(\Lambda) = 1$ for all $x \in M$ such that
    the function $(0,\infty) \times \Omega \ni (t, \omega) \mapsto 1_{\Lambda}(\omega) F_{t} \circ \theta_{t}(\omega) = 1_{\Lambda}(\omega) F_{t}(\theta_{t}\omega)$ is 
    $\mathcal{B}((0,\infty)) \otimes \EuScript{F}_{\infty}$-measurable;
    \item  
      the function $(0,\infty) \times M \ni (t, x) \mapsto E_{x}[F_{t}]$ is Borel measurable.
  \end{enumerate}
  Then, for any $t \in (0, \infty]$ and $x \in M$,
  \begin{equation} 
    E_{x}\biggl[ \int_{0}^{t} F_s \circ \theta_{s}\, dA_{s} \biggr]
    = 
    \int_{0}^{t} \int_M p_s(x, y) E_y[F_s]\, \nu(dy)\, ds.
  \end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Thm Theorem:MartingaleProblem-Lh of arXiv:2411.13765, 'Schr\"odinger Bridge Problem for Jump Diffusions'] Assume that Assumption \textup{(Assumption:MartingaleProblem-s,x of the paper)} holds for the jump-diffusion operator $L$ and $\mathbf{P}$ is the solution to the martingale problem for $(L,\rho_0)$. Let $h$ be a harmonic function that satisfies the mean-value property, and let $\mathbf{P}^h$ and $L^h$ be defined as in (equation Definition:h-transform,general case with r0 of the paper) and (equation Definition:L^h of the paper) respectively. Then $\mathbf{P}^h$ solves the martingale problem for $(L^h,\rho^h_0)$, where $\rho^h_0:=\frac{\mathbbm{1}_{A_0}}{r_0}\rho_0$ with $A_0$ and $r_0$ defined as in (equation definition_A0r0 of the paper). Moreover, the canonical process $\left\{ X_t \right\}_{[0,T]}$ under $\mathbf{P}^h$ is a strong Markov process.

body:
[Lemma le:Tbound of arXiv:2602.04673, 'Brownian paths as loop-decorated SLEs'] For $f:[0,\infty)\to [0,\infty)$, let $K_f\coloneqq\{ \mathcal{X}\in {\mathscr{R}}_0: \forall \epsilon>0, \ T_{\leq \epsilon}(\mathcal{X})\leq f(\epsilon)\}$.
  For $r>0$ and $\mathcal{X}\in{\mathscr{R}}$, let $\tilde{B}_{r}(\mathcal{X})$ be the ball in ${\mathscr{R}}_0$ with radius $r$ centred at $\mathcal{X}$ for the distance $\rho(\gamma,\gamma')+  d( \mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}'  )+d_{\infty,[0,1]}(\omega(\mathcal{L}),\omega(\mathcal{L}') )$.

  Then, for all $\mathcal{X}\in{\mathscr{R}}$,
  \begin{itemize}
  \item For all continuous function $f$ with $f(0)=0$, for all $\epsilon>0$, there exists $\delta>0$ (which depends on $\epsilon$, $f$, and $\mathcal{X}$)
  such that $\tilde{B}_{\delta}(\mathcal{X})\cap K_f\subseteq B_\epsilon(\mathcal{X})$.
  \item There exist continuous functions $(f_\epsilon)_{\epsilon>0}$ (which depend on $\mathcal{X}$) such that $f_\epsilon(\epsilon)\underset{\epsilon\to 0}\longrightarrow 0$ and such that
  for all $\mathcal{X}'\in {\mathscr{R}}_0$, if there exists an $\epsilon$-suited isomorphism $\phi$ from $\mathcal{X}$ to $\mathcal{X}'$, then $\mathcal{X}'\in  K_{f_\epsilon} $.

  In particular, $B_{\eta(\epsilon)} (\mathcal{X})\subseteq K_{f_\epsilon} $.
  \end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

DRAFT proof (unaudited), T421-W706-005 v1. The common-fixed-point conclusion of Theorem 1 as printed on p.7 of Bock-Weiss arXiv:2210.02070v1 does not follow from its hypotheses. On the closed set X=[0,2], the maps T(t,x)=x/2+2^(-t), t>=0, map X to X, contract uniformly by 1/2, and satisfy |T(t+1,x)-T(t,x)|=2^(-t-1). But their individual fixed points 2^(1-t) are different, so they have no common fixed point. The trajectories do converge to 0, the fixed point of the limiting map; common-fixed-point and limiting-fixed-point statements must be distinguished. This checks the printed statement only, not the validity of the paper as a whole.

body:
[Lemma 10 of arXiv:2604.09248, '\bfseries Limit laws for longest edges in empty region graphs'] Assume that {$S$ is as in \eqref{eq:SetswithoutRot} with a compact and star-shaped set $K\subset\RR^d$} and let $c>0$. Let $x,y,u,v \in \RR^d$ be such that $\lVert x-y \rVert \ge \lVert u-v \rVert$. Then,
\[
\vol(S(x,y)\setminus S(u,v)) \ge {1\over c+1}{\vol(K)\over {\rm diam}(K)} \Big\lVert \frac{x+y}{2} - \frac{u+v}{2} \Big\rVert \lVert x-y \rVert^{d-1},
\]
whenever {$\lVert \frac{x+y}{2} - \frac{u+v}{2} \rVert\leq c\,{\rm diam}(K) \lVert x-y \rVert$.}
title: Lemma 10 of arXiv:2604.09248

[Theorem 8 of arXiv:2607.13273, 'Asymptotics of transition densities for L\'evy processes with stochastic resetting'] Let $Y_t$ be a pure-jump isotropic unimodal L\'evy process in $\Rd$. 
         Assume that
    $\psi$ is regularly varying of index $\alpha\in (0,2)$ at zero, i.e.,
	\[
		\lim\limits_{x\to 0^+}\frac{\psi\left(\lambda x\right)}{\psi\left(x\right)}=\lambda^{\alpha},\quad\lambda>0.
	\]
    Then, for all $\lambda, t >0, x\in\Rd,$ the density $p_\lambda(t,\cdot)$ of the corresponding process with resetting exists  and satisfies
    \begin{equation}
       p_\lambda(t,x,y) \sim \frac{\mathcal{A}_{d,\alpha}}{\lambda} |y|^{-d} \psi(|y|^{-1}).
    \end{equation}

body:
[Defi Marking scheme A of arXiv:2607.19658, 'Hitting time mixing for random $k$-cycles'] At time $t^*$, mark all elements in $[n]\setminus S_{t^*}$. At time $t+1$,
sample a move $\sigma$ from the kernel $Q_{n,t}$.

The marked set is updated as follows.
\begin{itemize}
\item If the sampled move is a dummy move labelled by $i\in S_t$, then mark
$i$.
\item If $\sigma=(i_1\cdots i_k)$ with $i_1\in S_t$ and
$i_2,\ldots,i_k\in M_t$, then mark $i_1$. Thus, $M_{t+1} = M_t \cup \{i_1\}$ and $S_{t+1} = S_t \setminus \{i_1\}$.
\item In all remaining cases, namely when the ordinary $k$-cycle does not
mark exactly one new element, pull back the marked set under $\sigma$:
$$
M_{t+1}=\{i\in[n]:\sigma(i)\in M_t\}=\sigma^{-1}(M_t),
\qquad
S_{t+1}=\{i\in[n]:\sigma(i)\in S_t\}=\sigma^{-1}(S_t).
$$
\end{itemize}
title: Marking scheme A

[Theorem BEBT! of arXiv:2412.09290, 'Asymptotics of Harish-Chandra transform and infinitesimal freeness'] Let $A$ be a random Hermitian matrix of size $N$ and assume
  that for every $r \in \mathbb{N}$ one has
  \begin{equation}
    \lim_{N \rightarrow \infty} \log \mathbb{E} [H \text{} C (x_1, \ldots,
    x_r, 0^{N - r} ; \lambda_1 (A), \ldots, \lambda_N (A))] = \sum_{i = 1}^r
    \Psi (x_i), 
  \end{equation}
  where $\Psi$ is a smooth function in a neighborhood of $0$ and the above
  convergence is uniform in a neighborhood of $0^r$. Then for every $k \in
  \mathbb{N}$, the $k$-th moment of the random measure $\sum_{i = 1}^N
  \delta \left( N^{- 1} \lambda_i (A) \right)$ converges as $N \rightarrow \infty$ in
  probability to $\Psi^{(k)} (0) / (k - 1) !$.

[Lem 73 of arXiv:2511.20322, 'Dissertation'] Let $Z : \Om \to \R$ be a random variable and $\ph$ be an increasing function. Then $\ph(Z) \sim \Unif{[0,1]}$ if and only if 
\[\ph(t) = F_Z(t) := \P(Z\leq t), \quad \P_Z\text{-}a.s.\]
Similarly, if $\psi$ is decreasing, then $\psi(Z) \sim \Unif{[0,1]}$ if and only if 
\[\psi(t) = 1 - F_Z(t) = \P(Z <t), \quad \P_Z\text{-}a.s.\]

[Theorem recallTzero of arXiv:2608.09856, '\bf Mass erasure on measured $\bbR$-trees,\\ applications to L\'evy forests'] Let $\texttt Q_0 \! \in \!  \mathcal M_1( \mathbb{T}^0_{\! c})$ be such that 
 $\texttt Q_0\big( D \! \in \!  \mathbb{R}^*_+ \big)\!>\!0$ and $\texttt Q_0(Z_r^+\! <\! \infty)\! =\! 1$ for all $r \! \in\! \mathbb{R}_+$. Then the following assertions are equivalent.
\begin{compactenum}

\item[$(a)$] For every $r\! \in \!  \mathbb{R}_+$, the conditional distribution of $\mathtt{Abv}_r$ given $Z^+_r$ under $\texttt Q_0$ is $\texttt Q_0^{\oast Z^+_r} $. 

\smallskip

\item[$(b)$] $\texttt Q_0\! = \!  \texttt Q_{\xi,c}$ for some $c\! \in \! \mathbb{R}^*_+$ and some (sub)critical offspring distribution $\xi$ with $\xi (1)\! = \!  0$. 

\smallskip
\end{compactenum}  
In particular, if $(a)$ or $(b)$ hold true, then $\texttt Q_0$-a.s.~$r\! \in \!  \mathbb{R}_+ \! \mapsto \! Z^+_r$ is an $\mathbb{N}$-valued c{\`a}dl{\`a}g process. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

\]
for every Borel set $A \subset \mathbb{R}$.

P\preceq_{s,\lambda_\beta,\gamma}^{\rm CSD}Q

P\preceq_{\gamma,\beta}^{\rm MASD}Q

\Delta_\beta(P,Q)

[Theorem theo:wsobo of arXiv:2411.10235, '\textbf{Smooth transport map via diffusion process}'] For $\phi\in C^2(\mathbb{R}^d)$ satisfying $\phi(x)=a\|x\|^{1+s}$ for $\|x\|\geq K,$ with $ K,a,s>0$, define the measure $\mu$ having a density $d\mu(x) = \exp(-\phi(x))dx$ with respect to the $d$-dimensional Lebesgue measure. \end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

MDP $(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{A}, H, \mathbb{P}_m, r_m)$ is a $\xi$-approximate linear
MDP with a feature map $\phi : \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{A} \to \mathbb{R}^d$. Specifically, for each step $h \in [H]$, there exist $d$ unknown measures 
$\mu_h = \bigl(\mu_h^{(1)}, \ldots, \mu_h^{(d)}\bigr)$ over $\mathcal{X}$ and an unknown vector 
$\theta_h \in \mathbb{R}^d$ such that, for all $(x,a) \in \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{A}$,

\[
\bigl\|\mathbb{P}_{m,h}(\cdot \mid x,a) - \langle \phi(x,a), \mu_h(\cdot)\rangle\bigr\|_{\mathrm{TV}} \le \xi,\quad
\bigl|r_{m,h}(x,a) - \langle \phi(x,a), \theta_h\rangle\bigr| \le \xi.
\]
Here, we assume $\|\phi(x,a)\| \le 1$ for all
$(x,a) \in \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{A}$, and $\max\bigl\{\|\mu_h(\mathcal{X})\|,\|\theta_h\|\bigr\} \le \sqrt{d}$.

[Proposition 18 of arXiv:2609.01460, 'On cost-induced Santal\'o-type inequalities \\ in Polish measure spaces'] Let $X$ and $Y$ be geodesic vector spaces, and let $c: X \times Y \to \R$ be a cost function that is $1$-homogeneous in each variable. Let $K \subset X$ and $L \subset Y$ be compact, geodesically convex sets containing the origin in their respective interiors. Then, 
\[
\Ld c(\|\cdot\|_K)(y)=I_{K^{\circ, c}}(y) \quad \text{and} \quad \Lu c(\|\cdot\|_L)(x)=I_{L^{\star, c}}(x).
\]

body:
[Definition 3 (Polynomials and their coefficients) of arXiv:2606.19115, 'Finite free perpetuities'] Every polynomial $p\in \tilde\pols_{\leq n}(\C)$ can be written uniquely in the form
\begin{align*}
    p(z) &= \sum_{k=0}^n (-1)^k \binom{n}{k} \coef{k}{n}(p) z^{n-k}.
\end{align*}
In particular, if $p(z) = \prod_{i=1}^n (z-\lambda_i) \in \pols_n(\C)$, then
\[ \coef{k}{n}(p) = \binom{n}{k}^{-1} \sum_{1 \le i_1 < \dots < i_k \le n} \lambda_{i_1} \cdots \lambda_{i_k} \]
for $k\in\{1,\dots,n\}$, while $\coef{0}{n}(p) = 1$.

We say that a polynomial $p\in\tilde\pols_{\leq n}(\C)$ is $d$-monic, $d\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$, if $\coef{d}{n}(p)=1$. In particular, monic polynomials are $0$-monic. More precisely, this notion depends on both \(n\) and \(d\). We suppress the parameter \(n\) when it is clear from the context.
title: Polynomials and their coefficients

[Openproblem op:uniqueness of arXiv:2609.01557, '$L^\infty$ Variational Approximation of the Aubry Set'] Assume
\[
\int_{\mathbb T^n} u_k\,dx=0.
\]
Does the whole sequence \(u_k\) converge uniformly as \(k\to\infty\)?
Equivalently, can two different subsequences converge to different absolute
minimizers? By (cor:lowdim of the paper), when $n\leq 3$, every subsequential limit \(u\) satisfies
\[
D_u=\mathcal A,
\]
but this characterization alone does not determine \(u\) uniquely. (Stated as a problem by the paper; open unless the paper says otherwise.)
title: Uniqueness of the limit

[Theorem 19 of arXiv:2607.22441, 'The martingale representation theorem for cylindrical martingale valued measures'] Let $X$ be a separable, reflexive Banach space and let $(m_t: t \geq 0)$ be a cylindrical square integrable martingale on $X^*$ with operator quadratic covariation satisfying
$$\langle m(x^*_1), m(x^*_2)\rangle_t=\int_0^t \Bigl(\Phi (r)Q \Phi(r)^* x^*_1, x^*_2\Bigr)_H\,dr, \quad \forall x^*_1, x^*_2 \in X^*,$$ 
where $Q$ is a bounded, non-negative, self-adjoint operator on $H$ with  representation  \eqref{representationCovariaQDefiCylinWhineNoiseMeasure} and $\Phi: \Omega \times[0,T]  \rightarrow \mathcal{L}(H,X)$ is $ (\omega,t) \mapsto \Phi(\omega,t)h$ 
is $\mathcal{P}_{T}/\mathcal{B}(X)$-measurable for every $h \in H$ and such that for $\Psi(\omega,t)=\Phi(\omega,t) Q^{1/2}$, we have $\Psi(\omega,t) \Psi^{*}(\omega,t) \in \mathcal{K}^{+}(X)$. Then there exists a cylindrical Wiener process $B=(B_t: t \geq 0)$ in $H$ with covariance $Q$ defined on an extended probability space $(\Omega \times \widetilde{\Omega}, \mathcal{F} \times \widetilde{\mathcal{F}}, \Prob \times \widetilde{\Prob})$ adapted to the filtration $\{\mathcal{F}_{t} \times \widetilde{\mathcal{F}}_{t}\}$ such that
\begin{equation}

m_t(\omega)=\int_0^t \Phi(\omega, r)\, dB_r (\omega, \widetilde{\omega}).
\end{equation}

[Proposition 14 (Power sums and the kernel of \(\rho\)) of arXiv:2609.03881, 'Eulerian insertion operators and an Eulerian form of the Pieri rule'] We have
$\rho(p_m)=\delta^mE=\delta^{m-1}\G_1$.
Consequently, if \(\lambda\vdash n\), then
$\rho(p_\lambda)=\delta^nE^{\ell(\lambda)}$.
Moreover, $\ker\rho
  =
  \left\langle
    p_i p_{j+1}-p_{i+1}p_j:\ 1\leq i<j
  \right\rangle$.
In particular, for \(n\geq1\),
\[
  \rho(\Lambda_n)
  =
  \delta^n\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb Q}
  \{E,E^2,\ldots,E^n\},~
  \dim\ker(\rho|_{\Lambda_n})=p(n)-n,
\]
where \(p(n)\) is the number of partitions of \(n\).

and $T_n^{\, \bullet}=(T_n, X_n)$ has the uniform distribution on marked binary trees with size $n$.

[Definition eq:transience_r_def of arXiv:2607.18011, 'From local giants to locality in long-range percolation'] \thlabel{def:transience_renorm_scheme}
    Let $\varepsilon > 0$, and let $r_0 \in \mathbf{N}$ be a large constant.
    
    We define $s=s(\varepsilon)$ to be the least integer satisfying simultaneously $2(1+s)^2\ge (1+\varepsilon)/\varepsilon$.
    
    We set $
    \bar r_0=r_0$, set $m_0=0$, and for $i \geq 1$ we iteratively define 
    
    \begin{equation}
        
        m_i 
        =
        2 
        (i+s)^2
        \quad
        \text{and}
        \quad
        r_i
        =
        r_{i-1}
        m_i.
    \end{equation}
    
    Let $((\Tile{i}{j})_{j \geq 0})_{i \geq 0}$ be the renormalisation scheme associated to the renormalisation scales $(r_i)_{i \geq 0}$ in \thref{def:recursive_tiles}.
title: Definition eq:transience_r_def of arXiv:2607.18011

[Proposition prop:gauge-link of arXiv:2608.01253, 'The pseudo-quantum representation of \\finite reversible Markov chains'] Let $\mathcal{E}:=\operatorname{diag}\bigl(i^{\,n-k}\bigr)_{k=0}^{n}$, a fixed unitary diagonal
matrix independent of $t$, and let $\lvert \psi_\theta\rangle:=e^{-i\thetaJ_x}\lvert n\rangle$ be
the register coherent state of the imaginary slice. Then

\begin{equation}
\mathcal{E}\,J_x\,\mathcal{E}^{-1}=J_y,\qquad \mathcal{E}\lvert n\rangle=\lvert n\rangle,\qquad
\mathcal{E}\ket{\psi_{\theta}}=e^{-i\thetaJ_y}\lvert n\rangle,

\end{equation}

so $\ket{\sqrt{\pi_t}}=\mathcal{E}\ket{\psi_{\theta(t)}}$ and
$\sigma^{\mathrm{FR}}_t=\mathcal{E}\,\ketbra{\psi_{\theta(t)}}{\psi_{\theta(t)}}\,\mathcal{E}^{*}$.

[Lemma 10 of arXiv:2606.02786, 'Non-local SDEs, critical drifts and local blow-ups'] The following are true for every $\beta \in ]\frac{\alpha \gamma}{2},d+\gamma]$, for all $(t,x) \in \mathbb{R}^{1+d}$:

\smallskip

{\rm (\textit{i})}~For all $\rho>0$, we have
\begin{align*}
P_\gamma(\mathbf{1}_{C^c_\rho}f)(t,x)  \leq K \rho^{\frac{\alpha \gamma}{2}-\beta }M_\beta f(t,x), & \qquad K:=\frac{1}{\beta-\frac{\alpha\gamma}{2}}\bigl(-\frac{\alpha \gamma}{2}+d+\alpha\bigr), \\[2mm]
P_\gamma(\mathbf{1}_{C_\rho}f)(t,x)  \leq N \rho^{\frac{\alpha \gamma}{2}}Mf(t,x), & \qquad N:= \frac{2}{\alpha \gamma}\bigl(-\frac{\alpha\gamma}{2}+d+\alpha\bigr)
\end{align*}
for all $0 \leq f \in C_c(\mathbb{R}^{1+d})$.

\smallskip

{\rm (\textit{ii})}~$$
P_\gamma f(t,x) \leq C (M_\beta f(t,x))^{\frac{\alpha \gamma}{2}\frac{1}{\beta}}(M f(t,x))^{1-\frac{\alpha \gamma}{2}\frac{1}{\beta}}, \quad C:=K^{\frac{\alpha \gamma}{2}\frac{1}{\beta}}N^{1-\frac{\alpha \gamma}{2}\frac{1}{\beta}}. 
$$

[Proposition prop-psiconvp-bsdequadr of arXiv:2605.07832, 'A Bismut -Elworthy formula for BSDEs with degenerate noise'] Let $(X,Y,Z)$ be solution of the forward-backward system ((fbsde of the paper)),
and assume that hypotheses (ip_forward of the paper) and (ip-psiphi of the paper) hold
true and let $(Y^n,Z^n)$ be solution of the BSDE in the forward-backward system ((fbsde of the paper))
with generator  $\psi_n$ in the place of $\psi$, where $\psi_n$ is defined in ((infsupconvpsi of the paper)). Namely,
$(Y^n,Z^n)$ solve the following BSDE:
\begin{equation}
    \left\{\begin{array}{l}\displaystyle
 dY^{n,t,x}_\tau=-\psi_n(\tau,X^{t,x}_\tau,Y^{n,t,x}_\tau,Z^{n,t,x}_\tau)\;d\tau+Z^{n,t,x}_\tau\;dW_\tau,
  \\\displaystyle
  Y^{n,t,x}_T=\phi(X_T),
\end{array}\right.
\end{equation}
Then, for all $p\geq 1$, the unique solution of the markovian BSDE in ((fbsde of the paper)) is such that
\[
 \Vert Y-Y^n\Vert _{{\cal S}^p}+\Vert Z-Z^n\Vert_{{\cal M}^p}\rightarrow 0 \qquad \text{as }n\rightarrow \infty.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition prop-psiconvp-bsdequadr of arXiv:2605.07832

\]

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Test the d = 3 analogue of the Apollonian structure on the simplest candidates (diagonal matrices). Result: Gamma(Z^d) is the set of symmetric matrices A for which there is an integer-valued function on Z^d whose discrete Laplacian is at most the constant ... with quadratic growth A: g(x) = (1/2) x^T A x + (lower order) integer-valued superharmonic. Diagonal A = diag(a_1,...,a_d): g(x) = sum_i (1/2) a_i x_i^2 rounded is integer-valued; the discrete Laplacian of x -> ceil(a x^2 / 2) in one dimension is at most a + 1 ... in one dimension the maximal a with an integer superharmonic quadratic of curvature a is determined by the 1D odometer; for diagonal matrices the problem separates into d one-dimensional problems and the maximal diagonal elements are rational (the 1D maximal curvatures are rational, e.g. the 1D sandpile has only finitely many patterns). This gives rational maximal elements on the diagonal slice, but maximality in Gamma(Z^d) (not just among diagonal matrices) is not implied: a diagonal A might be dominated by a non-diagonal B. In d = 2 the LPS classification shows the maximal elements are dense in the boundary and rational; for d = 3 the analogue of the Apollonian packing would be a packing by spheres of a slab, whose tangency structure has more degrees of freedom (a sphere touching four others is not determined by rational data in general: Descartes-type relations in 3D involve a quadratic form on curvatures with generic irrational solutions unless the initial spheres are chosen integrally). This suggests that rationality may FAIL in d = 3 unless the initial configuration forces integrality via the Soddy-Gosset relation with integer curvatures; the analogue of the band packing in d = 3 has initial curvatures determined by the lattice (integer), and integral Apollonian-type packings in 3D do have all curvatures integral when the initial ones are (Soddy-Gosset gives a quadratic recursion preserving integrality). So rationality is plausible in d = 3 if the correspondence to packings persists, and isolation would be false (packings are dense in the boundary). Recorded as a conjectural picture with the Soddy-Gosset integrality argument as the reason to expect rational entries. Key identity: If the d = 3 maximal elements correspond to a sphere packing generated from integer initial curvatures, Soddy-Gosset integrality gives rational entries. Obstruction: No d = 3 analogue of the LPS correspondence between Gamma(Z^d) and packings.

[Thm 7 of arXiv:2604.11489, '2604.11489'] Let $\{X_n, n\ge 1\}$ be a sequence of independent and identically distributed random variables with common nonuniform distribution $\{p_i, i\ge 1\}$ satisfying $\ee|\ln p(X_1)|^{2+\delta} < \infty$. Assume that there exists an integer valued function $K(n)$ such that, for some $0< \delta<\frac{1}{2}$,
\beq
K(n)\le n^{\frac{1}{2}-\delta},\ \ n^{\frac{1}{2}+\delta}\ln n\sum_{i=K(n)}^{\infty}p_i \leq C
\ \ \text{and}\ \ -n^{\frac{1}{2}+\delta}\sum_{i=K(n)}^{\infty}p_i\ln p_i\leq C.
\deq
If there exists an $\epsilon \in (1/2, 1)$ with
\beq
\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}p_{i}^{1-\epsilon}<\infty,
\deq
then we have
\beq
\sup_x\left|\pp\left(\frac{\sqrt{n}}{\sigma}(\hat H_{JK}-H)\le x\right)-\Phi(x)\right|\le
Cn^{-\frac{\delta}{2}}+Cn^{\frac{1}{4}-\frac{\epsilon}{2}},
\deq
where $\Phi$ denotes the standard normal distribution function and $\sigma^2=Var(\ln p(X_1))$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Thm 7 of arXiv:2604.11489

body:
[Definition def:bs-Ho of arXiv:2412.05142, 'Strong convergence of the Euler scheme for singular kinetic SDEs driven by $\alpha$-stable'] For a function $f:{\mathbb R}^{2d}\to{\mathbb R}$,  the first-order difference operator is defined by
$$
\delta^{(1)}_hf(z):=\delta_hf(z):=f(z+h)-f(z),\ \ z, h\in{\mathbb R}^{2d}.
$$
For $M\in{\mathbb N}$, the $M$-order difference operator  is defined recursively by
$
\delta^{(M+1)}_hf(z)=\delta_h\circ\delta^{(M)}_hf(z).
$
title: Definition def:bs-Ho of arXiv:2412.05142

[Lemma pro: RangeOfConvergence of arXiv:2411.13465, 'Height-offset variables and pinning at infinity for gradient Gibbs measures on trees'] \mbox{}\\
\begin{enumerate}[a)]
    \item Let $\nu$ be the free measure (a GGM of height-period $2$, resp.) Assume that $\hat{\psi}^{free}(t)$ ($\hat{\psi}^{\bar{\mu}}_\star(t)$, resp.)
converges for real $t \in (-R,+R)$. Then the following holds true. The moment generating function  $\hat{\varphi}_\infty^\nu$ of $H^{\rho,0}$ converges for real $t \in \left(-(d+1)R,+(d+1)R\right)$ and is given as the pointwise limit of the family $(\hat{\varphi}_r^\nu)_{r \geq 1}$. 
 \item In the specific case of the free state let $\kappa_n^{free,\mathbb{T}^d}$ denote the $n$th cumulant for $H^{\rho,0}$ and let $\kappa_n^{free}$ denote the $n$th cumulant associated with $\hat{\psi}^{free}$. \\Then 
$\kappa^{free,\mathbb{T}^d}_n = \kappa^{free}_n \frac{d^{n-1}}{(d^{n-1}-1)(d+1)^{n-1}}$.
\end{enumerate}
title: Range of convergence for the moment generating function of $H$ and its cumulants

body:
[Lemma lem:conditional-convolution of arXiv:2608.26745, 'Moderate Deviations for the Largest Eigenvalue of a Randomly Deformed Gaussian Unitary Ens'] Let $X_N+Y_N$ be a decomposition with $Y_N$ measurable with respect to a
$\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal F_N$.  Let $a_N\to\infty$, and let $\alpha_N a_N\to\infty$.
Assume the following.

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.7em]
\item There are events $\mathcal G_N\in\mathcal F_N$ whose complements are
superexponentially small at the speeds
$a_N^{3/2}$, $a_N^3$, and $\alpha_N^2a_N^2$.
\item Uniformly on $\mathcal G_N$ and uniformly for $u$ in compact subsets of
$(0,\infty)$,
\begin{align*}
 \log\mathbb P(X_N>a_Nu\mid\mathcal F_N)
 =-a_N^{3/2}\left(\frac43u^{3/2}+o(1)\right),\\
 \log\mathbb P(X_N\le-a_Nu\mid\mathcal F_N)
 =-a_N^3\left(\frac1{12}u^3+o(1)\right).
\end{align*}
\item The variables $Y_N/a_N$ satisfy an MDP with speed
$\alpha_N^2a_N^2$ and rate $v^2/(2\sigma^2)$.
\end{enumerate}

Here and below, fixed versions of the conditional probabilities are used.
Uniformity on $\mathcal G_N$ means that the displayed deterministic error bounds hold
for almost every outcome in $\mathcal G_N$.

Then the six conclusions of (thm:main of the paper) hold with $Z_N$ replaced by
$X_N+Y_N$.

body: [Definition 1.1 (Connective constants) of arXiv:2604.02746, 'Zero-Freeness of the Hard-Core Model with Bounded Connective Constant'] For a family H of finite graphs, the k-depth connective constant of H for a fixed k, denoted by µk(H), is supG∈H µk(G). The lower connective constant of H, denoted by µinf(H), is infk≥1 µk(H). For an infinite graph G, let HG denote the set of all finite subgraphs of G. We establish the following relationship: for any infinite graph G with connective constant σ(G), µinf(HG) ≤σ(G).
title: Definition 1.1 (Connective constants) of arXiv:2604.02746: Zero-Freeness of the Hard-Core Model with Bounded Connective Constant

[Proposition explicit_prop of arXiv:2608.25513, 'Adaptive Regularization for Random Features: A Neighboring Early-Stopping Rule with Oracle'] For two KRR-RF estimators $f_{M,D,\lambda}(\mathop{\bf x})=\boldsymbol{u}_{M,D,\lambda}^T\phi_M(\mathop{\bf x})$ and $f_{M,D,\tilde{\lambda}}(\mathop{\bf x})=\boldsymbol{u}_{M,D,\tilde{\lambda}}^T\phi_M(\mathop{\bf x})$ with $\lambda, \tilde{\lambda} > 0$, there holds the following explicit equality:
$$\|(C_{M,D} + \lambda I)^{1/2} (\boldsymbol{u}_{M,D,\lambda} - \boldsymbol{u}_{M,D,\tilde{\lambda}})\|_2^2 =  \|f_{M,D,\lambda} - f_{M,D,\tilde{\lambda}}\|_D^2 + \lambda \|\boldsymbol{u}_{M,D,\lambda} - \boldsymbol{u}_{M,D,\tilde{\lambda}}\|_2^2 ,$$
where we denote the empirical norm of $f$ as $\|f\|_D^2 = \frac{1}{|D|} \sum_{i=1}^{|D|} f(\mathop{\bf x}_i)^2$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition explicit_prop of arXiv:2608.25513

body:
[Cor SSL0 of arXiv:2609.01751, 'Orthogonal polynomials which are eigenfunctions of a partial differential operator'] Let ${\kappa}_1,\ldots, {\kappa}_{d_2-1} > -1$ and ${\kappa}_{d_2} = -1$. The spectral operator ${\mathfrak D}_{{\boldsymbol{\kappa}}}^{{\mathbb S} \rtimes \Sigma} $ can be 
written as 
\begin{align} 
  {\mathfrak D}_{{\boldsymbol{\kappa}}}^{{\mathbb S} \rtimes \Sigma} & = 
   \frac{1}{{\mathsf W}_{{\boldsymbol{\kappa}}}^{{\mathbb S} \rtimes \Sigma} (\bm x, \bm y)}  
       \sum_{i=1}^{d_2-1} (\partial_{y_i} - \partial_{y_{d_2}}) y_i |{\bm y}|^{d_2} {\mathsf W}_{{\boldsymbol{\kappa}}}^{{\mathbb S} \rtimes \Sigma} (\bm x, \bm y)
         (\partial_{y_i} - \partial_{y_d}) \\
   & +  \frac{1}{|\bm y|^{d_1-1}} \frac{1}{{\mathsf W}_{{\boldsymbol{\kappa}}}^{{\mathbb S} \rtimes \Sigma} (\bm x, \bm y)}     
        \partial_{y_d}  \big( |\bm y|^{d_1} {\mathsf W}_{{\boldsymbol{\kappa}}}^{{\mathbb S} \rtimes \Sigma} (\bm x, \bm y) \partial_{y_d} \big)
        + \frac{1}{|\bm y|} \Delta_0^{(\bm x)}. \notag 

 \end{align}
In particular, it follows that 
\begin{align}  
    - &\int_{{\mathbb S}^{d_1-1}\! \rtimes {\mathbb R}_\Sigma^{d_2}}{\mathfrak D}_{{\boldsymbol{\kappa}}}^{{\mathbb S} \rtimes \Sigma} 
    f (\bm x,\bm y) \cdot g(\bm x, \bm y) {\mathsf W}_{{\boldsymbol{\kappa}}}^{{\mathbb S} \rtimes \Sigma} (\bm y) \mathrm{d} \sigma(\bm x, \bm y)  \\ 
  &   =  \int_{{\mathbb S}^{d_1-1}\! \rtimes {\mathbb R}_\Sigma^{d_2}}  \frac{1}{|\bm y|}  \sum_{1 \le i< j \le d_1}  D_{i,j}^{(\bm x)} f(\bm x, \bm y)  D_{i,j}^{(\bm x)} g(\bm x, \bm y) 
  {\mathsf W}_{{\boldsymbol{\kappa}}}^{{\mathbb S} \rtimes \Sigma}(\bm y)  \mathrm{d} \sigma({\bm x}, {\bm y})    \notag \\ 
  & + \int_{{\mathbb S}^{d_1-1}\! \rtimes {\mathbb R}_\Sigma^{d_2}}   \sum_{i=1}^{d_2-1} (\partial_{y_i} - \partial_{y_d}) f(\bm x,\bm y) \cdot 
    (\partial_{y_i} - \partial_{y_d})g(\bm x,\bm y)
  {\mathsf W}_{{\boldsymbol{\kappa}}}^{{\mathbb S} \rtimes \Sigma}(\bm y)  \mathrm{d} \sigma(\bm x, \bm y)    \notag \\
    &  +  \int_{{\mathbb S}^{d_1-1}\! \rtimes {\mathbb R}_\Sigma^{d_2}}  |{\bm y}|^{d_1} \partial_{y_d} f(\bm x,\bm y) \partial_{y_d} g(\bm x,\bm y) 
       |{\bm y}| {\mathsf W}_{{\boldsymbol{\kappa}}}^{{\mathbb S} \rtimes \Sigma}(\bm y)   \mathrm{d} \sigma(\bm x,\bm y).  \notag
 \end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: For an m by n real or complex matrix A with entries a_{ij} and singular values sigma_1 >= ... >= sigma_{min(m,n)} >= 0, the Frobenius norm is ||A||_F = sqrt(sum_{i,j} |a_{ij}|^2) = sqrt(trace(A* A)) = sqrt(sum_i sigma_i^2). The Frobenius norm is the norm induced by the trace inner product <A,B> = trace(A* B) on the space of m by n matrices, and it is submultiplicative: ||AB||_F <= ||A||_F ||B||_F whenever the product is defined. [standard, e.g. Horn and Johnson, Matrix Analysis]
title: Frobenius (Hilbert-Schmidt) Norm of a Matrix

[Lemma lem:cutoff of arXiv:2607.22220, 'Pathwise uniqueness for degenerate stochastic differential equations with H\"{o}lder conti'] For every $\vartheta>0$ there is $C_{\vartheta,R}$, independent of $n$, such that
\begin{equation}
\sum_{i=1}^K\mathfrak R_i(u)
\le
\vartheta\sum_{i=1}^K\frac{\Delta_i(s)}{d_i(s)^2}u_i^2
+C_{\vartheta,R}{\cal Q}_s(u).
\end{equation}
More generally, if $R_s(u)$ in (equation eq:R-cutoff-exact of the paper) is replaced by $R_s(y)$ and the neighbor $u_{i+1}$ in the middle term is replaced by a vector component $z_{i+1}$, then the final term on the right-hand side becomes
$C_{\vartheta,R}({\cal Q}_s(u)+{\cal Q}_s(y)+{\cal Q}_s(z))$.

[Definition 48 (Coalescent subtrees) of arXiv:2511.09517, 'From Cannings model to Brownian motion conditioned on local time profile'] For \(0\le j\le h^*\), define the collection of the coalescent subtrees at height \(j\) by
\[
\mathbf{T}_j=\mathbf{T}_j(n,h^*):=\big\{\mathscr{T}^n(v): v\in \cX_j\big\}.
\]
Each element of \(\mathbf{T}_j\) is a subtree rooted at a vertex at height \(j\) that admits at least one descendant at height \(h^*\). Note that \(|\mathbf{T}_j|=|\cX_j|=X_j\).

We then write \(\mathsf{T}_1,\ldots,\mathsf{T}_{|\mathbf{T}_j|}\) for a uniform random ordering of the elements of \(\mathbf{T}_j\). Concretely, conditionally on \(\mathscr{T}^n\), we first list the elements of \(\mathbf{T}_j\) according to the lexicographical order of their roots, denoted by \(\mathbf{T}_j^{(1)},\ldots,\mathbf{T}_j^{(|\mathbf{T}_j|)}\). Then we choose a permutation \(\pi\) uniformly at random from the symmetric group on \(|\mathbf{T}_j|\) elements, and define
\[
(\mathsf{T}_1,\ldots,\mathsf{T}_{|\mathbf{T}_j|})
:= (\mathbf{T}_j^{(\pi(1))},\ldots,\mathbf{T}_j^{(\pi(|\mathbf{T}_j|))}).
\]
Finally, we introduce the labeling map
\begin{align}
    \Lambda_j : \mathbf{T}_j \longrightarrow \{1,\ldots,|\mathbf{T}_j|\}, \qquad
\Lambda_j(\mathsf{T}_i) := i,
\end{align}
which assigns to each coalescent subtree its index in the random ordering.  
The random orderings (and hence the labeling maps \(\Lambda_j\)) are taken independently across different heights~\(j\).

[Proposition prop:W_lower of arXiv:2411.03609, 'Asymptotically optimal Wasserstein couplings for the small-time stable domain of attractio'] Let $\bm{X}$ be in the domain of non-normal attraction of an $\alpha$-stable process $\bm{Z}$ with $\alpha\in(0,2]$ and define $a(t)\coloneqq G(2t)/G(t)$ for $t>0$. Then, for all $t>0$ and $q\in(0,1]\cap(0,\alpha)$, 
\begin{align*}
2^{1-q/\alpha}\mathcal{W}_q(\bm{X}^t_1,\bm{Z}_1)
+a(t)^q\mathcal{W}_q(\bm{X}^{2t}_1, \bm{Z}_1) 
\geqslant 
|1-a(t)^q|\mathds{E}\big[|\bm Z_1|^q\big].
\end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Theorem 2.4 of arXiv:2110.05374, 'When Janson meets McDiarmid: Bounded difference inequalities under graph-dependence'] Let the Ω-valued random vector X be G-dependent and let f : Ω → R be forest-decomposable c-Lipschitz with respect to G. Then for every t > 0, P(f(X) − E[f(X)] ≥ t) ≤ exp(−2t²/D(G, c)), where D(G, c) := min over {(F_k, w_k)}_k ∈ FFC(G) of ( Σ_k w_k √( Σ_{{i,j}∈E(G[F_k])} (c_i + c_j)² + Σ_{T∈T(F_k)} c_{min,k,T}² ) )², with c_{min,k,T} := min{c_i : i ∈ T} for T ∈ T(F_k). By Remark 2.5 of the paper, D(G, c) ≤ χ_f(G)‖c‖₂², the denominator of Janson's inequality (take a fractional independent vertex cover).
c-Lipschitz (Definition 1.1 of the paper): Ω = Ω_1 × ... × Ω_n is a product of Polish spaces, c = (c_1, ..., c_n) ∈ R_+^n, and f : Ω → R is c-Lipschitz when |f(x) − f(x')| ≤ Σ_{i=1}^n c_i 1{x_i ≠ x'_i} for all x, x' ∈ Ω (Lipschitz for the c-weighted Hamming distance).
G-dependent (Definition 1.3 of the paper): X = (X_i)_{i∈V(G)} is G-dependent when for all disjoint S, T ⊂ V(G) with no edge of G between S and T, the families (X_i)_{i∈S} and (X_j)_{j∈T} are independent; this is stronger than pairwise independence of non-adjacent coordinates.
Fractional forest vertex cover: a family {(F_k, w_k)}_k with F_k ⊆ V(G), w_k ∈ [0, 1] and Σ_{k: v∈F_k} w_k = 1 for every v ∈ V(G), such that each F_k induces a forest G[F_k]; T(F_k) is the set of vertex sets of the trees of G[F_k], and FFC(G) is the set of all fractional forest vertex covers of G.
Forest-decomposable c-Lipschitz with respect to G (Section 2.2 of the paper): for every {(F_k, w_k)}_k ∈ FFC(G) there are (c_i)_{i∈F_k}-Lipschitz functions f_k : Ω_{F_k} → R with f(x) = Σ_k w_k f_k(x_{F_k}) for all x ∈ Ω. The paper's sentence puts 'for all x' before 'there exist f_k'; the f_k cannot depend on x, since constant f_k would then make every f decomposable.

\[
Z_m \vcentcolon= \frac{A_m(t - A_m)}{m(2n - m)}.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
Z_{n - 1} \succeq_{\mathrm{cx}} Z_n.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition d:derivative of arXiv:2510.13659, 'On the energy image density conjecture of Bouleau and Hirsch'] Suppose $f: X \to \mathbb{R}$ and $\phi=(\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_n): X \to\mathbb{R}^n$ are Lipschitz functions on a metric   space $(X,d)$. Then $f$ is \emph{differentiable with respect to $\phi$ at $x_0 \in X$} if there is a unique $\mathbf{a}=(a_1,\ldots,a_n) \in \mathbb{R}^n$ such that $f$ and the linear combination $a\cdot \phi = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i \phi_i$ agree to first order near $x_0$: 
		\[
		\limsup_{x \to x_0} \frac{\abs{f(x)-f(x_0)-\langle \mathbf{a}, \phi(x)-\phi(x_0) \rangle }}{d(x,x_0)}=0.
		\]
		Equivalently,  $\Lip g(x_0)=0$, where $g(\cdot)= f(\cdot)-\sum_{i=1}^n a_i \phi_i(\cdot)$. The tuple $a \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is the \emph{derivative of $f$ with respect to $\phi$} and will be denoted by $\partial_\phi f(x_0)$.
title: Definition d:derivative of arXiv:2510.13659

Let X = (X_1,...,X_n) have independent real coordinates. (Thm 1.1) If each X_i has density <= K a.e., then for every orthogonal projection P onto a d-dimensional subspace, PX has density <= (CK)^d a.e., C absolute. (Thm 1.2) For d = 1 the optimal constant is sqrt(2): if sum a_j^2 = 1, sum a_jX_j has density <= sqrt(2)K, attained by (X_1+X_2)/sqrt(2) with X_i uniform on [-1/(2K),1/(2K)]. (Cor 1.4) With L(Z,t) = sup_u P(||Z-u||_2 <= t): if L(X_i,t) <= p for all i, then L(PX, t sqrt(d)) <= (Cp)^d. (Thm 1.5) For every m x n matrix A and delta in (0,1), L(AX, t||A||_HS) <= (C_delta p)^{(1-delta) r(A)}, where r(A) = ||A||_HS^2/||A||^2 is the stable rank and C_delta depends only on delta; with densities <= K this reads L(AX, t||A||_HS) <= (C_delta K t)^{(1-delta) r(A)}.

body:
[Lemma 60 (Causal Borel limit selector) of arXiv:2608.04993, '2608.04993'] Let $E$ be a separable Banach space with base point $0$ and define
\[
 \operatorname{Lim}_E:E^{\N}\longrightarrow E,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{Lim}_E((z_n)_n)
 :=\begin{cases}
    \lim_nz_n,&(z_n)_n\text{ converges in }E,\\
    0,&\text{otherwise}.
   \end{cases}
\]
Then $\operatorname{Lim}_E$ is Borel.  Suppose
$F_n:[0,T]\times\Omega_H\to E$ are Borel and
\[
 F_n(t,r_sx)=F_n(t\wedge s,x)
 \qquad(n\ge1).
\]
The coordinatewise selector
$F(t,x):=\operatorname{Lim}_E((F_n(t,x))_n)$ is Borel and satisfies the same
stopping identity.  On every Borel set on which $(F_n)_n$ converges uniformly
in $C([0,T];E)$, $F$ is the resulting continuous path-valued limit.

body:
Let p be a prime, f a polynomial with coefficients in the p-adic integers Z_p (in particular any polynomial with integer coefficients), and a in Z_p with f(a) congruent to 0 modulo p and f'(a) not congruent to 0 modulo p. Then there is a unique alpha in Z_p with f(alpha) = 0 and alpha congruent to a modulo p. Concretely: a simple root of f modulo p lifts to a unique root modulo p^k for every k, and these lifts converge p-adically to the root alpha. The general form replaces the hypothesis by |f(a)|_p < |f'(a)|_p^2, which allows f'(a) to be divisible by p.
p prime, f in Z_p[x], a in Z_p
f(a) congruent to 0 mod p
f'(a) a p-adic unit (a SIMPLE root modulo p); the double-root case needs the general form |f(a)|_p < |f'(a)|_p^2

body: The set R of real numbers is uncountable: there is no surjection from N onto R, hence no bijection between N and R. Equivalently, for every sequence x_1, x_2, x_3, ... of real numbers there is a real number different from every x_n.

Let x_1, x_2, ... be any sequence in [0,1]. Choose for each x_n a decimal expansion x_n = 0.d(n,1) d(n,2) d(n,3) ... (each digit d(n,k) in {0, ..., 9}). Define a new number x = 0.b_1 b_2 b_3 ... by the diagonal rule: b_n = 5 if d(n,n) is not 5, and b_n = 6 if d(n,n) = 5. Then x lies in [0,1], and its expansion differs from the chosen expansion of x_n in the n-th digit for every n. Because all digits of x lie in {5, 6}, its expansion contains no infinite tail of 0s or of 9s, and a real number can have two distinct decimal expansions only when one ends in all 9s and the other in all 0s; hence x has exactly one decimal expansion. If x were equal to some x_n as a real number, the chosen expansion of x_n would be a decimal expansion of x differing from x's unique expansion (they differ in digit n), which is impossible. So x differs from every x_n, and no sequence lists all of [0,1]. Since [0,1] is a subset of R, no sequence lists R, so R is uncountable.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:81845b66a64fd9e8baa9830788af1d24ccfa7255e76ef65a7c1032858629b23b","revision_digest":"sha256:5217c7a5ca26073bea088c4a23a842fa0dd29c9f47c16b42b319b5cc59055627","source_id":"wikipedia:Cantor's_diagonal_argument","source_revision":"as-read-2026-08-02","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Definition 5 of arXiv:2609.02785, 'Characterization of Stanley-Reisner varieties by their automorphism group'] A \emph{Demazure root} of $\Delta$ is a vector $\beta-\mathbf{e}_i\in\ZZ^n$ with
$\beta\in\ZZ^n_{\geq0}$, $\beta_i=0$ and $\supp(\beta)\in\mathcal{A}_i(\Delta)$; that is,
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{R}(\Delta)=\bigl\{\beta-\mathbf{e}_i \;:\; \beta\in\ZZ^n_{\geq0},\ \supp(\beta)\in\Delta,\ i\in\operatorname{cl}(\supp\beta)\setminus\supp\beta\bigr\},
\end{equation}
with $\supp(0)=\emptyset$, so $\beta=0$ contributes the $-\mathbf{e}_i$ with $i\in c(\Delta)$.
We write $\mathcal{R}_i(\Delta):=\{\alpha\in\mathcal{R}(\Delta):\alpha_i=-1\}$.

[Proposition prop:lindeberg of arXiv:2607.22480, 'Distinguishability threshold for random geometric graphs'] There exist absolute constants $C>c>0$, such that the following holds.

Let $\xi \in \mathbb{R}^m$ be a vector with independent subgaussian coordinates, each with expectation $0$ and variance proxy at most $\sigma^2$.  Also, fix a symmetric zero-diagonal $m\times m$ matrix $M$, and a vector $\boldsymbol{a}\in\mathbb{R}^m$. Let us define
\[\delta_1=\max\big\{\sigma^2\|M\|_{op}, \sigma\|\boldsymbol{a}\|_\infty\big\} \text{  and }\delta_2=\sigma^4\|M\|_{HS}^2+\sigma^2\|\boldsymbol{a}\|_2^2.\]
If $\delta_1\leq c$, then
\begin{align*}
\log\mathbb{E} e^{\xi^TM\xi+\boldsymbol{a}^T\xi}
=\frac{1}{2}\Var(\xi^TM\xi+\boldsymbol{a}^T\xi)+O(e^{C\delta_2} \delta_1\delta_2)
\end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition prop:lindeberg of arXiv:2607.22480

body:
[Definition 14 (Locally bounded function) of arXiv:2605.18198, 'Large deviations of crowding in finite $\beta$-ensembles'] A measurable function $f:\mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ is said to be a locally bounded function if for every compact set
	$K \subset \mathbb{R}^2$,
		\[
	\|f\|_{L^\infty(K)}
	:=
	\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{x\in K} |f(x)|
	< \infty .
	\]
	In other words, $f$ is essentially bounded on every compact subset
	of $\mathbb{R}^2$. The space of all locally bounded functions on $\R^2$ is denoted by $L^\infty_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^2)$.
title: Locally bounded function

body:
[Lemma lem:ricci-removal of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] Let $P_z$ be the rank-one projector onto a unit decomposable bivector and
$C_z=P_z-N^{-1}I_W$.  If $L_z=-2z_{\rm mat}^2$ is the orthogonal
projector onto the plane of $z$, put
\[
 B_z=\frac{L_z-(2/n)I_H}{n-2}.
\tag{2.6.2}
\]
Then the orthogonal curvature decomposition is
\[
 C_z=W_z+X_{B_z},\qquad W_z\in\mathcal W,
 \qquad X_B(u\wedge v)=Bu\wedge v+u\wedge Bv,
\tag{2.6.3}
\]
with no scalar or $\Lambda^4H$ summand, and
\[
 \|B_z\|_\mathrm{op}=\frac1n,\qquad
 \|B_z\|_F^2=\frac{2}{n(n-2)},\qquad
 \|X_B\|_2^2=(n-2)\|B\|_F^2,\qquad
 \|X_B\|_\mathrm{op}\le2\|B\|_\mathrm{op}.
\tag{2.6.4}
\]

In the cumulative moving frame the transported $B_z$ are reverse
martingale differences.  If $\mathfrak B_r$ is their sum, then
\[
 \mathbb E\|\mathfrak B_r\|_F^2=\frac{2r}{n(n-2)},\qquad
 \mathbb E\|\mathfrak B_r\|_F^4
 \le C\frac{r^2}{n^2(n-2)^2},
\tag{2.6.5}
\]
and, for fixed $c$, uniformly over $r\le cN$,
\[
 \max_{r\le cN}\|\mathfrak B_r\|_\mathrm{op}=o_{\mathbb P}(1).
\tag{2.6.6}
\]
More quantitatively, for every fixed $L$ and $1\le p\le L\log n$,
\[
 \left(\mathbb E\max_{r\le cN}\|\mathfrak B_r\|_\mathrm{op}^p\right)^{1/p}
 \le C_{c,L}\left(
 \sqrt{\frac{p+\log n}{n}}+\frac{p+\log n}{n}
 \right)=o(1).
\tag{2.6.6a}
\]
The same martingale satisfies the dimension-free Frobenius estimate
\[
 \left(\mathbb E\max_{r\le cN}\|\mathfrak B_r\|_F^p\right)^{1/p}
 \le C_c\sqrt p,
 \qquad 2\le p\le L\log n.
\tag{2.6.6b}
\]

Finally let $A_i=\operatorname{ad}_{a_i}$.  For traceless symmetric $B$
on $H$ and arbitrary $Z\in\operatorname{End}(W)$, define
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \mathcal R_i(B,Z)&=\{X_B,[A_i,Z]\}a_i,&
 U_i(B,Z)&=\{X_B,Z\}a_i,\\
 E_i(B,Z)&=\{X_{[a_i,B]},Z\}a_i,&
 \bar E(B,Z)&=N^{-1}\sum_iE_i(B,Z).
\end{aligned}
\tag{2.6.7}
\]
Put $\Psi(T)=\sum_jA_jTa_j$ and
$H_B(Z)=-N^{-1}X_B\Psi(Z)$.  Then the exact two-gradient decomposition is
\[
 \boxed{\mathcal R_i=A_iU_i-(E_i-\bar E)
 -\frac1N\sum_jA_jV_j-H_B(Z)},
 \qquad
 \bar E=\frac1N\sum_jA_jV_j+H_B(Z),\qquad V_j=X_BZa_j,
\tag{2.6.8}
\]
and its star-normalized square functions obey
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \frac1N\sum_i\|U_i\|^2
 &\le\frac{4(n-2)}N\|B\|_F^2\|Z\|_\mathrm{op}^2,\\
 \frac1N\sum_j\|V_j\|^2
 &\le\frac{n-2}N\|B\|_F^2\|Z\|_\mathrm{op}^2,\\
 \frac1N\sum_i\|E_i-\bar E\|^2
 &\le\frac{64}{n-1}\|B\|_F^2\|Z\|_\mathrm{op}^2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2.6.9}
\]
The residue obeys
\[
 \|H_B(Z)\|
 \le\frac{2\sqrt{n-2}}N\|B\|_\mathrm{op}\|Z\|_2.
\tag{2.6.9a}
\]

body:
[Lem 21 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $\tilde{F}$ be the function from the statement of Lemma~\ref{l:fp-F-kirszbraun}. We then have
    \[\Big|F^{\ri}(\bG,\bXi,\hat{\by}(\bG,\bXi)) - \E [\tilde{F}(\bXi;\bG) | \bG]
    \Big| \le
    \frac{\epsilon'}{15}\]
with probability at least $1-e^{-cN}$.

\begin{proof}
    By Lemma~\ref{l:fp-gc} and
    \eqref{e:wishart.bound.repeated}, it holds with probability at least $1-e^{-cN}$ that $\bG$ satisifes \eqref{e:fp-F-kirszbraun-bG-event}, $\bXi$ satisfies \eqref{e:fp-F-kirszbraun-bXi-event}, and $\hat{\by} = \ytrunc$.
    On this event, $F^{\ri}(\bG,\bXi,\hat{\by}(\bG,\bXi)) = \tilde{F}(\bXi;\bG)$. It follows by gaussian concentration of measure (Lemma~\ref{l:lip.subgaus}) that
        \[\Big|\tilde{F}(\bXi;\bG) - \E [\tilde{F}(\bXi;\bG)
    \,|\,\bG] \Big| \le \frac{\epsilon'}{15}\]
with probability at least $1-e^{-cN}$, so the claim follows.
\end{proof}

body: [Lemma lem:rn_bound of arXiv:2411.13133, 'Connectivity of the adjacency graph of\\ complementary components of the $\SLE$ Fan'] Fix $\delta_2 > \delta_1 > 0$ and $\epsilon \in (0,\delta_1^2/2)$. Suppose that $\eta$ is an ${\rm SLE}_\kappa(\rho_1; \rho_2)$ process in $\mathbf{H}$ from $0$ to $\infty$ with force points located at $x_1 = -\delta \in (-\delta_2, -\delta_1)$ and $x_2= 0^+$.  Let $R_\epsilon$, $\sigma_{\epsilon}$ be as in Section~(subsec:single_force_point of the paper).  Then the law of $\eta|_{[0,\sigma_{\epsilon}]}$ is absolutely continuous with respect to that of an ${\rm SLE}_\kappa(\rho_2)$ process stopped at the corresponding time with Radon-Nikodym derivative which is at most $C$.

Own work method record, proof (unaudited), W719-T295-C016 v1; no specialist novelty asserted. Given a conditional Gaussian vector X with predictable mean mu and PSD covariance Sigma, predictable real vectors g,w, v_i=Sigma_ii and ell_i=3mu_i^2+3v_i-g_i^2, S=sum_i w_i(X_i^3-g_i^2 X_i) has conditional mean sum_i w_i[mu_i^3+(3v_i-g_i^2)mu_i] and variance (w*ell)^T Sigma(w*ell)+18(w*mu)^T Sigma^{circ 2}(w*mu)+6w^T Sigma^{circ 3}w. Here * and circ denote entrywise product and power. If Sigma<=sigma^2 I, the variance is at most sigma^2||w*ell||^2+18sigma^4||w*mu||^2+6sigma^6||w||^2. For the C015 phase-retrieval forward law, w=g/m gives centered signal-gradient innovations D_t with conditional mean zero in the post-backward-query filtration. Stop before any predictable budget sigma_t<=s, sum g_i^2/m<=G0, sum g_i^2 mu_(t,i)^2/m<=G1 or sum g_i^2 ell_(t,i)^2/m<=G2 fails. Then N_n=-eta sum_(t<n)1_(t<tau)D_t satisfies P(max_(n<=T)|N_n|>=u)<=T eta^2(s^2G2+18s^4G1+6s^6G0)/(m u^2). With s=K eta, eta=c/log d<=1, m=ceil(alpha*d), T<=C log^2 d and fixed budget constants, max|N_n|=O(1/sqrt(d log d)) with probability at least 1-1/log d. This is stopped unamplified fresh-noise control only; actual-path budgets and positive drift remain unproved. Proof: expand the centered coordinate polynomial as ell_i Z_i+3mu_i(Z_i^2-Sigma_ii)+(Z_i^3-3Sigma_ii Z_i). Gaussian mgf differentiation makes the three degrees orthogonal with covariances Sigma_ij, 2Sigma_ij^2 and 6Sigma_ij^3. Schur-product positivity bounds the entrywise covariance powers. Predictable stopping and conditional mean zero give orthogonal martingale increments; the squared-martingale maximal inequality yields the cumulative bound. No product of conditional characteristic functions or iid stopped Gaussian list is used. No actual-path budget survival, memory-dependent positive drift, amplified-noise bound, overlap growth or convergence follows from this conditional record.

body:
[Proposition 66 (exact verification of the coefficient record) of arXiv:2609.03593, '\textbf{New Homogeneous Einstein Metrics from Detection}'] Let $R_i(x)$, $i=1,\ldots,4$, denote respectively the coefficient rows
obtained directly from
\[
 [h^2]F_3,\qquad [h^2]F_4,\qquad [h^3]F_1,\qquad [h^3]F_2
\]
after substituting \eqref{eq:H4bal-k1}--\eqref{eq:H4bal-critical-relations}
and reducing in the quotient ring $\mathbb Q[x]/(P)$.  Let
$\widetilde R_i$ be the four rows of the displayed augmented system
$(\mathcal M\mid b)$.  Then
\[
 \widetilde R_i=\gamma_i(x)R_i\qquad\text{in }\mathbb Q[x]/(P),
\]
where
\[
\begin{aligned}
\gamma_1&=4(119164x^3-133361x^2+52500x-8937),\\
\gamma_2&=\frac{3492x^3-3743x^2+1420x-231}{8},\\
\gamma_3&=\frac{972x^3-961x^2+356x-57}{32},\\
\gamma_4&=\frac{1197228x^3-1337669x^2+524324x-89373}{2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
None of these multipliers vanishes at a root of $P$: the resultants of
$P$ with their numerators are respectively
\[
\begin{gathered}
485699642990788608,\qquad
70962905088,\qquad
1019215872,\qquad
728549464486182912,
\end{gathered}
\]
all nonzero.  Hence the appendix system is exactly equivalent to the
coefficient system obtained from the Ricci equations at the critical root.

Moreover direct determinant expansion gives
\[
 \det\mathcal M+\frac{C_*B_*}{256}\equiv0\pmod P,
 \qquad
 \det\mathcal M_\rho-2C_*A_*\equiv0\pmod P.
\]
Thus the Cramer formula \eqref{eq:H4bal-r2} follows from the displayed
coefficient record alone.

body:
[Definition 1 ($p$-variation) of arXiv:2506.09637, 'Nonlinear Stochastic Filtering with Volterra Gaussian Noises'] Let \(p\ge 1\). For a two-parameter map
    \(h:\Delta_{[a,b]}\to \mathcal V \), we set
    \[
        \|h\|_{p-var;[a,b]}
        :=
            \sup_{\mathcal P }\left(\sum_{i}\|h_{s_i,s_{i+1}}\|^p_{\mathcal V}
            \right)^{1/p},
    \]
    where the supremum is taken over all finite partitions $\mathcal P = \{s_i\}$ of $[a,b]$.
 We then
    write
    \[
        \mathcal{C}^p(\Delta_{[a,b]},\mathcal V)
        :=
        \left\{
            h:\Delta_{[a,b]}\to \mathcal V:
            \|h\|_{p\text{-var};[a,b]}<\infty
        \right\}.
    \]
    
Finally, for a path \(g:[a,b]\to \mathcal V\), we say that
\(g\in \mathcal{C}^p([a,b],\mathcal V)\) whenever its increment map
\[
    g_{s,t}:=g_t-g_s
\]
belongs to \(\mathcal{C}^p(\Delta_{[a,b]},\mathcal V)\). In this case we set
\(
    \|g\|_{p\text{-var};[a,b]}
    :=
    \|g_{\cdot,\cdot}\|_{p\text{-var};[a,b]} .
\)
title: $p$-variation

[Appendixtheorem 1 (Finite-noise planar branch junctions) of arXiv:2608.22334, 'Recovering Weighted Tangent Geometry from a Single-Scale Score Field'] Let $D=2$, $d=1$, and $0<\beta\leq1$.  Suppose that, near $x_0$, the measure is
a finite sum of half-branches $\gamma_j:[0,r_0]\to\R^2$ with densities
$\rho_j$ relative to arc length, plus a finite remainder supported a positive
distance from $x_0$.  Assume
\begin{equation}
 \gamma_j(0)=x_0,\quad \gamma_j'(0)=v_j,\quad \|v_j\|=1,
 \quad \|\gamma_j'(r)-v_j\|\leq L_\gamma r^\beta,
 \quad |\rho_j(r)-\rho_j(0)|\leq L_\rho r^\beta,
 
\end{equation}
where the $v_j$ are distinct and $\rho_j(0)>0$.  Then, for every compact
$Q\subset\R^2$ in the normalized coordinate $z=(x-x_0)/\sigma$, there are
$C_Q<\infty$ and $\sigma_0>0$ such that
\begin{equation}
 \sup_{z\in Q}\|\sigma s_\sigma(x_0+\sigma z)-F_\Lambda(z)\|
 \leq C_Q\sigma^\beta,
 \qquad 0<\sigma\leq\sigma_0,
 
\end{equation}
with $\Lambda=\sum_j\rho_j(0)\delta_{v_j}$.  In particular, $C^2$ branches
with $C^1$ positive densities give an $O(\sigma)$ bias. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Finite-noise planar branch junctions

\[

    -(1-\eta\lambda_j-y_{j,+})y_{j,-}^{k}}
    {y_{j,+}-y_{j,-}}\,\theta_j^* .
\]

[Corollary 22 (Target cover and target blanket criterion) of arXiv:2606.07931, 'Pointwise Complexity for Gaussian Fields:\\Upper Envelopes, Algorithmic Lower Bounds, and '] Assume that for some \(t>0\), \(H\subseteq V\), and \(\theta\in(0,1/\sqrt2)\),
\[
\sup_{x\in H}A_H(x;\delta/2)\le \theta\sqrt t.
\]
Then, under the law of the walk, with probability at least \(1-\delta\),
\[
(1-\sqrt2\,\theta)t
\le L_{\tau(t)}(x)
\le \Bigl(1+\sqrt2\,\theta+\frac12\theta^2\Bigr)t
\qquad \forall x\in H.
\]
In particular, \(\tau_H\le\tau(t)\) on this event, and
\[
\max_{u,v\in H}\frac{L_{\tau(t)}(u)}{L_{\tau(t)}(v)}
\le
\frac{1+\sqrt2\,\theta+\theta^2/2}{1-\sqrt2\,\theta}.
\]

body:
[Definition 20 (Frankenstein process on paths) of arXiv:2605.02499, '2605.02499'] Let $\bs w \in \{\ddownarrow,\uuparrow\}^\Nb$ and let $\sP^-$ be as in
Def.~\ref{def.quasiAIG}. Let $(T_k)_{k \geq 1}$
denote the times of interactive neutral events in the quasi-AIG, ordered increasingly. Let
$\gs_0\subseteq[N]$ and fix $S=R_{\gs_0}$. The \emph{Frankenstein process on the path $\bs w$}, denoted by
$\bigl(\overline{\Phi}_t(R_{\gs_0},\bs w, \sP^-)\bigr)_{t \geq 0}$, takes values in $\varSigma^R$, starts at
$\overline{\Phi}_0(R_{\gs_0},\bs w, \sP^-) = R_{\gs_0}$, and evolves as follows. Suppose that at some time the process is in state $C\in\Sigma^R$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item At the times of a coalescence or a relocation event $\coal{\alpha}{\beta}$, the process performs the transition $$C\mapsto\ocoal{\alpha}{\beta}(C).$$

\item At the times of a deleterious mutation $\timesa$, the process performs the transition $$C\mapsto\omutr{\alpha}(C).$$

\item At the times of a beneficial mutation $\circa$, the process performs the transition $$C\mapsto\omutb{\alpha}(C)=\varnothing.$$

\item At the times of an FTW event $\ftw{\alpha}{\Bs}$, the process performs the transition 
\begin{equation*}
C\mapsto \overline{C}, 
\end{equation*} 
where $\overline C$ is the single cylinder contained in $\oftw{\alpha}{\Bs}(C)$.

\item At the time $T_k$ of the $k$th interactive neutral event, the process performs the transition
$$C\mapsto \widehat{C}^{w_k},$$
\end{enumerate}
where $\widehat{C}^{w_k}$ is as in Prop.~\ref{prop_frankenstein_matching}.
title: Frankenstein process on paths

body:
[Definition Ideal gap of arXiv:2604.17170, 'CaTherine wheels from trees and Liouville quantum gravity'] A sequence of proper lines $\eta_i$ in $Z$ which are the convex hulls of 
$\lbrace e_i^L,e_i^R\rbrace$ for a sequence of nested intervals 
$[e_i^L,e_i^R]$ in $\mathcal E$ is said to be {\em end nested}.

A point $p\in Z$ together with an end nested sequence $\eta_i$ as above for which
$\bigcap_i [e_i^L,e_i^R]$ is empty and for which $p \in \bigcap_i \eta_i$ is
called an {\em ideal gap}. We define an equivalence relation on ideal
gaps as follows. Let $S$ and $S'$ be a pair of sequences of nested intervals
in $\mathcal E$ with empty intersection. We say $S$ refines $S'$ if $S'$ is a subsequence
of $S$. The relation of refinement is not an equivalence relation,
but it generates an equivalence relation on sequences of nested intervals
in $\mathcal E$ with empty intersection by
$S {\originalsim} S'$ if there is a finite sequence $S=S_0,S_1,\cdots,S_n=S'$ 
so that for each $i$ either $S_i$ refines $S_{i+1}$ or $S_{i+1}$ refines $S_i$.
Say that two ideal gaps are equivalent if their associated
sequences of nested intervals are related by this equivalence relation.

A point $p$ as above is said to lie in the {\em support} of the 
equivalence class of the given ideal gap.
title: Ideal gap

[Proposition prop_transitive_and_trichotomy of arXiv:2604.04672, 'Connected components and topological ends of stationary planar forests'] The relation $\cdot\in(\cdot,\cdot)_\Gamma$ is \emph{transitive}, that is, for all distinct $\gamma,\sigma',\sigma',\sigma''\in\Gamma$,
        \[\gamma\in(\sigma,\sigma')_\Gamma\setminus(\sigma,\sigma'')_\Gamma\implies\gamma\in (\sigma',\sigma'')_\Gamma.\]
    Furthermore, for all distinct $\sigma,\sigma',\sigma''\in\Gamma$, exactly one of the assertions $\sigma\in(\sigma',\sigma'')_\Gamma$, $\sigma'\in(\sigma,\sigma'')_\Gamma$ and $\sigma''\in(\sigma,\sigma')_\Gamma$ holds.

[Lem 17 of arXiv:2608.20552, 'One-point fluctuations for exponential last passage percolation under upper-tail condition'] Let $(x,y)\in\overline{U}_2^<$ with $y< x$. The roots of $\tpt$ are
\beq
	(\tzt^-,\tzt^+)
	=\left(\frac{\bc y}{\mv\pp},\pp\right), 
\eeq
and $\tzt^-=\tzt^+$ if and only if $(x,y)$ lies on the boundary between $U_2^<$ and $U_3^<$.
When $\mv\ne\lv$, the roots of $\tpr$ are
\beqq
	(\tzra,\tzrb)
	=\left(\pp,\frac{\bc(y-1)}{(\mv-\lv)\pp}\right).
\eeqq
The roots are ordered as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item If $\mv>\lv$, then
\beqq
	-1<\tzo^-<\tzt^-\le\tzt^+=\tzo^+=\tzra=\pp\le\tzrb,
\eeqq
where
\beqq
	\text{$\tzrb\in [\pp, 0)$ for $y>1$;}
	\qquad
	\text{$\tzrb=0$ for $y=1$;}
	\qquad
	\text{$\tzrb>0$ for $y<1$,}
\eeqq
and $\tzrb=\pp$ if and only if $(x,y)$ lies on the boundary between $U_1$ and $U_2^<$.

\item 
If $\mv<\lv$, then
\beqq
	\tzrb<\tzo^-<\tzt^-\le\tzt^+=\tzo^+=\tzra=\pp<0,
\eeqq
where
\beqq
	\text{$\tzrb<-1$ for $x>1$;}
	\qquad
	\text{$\tzrb=-1$ for $x=1$;}
	\qquad
	\text{$\tzrb\in (-1, \tzo^-)$ for $x<1$.}
\eeqq
\end{itemize}

body:
Let a finite nonempty deterministic path family visit exactly one site in each of finitely many layers t. In layer t there are m_t independent N(0,sigma_t^2) weights, and all layers are independent. For deterministic positive a_p and finite beta, put F=log(sum_p a_p exp(beta sum_t omega(t,p_t))). If A_t is the layer mean and R(t,x)=omega(t,x)-A_t, then Var(F)=beta^2 sum_t sigma_t^2/m_t+Var(F(R)). For M=max_p sum_t omega(t,p_t), Var(M)=sum_t sigma_t^2/m_t+Var(M(R)). In the unrestricted n-vertex up/right model with unit Gaussian weights, this gives Var(M_n)>=H_n; in any n-layer width-W family it gives Var(M)>=n/W.
Finite nonempty deterministic path family
One selected site per layer
Independent centered Gaussian weights with common variance within each layer
Deterministic positive coefficients for F
Finite beta for F

[Proposition prop:DL_all_coal of arXiv:2505.09604, 'Exceptional force, uncountably many solutions in the KPZ fixed point'] [Busa-Sepp-Sore-22a]
On a single event of full probability, the following hold across all directions $\xi \in \mathbb{R}$ and signs ${\scaleobj{0.9}{\boxempty}} \in \{-,+\}$. Let $K$ be a compact set. Then, there exists $S < \inf\{t:(x,t) \in K\}$ such that, for any $\xi {\scaleobj{0.8}{\boxempty}}$ geodesics $g_1$ and $g_2$ rooted at points in $K$, we have $g_1(s) = g_2(s)$ for all $s \le S$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: In the classical theory of Ambrosio-Gigli-Savaré, metric gradient flows require a rigorous characterization of absolutely continuous curves and metric derivatives. By establishing that every curve in $AC^p(\mathbb{FP}_p)$ can be represented as an adapted flow on a single probability space, Acciaio, Krsek, Pammer, and Rodrigues provide the foundational prerequisite for defining subdifferentials and gradient flows in the space of filtered processes.
title: Foundations for Gradient Flows in Adapted Wasserstein Spaces

[Corollary 38 (The boundary memory equation) of arXiv:2609.01826, 'An extension theory for fully fractional Schr\"odinger equations with memory'] Under the hypotheses of Proposition~\ref{P:boundary-Duhamel}, the boundary
trace $u$ of the mild solution of the memory problem satisfies, for $0<t\le T$,
the Volterra integral equation
\begin{equation}
u(x,t)
=
\mathbb T_a^\star(\mathcal P_su_0)(x,0,t)
\;+\;
\frac{\mu}{\G(s)}
\int_0^t
\frac{1}{\sigma^{1-s}}\,
S(\sigma)\bigl(|u(\cdot,t-\sigma)|^{p-1}u(\cdot,t-\sigma)\bigr)(x)\,d\sigma ,
\end{equation}
the identity holding in $L^q_t(I;L^r_x(\Rd))$ in the sense described in
Proposition~\ref{P:boundary-Duhamel}.

[Lemma 8 of arXiv:2609.00254, 'On the geometry and cohomology of almost abelian solvmanifolds'] Let $U\subseteq M$ be an open set and let $\rho=\exp(B+\mathbf i\omega) \wedge \Omega$ be a
    non-degenerate pure spinor on $U$ where $B,\omega \in C^\infty(U,\bigwedge^2 T^*_M)$ and
    $\Omega = \theta_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge \theta_k$. Assume that 
    $\theta_1,\dots,\theta_k\in C^\infty(U,T^*_M\otimes\mathbb C)$ are pointwise linearly independent. Write $\beta:=B+\mathbf i\omega$.
    Then the almost generalized complex structure determined by $\rho$
    (Lemma \ref{lem:spinor-determines-J}) is integrable on $U$ if and only if there exists a section
    $X+\xi \in C^\infty(U,(T_M \oplus T_M^*)\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb{C})$ such that
    \begin{itemize}
        \item[(a)] $\iota_X\Omega = 0$,
        \item[(b)] $\d\Omega = \alpha\wedge\Omega$, where $\alpha:=\xi + \iota_X \beta$,
        \item[(c)] $\d\beta \wedge \Omega = 0$.
    \end{itemize}

body:
[Definition def2.10 of arXiv:2411.13266, '\bf A new maximal regularity for parabolic equations and an application'] Let $p\in [1,+\infty]$ and $\alpha\in [0,1)$, we denote by
 $L^p(\mathbb{R};{\mathcal C}_{l,d}^{\alpha,\rho}({\mathbb R}^n))$ (locally bounded Lebesgue--H\"{o}lder--Dini space)   the set  consisting of all Borel measurable functions $h\in L^p(\mathbb{R};{\mathcal C}({\mathbb R}^n))$ satisfying
 $|h(t,x)-h(t,y)| \leqslant f(t)|x-y|^\alpha\rho(|x-y|)$  for every $x,y\in {\mathbb R}^n$ with $|x-y|\leqslant 1$ and some integrable function $f\in L^p(\mathbb{R})$\,.
Moreover, we denote by $L^p(\mathbb{R};{\mathcal C}_{l,\varsigma}^{\alpha,\rho}({\mathbb R}^n))$ ($\varsigma\in \{s,c,w\})$~(locally bounded Lebesgue--H\"{o}lder spaces)  the set consisting all elements  belong to $L^p(\mathbb{R})$ as ${\mathcal C}_{l,\varsigma}^{\alpha,\rho}({\mathbb R}^n)$-valued functions.

\smallskip
Further,  we say  $h\in L^p(\mathbb{R};{\mathcal C}_{l,\varsigma}^{k+\alpha,\rho}({\mathbb R}^n))$ ($\varsigma\in \{d,s,c,w\}$ and $0<k\in \mathbb{N}$) if
$h\in L^p(\mathbb{R};{\mathcal C}({\mathbb R}^n))$ and for $1\leqslant j\leqslant k, \ 1\leqslant i_1,_{\cdots},i_j\leqslant n$, $\partial^j_{x_{i_1},\cdots,x_{i_j}}h\in L^p(\mathbb{R};{\mathcal C}_b({\mathbb R}^n))$ (the subscript $b$ means the functions are bounded), and for $1\leqslant i_1,_{\cdots},i_k\leqslant n$, $[\partial^k_{x_{i_1},\cdots,x_{i_k}}h(t,\cdot)]_{\alpha,\rho}\in L^p(\mathbb{R})$.  For $h\in L^p(\mathbb{R};{\mathcal C}_{l,\varsigma}^{k+\alpha,\rho}({\mathbb R}^n))$ ($\varsigma\in \{d,s,c,w\}$), we define the norm by
\begin{eqnarray}
\|h\|_{L^p(\mathbb{R};{\mathcal C}_{l,\varsigma}^{k+\alpha,\rho}({\mathbb R}^n))}&=&\Bigg[\int\limits_{\mathbb{R}}\Big(\|(1+|\cdot|)^{-1}h(t,\cdot)\|_0
+\sum_{j=1}^k\|\nabla^jh(t,\cdot)\|_0+[\nabla^k h(t,\cdot)]_{\alpha,\rho}\Big)^pdt\Bigg]^{\frac{1}{p}}\nonumber \\ &=&: \Bigg[\int\limits_{\mathbb{R}}\Big(\|h(t,\cdot)\|_{l,k,0}+[\nabla^k h(t,\cdot)]_{\alpha,\rho}\Big)^pdt\Bigg]^{\frac{1}{p}}
\nonumber \\
&=&:\Bigg[\int\limits_{\mathbb{R}}\|h(t,\cdot)\|_{l,k+\alpha,\rho}^pdt\Bigg]^{\frac{1}{p}},
\end{eqnarray}
where  the integrals in ((2.13 of the paper)) are interpreted as the essential supermum when $p=+\infty$.
Then $L^p(\mathbb{R};{\mathcal C}_{l,\varsigma}^{k+\alpha,\rho}({\mathbb R}^n))$ are Banach spaces  under the norm ((2.13 of the paper)). Similarly, if $h$ is bounded as well, we define the norm for $h\in L^p(\mathbb{R};{\mathcal C}_{b,\varsigma}^{k+\alpha,\rho}({\mathbb R}^n))$ ($\varsigma\in \{d,s,c,w\}$) by
\begin{eqnarray*}
\|h\|_{L^p(\mathbb{R};{\mathcal C}_{b,\varsigma}^{k+\alpha,\rho}({\mathbb R}^n))}&=&\Bigg[\int\limits_{\mathbb{R}}\Big(\sum_{j=0}^k\|\nabla ^jh(t,\cdot)\|_0+[\nabla^k h(t,\cdot)]_{\alpha,\rho}\Big)^pdt\Bigg]^{\frac{1}{p}}\nonumber \\  &=&: \Bigg[\int\limits_{\mathbb{R}}\Big(\|h(t,\cdot)\|_{b,k,0}+[\nabla^k h(t,\cdot)]_{\alpha,\rho}\Big)^pdt\Bigg]^{\frac{1}{p}}=:
\Bigg[\int\limits_{\mathbb{R}}\|h(t,\cdot)\|_{b,k+\alpha,\rho}^pdt\Bigg]^{\frac{1}{p}}.
\end{eqnarray*}
Moreover, for every open or closed domain $D\subset\mathbb{R}$, we define spaces $L^p(D;{\mathcal C}_{\vartheta,\varsigma}^{k+\alpha,\rho}({\mathbb R}^n))$ and $W^{1,p}(D;{\mathcal C}_{\vartheta,\varsigma}^{k+\alpha,\rho}({\mathbb R}^n))$ ($\vartheta\in \{l,b\}, \, \varsigma\in \{d,s,c,w\}$) in a similar way.

There exist universal C0,D0,K0,R0>0 such that for every real p>0, integers w>=ceil(exp(C0*(p+2))), m>=w with no upper bound, d>=D0*w, and each deterministic ||x||=sqrt(d), the independent Gaussian zero-bias ReLU network f(x)=a^T*rho(B*rho(A*x)), A_ij~N(0,1/d), B_ij~N(0,1/w), a_i~N(0,1/m), has the following property. Put xi=A*x, h=rho(xi), n=#{xi_i>0}, S=K0*sqrt((p+2)*log(w)), s=S*sqrt(w)*||h||/n for n>0 (else zero), tau=sign(f(x)), and x_s=x-tau*s*grad f(x). With probability at least 1-w^(-p), tau*f(x_s)<0 and ||x_s-x||<=R0*sqrt((p+2)*log(w)). Zero initial output is counted as failure. Constants are independent of p,w,m,d,x; the displayed step and threshold give all p-dependence. The input quantifier is pointwise, not simultaneous. Novelty is not established.

[Lemma 9 of arXiv:2608.30554, 'Strong law of large numbers for generalized operator means II'] Let $f$ be an operator monotone function on $(0, \infty)$ such that $f(1) = 0$ and $f'(1) = 1$.
 Let $Y_1, Y_2, \hdots$  be a sequence of i.i.d. random variables with probability law $\mu$ on $\mathbb{P}$ such that
     $$ \int_\mathbb{P} \|f(y)\|\log^{+}\|f(y)\| \: d\mu(y) < \infty.$$ 
     For any initial $S_1\in\mathbb{P}$, the stochastic resolvent iteration $$S_{n+1}=J_{1 \over n+1}(Y_{n+1},S_n) \qquad n \geq 1$$ is almost surely bounded.
title: Lemma 9 of arXiv:2608.30554

$$
\lim_{\delta\rightarrow 0^+} Z_\upsilon(\Sigma,G) \mathbb{P}_{\operatorname{YM}}^{{\rm free}}\left(\Phi|\mathbf{Hol}_0\in B_\delta(\operatorname{Id}_G)\right)
$$
exists and is equal to
$$
\int_{\Omega\times G^{2g}}\Phi d\mathbb{M}_{\operatorname{YM},r}:=\int_G \mathbb{P} _{\operatorname{YM}}^{{\rm free}}\left(\Phi|\operatorname{\mathbf{Hol}}_r=\mathrm{g}\right)p_{\mathbf{Hol},r}(\mathrm{g})p_{\upsilon(\Sigma)-\mathscr{A}_{r}(1)}(\mathrm{g})\mu_G(d\mathrm{g}),
$$
where $p_t$ is the heat kernel on $G$, $p_{\mathbf{Hol},r}$ is defined in Lemma~(lemm:lawHolcombi of the paper) and $\mathscr{A}_{r}(1)=\int_\Sigma[\blacktriangle(\gamma_r)]\upsilon.$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition 8 of arXiv:2511.09517, 'From Cannings model to Brownian motion conditioned on local time profile'] \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), ref=\roman*]
    \item For any continuous profile \(\ell\) with \(h(\ell)<\infty\), the local time profile of \(W^\ell\) is \(\ell\); that is, a.s. for every non-negative measurable \(f\) on \(\mathbb{R}_+\),
\begin{align}
    \int_{0}^{I(\ell)} f\big(W^\ell_t\big)\,\mathrm{d}t \ = \ \int_{0}^{\infty} \ell(s)\,f(s)\,\mathrm{d}s.
\end{align}
In particular, the total time duration of $W^\ell$ is $I(\ell)$.
\item The process $W^\ell$ is a bridge from $0$ to $0$ on the time interval $[0,I(\ell)]$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 15 of arXiv:2609.03750, '\bf Pullback Measure Attractors, Zero-Noise Limits, and Moderate Deviations for 2D Stochas'] Suppose Hypotheses \ref{PEeqAssum-2.2}, \ref{PEeqAssum-2.3}, \ref{PEeqAssum-2.4} and \eqref{PETNs-3.01} hold. For $\tau\in\mathbb R$, set
	\[
	\mathscr M_0(\tau)
	=\mathcal R_1\left(
	1+\int_{-\infty}^{\tau}e^{-\kappa(\tau-s)}|g(s)|^4\,ds
	\right),
	\]
	and
	\[
	\mathscr M_z(\tau)
	=\mathcal R_3\left(
	1+\int_{-\infty}^{\tau}e^{-\kappa(\tau-s)}
	|\partial_zg(s)|^4\,ds
	\right).
	\]
	Define
	\[
	\mathscr K(\tau)
	=
	\left\{
	\mu\in\mathcal P_{4,z}(H):
	\int_H|\zeta|^4\,\mu(d\zeta)\le\mathscr M_0(\tau),\
	\int_H|\partial_z\zeta|^4\,\mu(d\zeta)\le\mathscr M_z(\tau)
	\right\}.
	\]
	Then $\mathscr K=\{\mathscr K(\tau):\tau\in\mathbb R\}$ belongs to $\mathfrak D$ and is a closed $\mathfrak D$-pullback absorbing family for $S_\epsilon$, uniformly for $\epsilon\in(0,\epsilon_0)$.

DRAFT; author proof, independent mathematical review pending. For n>=81 put t=floor(sqrt(n)), a=t, b=2t+1, m=floor(n/2) and form the Jordan domain D_n from [0,a/n]x[0,1], [b/n,1]x[0,1], and the corridor [a/n,b/n]x[(m-1/2)/n,(m+1/2)/n], taking the interior of their union. Normalize the disk Riemann map f_n by f_n(0)=(1/2,1/2), f_n'(0)>0. Its Jordan boundary extension satisfies |f_n^{-1}(0,1)-f_n^{-1}(0,0)|<=8/n. The boundary arc containing both corners lies behind a height-1/n gate at x=b/n. Brownian motion must hit this gate before exiting on that arc. The half-plane Poisson kernel bounds its harmonic measure by 1/[pi*n*(1/2-b/n)]<=4/(pi*n); the preimage arc has angular length <=8/n. Thus Euclidean corner convergence, even with unmarked kernel and boundary Hausdorff convergence, does not imply marked-prime-end convergence.

[Lemma lemma_annihilation of arXiv:2412.09532, 'Percolation on the stationary distributions of the voter model with stirring'] For any $A \subset \mathbb{Z}^d$ finite,~$\beta \in (0,1)$ and~$\mathsf v \ge 0$ we have

body:
[Proposition prop:component-energy-decomposition of arXiv:2608.22910, 'A Commutator Framework for Selective Spectral Alignment in Deep Neural Networks'] For
\[
\mathcal E_\ell^\nu:=\|T_\ell^\nu\|_F^2,
\qquad
\mathcal I_\ell^{\nu,\eta}
:=2\langle T_\ell^\nu,T_\ell^\eta\rangle_F,
\qquad
\nu,\eta\in
\{\mathrm{tr},\mathrm{imb},\mathrm{fluc},\mathrm{gate}\},
\]
one has
\begin{equation}
\|C_\ell^{\mathrm{int}}\|_F^2
=
\sum_\nu\mathcal E_\ell^\nu
+
\sum_{\nu<\eta}\mathcal I_\ell^{\nu,\eta}.
\end{equation}
If \(\sum_\nu\|T_\ell^\nu\|_F>0\), the aggregate cancellation ratio
\begin{equation}
\chi_\ell
:=
\frac{\|C_\ell^{\mathrm{int}}\|_F}
{\sum_\nu\|T_\ell^\nu\|_F}
\end{equation}
satisfies \(0\leq\chi_\ell\leq1\). Small \(\chi_\ell\) indicates strong
matrix-valued cancellation among the source components. If the denominator in
(equation eq:aggregate-cancellation-ratio of the paper) vanishes, then every component and
\(C_\ell^{\mathrm{int}}\) vanish, and \(\chi_\ell\) is left undefined.

[Proposition prop:X_T of arXiv:2411.12315, 'A pursuit problem for squared Bessel processes'] Let us denote by $\theta$ the first positive zero of the hypergeometric function $F_{\alpha,\beta}$: 
$$\theta = \inf\left\{s\geq0,\, F_{\alpha, \beta}(s)=0  \right\}.$$
Under $\mathbb{P}_{(0,y)}$ the stopping time $T$ is a.s. finite and the Mellin transform of $X_{T}$ is given by:
$$ \mathbb{E}_{(0,y)}\left[ X_{T}^{s} \right]= \frac{(2y)^s}{F_{\alpha,\beta}(s)  },\qquad s\in[0,\theta).$$
In particular, $\theta$ is equal to  $1$  when $\alpha=\beta$. Otherwise,  $\theta<1$ when $\alpha < \beta$, and  $\theta>1$ when $\alpha>\beta$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition prop:X_T of arXiv:2411.12315

body: [Lemma 30 of arXiv:2606.19115, 'Finite free perpetuities'] Let $(a_n)_{n \ge 1}$ be a sequence of complex numbers and let $c \in\C$ be such that $|c|<1$. Assume that the sequence $(a_n - ca_{n-1})_{n\ge 2}$ converges. Then, $(a_n)_{n\ge 1}$ converges.

[Corollary cor:recover-liu-wasserstein-poc of arXiv:2607.00149, '\bf Uniform-in-time Propagation-of-Chaos for\\ Stein Variational Gradient Descent'] Consider the affine Gaussian kernel (equation eq:affine-kernel of the paper) and the
standard Gaussian target on $\mathbb R^d$.  Assume that
\[
        \widetilde\mu_0=N(m_0,\Sigma_0),
        \qquad \Sigma_0>0,
\]
and let $Y_1(0),\ldots,Y_N(0)$ be i.i.d. with law $\widetilde\mu_0$.  Let
$\widetilde\mu_t$ denote the mean-field solution and let
\[
        \widetilde\mu_t^N:=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\delta_{Y_i(t)}
\]
be the empirical measure of the particle system.  Then there is a constant
$C=C(d,m_0,\Sigma_0)<\infty$ such that, for all $N$ sufficiently large,
\begin{equation}
        \mathbb E \left[\sup_{t\ge0}\, W_2^2(\widetilde\mu_t^N,\widetilde\mu_t)\right]
        \le
        C r_d(N),
\end{equation}
where
\[
        r_d(N):=
        \begin{cases}
        N^{-1}\log\log N, & d=1,\\
        N^{-1}(\log N)^2, & d=2,\\
        N^{-2/d}, & d\ge3.
        \end{cases}
\]
Moreover, for fixed \(k\ge1\), writing $\mathcal L(Y_1^N(t),\ldots,Y_k^N(t))$ for the joint law of $Y_1^N(t),\ldots,Y_k^N(t)$,
\begin{equation}
        \sup_{t\ge0}
        W_2^{(k)}\left(\mathcal L(Y_1^N(t),\ldots,Y_k^N(t)),\widetilde\mu_t^{\otimes k}\right)^2
        \le
        C'\left(k r_d(N)+\frac{k^2(k-1)}{N}\right),
\end{equation}
for some constant
$C'=C'(d,m_0,\Sigma_0)<\infty$.

[Corollary 13 (Finite-time Hopf torus trajectories) of arXiv:2609.00501, 'Uniqueness of Finite-Time Varifold Limits for the M\"obius-Invariant Willmore Flow'] Suppose that the MIWF starts from a smooth parametrization \(F_0\) of
a smooth Hopf torus in the sense of Pinkall \cite{Pinkall}, that
\(W(0)\leq8\pi\), and that
\(T=T_{\max}(F_0)<\infty\).  Then there exists a unique unrenormalized
limiting integral varifold \(\Var_T\).  Its support is an embedded
\(C^1\) Hopf torus, and the convergence is both weak varifold
convergence and Hausdorff convergence.  Moreover,
\eqref{eq:conformal-limit}--\eqref{eq:limit-measure} hold
for a uniformly conformal bi-Lipschitz parametrization of the limiting
Hopf torus.  In particular, among the alternatives of
Corollary~\ref{cor:four-way}, every such finite-time Hopf trajectory
lies in alternative \textup{(D)}.

[Thm 10 (Homogeneous coupling) of arXiv:2604.12853, 'Coupling Markov Chains \\with a Common Image Chain'] Consider time-homogeneous Markov chains  $\Xoriginal$, $\Yoriginal$, and $\Zoriginal$ with time indexed by  $t=0,1,2,\dots$, and countable state spaces $A$, $B$, and $C$ respectively. 
    Suppose for maps $f: A \to C$ and $g: B \to C$ that
    \[\bigl(f(\Xoriginal_t)\bigr)_{t \ge 0} \eqdist \Zoriginal \eqdist \bigl(g(\Yoriginal_t)\bigr)_{t \ge 0}\,.\]
    Then there exists a homogeneous Markov chain $(\Xcopy_t, \Ycopy_t)_{t\geq0}$ such that 
     \[(\Xcopy_t)_{t \ge 0} \eqdist \Xoriginal \;\text{ and } \; (\Ycopy_t)_{t \ge 0} \eqdist \Yoriginal\,,\]
     and
     $$f(X_t)=g(Y_t)\text{ for all }t\geq 0.$$
     Writing $\Zcopy_t =f(\Xcopy_t) = g(\Ycopy_t)$ (so that $\Zcopy \eqdist \Zoriginal$), the marginal processes
     $X$ and $Y$ may be taken to be conditionally independent given the process $Z$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Conservation, explicit coupling reduction, exact law comparison or spectral calculation Result: For a stabilizable stationary system, mass transport preserves the mean particle density: send one unit from every initial particle to its final sleeping site. Thus any local subsequential limit of the bounded occupation indicators has one-site mean zeta_c. This still does not imply almost-sure density. To see the precise gap, fill consecutive blocks of length m with iid Bernoulli(rho) values, constant within a block, and randomize the block origin uniformly. Each resulting process is stationary ergodic with density rho. As m tends to infinity its local law converges to the mixture rho*delta_all_ones+(1-rho)*delta_all_zeros, whose density is random. Check: A fixed window crosses a block boundary with probability at most its diameter/m. Away from a boundary it sees a single Bernoulli variable. Ergodicity of each finite-block process follows by iid block ergodicity and the cyclic action on the random phase. Obstruction: Need control of correlations or ergodic components that is uniform near criticality, together with uniqueness and independence from the initial law. Conservation of mean does not supply any of these.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-p0376-universal-critical-limit-obtained-by-sprinkling-subcritical-arw-states
No independent review
