{"artifact_digest":"sha256:e071b07d0c27b01893917b028901da962245565a5c940128c22652d92312e107","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/e0/e071b07d0c27b01893917b028901da962245565a5c940128c22652d92312e107.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:61f6c6565be7cce899cefc37a16589ec9041ee0c312ca24e3a354ad3a458d566","bundle_entry_key":"unrestricted-vc-frontier","bundle_id":"population.t379-unrestricted-vc-verifier-frontiers-20261020","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"statistical learning; calibrated generation; minimax decision theory","draft":"w709/bundle_002.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:learning.calibration:paired-vc-unrestricted-vc-frontier","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Exact all-generator frontier for an annotated paired VC version space

Candidate T379-C004 v1. Own-work draft; proof (unaudited).
Kind: narrowed, target 1, subject to review of whether this experiment qualifies.
This is an annotated-training, robust-calibration experiment. It does not
settle the ordinary factual-training problem. The hardest remaining piece
is the posterior coarsening bound after factual identities have been seen:
then the posterior mean factual distribution is no longer uniform.

## Experiment and decision criterion

Let d>=1, N>=2d+1, n>=0, K>=2 and 1<=r<K be integers. Set
beta=r/K, kappa=1-beta, and a=d/N. The universe is [N] x [K].
There are d disjoint pairs of contexts, each with exactly one arbitrary
(A) and one systematic (S) context. The other N-2d contexts are known S.
The class of 2^d pair orientations has VC dimension d: one representative
per pair is shattered, while there are only 2^d classifiers. Every S
context has all K candidates true; every A context has an independent
uniform random r-subset true. A world's factual law p chooses a context
uniformly, then a true candidate uniformly. A world specifies orientations
and true subsets, not just their distribution.

The training data D comprise n independent uniform context indices and
their exact A/S tags, and NO candidate identities. A consistent ERM
version space knows the orientation of every pair touched by D; the
remaining U pairs have both orientations possible. Write m=U/N and
w=(d-U)/N=a-m. Known A contexts have uniform-law mass w; contexts in
unknown pairs have mass 2m. There is always a nonempty fixed S reservoir.

Fix c in [0,1]. For every arbitrary probability law g on the whole
universe, form the Kalai--Vempala source output bins Pi(g), either exact
probability levels or any specified grouping of complete levels (including
every source finite-bin choice). Let p_Pi(y)=p(B)/|B| for y in B and
Mis(g,p)=TV(p_Pi,g), with TV half the l1 distance. Binning is a function of
g alone. Require Mis(g,p)<=c for EVERY world consistent with D. Minimize
the worst-world false-output mass H(g). There is no within-context or
within-block restriction on the competing generators.

The exact conditional value is

 V(c,U)=kappa max{a-c, (a+m-c)/2, 0}
       =kappa[(a-c)_+ + (m-|a-c|)_+/2].                 (1)

The same conditional value holds if both the calibration constraint and
the objective are posterior averages under uniform consistent orientations
and uniform independent true subsets. This latter statement concerns a
Bayes experiment, not a lower bound for every fixed world and generator.

## Lower bound, including bins that mix types or split contexts

Average over uniform consistent orientations and independent uniform
r-subsets. In EVERY context the posterior mean factual probability of
each candidate is lambda(y)=1/(NK): an A candidate has probability r/K
of being true and then receives 1/(Nr). For fixed g, Pi(g) is fixed.
Uniform coarsening is linear in p and leaves lambda fixed. Consequently

 E[p_Pi(y)|D]=lambda(y),
 TV(lambda,g)<=E[TV(p_Pi,g)|D].                       (2)

The inequality is the finite triangle inequality, coordinate by coordinate;
there is no pushforward-TV substitution and no assumption about bins being
pure. Robust feasibility therefore implies TV(lambda,g)<=c. The same is
true under average calibration. Randomized decisions are covered by first
conditioning on their random seed; if the budget is only averaged over
that seed as well, average the following linear inequalities over it.

Let q_A=g(known A) and q_M=g(unknown pair contexts). The posterior false
probability is kappa on known A, kappa/2 on unknown pairs, and zero on
known S. Thus E[H(g)|D]=kappa(q_A+q_M/2). For t=TV(lambda,g), the event
inequality q(E)>=lambda(E)-t gives

 q_A+q_M/2 = [q(A)+q(A union M)]/2 >= a-t,
 q_A+q_M/2 >= q(A union M)/2 >= (a+m-t)/2,
 q_A+q_M/2 >= 0.

Use t<=c. A worst-world H dominates its posterior average, proving (1)'s
lower bound for unrestricted g. For calibration averaged over random seed,
the same three affine inequalities give the same bound after averaging.

## Attainment in every compatible world

Start with lambda. Remove total mass t1=min(c,w) uniformly from known A
contexts. Remove total mass t2=min((c-w)_+,2m) uniformly from unknown pair
contexts. Interpret removal from an empty group as zero. Add t=t1+t2
uniformly to the fixed S reservoir; leave observed S contexts alone.
Within each context keep all K candidate probabilities equal. No
probability becomes negative and total mass is one.

Each output level, including zero, is a union of whole context fibres.
Every world has p(context)=1/N, so p_Pi=lambda for every grouping of these
levels. Hence Mis=t<=c, for every compatible world and every source bin
count, even if levels happen to merge. Since exactly half of the unknown
contexts are A, in every such world

 H=kappa[(w-t1)+(m-t2/2)].                            (3)

For c<=w, w<=c<=w+2m, and c>=w+2m this is respectively kappa(a-c),
kappa(a+m-c)/2, and zero. This proves (1) and the equivalent positive-part
formula, including U=0, c=0, and all zero-output cases.

Given the complete partition but still no true-subset identities, the
same posterior argument and removal from known A contexts give the exact
oracle value kappa(a-c)_+. Thus the excess is exactly the second term of
(1). In particular the penalty can vanish away from c=a: a uniform claim
that it is always proportional to classification error would be false.

## Expected minimax value and ERM learning error

Among algorithms satisfying the conditional robust budget for every D,
the minimax expected H over fixed worlds equals E[V(c,U)]. To prove the
lower bound, place the uniform prior on orientations and true subsets.
Context sampling and tags leave precisely the posterior used above.
Average the conditional lower bound over D; a maximum over fixed worlds
dominates this Bayes average. For the upper bound, construction (3)
has H=V(c,U) in every fixed world. The law of U is independent of the
world, so the same expected upper value holds for every world. This
argument does not replace a supremum and expectation without justification.

For missing-pair indicators I_j,

 E[U]=d(1-2/N)^n,
 E[z^U]=sum_{j=0}^d binom(d,j)(z-1)^j(1-2j/N)^n.       (4)

Expand product_j[1+(z-1)I_j]. The joint missing event for j specified
pairs has probability (1-2j/N)^n. The indicators are NOT independent.
Coefficient extraction gives

 P(U=u)=binom(d,u) sum_{j=0}^{d-u} (-1)^j binom(d-u,j)
                         (1-2(u+j)/N)^n.

Consequently the exact expected excess for any c is

 kappa/(2N) E[(U-|d-Nc|)_+].                          (5)

At the informative calibration budget c=a=d/N, this simplifies to

 minimax E[H] = kappa d/(2N)(1-2/N)^n.                (6)

The oracle is zero here. Fair completion of unseen orientations is a
consistent randomized ERM. Its minimax expected partition-classification
error under the uniform context law is R=d/N(1-2/N)^n: each unseen pair
has mass 2/N and a fair orientation guess errs with probability 1/2.
The matching lower bound follows by the independent fair orientation prior
and conditioning on unseen pairs. Equation (6) is exactly kappa R/2.
The generator itself uses the ERM VERSION SPACE (which pairs remain
undetermined), rather than claiming to plug in one ERM classifier.

The version space can be represented by d flags and observed orientations;
training processing costs O(n+d), without enumerating its hypotheses.
The constructed generator samples a context from its constant-size group
mixture then a uniform candidate. Integer/rational sampling implements
the law in expected polynomial bit complexity for rational c. Sampling
indices uniformly need not allocate an array of size NK.

For every fixed world, P(U>0)<=d(1-2/N)^n<=d exp(-2n/N).
Thus n>=(N/2)log(d/delta) ensures the exact oracle frontier simultaneously
for all c with probability at least 1-delta. The sharper samplewise
certificate is the observed U and (1); at c=a, Markov also gives
H<=kappa min(d,d(1-2/N)^n/delta)/(2N) with probability >=1-delta.
These probability claims use no independence of the missing events.

## Scope, literature, and verification

Source for the calibration definition: Kalai--Vempala, arXiv:2311.14648v3,
Definitions 1--2 and equation (2), printed pp.8--9. Its Theorem 1 and
Lemma 3 do not state this annotated version-space experiment. General
TV event inequalities and finite convexity are standard; no novelty is
claimed for them, occupancy, VC shattering, or the missing-pair rate.
Prior literature searches and the primary-source comparison are recorded
in SOURCES.jsonl and route/source logs; absence of a matching hit does not
establish novelty. The proposed new contribution is the exact calibrated
generation frontier (1) with an unrestricted lower bound in this explicit
infinite family, conditional on the stated annotated experiment.

No candidate identities are observed; systematic facts here are all
candidates, not a general learned semantic rule. Robust calibration is
stronger than a single-world high-probability calibration requirement.
Equation (2) is invalid with uniform lambda after ordinary factual
training, and no such extension is claimed. The unrestricted lower bound
also holds for the specified posterior-average calibration criterion,
but that does not silently establish a general frequentist calibration
criterion. Independent priority/scope audit is required.

The finite verification script uses Fraction throughout. It checks actual
world distributions, arbitrary generators and probability-level groupings,
the constructive upper bound, and joint occupancy identities. These checks
supplement the general proof above; they are not a proof by numerical
extrapolation. There is no Lean certificate: earlier compiler attempts

[Lemma 23 of arXiv:2608.30743, 'Perspectives on the Bott spectral sequence for Lie groupoids'] Consider a vector bundle $b: V \rightarrow M$. Furthermore consider a fibrewise linear action $L$ of a Lie groupoid $G$ on $V$ that covers an action $\underline{L}$ of $G$ on $p: M \rightarrow G_0$ and an action $K$ of $G$ on $p': N \rightarrow G_0$. Now consider an equivariant map $f: N \rightarrow M$. Then there is a natural linear action of $G$ on $f^* V$ covering the action on $N$ and the map
	\[
	f^*: \Gamma(M, V) \rightarrow \Gamma(N, f^* V)
	\]
	restricts to the equivariant sections
	\[
	f^*: \Gamma(M, V)^G \rightarrow \Gamma(N, f^* V)^G.
	\]

[Definition 26 of arXiv:2606.31455, 'Discrete time-multidimensional renewal theory and applications'] Let $q_1,q_2\in(0,1)$, $\beta_1,\beta_2>0$, and $\theta\in(0,1]$.
A random vector $X=(X_1,X_2)$ on $\mathbb{N}_0^2$ is said to follow the bivariate discrete Weibull
model (as used in this paper) if its joint survival function is

\begin{equation*}
S(k_1,k_2)
=
\mathbb{P}(X_1\ge k_1,\;X_2\ge k_2)
=
q_1^{k_1^{\beta_1}}\,q_2^{k_2^{\beta_2}}\,\theta^{\,k_1^{\beta_1}k_2^{\beta_2}},
\qquad (k_1,k_2)\in\mathbb{N}_0^2,
\end{equation*}

and the pmf is computed from $S$ via \eqref{eq:pmf-from-survival}.
The marginals satisfy $S(k_1,0)=q_1^{k_1^{\beta_1}}$ and $S(0,k_2)=q_2^{k_2^{\beta_2}}$,
so each component is a (univariate) discrete Weibull distribution in the sense of
Nakagawa--Osaki \cite{nakagawa1975discrete}.
The case $\theta=1$ yields independence (product survival).

\rho^{*}_t(x) \equiv \gamma(x).

The minimal entropy equals the entropy of $\gamma$,

H^* = h_\mathbb{R}(\gamma).
\]

body:
[Lemma 39 of arXiv:2608.15914, 'Absorption cutoff and stationary singularities for rounded Gaussian random dynamical syste'] For every $0\leq\beta<N$, the operator $\Lcal_{A,N,\beta}$ is bounded on
  $C(\mathbb S^{N-1})$ and satisfies
  \begin{equation}
    \Lcal_{A,N,\beta}\varphi(\theta)
    =
    \mathcal M_{A,N}(\beta)
    \int_{\mathbb S^{N-1}}\varphi\,\mathrm{d}\bar\sigma_N,
    \qquad
    \theta\in\mathbb S^{N-1},
  \end{equation}
  where
  \begin{equation}
    \mathcal M_{A,N}(\beta)
    :=
    \Ee\norm{\mathsf W_A^{(N)}\theta}_2^{-\beta}
    =
    \left(\frac{\sqrt N}{A}\right)^\beta
    2^{-\beta/2}
    \frac{\Gamma((N-\beta)/2)}{\Gamma(N/2)}.
  \end{equation}
  Consequently, its spectral radius $r_{A,N}(\beta)$ is given by
  \begin{equation}
    r_{A,N}(\beta)
    =
    \mathcal M_{A,N}(\beta)
    =
    A^{-\beta}\mathcal M_{1,N}(\beta).
  \end{equation}

body:
Measured 2026-09-05 on the EMIT and OCO-2 stacking pools (70 cells, the pool protocol, full calibration, paired). Given that the long-only gain is the estimation variance the constraint removes at the rows the stack is scored on, the amount of constraint was chosen with the evaluation inputs: a blend w(t) between the simplex and least-squares stacks with t minimising the cross-validated calibration error plus the excess bootstrap variance of the blend at the evaluation rows over the calibration rows, and a per-row version t_i = 1/(1 + kappa v_i/median v) that leans to the simplex where least squares is uncertain. P24 (a) HELD: on EMIT the per-cell blend reads +0.08 vs the simplex and beats least squares on 39 of 40 cells; (b) HELD: on OCO-2 t* is at or above 0.5 on 30 of 30 cells and the blend reads +0.66 vs least squares; (c) REFUTED: the per-row blend vs the per-cell blend is +0.70 on Y2 and -0.14 on EMIT overall; falsifier (blend worse than the simplex by more than 1 on EMIT, or than least squares by more than 0.3 on OCO-2) not triggered. Fresh-split replication (P25, split C, SPLIT_SEED 11, the criterion uses no evaluation targets): P25 (a) HELD: on split C the EMIT blend reads +0.63 vs the simplex and beats least squares on 35 of 40 cells; (b) HELD: on OCO-2 the blend reads +0.84 vs the simplex (wins 30 of 30) and +0.65 vs least squares; (c) HELD: t* averages 0.34 on EMIT and 0.67 on OCO-2; falsifier (blend worse than the simplex by more than 1 on EMIT, or than least squares by more than 0.3 on OCO-2) not triggered. Bootstrap-size stability (P28, B = 16 against B = 8 on split B): P28 (a) HELD: t*(16) equals t*(8) on 86 pct of the 70 cells and is within 0.2 on 100 pct; (b) HELD: the blend's mean gain against the simplex moves from +0.08 to +0.06 on EMIT and from +0.83 to +0.83 on OCO-2, and the both-endpoints win count on OCO-2 is 30 of 30 at B = 16; falsifier (agreement below 50 pct or a gain moving by more than 0.5) not triggered. Break test: a fixed midpoint t = 0.5 matches the criterion on OCO-2 (+0.96 / +1.01 against +0.83 / +0.84 on the two splits) but loses 1.6 and 4.4 pct on EMIT where the criterion stays at +0.08 and +0.63 - the criterion's value is knowing, without labels, when not to leave the simplex; the EMIT shortfall against the hindsight-best t is the bias-shift term of the risk identity.
the members' predictions on the rows to be scored are available (transductive setting); their targets are not
the blend w(t) = (1 - t) w_simplex + t w_leastsquares is linear in t, so the cross-validated and bootstrap predictions of every t come from the two base estimators' predictions; the criterion is the 5-fold cross-validated squared relative error on the calibration rows plus the excess pairs-bootstrap variance (B = 8) of the blend at the evaluation rows over the calibration rows

body:
[Proposition 6 (Stability and uniqueness) of arXiv:2606.11369, 'Mean-field limits for stochastic particle systems on dense graphs'] Let $(\mu_t)_{t\in[0,T]}$ and $(\nu_t)_{t\in[0,T]}$ be two weak solutions of
\eqref{eq:weak_limit} satisfying the assumptions of Lemma \ref{lem:moment_limit}.
For $k\ge0$, write
\[
\mu_t^k(du):=\mu_t(du,\{k\}),\qquad
\nu_t^k(du):=\nu_t(du,\{k\}),
\]
and set
\[
\Delta_t^k:=\mu_t^k-\nu_t^k .
\]
Define
\[
\Theta(t):=\sum_{k\ge0}(1+k)|\Delta_t^k|([0,1]).
\]
Then there exists a constant $C_T>0$ such that
\[
\Theta(t)\le e^{C_Tt}\Theta(0),
\qquad t\in[0,T].
\]
In particular, if $\mu_0=\nu_0$, then $\mu_t=\nu_t$ for every $t\in[0,T]$.

[Corollary 3 of arXiv:2604.08623, 'Central limit theorem for the Allen-Cahn equation with supercritical random initial condit'] Under the same notations, we have for any $\eps > 0$, $t>0$ and $x,y\in \mathbb{R}^d$, the estimate
  \begin{equation}
    0\leq D_{y} u_\eps(t,x) \leq p_t * \rho_\eps (x-y).
  \end{equation}
  Consequently, for any $p\geq1$, we get the following bounds on the $p$-th moment of $Du(t,x)$ and 
  $\langle Du(t,\cdot),\phi\rangle$ where $\phi$ is any test function.
  \begin{align*}
    \mathbf{E}\left[ \|D u_\eps(t,x)\|_{\mathcal{H}}^p\right] & \leq \|p_t * \rho_\eps\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)}^p,\\ 
    \mathbf{E}\left[ \|\langle D u_\eps(t,\cdot),\phi\rangle\|_\mathcal{H}^p\right] 
    & \leq \|p_t * \rho_\eps * |\phi|\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)}^p.
  \end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Then, for almost every $t>0$,
\begin{equation}

\frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{dt}\|u(t)\|_{L^2}^2
+ \nu \|\nabla u(t)\|_{L^2}^2
+ \int_{\omega} K(\rho(t))\,|u(x,t)|^2\,dx
\le 0.
\end{equation}
Equivalently, for almost every $s\ge 0$ and every $t\ge s$,
\begin{equation}

\frac{1}{2}\|u(t)\|_{L^2}^2
+ \nu \int_s^t \|\nabla u(\tau)\|_{L^2}^2\,d\tau
+ \int_s^t \int_\omega K(\rho(\tau))\,|u(x,\tau)|^2\,dx\,d\tau
\le \frac{1}{2}\|u(s)\|_{L^2}^2.
\end{equation}

body: [Lem 35 of arXiv:2608.30990, 'Convergence of symmetries: nilpotency, dimension, and perfectness'] Let $\phi_i : G_i \to G$ be a sequence of local good approximations with regular neighborhoods $A_i \subset G_i$ and $A \subset G$. If $G$ is metrizable, then for any open set $B \subset A$ there is a sequence of open sets  $B_i \subset A_i$ that approximates $B$. Moreover, if $B$ is symmetric, the sets $B_i$ can be taken to be symmetric. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Definition 16 (Graph) of arXiv:2608.07239, 'Unified framework for asymptotically uniform iterative construction of generalised random '] A \emph{graph} is a tuple $G=(V,E)$ with $V$, a finite set of vertices, and $E$, a set of edges, which are unordered pairs of vertices. In a \emph{multigraph}, $E$ and its elements are multisets, which allows \emph{self-loops} and \emph{multi-edges}. To emphasize the distinction from a multigraph, a graph may be referred to as a \emph{simple graph}.

[Definition def:g-gl-fib-orth-spc of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] A map $f\colon X\to Y$ in $\cat{$\bm G$-$\textbf{\textup{L}}$-Top}$ is called a \emph{$G$-global fibration} if it is a $G$-global level fibration and for all $H$-representations $V,W$ such that $V$ is faithful the naturality square
    \[
        \begin{tikzcd}
            X(V)\arrow[r]\arrow[d,"f(V)"'] & X(V\oplus W)\arrow[d,"f(V\oplus W)"]\\
            Y(V)\arrow[r] & Y(V\oplus W)
        \end{tikzcd}
    \]
    is a homotopy pullback in the $\mathcal G_{H,G}$-equivariant model structure on $\cat{$\bm{(H\times G)}$-Top}$.

    A $G$-orthogonal space $X$ is called \emph{static} if $X\to1$ is a $G$-global fibration, i.e.\ if the transition map $X(V)\to X(V\oplus W)$ is a $\mathcal G_{H,G}$-weak equivalence for all $V,W$ as above.

[Definition def:Ck1 of arXiv:2608.17022, 'Sharp hypocoercive convergence estimates for underdamped Langevin dynamics with specular r'] Let $k\ge0$ be an integer. A bounded open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ has
\emph{boundary of class $C^{k,1}$}, written $\partial\Omega\in C^{k,1}$, if for
every $x_0\in\partial\Omega$ there exist $r,h>0$, an orthonormal coordinate
system $y=(y',y_d)\in\mathbb{R}^{d-1}\times\mathbb{R}$ centered at $x_0$, and a function
$\varphi\in C^{k,1}(\overline{B'_r})$ with $\varphi(0)=0$ and
$\sup_{B'_r}|\varphi|<h$, such that, writing
$B'_r:=\{y'\in\mathbb{R}^{d-1}:|y'|<r\}$ and $V:=B'_r\times(-h,h)$,
\begin{equation}
\Omega\cap V=\big\{(y',y_d)\in V:\ y_d>\varphi(y')\big\},
\qquad
\partial\Omega\cap V=\big\{(y',y_d)\in V:\ y_d=\varphi(y')\big\}.
\end{equation}
Here $C^{k,1}(\overline{B'_r})$ denotes the space of functions of class $C^k$
on $\overline{B'_r}$ all of whose partial derivatives of order $k$ are
Lipschitz continuous. By compactness of $\partial\Omega$, finitely many charts
(equation eq:local-graph of the paper) cover $\partial\Omega$, and the $C^{k,1}$ norms of the
corresponding $\varphi$'s may be taken uniformly bounded. On a compact
boundary, $C^{k+1}\subset C^{k,1}\subset C^k$; in particular a $C^3$ boundary
is $C^{2,1}$. This is the standard local-graph definition; see e.g.\ [Grisvard85] or [GilbargTrudinger01].
title: $C^{k,1}$ boundary

body:
Let phi be real-analytic near 0 in R^n, phi(0) = 0, and psi smooth with small support. Then int e^{i lambda phi} psi has an expansion sum_k sum_{j=0}^{n-1} a_{j,k} lambda^{-r_k} (log lambda)^j with rational r_k (resolution of singularities). For n = 2 (Varchenko 1976): adapted coordinates exist, the leading exponent is 1/h, where the height h is the Newton distance in adapted coordinates, and |int e^{i lambda phi} psi| <= C lambda^{-1/h} (log lambda)^nu with nu in {0,1}, sharp in the exponents. Karpushkin (1984): for n = 2 this bound holds uniformly under small real-analytic perturbations of phi. For n >= 3 the oscillation index can differ from 1/h and such stability fails (Varchenko). Phong-Stein-Sturm (1999) reprove the existence of adapted coordinates in two variables (Puiseux series) and study stability of sublevel and oscillatory estimates.

\frac{dP_m^0}{dP_\infty^0}
\right)
\right\|_{L^\infty(P_\infty^0)}
\longrightarrow 0.
\]
For each pair $(k,m)$ and each $k$ define, respectively
\[
Q_{k,m}
:=
\arg\min_{P\in\mathbb{P}_k} D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|P_m^0), \qquad
Q_k^\infty
:=
\arg\min_{P\in\mathbb{P}_k} D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|P_\infty^0),
\]
and further define $
Q_\infty
:=
\arg\min_{P\in\mathbb{P}} D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|P_\infty^0).
$
Assume the hypotheses of Theorems~(thm:mtd1_converges of the paper) and~(thm:mtd2_converges of the paper) hold. Then there exists an increasing sequence of indices $m(k)\to\infty$ such that $Q_{k,m(k)} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{TV}} Q_\infty$.

body: A prime is an integer p > 1 whose only positive divisors are 1 and p; an integer > 1 that is not prime is composite. Equivalent (Euclid's-lemma) characterization in the integers: p is prime iff p | ab implies p | a or p | b. Primes are the multiplicative building blocks - the fundamental theorem of arithmetic says every integer > 1 factors uniquely into primes - and there are infinitely many (Euclid).
title: Prime Number

[Definition def:S-cc of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] Let $S\subset T$ be a cleft. A $T$-$\infty$-category is called \emph{$S$-cocomplete} if it is fiberwise cocomplete and $\ul\Spc_{S\triangleright T}$-cocomplete, and it is called \emph{$S$-presentable} if it is in addition fiberwise presentable. A functor $F\colon{\mathcal{C}}\to{\mathcal{D}}$ of $S$-cocomplete $T$-$\infty$-categories is called \emph{$S$-cocontinuous} if it is fiberwise cocontinuous and $\ul\Spc_{S\triangleright T}$-cocontinuous.
    We write $\CAT_T^\text{$S$-cc}\subset\CAT_T$ for the subcategory spanend by the $S$-cocomplete $T$-$\infty$-categories and $S$-cocontinuous functors. We moreover write $\textup{Pr}^S_T\subset\CAT_T^\text{$S$-cc}$ for the full subcategory spanned by the $S$-presentable $T$-$\infty$-categories.
title: Definition def:S-cc of arXiv:2608.28504

[Proposition p:exp.clique of arXiv:2601.12677, 'Stable and Fréchet limit theorem for subgraph functionals in the hyperbolic random geometr'] Let $\frac{2m-3}{2m-2} < \alpha < 1$ and $\gamma \in (\frac{1}{2\alpha}, 1)$. \\
$(i)$  As $n\to\infty$, 
$$
\nu_{m,n}(u) \le \big( 1+o_n(1) \big) C_{m,\alpha} e^{\frac{1}{2} (d-1)u}, 
$$
uniformly over $u\in (0,{\gamma R_n})$. \\
$(ii)$ There exists $C\in (0,\infty)$, independent of $n$ and $u$, such that 
$$
\nu_{m,n}(u)\ge \Big\{ \big( 1+o_n(1) \big) 2^{d-1}\xi_{d-1} \big( s_{d-1}^{-1}\alpha (d-1) \big)^{m-1} \ell(u) - C \ell'(u)  \Big\}_+e^{\frac{1}{2} (d-1)u}, 
$$
uniformly over $u\in (0,{\gamma R_n})$, where $\ell'(u)$ is defined in (equation e:def.ell' of the paper). \\
$(iii)$ There exist $C, c_0 \in (0,\infty)$, independent of  $n$ and $u$, such that for all $n\ge1$ and $u\in (0,R_n)$, 
$$
\nu_{m,n}(u) \le Ce^{c_0\omega_n} \cdot  e^{\frac{1}{2}(d-1)u}. 
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[2 11 of arXiv:2607.12303, 'Marginal Stationary Distributions and Convergence Rates of Higher Order Markov Chains'] Suppose that $\{X_t\}_{t=1}^{\infty}$ is an $(m-1)$th order Markov chain   on state space $S$ with a transition tensor $\mathcal{P}$. If the chain is regular, then it has a unique marginal stationary distribution $\pi$. Moreover, 
$$
\lim_{t \to \infty} \xi^{(t)}_{i} =  \lim_{t \to \infty} \Pr(X_t=i) =  \pi_i, \ \ \forall i \in S. 
$$
Thus, $\pi$ is the limiting probability distribution of $X_t$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let d>=1, fix any norm on R^d and epsilon>=0, and let P_+,P_- be Borel class-conditional probability laws with equal class priors1/2. A perturbation can move a labeled example x to any point in its closed radius-epsilon norm ball. Define R_epsilon(h)=0.5*P_+{x: some z with ||z-x||<=epsilon has h(z)=-1}+0.5*P_-{y: some z with ||z-y||<=epsilon has h(z)=+1}. With probabilities interpreted on their completions as needed, inf_h R_epsilon(h)=0.5*sup_(pi in Pi(P_+,P_-)) pi{(x,y): ||x-y||<=2epsilon}. The infimum is over measurable binary classifiers and is attained. Both classes have the same perturbation ball and balanced priors; the factor2 in the distance threshold and factor1/2 in risk are essential. This is the norm-ball specialization of the source theorem for Polish spaces with nonempty closed upper-hemicontinuous neighborhoods.
Finite-dimensional real normed space; epsilon>=0; closed perturbation balls identical for both classes
Borel class-conditional laws with priors1/2; arbitrary measurable binary classifiers; standard pointwise worst-case0-1 risk

[Definition def:admissible_operators of arXiv:2609.01697, 'Unique ergodicity of projective cocycles over the 2D stochastic Navier--Stokes equations'] A linear operator $A \colon \mathcal{S} \to \mathcal{S}$ is \emph{admissible} if it is continuous in the Fr\'echet topology of $\mathcal{S}$. (Differential operators with smooth coefficients, while possibly unbounded on $L^2$, are continuous on $\mathcal{S}$).
  \begin{itemize}
    \item   We denote with $\mathrm{Op}^{\infty}$ the set of
      admissible operators on $\mathcal{S}$.
    \item We denote with $\mathrm{Op}^{\beta_\star} \subseteq \mathrm{Op}^{\infty}$ the
      subset of admissible operators that extend (uniquely) to bounded linear operators $H^{\beta_\star} \to \mathcal{H}$, with $\beta_\star$ as in~(equation eq:X_star of the paper). We endow $\mathrm{Op}^{\beta_\star}$ with the operator norm topology of $\mathcal{L}(H^{\beta_\star};\mathcal{H})$, and write $\|A\|_{\mathrm{Op}^{\beta_\star}} \overset{\mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle def}}{=} \|A\|_{\mathcal{L}(H^{\beta_\star};\mathcal{H})}$ for the corresponding norm.
  \end{itemize}

[Proposition 12 (Early-stopping for compactly supported data) of arXiv:2607.25685, 'Mimicking diffusion processes with differential equations'] Assume \textup{(E1)}.
 Let $X=(X_t)_{t\in[0,T]}$ be the solution of the linear SDE with drift $f(x,s)=-\beta(s)x,\ \beta\in L^\infty(0,T)$:
 $$ dX_t= -\beta(t)X_t dt +\sigma(t) dW_t,\qquad X_0\sim \mu_0$$
where $\mu_0\in{\cal P}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ is a
probability  measure on $\mathbb{R}^d$ with compact support $\supp \mu_0\subset B_R$. No absolute continuity, regularity, or log-concavity of $\mu_0$  is assumed. 
Let $0<\delta<T$ and  $m_s,\varsigma_s$ as in
Proposition~\ref{prop:linear},
\[
\varsigma_{\min}^2:=\inf_{s\in[\delta,T]}\varsigma_s^2>0,\qquad
  m_{\max}:=\sup_{s\le T}m_s<\infty .
\]
Then the density $p_t$ of $X_t$ satisfies \textup{(S)}  on $[\delta,T]$, with the explicit constants
\begin{align}
\bigl\|[\Delta\log p_s]^+\bigr\|_{L^\infty}
\le
d\left(
\frac{m_s^2R^2}{\varsigma_s^4}
-
\frac1{\varsigma_s^2}
\right)^+
\le
d\,m_{\max}^2R^2\varsigma_{\min}^{-4}, &&\text{giving \textup{(S3)}},
  \\
  \|\nabla^2\log p_s\|_{\mathrm{op}}
\le
\varsigma_s^{-2}
+m_s^2R^2\varsigma_s^{-4}
\le
\varsigma_{\min}^{-2}
+
m_{\max}^2R^2\varsigma_{\min}^{-4}
  &&\text{giving \textup{(S2)}},
  \\
  |\nabla\log p_s(x)|
\le
\varsigma_{\min}^{-2}
\max\{1,m_{\max}R\}(1+|x|),
  &&\text{giving \textup{(S4)}} .
  
\end{align}
In addition,
\[
\nabla^2\log p_s\ge-\varsigma_s^{-2}I,
\qquad
\bigl\|[\Delta\log p_s]^-\bigr\|_{L^\infty}
\le d\varsigma_{\min}^{-2}.
\]

Fix an integer k>=1 and c>0. Let N/d^k -> c, with independent uniform unit feature directions in R^d and population inputs uniform on the sphere of radius sqrt(d). Let sigma be a fixed activation of polynomial growth with normalized Gaussian Hermite coefficients mu_0,...,mu_k all nonzero and T=sum_{j>k}mu_j^2>0. For each d, let the target have zero coefficients below degree k and independent centered Gaussian spherical-harmonic coefficients at degrees j>=k, independent of the feature directions, with variance F_j^2/D_{j,d} per coordinate. The nonnegative masses F_j^2 are independent of d and have finite sum; D_{j,d} is the degree-j harmonic dimension. Put psi=c*k!, z=T/mu_k^2, and B=(1-psi-z+sqrt((1+psi+z)^2-4*psi))/2. The minimum population squared approximation error over the span of the N sigma features converges in L1 over directions and target coefficients to F_k^2*B+sum_{j>k}F_j^2. In particular F_k=0 is allowed. The ratio z is the ACTIVATION tail-to-critical mass, not the target ratio in general. This is population approximation with unrestricted coefficients, not arbitrary positive population ridge.

$q=e^{h/2}$,
$K_j=e^{hH_j/2}$,
$\mathcal R=D\Psi$ with
$\Psi=\Theta_{\mathrm{HL}}^{-1}$ as in
\eqref{eq:HL-R-convention}, and
$g=K_{-2\rho}=u\mathbf r^{-1}$, the continuous Hopf
automorphism
\[
 \vartheta_h(H_j)=-H_{n+1-j},\qquad
 \vartheta_h(E_i)=E_{n-i},\qquad
 \vartheta_h(F_i)=F_{n-i}
\]
is a ribbon Hopf automorphism:
\[
 (\vartheta_h\otimes\vartheta_h)(\mathcal R)=\mathcal R,
 \qquad
 \vartheta_h(g)=g,
 \qquad
 \vartheta_h(\mathbf r)=\mathbf r.
\]

[Lemma l:easy-useful-heat-kernel of arXiv:2607.24640, 'The Yang-Mills measure on surfaces via Morse theory'] Let $\tau>0$ and let $\mathrm{h}_1,\mathrm{h}_2$ be two elements in $G$. Then, for any bounded and measurable function $\Psi:G\rightarrow\mathbb{C}$, one has
$$
\forall \mathrm{g}\in\mathbb{C},\quad\int_Gp_{\tau}\left(\mathrm{g}\mathrm{g}_1^{-1}\right)\Psi(\mathrm{h}_1\mathrm{g}_1\mathrm{h}_2)\mu_G(d\mathrm{g}_1)=e^{\frac{\tau\Delta_G}{2}}(\Psi)(\mathrm{h}_1\mathrm{g}\mathrm{h}_2).
$$
If, in addition, $\Psi$ is a central function, then one has 
$$
\forall \mathrm{g}\in\mathbb{C},\quad\int_Gp_{\tau}\left(\mathrm{g}\mathrm{g}_1^{-1}\right)\Psi(\mathrm{h}_1\mathrm{g}_1\mathrm{h}_2)\mu_G(d\mathrm{g}_1)=e^{\frac{\tau\Delta_G}{2}}(\Psi)(\mathrm{h}_2\mathrm{h}_1\mathrm{g}).
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Thrm 5 of arXiv:2604.17732, 'Exact Simulation from Tempered Stable Distributions with Infinite Variation ($\alpha\ge1$)'] Fix $\epsilon\in(0,1)$ and let
$$
m^\sharp_\epsilon = \frac{2}{\pi}\left(1-\log(\ell\epsilon)\right).
$$
1. For $x\le m^\sharp_\epsilon$ and $- \frac{\pi}{2}<\theta\le \frac{\pi}{2}$, we have 
$$
g^*(x,\theta) \le C_1 f^*(x,\theta),
$$
where
$$
C_1 = C e^{m^\sharp_\epsilon/\ell} = e^{\frac{2}{\pi\ell}\left(1-\log \epsilon\right)}.
$$
2. For $x> m^\sharp_\epsilon $ and $- \frac{\pi}{2}<\theta\le \frac{\pi}{2}$, we have
$$
g^*(x,\theta) \le C_{2} \frac{1}{\pi} e^{-\xi(x-m_\epsilon(\theta))^2/2}\sqrt{\frac{2\xi}{\pi}} ,
$$
where
$$
\xi = \frac{\pi}{2\ell}, \ \ \ 
m_\epsilon(\theta) = \frac{2}{\pi}\log\left(\frac{2}{\epsilon \ell\pi V(\theta)}\right),
$$
and
$$
C_{2} =\frac{\pi\sqrt\ell}{2e(1-\epsilon)} \epsilon^{-\frac{2}{\pi\ell}} .
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:624750b2f92ed08c839d604b23608831ec4730dbeb4c1b9e57be6064828c2d3b","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/62/624750b2f92ed08c839d604b23608831ec4730dbeb4c1b9e57be6064828c2d3b.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:582e938d316bd3d34c589b3a80a45bdb233a32e507f3c6bf8d8bdb2f6a801459","bundle_entry_key":"stein-spectral-order","bundle_id":"population.t311-positive-hermite-and-stein-spectral-order-001","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"analysis","draft":"w722/bundle_001.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:analysis.stein:w722-t311-stein-spectral-order","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Gaussian RBF Stein spectrum: a two-sided rate-order theorem

Status: proof (unaudited). Target 2. This proves order up to explicit factors, not an asymptotic equivalent with a single leading constant. It does not prove nonlinear KL decay or propagation of regularity.

Let pi=N(0,1), h>0, k_h(x,y)=exp(-(x-y)^2/(2h^2)), and T the associated kernel integral operator on L2(pi). Let D=d/dx, D*=-d/dx+x. Let A be the bounded positive extension of D*T D, with its constant zero mode removed. Denote its positive eigenvalues in decreasing order by lambda_1, lambda_2, ... . Define

q=sqrt(1+4/h^2), B=(q-1)/(q+1), mu_j=(1-B)B^j,
d_j=(j+1)mu_j, j=0,1,... .

Let d_j^down denote the decreasing rearrangement of the sequence d_0,d_1,..., indexed from zero. Then for every j>=0,

q^(-1) d_j^down <= lambda_(j+1) <= q d_j^down.                 (1)

For every fixed h, d_j^down=d_j for all sufficiently large j. Consequently

lambda_(j+1) is comparable to (j+1) B^j as j tends to infinity, (2)

with explicit eventual factors (1-B)/q and q(1-B). In particular,

lim_(j->infinity) log(lambda_(j+1))/j = log B.                  (3)

When h>=1/sqrt(2), B<=1/2 and d_j is already decreasing, so the unrearranged bounds in (1) hold for every j. The bounds imply that in the j-th Stein eigenvector the linearized amplitude decays as exp(-lambda_(j+1)t), bracketed by exp(-q d_j^down t) and exp(-d_j^down t/q). They do not identify a Hermite polynomial as an eigenvector.

## Inputs taken as established

The dossier supplies A=D*T D and equality of its nonzero spectrum with that of S=T^(1/2)(DD*)T^(1/2). It also supplies the Gaussian Mercer eigenvalues mu_j, with eigenfunctions which become squeezed Hermite functions under the unitary map U f=sqrt(pi)f. The latter is the Gaussian-measure squared-exponential Mercer decomposition in Rasmussen and Williams, Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning, Section 4.3.1. Those established inputs are not re-derived here.

## Proof of the new comparison

1. Work in flat L2(dx) using U, and suppress U from the operator names. Put c=q/4. Then

U(DD*)U^(-1) = H = -d^2/dx^2 + x^2/4 + 1/2.

The normalized eigenfunctions psi_j of T are oscillator eigenfunctions for

Q = -(1/(4c)) d^2/dx^2 + c x^2 + 1/2,
Q psi_j=(j+1)psi_j.

Indeed the unshifted oscillator -d^2/dx^2+4c^2 x^2 has eigenvalues 2c(2j+1); dividing by 4c and adding 1/2 gives the asserted eigenvalues. This checks the frequency and the shift explicitly.

2. Since q=4c>=1, direct comparison of the nonnegative derivative, position and norm terms gives the quadratic-form inequalities

q^(-1) Q <= H <= q Q.                                       (4)

For clarity, their differences are

H-q^(-1)Q = (1-q^(-2))(-d^2/dx^2)+(1-q^(-1))/2,
qQ-H = (q^2-1)x^2/4+(q-1)/2.

Both are nonnegative forms on the common form domain {g in H1(dx): xg in L2(dx)}. No commuting of H and T is used.

3. Q and T commute in their common basis psi_j, so

R=T^(1/2)Q T^(1/2)=QT,
R psi_j=d_j psi_j.

The sequence d_j is positive and summable. The map T^(1/2) sends all of L2 into the form domain of Q because sup_j (j+1)mu_j is finite. By (4) it also sends all of L2 into the form domain of H. Sandwiching (4) therefore gives bounded positive quadratic forms

q^(-1)R <= S=T^(1/2)H T^(1/2) <= qR.                         (5)

There is no domain omission in this sandwich: for f=sum f_j psi_j, the Q form of T^(1/2)f is sum d_j |f_j|^2, and (4) controls its H form. S is trace class: summing <psi_j,S psi_j><=q d_j yields a finite trace. In particular S is compact.

4. The compact positive-operator min-max principle applied to (5) proves

q^(-1) lambda_(j+1)(R) <= lambda_(j+1)(S) <= q lambda_(j+1)(R).

Here lambda_(j+1)(R)=d_j^down, including multiplicities. The nonzero spectra of S and A agree, giving (1).

One may also justify that equality of spectra directly at the level of bounded operators. For this paragraph return to the original L2(pi), with D=d/dx and D*=-d/dx+x; all the flat-space forms are transported by U. C=D*T^(1/2) is bounded and Hilbert-Schmidt, since ||Cf||^2=<f,Sf> and tr S<infinity. Then C*C=S and CC* is the bounded extension of D*T D from smooth compactly supported functions. The usual equality of positive eigenvalues of C*C and CC* applies. Constants lie in ker CC*. Conversely if C*f=0 then <f,D*g>=0 for every g in the finite span of the Mercer eigenfunctions (their finite linear combinations lie in the range of T^(1/2)). That span is a core for the D* graph norm: its U-image is a form core for Q, and (4) identifies this form norm with the H form norm ||D*g||^2+||g||^2. Thus the distributional derivative of f vanishes and f is constant. This identifies the sole zero mode and justifies restricting A to the mean-zero subspace.

5. The successive ratio d_(j+1)/d_j=B(j+2)/(j+1) decreases to B<1. Hence d_j is eventually strictly decreasing and tends to zero. Choose J beyond the maximum with d_J<=d_0. All earlier terms then exceed every later term: before the maximum the smallest term is d_0, and after the maximum the sequence decreases. Sorting therefore permutes only the first J terms, and d_j^down=d_j for j>=J. Equations (2) and (3) follow. If B<=1/2 the ratio is at most one already at j=0, giving the stated all-index case. QED.

## Limits and the next unpaid step

The two-sided comparison does not prove convergence of lambda_(j+1)/((j+1)B^j); the dossier's numerical leading constant remains a separate question. The nonlinear flow still needs a preserved regularity class and control of the nonlinear remainder. Nothing in this proof supplies that. The least routine functional-analytic step for independent review is the core/closure identification of CC* with the intended linearized Stein generator; the comparison of bounded forms S and R itself is explicit.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:18618181c1e55723453d3fd0280a04028682b29877205fda162197655ca2b74e","revision_digest":"sha256:5d6954c77a1ed578f79822dcffe44df16d9856572f171fa069e95c4559665fd3","source_id":"own-work:w722:T311:w722-spectral-order-v1","source_revision":"w722-spectral-order-v1","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

    \[

\]

[Theorem thm:bv of arXiv:2510.22778, 'Free denoising diffusion models'] For $\mu,\nu$ with finite second moment,
$W_{2}^{\mathrm{free}}(\mu,\nu)=W_{2}(\mu,\nu)$, the classical quadratic Wasserstein
distance on $\mathbb{R}$. The infimum in (equation eq:freeW of the paper) is attained by a pair of

body: [Theorem thm:impossible of arXiv:2608.23638, 'Replicable Conformal Prediction'] \emph{(a)} If $\varepsilon+\delta<\min(\alpha,1-\alpha)$, no $(1,\delta)$-list-replicable procedure is uniformly $\varepsilon$-valid. Every seedless $\rho$-replicable procedure is $(1,\rho)$-list replicable, so no seedless procedure is uniformly $\varepsilon$-valid and $\rho$-replicable when $\varepsilon+\rho<\min(\alpha,1-\alpha)$. \emph{(b)} With a shared seed $R$, any exactly ($0$-)replicable procedure equals a fixed measurable $v_\star(R)$ almost surely under every $P\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{ac}}$, so its output law is $P$-independent, and if it is also uniformly $\varepsilon$-valid, there is a fixed kernel $p$ with $p(x,y)\in[1-\alpha-\varepsilon,1-\alpha+\varepsilon]$ for a.e.\ $x$ and every $y$, coverage under every $P$ equals $\mathbb{E}_P[p(X,Y)]$, and $(1-\alpha-\varepsilon)K\le\mathbb{E}|\widehat\mathcal{C}(x)|\le(1-\alpha+\varepsilon)K$ for a.e.\ $x$. (Proof: Appendix~(app:impossible of the paper).) (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Theorem 6 (Bulk regime) of arXiv:2511.12623, 'The eigenvector bead process'] Let $K \ge 1$ and fix an energy level
\(
E \in \bigl((1-\sqrt{q})^2,\,(1+\sqrt{q})^2\bigr), q = \frac{N}{T} \in (0,1),
\)
kept constant as $N,T \to \infty$. We recall the notation for $\rho_{\mathrm{MP}}$ (see Equation~\ref{eq:MP-law}).
Define the point process
\[
\Theta_N^{(s)}
\;=\;
\sum_{j=1}^{N+s}
\delta_{2\pi\rho_{\mathrm{MP}}(E)\,(\lambda_j^{(s)} - E T)},
\qquad 0 \le s \le K.
\]
Then $\bigl(\Theta_N^{(s)}\bigr)_{s=0}^K$ forms a Markov chain, and as $N,T\to\infty$,
it converges in distribution to the Markov chain
\(
\Theta^{(s+1)} = \mathcal{D}\bigl(\Theta^{(s)},\,\Gamma^{(s)},\,h\bigr)
\)
described in \cite[Eq.\,(1.4)]{huang2022},
with level parameter
\[
h(E, q)
= -\,\frac{q\,\big(E + q - 1\big)}{2\,\sqrt{\big((1+\sqrt{q})^{2} - E\big)\,\big(E - (1-\sqrt{q})^{2}\big)}}\,.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Bulk regime

	\frac{G_R(t)-G_R(s)}{\sqrt R}
	\right|^p
	\right]

	\]

body: For an elliptic curve E over a number field K, the group E(K) of K-rational points is finitely generated: E(K) is isomorphic to a finite torsion group times Z^r, where r is the rank. The proof combines the weak Mordell-Weil theorem (E(K)/mE(K) finite, via Kummer theory and finiteness of class and unit groups) with a descent using height functions. Ranks are computable in practice but no general algorithm is proven; the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture ties r to the order of vanishing of the L-function at s = 1.
title: Mordell-Weil Theorem

body:
[Conj 91 of arXiv:2509.01797, 'Relation between Wick powers and excursion clusters of the 2D GFF'] Let $n\geq 1$.
For $\varepsilon>0$, consider the family of random variables
\begin{displaymath}
(B([0,\zeta_M]), (Z_{j,\varepsilon},[\Gamma_{Z_{j,\varepsilon}}])_{1\leq j\leq n}).
\end{displaymath}
As $\varepsilon\to 0$, this family converges in law towards
\begin{displaymath}
(B([0,\zeta_M]),(Z_{j},[\Gamma_{j}])_{1\leq j\leq n}),
\end{displaymath}
with the following properties.
\begin{itemize}
\item $B([0,\zeta_M])$ is the same Brownian trajectory as previously.
\item $(Z_{j})_{1\leq j\leq n}$ are random points on $B([0,\zeta_M])$,
sampled, conditionally on $B([0,\zeta_M])$, in an i.i.d. way according to the probability measure
$\Theta_{\zeta_{M}}/\zeta_{M}$, 
where $\Theta_{\zeta_{M}}$ is the occupation measure \eqref{Eq occup meas}.
\item The family of equivalence classes of loops
$([\Gamma_{j}])_{1\leq j\leq n}$
is \textbf{independent} from
$(B([0,\zeta_M]),(Z_{j})_{1\leq j\leq n})$,
with an i.i.d. distribution according to the measure
$\hat{\mu}^{\rm loop}_{\text{SLE}_{8/3}}$.
\end{itemize} (Stated as a conjecture by the paper; open unless the paper says otherwise.)
title: Conjecture 91 of arXiv:2509.01797

  L_D(W^\circ+H)=L^{\star}_{D}+\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\lVert Hx_i\rVert^2 .

body:
Own-work draft; proof (unaudited); reconstruction of a compactness technique, no novelty claim. Let Z be compact metric, let R_n,R be closed relations on Z, and suppose every convergent sequence of edges of R_n has its limiting edge in R. Let nonempty compact K_n converge to K in Hausdorff distance. Suppose every point of K_n has incoming and outgoing edges in R_n restricted to K_n x K_n, and K_n is internally chain transitive for that restricted relation. Then K has the same incoming/outgoing property and is internally chain transitive for R restricted to K x K. Chains mean finitely many true relation edges joined by arbitrarily small metric jumps. A finite epsilon/8-chain can be shortened, using a finite epsilon/8-cover, to at most one plus the cover size true edges with jumps smaller than3epsilon/8; keeping last occurrences of cells prevents accumulated shortcut error.
common compact metric ambient Z
closed relations R_n,R with the stated upper graph convergence
nonempty compact K_n converging in Hausdorff distance
restricted incoming/outgoing edges at every point
internal chain transitivity for each restricted relation

Editorial clarification;
existing compact closed-relation chain-limit statement is unchanged.
This is not a new frontier result or an independent proof audit.

CONVENTION
An epsilon-chain from x to y consists of at least one true edge
(a_j,b_j), all endpoints in the compact set under consideration,
a_0=x, successive jumps d(b_j,a_(j+1))<epsilon, and a final jump
d(b_last,y)<epsilon. The last target is not required to equal y.

FINITE LAST-OCCURRENCE COMPRESSION
Let a chain have m true edges and jump tolerance eta>0. Assign every
source a_j to one of N fixed cover cells of diameter at most D.
Keep edge0. If the current retained original index i is not m-1,
let k=i+1 be its ORIGINAL successor index. Retain edge j where j is
the LAST occurrence, among indices k,...,m-1, of the cell assigned to
a_k. Replace the intervening segment by the single jump b_i to a_j.
Then
 d(b_i,a_j)<=d(b_i,a_k)+d(a_k,a_j)<eta+D.
The next step starts from retained original edge j and its original
successor j+1; previously accumulated errors are never added.
The retained indices increase strictly. Every selected cell is absent
from all later sources, by its last-occurrence definition. Hence at
most N such selections follow edge0: length at most N+1.
The procedure necessarily reaches original last edge m-1. Its final
jump to y is unchanged and remains <eta. First source x is unchanged.
This handles m=1 as well, with no selections or altered jumps.

COMPACT LIMIT
For a fixed desired epsilon choose balls of radius epsilon/8, assign
each point to one covering ball, and put D<=epsilon/4. Start with
eta=epsilon/8 chains. Compressed successive jumps are <3*epsilon/8;
the final jump is <epsilon/8. The weaker common bound3*epsilon/8 also
works for the final jump. Length is uniformly bounded by N+1.

For jointly closed relations and Hausdorff-convergent compact sets,
extract a subsequence with fixed compressed length and convergent
sources and targets. Closedness makes each limiting edge a true edge;
Hausdorff convergence keeps its endpoints in the limiting set.
If x_n->x and y_n->y, the first source is exactly x and final jump is
at most epsilon/8 (or, using the weaker bound, at most3*epsilon/8).
Successive limiting jumps are at most3*epsilon/8<epsilon.
This is an epsilon-chain under the stated convention. It does not
show the final target equals y, and that stronger claim is unnecessary.

SCOPE
All ambient compactness, joint relation closedness, and internal chain

[Proposition of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] Given a variable $f:X\to\mathbb R$ which follows the uniform law of $[a,b]$, its cumulative distribution function (CDF) is as follows,
$$\xymatrix@R=18pt@C=25pt{
&&&\\
&&&&&\\
&&1\ar@.[uu]&&&\ar@{-}[rr]&&\\
\ar@{-}[rr]&&0\ar@{.}[u]\ar@{-}[r]&a\ar@{.}[rr]\ar@{-}[urr]&&b\ar@.[rr]&&}$$
and the converse holds too, in the sense that having this CDF means that our variable $f:X\to\mathbb R$ must follow the uniform law of $[a,b]$.

body:
[Definition of arXiv:2411.04590, 'Singular stochastic delay equations driven by fractional Brownian motion: Dynamics, longti'] Let $\mathcal{B}$ be a real Banach space. A strongly continuous semigroup of linear operators, or a $C_0$-semigroup, is a one-parameter family $\{T_t\}_{t \geq 0}$ of bounded linear operators on $\mathcal{B}$ that satisfies the following properties:
			
			\begin{enumerate}
				\item \textbf{Semigroup Property:} For all $t, s \geq 0$, we have
				\[
				T_{t+s} = T_t\circ T_s.
				\]
				\item \textbf{Identity at Zero:} The operator $T_0$ is the identity operator on $\mathcal{B}$, i.e.,
				\[
				T_0 = I.
				\]
				\item \textbf{Strong Continuity:} For every $x \in \mathcal{B}$, the map $t \mapsto T_t x$ is continuous from $[0, \infty)$ to $\mathcal{B}$.
			\end{enumerate}
			To every $C_0$-semigroup $\{T(t)\}_{t \geq 0}$ on a Banach space $\mathcal{B}$, we can associate an infinitesimal generator $L$ defined by
			
			\[
			{L} z = \lim_{t \to 0^+} \frac{T(t) z - z}{t},
			\]
			
			for all $z \in \mathcal{D}(L)$. The domain of the generator $L$, denoted by $\mathcal{D}(L)$, is given by
			
			\[
			\mathcal{D}(L) = \left\{ \varphi \in \mathcal{B} \mid \lim_{t \to 0^+} \frac{T(t) \varphi - \varphi}{t} \text{ exists and is finite} \right\}.
			\]
			
			In other words, $\mathcal{D}(L)$ consists of all elements $\varphi \in \mathcal{B}$ for which the limit above exists. The generator $\mathcal{L}$ is a densely defined linear operator mapping $\mathcal{D}(L)$ into $\mathcal{B}$.
title: Unnumbered definition of arXiv:2411.04590, 'Singular stochastic delay equations driven by fractional Bro'

[Theorem thm: main 2 of arXiv:2607.20097, 'Phase transition for the asymptotic entropy of branching random walks on groups'] For each $n \in \mathbb{N}$, let $\{X_{n,k}\}_{k=1}^{\rho^n}$ be i.i.d. $G$-valued random variables with common law $X_{n,1} \sim \mu^{*n}$. Define the empirical measure
$$\widehat{\mathcal{M}}_n(x) := \frac{1}{\rho^n}\sum_{k=1}^{\rho^n} \mathds1_{\{X_{n,k} = x\}}, \qquad x \in G,$$
and $H(\widehat{\mathcal{M}}_n)$ as in (equation eq:shannon-emp-distr of the paper) with $\widehat{\mathcal{M}}_n(x)$ instead of $\widehat{M}_n$.
If $\mu$ has  finite entropy and $\rho>1$, then the following holds. 
\begin{enumerate}[label = (\roman*)]
\setlength\itemsep{0em}
    \item \textbf{Small-$\rho$ regime.} If $\rho\leq \mathsf{e}^{\textsf{h}(\mu)}$, then almost surely
    $$\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{H(\widehat{\mathcal{M}}_n)}{n}=\log\rho.$$
    \item  \textbf{Large-$\rho$ regime.} If $\rho> \mathsf{e}^{\textsf{h}(\mu)}$, then almost surely
    $$\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{H(\widehat{\mathcal{M}}_n)}{n} = \textsf{h}(\mu).$$
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Independent random walks

body:
[Prop virasoro-defect-degeneration of arXiv:2609.01300, 'Virasoro Constraints for Orbifold Curves'] Use the relative-data notation fixed at the beginning of this section.
Assume that the coarse curve underlying \(\mathcal C_0\)
has genus zero.
Let
\[
\mathbf B=
\prod_{i=1}^{u}\tau_{a_i}(\mathbf 1)
\prod_{j=1}^{v}\tau_{b_j}(\omega)
\mathbf A'\mathbf A_0,
\]
where \(\mathbf A'\) and \(\mathbf A_0\) are the ordered products of the
remaining insertions supported on \(\mathcal C'\) and \(\mathcal C_0\), respectively. We fix a partition \(\{1,\ldots,v\}=T\sqcup T'\), such that for $j\in T$, the representative of $\omega$ in $\tau_{b_j}(\omega)$ is chosen to be $(\omega',\omega_0)=(0,\omega)$, while for $j\in T'$, the representative of $\omega$ in $\tau_{b_j}(\omega)$ is chosen to be $(\omega',\omega_0)=(\omega,0)$. For \(S\subset\{1,\ldots,u\}\), set
\[
\mathbf B'(S)
=
\prod_{i\notin S}\tau_{a_i}(\mathbf 1)
\prod_{j\notin T}\tau_{b_j}(\omega)
\mathbf A',
\qquad
\mathbf B_0(S)
=
\prod_{i\in S}\tau_{a_i}(\mathbf 1)
\prod_{j\in T}\tau_{b_j}(\omega)
\mathbf A_0.
\]

Then, for every \(k\geq-1\),
\begin{equation}

\begin{aligned}
&
\Delta_{k,d}^{\mathcal C/Q}
\left(
\mathbf B
\ \middle|\
\boldsymbol\eta
\right)
\\
&=
\sum_{S\subset\{1,\ldots,u\}}
\sum_{\mu\vdash d}
\mathfrak z(\mu)
\Bigg[
\Delta_{k,d}^{\mathcal C'/(Q'\cup\{p\})}
\left(
\mathbf B'(S)
\ \middle|\
\boldsymbol\eta',\mu
\right)\cdot
\left\langle
\mathbf B_0(S)
\ \middle|\
\boldsymbol\eta_0,\mu
\right\rangle^{\bullet,\,\mathcal C_0/(Q_0\cup\{p\})}_{d}
\\
&\hspace{25mm}
+
\left\langle
\mathbf B'(S)
\ \middle|\
\boldsymbol\eta',\mu
\right\rangle^{\bullet,\,\mathcal C'/(Q'\cup\{p\})}_{d}\cdot
\Delta_{k,d}^{\mathcal C_0/(Q_0\cup\{p\})}
\left(
\mathbf B_0(S)
\ \middle|\
\boldsymbol\eta_0,\mu
\right)
\Bigg].
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

[Lemma of arXiv:2608.25065, 'Detection of first homology via random geometric graphs in the thermodynamic regime'] \label[lemma]{topology}
    There exists $R_0=R_0(Q,c)< \infty$
    such that for all $R \ge R_0$ the following holds.
    Assume $0 < c < Q/2$ and suppose $E'_x$ holds.
    Then $x + [-Q \log R, Q \log R]^d$
    supports a cycle $z \in Z_1(G^\nu)$
    such that the following hold.
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item If $w \in Z_1(G^\nu)$
        is such that $w-z$ is a sum
        of cycles of diameter
        at most $(c/100) \log R$
        with support lying in $x + [-Q \log R, Q \log R]^d$,
        $|w|$ must intersect
        $x + [-(Q/2)\log R, (Q/2)\log R]^d$.

        \item If, in addition, $E_x$ holds, then $z$ lies in a connected component
        of $G^\nu \cap [-Q \log R, Q \log R]^d$ of Euclidean diameter at least $Q \log R$.
    \end{enumerate}

[Definition eq:critical-count-ceiling of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[definition]{def:critical-count-ceiling}
We say that the array satisfies \({\rm(CC)}_p\) if there are deterministic
finite numbers \(D_{N,p}\) such that, almost surely,
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{Crt}_N^J(\mathbb R)\le D_{N,p},
 \qquad
 \limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log D_{N,p}\le\log(p-1).
\end{equation}
This is the exact counting input used by the localized upper bounds
below; it requires neither nondegeneracy nor absolute continuity.
Algebraic genericity is a convenient sufficient condition, with
\(D_{N,p}=2\{(p-1)^N-1\}/(p-2)\).
title: Exponential critical-count ceiling

[Lemma tensorization2 of arXiv:2504.15992, 'Repeated singular values of a random symmetric matrix and decoupled singular value estimat'] Fix $d<n$ and $k\geq 0$. Consider $W$ a $2d\times(k+2\ell)$ matrix and $H$ a $(n-d)\times 2d$ random matrix with i.i.d. rows. Consider $\tau\in\mathbb{R}^{2d}$ a random vector having the same distribution as a row of $H$. Then if we take $\beta\in(0,\frac{1}{8})$, we have
    $$
\mathbb{P}_H(\|HW\|_{HS}\leq\beta^2\sqrt{(k+2\ell)(n-d)})\leq (32e^{2\beta^2(k+2\ell)}\mathcal{L}(W^T\tau,\beta\sqrt{k+2\ell}))^{n-d}.
    $$

body:
[Lemma symmeqa of arXiv:2607.29020, 'Entropic Symmetrization Resistance'] \label[lemma]{lem:Sr_restriction_of_symmetrizers_produces_symmetrizers}
Let $f \in \Sym$ and let $r > 0$ satisfy $\supp(f) \cap S^r \ne \emptyset$. 
Then 
\( g := (\frac{1}{c}) f \mathds{1}_{S^r} \in \Sym^r, \)
where $c = \sum_{z \in S^r} f(z)$. 
Moreover, if $c < 1$, then $\frac{f-cg}{1-c} \in \Sym$. 

\begin{proof}
Fix $r \in [0,\infty)$ and denote $ F_z = \{\pm z,-z\pm2,z\pm2\}$ for $z \in \mathbb{R}$. 
Writing one of $z = 2k - r$ (or $z = 2k + r$) for some $k \in \mathbb{Z}$, we have $-z = -2k+r$ (or $-z = -2k -r$); either way, $-z \in S^r$. 
Also, $z \in S^r$ implies $\{z \pm 2\} \subseteq S^r$ and $-z \in S^r$ implies $\{-z \pm 2\} \subseteq S^r$. 
Thus $z \in S^r$ if and only if $F_z \subseteq S^r$. 

Next, write $g = (\frac{1}{c}) f \mathds{1}_{S^r}$ and consider the symmetry equations 
\begin{align}
 q\varphi(z+2) + p\varphi(z) 	&= q\varphi(-z) + p\varphi(-z-2) \\
 q\varphi(z) + p\varphi(z-2)   	&= q\varphi(-z+2) + p\varphi(-z)  . 
\end{align}
Note that $\varphi$ is only evaluated at elements of $F_z$ in ((symmeqa of the paper)-(symmeqb of the paper)). 
When $z \in S^r$, clearly $\varphi=f$ solves ((symmeqa of the paper)-(symmeqb of the paper)); since both equations are linear and $g = \frac{1}{c}f$ on $F_z$, $g$ is also a solution. 
When $z \not\in S^r$, $g = 0$ on $F_z$ and solves ((symmeqa of the paper)-(symmeqb of the paper)) trivially. 
Thus $g \in \Sym$, and indeed $g \in \Sym^r$.

Finally, when 
$c < 1$, we have $(\frac{1}{1-c}) f \mathds{1}_{\mathbb{R} \setminus S^r} = \frac{f-cg}{1-c} \in \Sym$ by (lem:closure_under_subtraction of the paper).
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma symmeqa of arXiv:2607.29020

body: [Lemma 7 of arXiv:2604.13845, 'Minkowski content construction of\\ the CLE gasket measure'] Let $D \subseteq \C$ be a simply connected domain and $K \subseteq D$ a compact set. For each $\dsep>0$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there exists $\delta>0$ such that the following holds. Suppose that $(D;\ul{x};\beta) \in \eldomain{2N}$ and the distances between distinct points in $\ul{x}$ are at least $\dsep$. Let $\CI$ be a non-empty collection of even boundary arcs as described above. Let $\mcclelaw{D;\ul{x};\beta}$ be the law of a multichordal \clek{} in $(D;\ul{x};\beta)$, and $\p_D$ the law of a nested \clek{} in $D$. Then, for each $E \in \CE_K$ with $\p_D[E(\Upsilon)] < \delta$, we have $\mcclelaw{D;\ul{x};\beta}[E(\Upsilon_\CI)] < \varepsilon$, and vice versa. The same holds for $\mcclelaw{D;\ul{x};\alpha}$ where $(D;\ul{x};\alpha) \in \ildomain{2N}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Definition D:indexSpace of arXiv:2606.03079, 'Mean Field Limits for Stochastic, Underdamped Reactive Langevin Dynamics Models'] To describe the dynamics of $\nu_t$, we will sample vectors containing the indices of the specific substrate particles participating in a single $\ell$-type reaction from the substrate index space
$$
\mathbb{I}^{(\ell)}=(\mathbb{N} \backslash\{0\})^{|\alpha^{(\ell)}|}.
$$
For the allowable reactions considered in this work, we label the elements of $\mathbb{I}^{(\ell)}$ according to their species types:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item For $\mathcal{R}_{\ell}$ of the form $\varnothing \rightarrow \cdots$
    $$
\mathbb{I}^{(\ell)}=\varnothing.
$$
    \item For $\mathcal{R}_{\ell}$ of the form $S_j \rightarrow \cdots$
    $$
\mathbb{I}^{(\ell)}=\{i_1^{(j)}\in\mathbb{N}\backslash\{0\}\}.
$$
    \item For $\mathcal{R}_{\ell}$ of the form $S_j + S_k \rightarrow \cdots$ with $j<k$
        $$
\mathbb{I}^{(\ell)}=\{(i_1^{(j)},i_1^{(k)})\in (\mathbb{N}\backslash\{0\})^2\}.
$$
    \item For $\mathcal{R}_{\ell}$ of the form $2S_j \rightarrow \cdots$
           $$
\mathbb{I}^{(\ell)}=\{(i_1^{(j)},i_2^{(j)})\in (\mathbb{N}\backslash\{0\})^2\}.
$$
\end{enumerate}
We write a particular sampled set of substrate indices $\bm{i}\in \mathbb{I}^{(\ell)}$ as
$$
\bm{i}=\bigl(i_{1}^{(1)}, \cdots, i_{\alpha_{\ell 1}}^{(1)}, \cdots, i_{1}^{(J)}, \cdots, i_{\alpha_{\ell J}}^{(J)}\bigr).
$$

body: [Defn def-proper of arXiv:2412.03067, 'Geodesic Trees and Exceptional Directions in FPP on Hyperbolic Groups'] We say that an embedding $i:(Y,y_0,d_Y) \to (X,x_0, d_X)$ of metric spaces with  base-points $y_0, x_0$ is proper if  there exists a proper function $M: {\mathbb N} \to {\mathbb N}$ such that  if $d_Y(y_0,y) \geq n$, then $d_X(x_0,i(y)) \geq M(n)$.

body:
Let X be the centered, unit-variance, automorphism-invariant Gaussian eigenvector process on the cubic tree T_3 with eigenvalue lambda=-2sqrt(2). On any fixed bi-infinite path, Cov(X_0,X_k)=(-1/sqrt(2))^{|k|}(1+|k|/3). Its path marginal is the stationary Gaussian AR(2) process X_i=-sqrt(2)X_{i-1}-(1/2)X_{i-2}+epsilon_i, where the epsilon_i are iid N(0,1/12), independent of the entire past. In particular the adjacent covariance is -2sqrt(2)/3 and the distance-two covariance is 5/6. For L>=2 the covariance determinant of L consecutive path values is (1/9)(1/12)^{L-2}. Pathwise AR(2) describes a marginal law; finite-graph transfer uses the source linear-FIID approximations to the critical wave.

[Theorem 13 of arXiv:2608.30138, 'High-frequency wave propagation for the viscoelastic wave equation with singular memory'] Fix $k\in\{1,2,\dots\}$, $T>0$, and $0\leq\varepsilon\leq\varepsilon_0$.
Assume \r{m0}, \r{m-monotone}, and \r{m-int-k}, and suppose that
$(u_0,v_0,u_-,f)$ satisfies the regularity and compatibility conditions of
order $k$ in Definition~\ref{def:compatibility}, for this value of
$\varepsilon$. Then \r{full_eq}, with $u(0)=u_0$, $u_t(0)=v_0$, the
prescribed prehistory $u_-$, and the homogeneous Dirichlet boundary
condition, has a unique weak solution. This solution is strong and satisfies
\[
\partial_t^j u\in C\bigl([0,T];H^{k+1-j}(\Omega)\cap H_0^1(\Omega)\bigr),
\quad 0\leq j\leq k,\qquad
\partial_t^{k+1}u\in C\bigl([0,T];L^2(\Omega)\bigr).
\]
Moreover, $\partial_t^j u(0+)=U_j$ for $0\leq j\leq k+1$; hence the
forward and prehistory jets agree through order $k$. 
The solution depends continuously on the data in these spaces.

[Proposition prop:boundary-source-RI-defect of arXiv:2607.03639, '\vspace{-0.6in}An AI-Assisted Solution to the Signed BAR Conjecture: Uniqueness in the Har'] Assume the semigroup is strongly continuous on $C_0(E)$ and that the zero-potential construction of (prop:zero-potential-correction of the paper) is available for a centered source $\chi$.  Write
\[
 Q\chi=(U\chi,\Theta\chi),
 \qquad
 U\chi=\int_0^\infty\chi P_t\,dt,
 \qquad
 \Theta_i\chi=\sum_{n=0}^\infty(\chi P_n)K_i.
\]
If $\zeta\in\mathsf M_\partial$ satisfies $\partial_R\zeta=\chi$, then
\begin{equation}
 Q\chi+(0,\zeta)
 =(U\chi,\Theta\chi+\zeta)
 \in\ker\mathcal A.
\end{equation}
Its image under the map in (lem:RI-defect-quotient of the paper) is the class $[U\chi]\in\mathcal Q_{\rm RI}$, and
\begin{equation}
 \mathfrak r(U\chi)(\lambda,h)
 =-\int_E R_\lambda h\,d\chi,
 \qquad \lambda>0,\quad h\in C_0(E).
\end{equation}
In particular, if $\chi\ne0$, then $[U\chi]\ne0$ in $\mathcal Q_{\rm RI}$.
title: Boundary sources give RI-defect classes

body: [Lemma g has two turning points of arXiv:2411.10296, 'Parking on a random rooted binary tree'] Let $\alpha > 2 - \sqrt{2}$. Then $g$ has two turning points, $t_1$ and $t_2$, which satisfy $0 < t_1 < t_2 < 1$. Both $t_1$ and 1 are roots of $g$, and $t_1$ is the point at which $G$ switches branches. Furthermore, $g$ is monotonically decreasing on $(0, t_1)$, increasing on $(t_1, t_2)$, and decreasing on $(t_2, 1)$.
title: Lemma g has two turning points of arXiv:2411.10296

[Lemma thm_rel_energy_est of arXiv:2603.26307, '\LARGE The incompressible Navier--Stokes--Fourier system with thermal noise'] Let Assumption (Ass:noise of the paper) hold and $(\Omega,\mathfrak{A},\mathbb{P})$, $\mathscr{F}$, $(W_n)_{n\in \mathbb{Z}^3}$, $(B_n)_{n\in \mathbb{Z}^3}$, 
	$(u,\psi ,q)  $ be a weak  martingale solution to (equation Eq_new_var of the paper) with initial value 
	$u_0 \in L^2(\mathbb{T}^3; \mathbb{R}^3)$ divergence-free and $\psi_0\in L^2(\mathbb{T}^3)$ non-negative. Assume additionally that, on the same stochastic basis, there exists a local strong solution $(V,\Phi)$ to (equation Eq_new_var of the paper) until a stopping time $\tau>0$. Then it holds
	\begin{align}\begin{split}&
			\mathcal{E}( u_t,\psi^+_t | V_t,\Phi_t ) \,=\, 	\mathcal{E}( u_0,\psi_0  | V_0,\Phi_0 ) \,+\, \frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathbb{T}^3} |u_t|^2 + (\psi_t^+)^2- |u_0|^2 - \psi_0^2\,\mathrm{d} x 
			\\&\qquad  +\, 2 \int_0^t  
			\int_{\mathbb{T}^3} \nabla_{\mathrm{sym}} V:  \nabla_{\mathrm{sym}}  u + \nabla  \psi \cdot  \nabla \Phi 	\,\mathrm{d} x\, \mathrm{d} s  \,-\,
			\int_0^t \int_{\mathbb{T}^3}  \frac{\psi}{\Phi} \bigl(
			|\nabla \Phi|^2+|\nabla_\mathrm{sym} V|^2
			\bigr)\,\mathrm{d} x \,\mathrm{d} s \,-\, \int_{[0,t] \times \mathbb{T}^3}     \Phi   \,\mathrm{d} q
			\\&\qquad + \,  \int_0^t \int_{\mathbb{T}^3}   u \cdot      (( V \cdot \nabla)  V )-  \nabla   V:  u\otimes u \,\mathrm{d} x\,\mathrm{d} s \,  + \, \int_0^t \int_{\mathbb{T}^3}\psi V\cdot \nabla \Phi -\nabla \Phi \cdot (\psi u ) \,\mathrm{d} x \,\mathrm{d} s,
	\end{split}\end{align}
	for all $t\in [0,T \wedge \tau)$,
	$\mathbb{P}$-almost surely. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 23 of arXiv:2609.03098, 'Standing waves for Schr\"odinger equations with Kato class potentials and $L^\infty$-bound'] {\em (See \cite[Ch. I, Th. 11.1]{rybakowski})}
Assume that a $C_0$ semigroup $\{T(t)\}_{t\geq 0}$ of bounded linear operators on a Banach space $X$ is hyperbolic (see, e.g., \cite[Def. V.1.14]{Engel}). If the dimension $\dim X_u=k$ of the unstable subspace $X_u$ \footnote{\ The unstable space $X_u$ is equal to $\ker P$, where $P$ is the spectral projection corresponding to $\{\lambda\in\sigma(T(t_0))\mid |\lambda|<1\}$ for some $t_0>0$.} is finite, then $\Phi\colon [0,+\infty) \times X\to X$, given by $\Phi(t,x):=T(t)x$, is a semiflow on $X$, $\{ 0\}$ is the maximal bounded invariant set with respect to $\Phi$, $(\Phi, \{ 0 \})\in {\mathcal I}(X)$ and $h(\Phi, \{ 0\})=\Sigma^k$ where $\Sigma^k=[(S^k, \overline s)]$  is the homotopy type of the pointed $k$-dimensional sphere.\hfill $\square$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 23 of arXiv:2609.03098

[Theorem 20 of arXiv:2608.30549, '\vspace{-1cm}Maximally Spread Out Measures and Implications\\{} for Phase Transitions in A'] Let $\emptyset \ne \Omega \subset \RR^d$ be an arbitrary bounded domain.
Let $A_1,A_2\in \{B,F\}$.
Let $s_1,s_2\in \RR$ and let $0<p_1,q_1,p_2,q_2 \le \infty$ (with $p_i<\infty$ if $A_i=F$).
Assume that 
\begin{equation*}
   s_1 > s_2 
   \quad \text{and} \quad
    s_1 - \frac{1}{p_1} > s_2 -\frac{1}{p_2}.
\end{equation*}
Let $\SC$ denote the unit ball of $S^{s_1}_{p_1,q_1}A_1(\Omega)$
and let $\XX= S^{s_2}_{p_2,q_2}A_2(\Omega)$, endowed with the \mbox{(quasi-)}\allowbreak metric
induced by $\norm{\cdot\mid S^{s_2}_{p_2,q_2}A_2(\Omega)}$.
Then $\md(\SC)=\frac{1}{s_1-s_2}$ and there exists a Borel probability measure
on $\XX$ that is critical for $\SC$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 20 of arXiv:2608.30549

[Theorem thm:conc_density of arXiv:2609.01581, 'Concentration of additive functionals of Stratonovich-type'] Let $(X_t)_{t \geq 0}$ be an ergodic diffusion with invariant measure $\mu$, let
$\overline{\rho}_t(V)$ denote the empirical density according to Definition~(def:empirical_density of the paper) with 
ergodic (time-independent) mean $\E^\mu[\overline{\rho}_t]$, and
let $\nu \ll \mu$ with $\mathrm{d}\nu/\mathrm{d}\mu \in L^2(\mu)$. 
Then for all $t > 0$ and
$a > 0$,
\begin{align}
  \mathbb{P}^\nu\left(\overline{\rho}_t(V) - \E^\mu[\overline{\rho}_t] \geq a\right)
  \leq
  \left\|\frac{\mathrm{d}\nu}{\mathrm{d}\mu}\right\|_{L^2(\mu)}
  \exp\bigl[-t I^\rho(\E^\mu[\overline{\rho}_t] + a)\bigr],
  
\end{align}
where the Cram\'er transform
\begin{align}
I^\rho(s) \equiv \sup_{k \in \mathbb{R}}\bigl[k s - \Lambda^\rho(k)\bigr],

\end{align}
is defined as the Legendre conjugate of the principal eigenvalue $\Lambda^\rho(k)$~(equation eq:Lambda_rho_dirichlet of the paper).

[Proposition 7 of arXiv:2603.28226, '2603.28226'] Assume the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:stein-gundy}. Let $\lambda>0$ and $\theta\ge0$. Then one can write
\[
 f=g_{\theta}+h_{\theta}+k_{\theta}
\]
where $g_{\theta}$ and $h_{\theta}$ satisfy the same estimates as in Theorem~\ref{thm:stein-gundy}\textup{(a)--(b)}, and
\begin{equation}

 0\le k_{\theta}\le(1+\theta)\lambda\quad\text{a.s.},
 \qquad
 \|k_{\theta}\|_1\le \|f\|_1,
 \qquad
 \|k_{\theta}\|_2^2\le(1+\theta)\lambda\|f\|_1.
\end{equation}
More precisely,
\[
 k_{\theta}=k^{\mathrm{st}}_{\theta}+k^{\mathrm{pr}}_{\theta},
\]
where
\[
 k^{\mathrm{st}}_{\theta}:=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\gamma_j\mathbf1_{\{s_{\theta}\ge j\}},
 \qquad
 k^{\mathrm{pr}}_{\theta}:=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\mathbb E_{j-1}[\varepsilon_j]\mathbf1_{\{s_{\theta}\ge j\}},
\]
and
\[
 0\le k^{\mathrm{st}}_{\theta}\le \lambda,
 \qquad
 0\le k^{\mathrm{pr}}_{\theta}\le \theta\lambda
 \quad\text{a.s.}

[Proposition 40 (Coefficient-map transfer) of arXiv:2607.16724, 'Algebraic Transfer for Operator-Valued Gaussian Chaoses: Oriented Schatten Profiles and Si'] Assume $\kappa_r(\Phi)<\infty$ and that $\Phi$ maps finite-rank operators to
finite-rank operators.  Let
$K\in\cK_m^{\mathrm{alg}}$, and let $\Phi_\#K$ be obtained by applying
$\Phi$ to every deterministic coefficient of $K$.  Then
\begin{equation}

 \norm{\Flat_S(\Phi_\#K)}_{\Sch_r}
 \le\kappa_r(\Phi)\norm{\Flat_S(K)}_{\Sch_r}
\end{equation}
for every cut.  Hence
\[
 \Prof_{m,r}(\Phi_\#K)\le\kappa_r(\Phi)\Prof_{m,r}(K).
\]
For $1\le r<\infty$, $\Phi_\#$ therefore extends uniquely to a bounded map
between the corresponding simultaneous profile completions.

body:
[Corollary cor:hilbert-strata of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Fix $h\geq1$, $k\geq2$, and a field $K$.  Recall the open normalized
exponent-shape simplex
\[
 \mathcal S_k=
 \{x\in\mathbb R^k:0=x_1<x_2<\cdots<x_k=1\}
\]
and put
\[
 N_h(x)=\left|\{u\cdot x:u\in\mathcal U_{h,k}\}\right|.
\]
For every $n\in\mathcal R(h,k)$, the locus
\[
 \mathcal H_{h,k}(n)=\{x\in\mathcal S_k:N_h(x)=n\}
\]
is a finite disjoint union of relatively open rational polytopes, and
\begin{equation}
 \max\{\dim P:P\text{ is a cell of }\mathcal H_{h,k}(n)\}
 =k-2-r_{h,k}(n).
\end{equation}
For rational $x\in\mathcal S_k$, choose $D\geq1$ with
$Dx\in\mathbb Z^k$ and let $C_x\subset\mathbb P^{k-1}$ be the projective
monomial curve defined by the kernel of
\[
 K[X_1,\ldots,X_k]\longrightarrow K[s,t],
 \qquad X_i\longmapsto s^{D(1-x_i)}t^{Dx_i}.
\]
The kernel is independent of the choice of $D$, and
\[
 H_{C_x}(h)=N_h(x).
\]
Consequently, $r_{h,k}(n)$ is exactly the codimension in exponent-shape
space of the largest stratum with degree-$h$ Hilbert value $n$.
If $h\geq2$, $k\geq3$, and $A_q$ is uniform in $\binom{[q]}k$, then
\begin{equation}
 \mathbb P(|hA_q|=n)
 =k!c_{h,k,n}q^{-r_{h,k}(n)}
  +O_{h,k}(q^{-r_{h,k}(n)-1}),
\end{equation}
and hence the same integer has the four equivalent descriptions
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{
 r_{h,k}(n)
 =k-\deg F^{(k)}_{h,n}
 =\operatorname{codim}_{\mathcal S_k}\mathcal H_{h,k}(n)
 =-\lim_{q\to\infty}
   \frac{\log\mathbb P(|hA_q|=n)}{\log q}.}
\end{equation}
Here the codimension of a finite polyhedral union means the codimension of
its largest-dimensional cell.

body: Hurwitz's theorem is often quoted as 'a locally uniform limit of zero-free holomorphic functions is zero-free'. Three hypotheses carry that conclusion. (1) Connectedness of the domain. On U = D(0,1) union D(3,1) put f_n = 1/n on the first disk and f_n = 1 on the second; each f_n is holomorphic and zero-free on U and f_n converges locally uniformly, but the limit is 0 on one component and 1 on the other: neither zero-free nor identically zero. The correct statement is the dichotomy component by component. (2) The degenerate alternative cannot be dropped even on a connected domain: f_n(z) = exp(z)/n is zero-free on C and converges locally uniformly to the identically zero function. Likewise the injectivity version must allow constants: f_n(z) = z/n is injective on D and converges to the constant 0. (3) Holomorphy, not just real analyticity: on the real line f_n(x) = x^2 + 1/n has no real zeros and converges uniformly on compacts to x^2, which has a zero; the complex statement survives because the complex zeros ±i/sqrt(n) move to 0. (4) The counting form requires that the boundary circle avoid the zeros of the limit: f_n(z) = z - 1 + 1/n has one zero in the unit disk for every n, while f_n(z) = z - 1 - 1/n has none, and both converge to z - 1, whose only zero sits on the circle |z| = 1. Never conclude equal zero counts from a circle through a zero of the limit.
title: Pitfall: Hurwitz's theorem needs connectedness, holomorphy, and allows the degenerate limit

In Asymptotic theory of in-context learning by linear attention, arXiv:2405.11751v3, Lu, Letey, Zavatone-Veth, Maiti and Pehlevan analyze a reduced linear-attention predictor linear in an effective d by (d+1) matrix, estimated by ridge-regularized pretraining and then considered in its ridgeless asymptotic limit. Their parameters are alpha=ell/d, kappa=k/d and tau=n/d^2, where ell is context length, k is the number of Gaussian tasks drawn once into a fixed pool, and n is the number of training contexts. Section III.E equation (18), printed p.11, predicts, in the additional joint limit alpha,tau -> infinity with fixed c_*=alpha/tau>0, that the task-generalization gap g_task=e_ICL-e_IDG equals (1-kappa)[1+rho*c_*/(1+rho)] for kappa<1 and 0 for kappa>1. Here rho>=0 is the label-noise variance. The displayed equation omits kappa=1. The transition location is kappa_c=1 in this specified limit; this is not a general finite-(alpha,tau) threshold formula. Section III.D equation (17) instead studies alpha -> infinity at fixed tau and gives a ridgeless ICL-error divergence boundary kappa<=min(tau,1). Preserve the different limit orders. The source explicitly discloses heuristic steps in Section III.B p.8 and the SI opening p.18. Record the final learning-curve asymptotics as qualified predictions, not as a fully rigorous theorem. [Proposition 33 (Intrinsic chart and representation equivalence) of arXiv:2608.04993, '2608.04993'] The cocycle chart
\[
 \operatorname{ch}_\tau(g):=(x,A,q)
\]
is a causal isometric homeomorphism from
$\mathsf Z_{\eta;\mathfrak I,1}(H)$ onto the triple presentation in which
$(1,x,\frac12x^{\otimes2}+A)\in G\Omega^2_{\eta,\mathfrak I}(H)$,
$q\in C_0^{0,2\eta}(\mathcal S_{1,\rm sa})$, and
\begin{equation}

 A_{s,t}=A_{s,u}+A_{u,t}
 +\Anti(x_{s,u}\otimes x_{u,t}).
\end{equation}
In this chart,
\[
 \mathbb X^S_{s,t}=\frac12x_{s,t}^{\otimes2}+A_{s,t},
 \qquad
 \mathbb X^I_{s,t}=\mathbb X^S_{s,t}-\frac12q_{s,t},
 \qquad
 \widehat j_t=\mathbb X^I_{0,t}.
\]
Thus $(x,A,q)$ is a canonical global chart of the intrinsic group-valued
state.

[Theorem 27 of arXiv:2606.09904, 'Non-explosion principles for branched rough differential equations with unbounded coeffici'] Supposing Assumption~\ref{as:growth} and \(b\) has sub-linear growth
  in its radial direction, i.e. there exists some \(\delta > 0\) such that
  \begin{equation}
    \<x, b(x)\> \lesssim \|x\|(1 + \|x\|)^{1 - \delta},\qquad \forall x \in \mathbb{R}^d.
  \end{equation}
  Then, the unique global solution \((x_t)\) of the branched RDE~\eqref{eq:bRDE} satisfies
  \[\sup_{s \in [0, t]}\|x_s\| \lesssim \|\mathbf{X}\|_{\gamma; [0, t]}^\eta\]
  for any \(t \in [0, T]\) where
  \(\eta := (N^2 - N + 1)\left(\left(\frac{1}{\delta} + \frac{N + 1}{(1 - \delta)\lambda}\right) 
    \vee \left(\frac{1}{\delta} + \frac{1}{(1 - \delta)(1 - \theta)\gamma} - 1\right)\right)\)
  and \(\lambda := (1 - \theta + \kappa)\gamma\). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 27 of arXiv:2606.09904

[Proposition prop:fdd of arXiv:2412.03325, 'Functional limit theorem for branching processes \\ in nearly degenerate varying environme'] Assume that the BPVE $(X_n)_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ satisfies conditions (C1)--(C3) and for $k \geq 0, \ell \geq 0$ let 
$0 < t_{-k} < t_{-k+1} < \ldots < t_{-1} < t_0 = 1 < t_{1} < 
\ldots < t_{\ell} < \infty$, and $x_i \in \mathbb{N}$, $i = -k, \ldots, \ell$. 
Then
\[
\begin{split}
& \lim_{n \to \infty}
\mathbf{P} ( X_{A(n t_i)} = x_i, i= -k, \ldots,  \ell | 
X_{A(n)} > 0) \\
& = \mathbf{P}_{t_{-k}} ( U(t_i) = x_i, i= -k, \ldots, \ell | U(1) > 0),
\end{split}
\]
where $\mathbf{P}_{t_{-k}}$ denotes the law of $(U(t))_{t \geq t_{-k}}$ with 
initial distribution $U(t_{-k}) \sim \textrm{Geom}(\tfrac{2}{2+\nu})$.
title: Proposition prop:fdd of arXiv:2412.03325

[Definition 50 (Fractional Sobolev spaces) of arXiv:2605.14630, '2605.14630'] For $s\geqs0$, the \emph{fractional Sobolev space} $H^s(\Lambda)$ is the 
space of functions $f\in \H = L^2(\Lambda)$ such that 
\begin{equation}
 
 \norm{f}_{H^s}^2 := \sum_{k\in\Z^d} \lambda_k^s \abs{\hat f(k)}^2 < \infty\;.
\end{equation} 
In particular, $H^0(\Lambda) = L^2(\Lambda)$. For $s<0$, $H^s(\Lambda)$ is 
the closure of $L^2(\Lambda)$ under the norm \eqref{eq:Sobolev_norm}.

[Corollary 11 of arXiv:2608.07365, 'A pathwise Ito formula \\for weakly differentiable functions'] Let $\omega \in C([0,T], \Rr^d)\cap Q^\pi([0, T], \mathbb{R}^d)$ and $f\in C^2_b(\mathbb{R}^d, \Rr)$. Then the following limit change of variable formula holds
$$
f(\omega(T)) = f(\omega(0)) + \int_0^T \nabla f(\omega)d^\pi\omega + \frac{1}{2}[\nabla f(\omega), \omega]_\pi(T).
$$
where the integral $ \int_0^T \nabla f(\omega)d^\pi\omega$ is defined as the limit of left Riemann sums along the sequence of partitions $(\pi_n)_{n\geq 1}$:
\[
 \int_0^T \nabla f(\omega)d^\pi\omega:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{\pi_n} \nabla f(\omega(t^n_k))\cdot \left(\omega(t^n_{k+1}) - \omega(t^n_k)\right).
\]
